LeetCode & System Design — Rust · C · C++ · Python (EN)

LeetCode & System Design — Rust · C · C++ · Python

War notebook for technical interviews, calibrated for the profile: 5 years of professional Python + the ambition to master Rust, C++, and C.

How this book is used

Two tracks, like a real senior-level interview:

  1. Coding — every problem has a solution in all 4 languages, in the template format: problem statement → pattern (what to memorize) → Python → Rust → C++ → C → complexity → pitfalls → review card.
  2. System Design — heavy weight for a 5-year-experience profile: method + classic problems designed end to end, as if narrated in a 45-minute interview.

Strategy by language (for your profile)

LanguageInterview roleWhy
PythonSpeed — the primary5 years of baggage: in the interview, clean and fast code matters more than exoticism
RustDifferentiatorSignals depth (ownership, memory, concurrency); impresses in infra/systems
C++VersatilityThe most requested language for product/performance roles, along with Python
CFoundationMastering C is mastering how everything works underneath; pointers and memory with no magic

Working rule: understand and solve in Python first (the pattern), then reimplement in Rust → C++ → C (the depth). The Languages sections are interview cheat sheets: what to use, complexity, idioms, and pitfalls for each.

Conventions

  • Comments in code: English.
  • Python: 3.10+, stdlib, type hints (like a real code review).
  • Rust: std only, idiomatic (iterators, Option/Result).
  • C++: C++20, STL, no boost; LeetCode-style signatures.
  • C: C11, stdlib.h/string.h; LeetCode-style signature with returnSize/returnColumnSizes where applicable.
  • Every solution records time and space complexity.

Study method

Double goal: (1) recognize a problem’s pattern in seconds and write the solution from memory; (2) design systems end to end while narrating the trade-offs — the two pillars of the senior interview.

Coding — the per-problem cycle

  1. Try it alone (25 min max) in Python before reading any solution.
  2. Read the page: understand the why of the pattern, not the code.
  3. Rewrite from memory in Python — it’s the interview language.
  4. Reimplement in Rust, then C++, then C (in that order; one per day, not all on the same day — spacing is what sticks).
  5. Check the review card at the end of the page.

Spaced review (coding)

Rewrite from memory (don’t just re-read!) at:

ReviewWhen
R11 day later
R23 days later
R37 days later
R421 days later
R560 days later

Missed one? The cycle resets (back to R1). From R3 onward, change the review language (Python → C++ → Rust…) to force the pattern, not muscle memory.

System Design — the weekly cycle

1 problem per week, timed like a real interview:

  1. 10 min — requirements + clarifying questions (functional and non-functional) and estimates (QPS, storage, bandwidth).
  2. 10 min — API + data model + high-level design.
  3. 20 min — deep dive into whichever bottleneck the “interviewer” picks (consistency? cache? fan-out?).
  4. 5 min — final trade-offs and what I’d improve with more time.

Narrate out loud. System design is 50% drawing, 50% communication — record yourself once a month and listen.

The pattern rule (what you actually memorize)

Before code, the statement clue → pattern table: “sorted + pair that sums” → two pointers · “contiguous substring + limit” → sliding window · “next greater/smaller” → monotonic stack · “top K” → heap · “shortest path, unweighted” → BFS · “optimal subproblem” → DP · “all combinations” → backtracking · “intervals” → sort by start.

Profile checklist (5 years of Python)

  • Blind 75 (first full pass in Python)
  • Blind 75 reimplemented in Rust (at least the 25 most asked)
  • NeetCode 150
  • 8 System Design problems narrated and timed
  • The 4 language cheat sheets re-read the night before each interview
  • 2 complete mock interviews (coding + design) before the real cycle

The 7 mother patterns (if you can only memorize one thing)

  1. Hash map trades O(n) lookup for O(1) — complements, counts, indices.
  2. Two pointers exploit sorting/monotonicity with no extra memory.
  3. Sliding window = two pointers maintaining a valid window.
  4. Layered BFS = shortest path with no weights; Dijkstra = with weights.
  5. Backtracking = DFS that does, tries, undoes (choices).
  6. DP = optimal subproblem + memo; find the recurrence and the fill order.
  7. Sort first — half of greedy/interval problems are born from a sort.

Anki — automatic spaced review

The whole book becomes a deck: download leetcode-kr-en.apkg (~1 MB). Import it into Anki (desktop or mobile) and the spaced review handles the R1–R5 calendar of the method by itself — the review cards on the pages become redundant.

How to use it well

  • Filter by tags: every problem has topic tags (arrays, dp, graphs…), difficulty (easy/medium/hard), number (lc146) and premium. E.g., tag:hard tag:graphs for a hard-graphs-only session.
  • Don’t want all 4 languages? Suspend the C/C++ cards (browse → select → toggle suspend) and keep Python + Rust + Recognition.
  • Flow with the book: solve the problem on the site → import/update the deck → let Anki drive the reviews (it implements R1/R2/R3… automatically).
  • Write from memory first, compare with the back afterward — never just “recognize” the solution.

Template — System Design problem

# <System name>

> Category: <e.g., key-value, fan-out, streaming> · Difficulty: <classic/advanced>

## 1. Requirements

**Functional:** what the system DOES (3–5 bullets).
**Non-functional:** scale (QPS/read-write), latency, availability

**Estimates:** users, QPS, data size, 5-year storage, bandwidth.

## 2. API + data model

Essential endpoints (method, path, payload) and tables/collections with keys.

workers. One sentence per box explaining WHY it exists.

## 4. Deep dive

The 2–3 points where the offer is won: consistency, partitioning, cache

## 5. Trade-offs and bottlenecks

What breaks first, what you'd sacrifice, what you'd do with 10× more time.

- [ ] Narrated out loud, timed (45 min) · [ ] R1 (+7d) · [ ] R2 (+30d)

Python — your home turf

With 5 years of Python, your edge is writing speed. The goal of this page: make sure no stdlib detail costs you 2 minutes in a 45-minute interview.

Core structures and complexity

StructureUseO(1) operationsWatch out
dict / sethash mapin, get, insert, deletekeys must be immutable
listdynamic arrayappend, pop() (end)pop(0)/insert(0) are O(n)
collections.dequequeue/stackappend/pop at both endsno fast indexing
heapqheappush/pop O(log n)it’s a min-heap; max-heap = negate values
bisectbinary searchbisect_left/right, insortthe list must be sorted

Stdlib that solves the problem by itself

from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque
Counter("aab")                       # {'a': 2, 'b': 1}
defaultdict(list)                    # no more `if key not in d`
from itertools import accumulate, pairwise, product, combinations
accumulate([1,2,3])                  # prefix sum: 1 3 6 — used ALL the time

Idioms that impress (and save a line)

for i, x in enumerate(nums): ...          # index + value
for a, b in zip(xs, ys): ...              # pairs
s[::-1]                                   # reverse string/list
nums[l:r]                                 # slice (a copy — watch the cost)
if (j := d.get(k)) is not None: ...       # walrus: single lookup
[x*x for x in nums if x > 0]              # comprehension
a, b = b, a                               # swap without a temp
float("inf"), float("-inf")               # sentinels

Patterns encoded in Python

  • Two pointers: l, r = 0, len(nums)-1 + while l < r.
  • Sliding window: for r, x in enumerate(nums): + while that shrinks l.
  • Monotonic stack: a list with append/pop.
  • Top K: heapq.nlargest(k, xs) / nsmallest (or a manual k-sized heap).
  • BFS: deque + popleft().
  • Union-Find: parent = list(range(n)) + find with path compression.
  • Trie: nested defaultdict or a dict of dicts.

Classic pitfalls

  • Recursion: default limit ~1000 frames. Deep DFS → convert to iterative with an explicit stack (or sys.setrecursionlimit, naming the cost).
  • // is floor division (with negatives: -7 // 2 == -4). “C-style truncated” division: int(a / b) or math.trunc.
  • is compares identity, == compares value. Never is with literals.
  • A mutable default argument (def f(xs=[])) is shared across calls.
  • Integers don’t overflow (arbitrary precision) — an edge over C/C++, but a giant int stops being O(1) per operation.
  • Strings are immutable: concatenation in a loop = O(n²). Use "".join(parts).
  • sort(key=...) and sorted are stable; list.sort() is in-place, sorted() copies.

        # 1) degenerate case
        if not nums:
            return 0
        # 2) pattern structure
        ...

Rust — the differentiator

Rust in an interview signals depth: ownership, memory without GC, explicit error handling. This page is the minimum for writing LeetCode solutions without fighting the borrow checker.

Core structures

StructureEquivalentNotes
Vec<T>list/vectorpush, pop() -> Option<T>, index with [i] (panics out of range)
HashMap<K,V> / HashSet<T>dict/setentry(k).or_insert(v) is the key idiom
BTreeMap / BTreeSetsorted dict/setrange queries (range(a..b))
VecDeque<T>dequepush_back/pop_front
BinaryHeap<T>heapqit’s a MAX-heap; min-heap = Reverse(x) or negate
String / &strstrowned vs borrowed; .chars(), .bytes()

Idioms that save lines

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
nums.iter().enumerate()                 // (i, &x)
nums.iter().copied().sum::<i64>()       // sum
nums.iter().max()                       // Option<&T>
xs.windows(2)                           // sliding pairs [a,b]
xs.chunks(k)                            // slices of k
map.entry(k).or_insert(0);              // counter without an if
map.entry(k).or_default();
*v += 1;
xs.retain(|&x| x > 0);                  // in-place filter
(0..n).map(|i| ...).collect::<Vec<_>>() // build
}

Patterns encoded in Rust

  • Two pointers: let (mut l, mut r) = (0i32, n - 1); with while l < r and indexing nums[l as usize] (or work in usize and mind the -= 1).
  • Sliding window: for (r, &x) in nums.iter().enumerate() + a while that shrinks l.
  • Monotonic stack: Vec with push/pop() -> Option.
  • BFS: VecDeque + pop_front().
  • DP: vec![0u64; n + 1]; 2D = vec![vec![0; cols]; rows].

Borrow checker in the interview (survival)

  • Recursive helper functions that mutate state: pass &mut explicitly or close over everything in an inner fn; if you get stuck, a point-wise clone is acceptable — comment “pragmatic clone here; a reference in production”.
  • Iterating and mutating the same collection at once doesn’t compile: collect the indices/decisions first, apply later (or use retain).
  • &str from String: &s. String from &str: s.to_string().

Classic pitfalls

  • BinaryHeap is a max-heap (Python/C++ default to min) — flip the sign or use std::cmp::Reverse.
  • Overflow: in dev/debug it panics; release wraps. LeetCode = use i64 when the math can exceed i32 (multiplications, prefix sums).
  • usize has no negatives: i - 1 with i = 0 panics. Safe pattern: i.checked_sub(1) or compare first.
  • s.chars().nth(i) is O(n) — for random access use s.as_bytes()[i] (ASCII) or let v: Vec<char> = s.chars().collect();.
  • Option/Result: unwrap() only where the problem guarantees it; prefer a commented expect("...") or a pattern match.
  • Integer division truncates toward zero (like C) — unlike Python.

Submission scaffold

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn problem_name(nums: Vec<i32>, k: i32) -> i32 {
        // 1) degenerate case
        if nums.is_empty() { return 0; }
        // 2) pattern structure
        let mut seen = std::collections::HashMap::new();
        // 3) main loop
        for (i, &x) in nums.iter().enumerate() {
            if let Some(&j) = seen.get(&(k - x)) {
                return j as i32;
            }
            seen.insert(x, i);
        }
        0 // unreachable
    }
}
}

C++ — the versatile one

C++ is, along with Python, the most widely accepted language in product and performance interviews. The goal: a sharp STL and zero type surprises.

Core structures (STL)

StructureEquivalentComplexityNotes
vector<T>list/Vecpush_back amortized O(1)reserve(n) avoids reallocation
unordered_map/setdict/setO(1) averagehash; worst case O(n)
map/setTreeMap/BTreeO(log n)sorted; lower_bound
priority_queue<T>heapqO(log n)MAX-heap by default!
deque<T>dequeO(1) endssliding window maximum
stack/queue—O(1)adapters (backed by deque)
stringstrmutable+= amortized O(1); unlike Python/Rust

Min-heap: priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> pq;

Idioms

for (int x : nums) ...                  // range-for (by value)
for (auto& [k, v] : map) ...           // structured binding (C++17)
nums.emplace_back(x);                   // constructs in place
sort(nums.begin(), nums.end());         // O(n log n) introsort
sort(nums.begin(), nums.end(), greater<int>());
*max_element(nums.begin(), nums.end());
auto it = lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x);   // binary search
accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL);    // 0LL forces long long summation!
to_string(x), stoi(s), stol(s);
s.substr(i, len);

Encoded patterns

  • Two pointers / sliding window: int indices + while.
  • Monotonic stack: vector<int> with push_back/pop_back (or stack).
  • Top K: a k-sized priority_queue with greater<int>.
  • BFS: queue<pair<int,int>> + visited.
  • DP: vector<vector<long long>> dp(n+1, vector<ll>(m+1, 0));
  • Union-Find: vector<int> parent(n); iota(parent.begin(), parent.end(), 0);

Classic pitfalls

  • int overflow: large multiplication/sum → long long. The classic accumulate(..., 0) truncates: use 0LL.
  • priority_queue is a max-heap (unlike Python) — top-K smallest = greater<>.
  • Iterator invalidation: inserting/removing in a vector during a loop invalidates iterators — use indices or collect first.
  • v[i] has no bounds check (silent UB); .at(i) checks and throws.
  • unordered_map worst case O(n) under adversarial collisions (rare in interviews; use map if you want an O(log n) guarantee).
  • Signed/unsigned: nums.size() is size_t — i < nums.size() - 1 with an empty vector underflows. Explicit cast: (int)nums.size().
  • Pass containers by reference in helpers: void f(vector<int>& v) — a copy is O(n) and sometimes the TLE bug.

Submission scaffold

class Solution {
public:
    int problemName(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
        if (nums.empty()) return 0;
        unordered_map<int, int> seen;
        seen.reserve(nums.size());
        for (int i = 0; i < (int)nums.size(); ++i) {
            auto it = seen.find(k - nums[i]);
            if (it != seen.end()) return it->second;
            seen.emplace(nums[i], i);
        }
        return -1; // unreachable
    }
};

C — the foundation

C isn’t for interview speed; it’s for understanding the machine. Whoever masters C understands what Python/C++/Rust do underneath: manual memory, pointers, layout. LeetCode accepts C with specific signatures (returnSize, returnColumnSizes).

The minimal kit

#include <stdlib.h>   // malloc, calloc, free, qsort, abs
#include <string.h>   // memset, memcpy, strlen, strcmp
#include <stdbool.h>  // true/false

Allocation — the discipline

int* v = malloc(n * sizeof(int));        // not initialized
int* z = calloc(n, sizeof(int));         // zero-initialized (prefer for DP)
int** m = malloc(rows * sizeof(int*));   // matrix = array of pointers
for (int i = 0; i < rows; i++) m[i] = calloc(cols, sizeof(int));
free(v);                                  // every malloc has its free

Interview rule: LeetCode frees what you return — but free what’s temporary (like the Two Sum hash map).

Sorting: qsort

int cmp_int(const void* a, const void* b) {
    int x = *(const int*)a, y = *(const int*)b;
    return (x > y) - (x < y);       // NEVER "x - y" (overflow!)
}
qsort(nums, numsSize, sizeof(int), cmp_int);

For [i, value] pairs, sort by column: a struct + a comparator that reads ((const int*)a)[1].

Hash map: there isn’t one — three exits

  1. Counting array when the domain is small (int cnt[26] for letters; cnt[20001] for values in ±10⁴).
  2. Hand-rolled open addressing (like this house’s Two Sum): an entry array {key, value, used} with power-of-2 capacity and linear probing.
  3. Sort + binary search (bsearch) when a hash isn’t needed.

LeetCode-style signature

/**
 * Return an array of arrays of size *returnSize.
 * The sizes of the arrays are returned as *returnColumnSizes array.
 */
int** problemName(int** grid, int gridSize, int* gridColSize,
                  int* returnSize, int** returnColumnSizes) {
    int** answer = malloc(gridSize * sizeof(int*));
    *returnColumnSizes = malloc(gridSize * sizeof(int));
    *returnSize = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < gridSize; i++) {
        answer[*returnSize] = malloc(2 * sizeof(int));
        (*returnColumnSizes)[*returnSize] = 2;
        (*returnSize)++;
    }
    return answer;
}

Classic pitfalls

  • x - y in a comparator overflows with extremes (INT_MIN): use (x > y) - (x < y).
  • Off-by-one: loops for (i = 0; i < n; i++); a string’s size is strlen(s) + 1 counting the \0.
  • malloc(n * sizeof(T)) can overflow with a huge n: in production code, reallocarray/a check; in an interview, mention it.
  • Dangling pointer: never return the address of a local variable.
  • char* from a literal is read-only: char* s = "abc"; s[0]='x'; is UB. Use char s[] = "abc"; for mutability.
  • Integer overflow is UB (not wrapping like Rust release, nor arbitrary like Python): big sum/multiplication → long long.
  • No native bool before C23: include stdbool.h.
  • Struct by value vs pointer: pass const T* in helpers to avoid copies.

Submission scaffold

int* twoSum(int* nums, int numsSize, int target, int* returnSize) {
    *returnSize = 2;
    int* answer = malloc(2 * sizeof(int));
    /* ... open-addressing hash pattern ... */
    return answer;
}

1. Two Sum (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/two-sum/ · Topic: Arrays & Hashing

Problem (summary)

Given nums and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. There is exactly one solution; you may not use the same element twice.

nums = [2,7,11,15], target = 9  →  [0,1]   (2 + 7 = 9)

Pattern — what to memorize

One-pass hash map: for each element x, the question is “have I seen target - x?”. If yes, found the pair; if not, store x → index and keep going. This trades the brute-force O(n²) for O(n) at the cost of O(n) memory. Clue in the statement: pair adding up to a value + indices → complement hashmap.

Python

def twoSum(nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
    seen: dict[int, int] = {}                  # value -> index
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        # has the complement shown up before me?
        if (j := seen.get(target - x)) is not None:
            return [j, i]
        seen[x] = i
    raise ValueError("no solution")            # the problem guarantees one

The interview version: 5 lines, dict is O(1), the walrus operator avoids a double lookup. This is the one you write on the spot — the others are for depth.

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashMap;

pub fn two_sum(nums: Vec<i32>, target: i32) -> Vec<i32> {
    let mut seen: HashMap<i32, usize> = HashMap::new();
    for (i, &x) in nums.iter().enumerate() {
        // Has the complement shown up before me?
        if let Some(&j) = seen.get(&(target - x)) {
            return vec![j as i32, i as i32];
        }
        seen.insert(x, i);
    }
    unreachable!() // the problem guarantees a solution
}
}

C++

#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> twoSum(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
        unordered_map<int, int> seen;                 // value -> index
        seen.reserve(nums.size());                    // avoids rehash (a senior detail)
        for (int i = 0; i < (int)nums.size(); ++i) {
            auto it = seen.find(target - nums[i]);
            if (it != seen.end()) {
                return {it->second, i};
            }
            seen.emplace(nums[i], i);
        }
        return {};                                    // unreachable
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

/* Simple open-addressing hash map (i32 key → index). */
typedef struct { int key; int index; int used; } Entry;

int* twoSum(int* nums, int numsSize, int target, int* returnSize) {
    /* Power-of-2 capacity ≥ 2*n to keep load factor < 0.5 */
    int cap = 16;
    while (cap < numsSize * 2) cap <<= 1;
    Entry* map = (Entry*)calloc(cap, sizeof(Entry));

    int* res = (int*)malloc(2 * sizeof(int));
    *returnSize = 2;

    unsigned mask = (unsigned)cap - 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < numsSize; i++) {
        int complement = target - nums[i];
        /* look up the complement */
        unsigned h = ((unsigned)complement * 2654435761u) & mask; /* Knuth multiplicative */
        while (map[h].used) {
            if (map[h].key == complement) {
                res[0] = map[h].index;
                res[1] = i;
                free(map);
                return res;
            }
            h = (h + 1) & mask; /* linear probing */
        }
        /* insert nums[i] → i */
        h = ((unsigned)nums[i] * 2654435761u) & mask;
        while (map[h].used) h = (h + 1) & mask;
        map[h].key = nums[i];
        map[h].index = i;
        map[h].used = 1;
    }
    free(map);
    return res; /* unreachable: there is always a solution */
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one pass; every lookup/insert is amortized O(1).
  • Space: O(n) — the map stores at most n entries.

Pitfalls

  • Return indices, not values; and the smaller index first (LeetCode order: [j, i] with j < i).
  • Negative numbers in target/nums — the C hash must handle negative int (the cast to unsigned handles it).
  • In C: who frees map? (here we free before returning; LeetCode frees res).
  • Duplicates: [3,3] target 6 works because the complement is looked up before inserting the current one.

242. Valid Anagram (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-anagram/ · Topic: Arrays & Hashing

Problem (summary)

Check whether t is an anagram of s — same letters, same count of each one. You may assume lowercase letters from a to z.

s = "anagram", t = "nagaram"  →  true
s = "rat",     t = "car"      →  false

Pattern — what to memorize

Frequency count in a fixed 26-slot array: count each letter of s, decrement with each letter of t; at the end everything must be back to zero. The small domain (26 lowercase letters) makes a hash map unnecessary — a fixed array is O(1) space and cache-friendly. Clues in the statement: same letters + lowercase → count vector; different lengths → immediate false.

Python

class Solution:
    def isAnagram(self, s: str, t: str) -> bool:
        if len(s) != len(t):
            return False
        count = [0] * 26
        for c in s:
            count[ord(c) - ord("a")] += 1
        for c in t:
            count[ord(c) - ord("a")] -= 1
        return all(x == 0 for x in count)

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn is_anagram(s: String, t: String) -> bool {
        if s.len() != t.len() {
            return false;
        }
        let mut count = [0i32; 26];
        for &b in s.as_bytes() {
            count[(b - b'a') as usize] += 1;
        }
        for &b in t.as_bytes() {
            count[(b - b'a') as usize] -= 1;
        }
        count == [0; 26]
    }
}
}

C++

#include <string>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    bool isAnagram(string s, string t) {
        if (s.size() != t.size()) return false;
        int count[26] = {};
        for (char c : s) count[c - 'a']++;
        for (char c : t) {
            if (--count[c - 'a'] < 0) return false;  // early exit
        }
        return true;
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <string.h>

bool isAnagram(char* s, char* t) {
    if (strlen(s) != strlen(t)) return false;
    int count[26] = {0};
    for (int i = 0; s[i]; i++) count[s[i] - 'a']++;
    for (int i = 0; t[i]; i++) {
        if (--count[t[i] - 'a'] < 0) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n + m) — two passes; the C++/C early exit cuts it in half.
  • Space: O(1) — 26 fixed slots, regardless of string length.

Pitfalls

  • Different lengths ⇒ false without counting anything (the very first check).
  • Characters outside a–z: the problem guarantees lowercase, but an uppercase letter or symbol would run c - 'a' off the array. In an interview, say you’re “assuming lowercase per the statement; I’d generalize with a Counter/hashmap”.
  • Unicode (accents, emoji): a–z bytes are 1 byte each, but anything else breaks the ASCII assumption — in the other 3 languages - 'a' needs the same rework.
  • Python all(...) is clean; a two-loop version with return count == [0]*26 works too.
  • In Rust, as_bytes() is O(1); s.chars() would be needlessly expensive here.

49. Group Anagrams (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/group-anagrams/ · Topic: Arrays & Hashing

Problem (summary)

Given a list of strings, group them by anagram: words with the same letters (same counts) land in the same group. The order of groups and the order within each group is free.

["eat","tea","tan","ate","nat","bat"]  →  [["bat"],["nat","tan"],["ate","eat","tea"]]
[""]                                   →  [[""]]

Pattern — what to memorize

You never compare anagram to anagram: compute a canonical key for each word and group by it in a hash map key → list. Two classic keys:

  1. Sort-key — key = sorted letters ("eat" → "aet"). Cost O(k log k) per word; shortest to write and what C does with qsort.
  2. Count-key — key = a 26-count vector ("eat" → [1,0,0,1,0,1,...]). Cost O(k) per word; the “optimal” one and the interview favorite (no sort).

Total: O(n·k) per word with the count-key (O(n·k log k) with the sort-key), space O(n·k). The trick is not sorting strings — it’s noticing that an anagram is the same letter-frequency vector, and that vector becomes a hash key.

Python

from collections import defaultdict

class Solution:
    def groupAnagrams(self, strs: list[str]) -> list[list[str]]:
        groups: dict[tuple, list[str]] = defaultdict(list)
        for s in strs:
            count = [0] * 26
            for c in s:
                count[ord(c) - ord("a")] += 1
            groups[tuple(count)].append(s)   # canonical key: tuple of counts
        return list(groups.values())

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashMap;

impl Solution {
    pub fn group_anagrams(strs: Vec<String>) -> Vec<Vec<String>> {
        let mut groups: HashMap<String, Vec<String>> = HashMap::new();
        for s in strs {
            let mut count = [0u8; 26];
            for &b in s.as_bytes() {
                count[(b - b'a') as usize] += 1;
            }
            // canonical key: counts joined by commas
            let key = count
                .iter()
                .map(|n| n.to_string())
                .collect::<Vec<_>>()
                .join(",");
            groups.entry(key).or_default().push(s);
        }
        groups.into_values().collect()
    }
}
}

C++

#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<vector<string>> groupAnagrams(vector<string>& strs) {
        unordered_map<string, vector<string>> groups;
        for (string& s : strs) {
            string key = s;
            sort(key.begin(), key.end());      // sort-key: sorted letters
            groups[move(key)].push_back(s);
        }
        vector<vector<string>> res;
        res.reserve(groups.size());
        for (auto& [key, list] : groups) res.push_back(move(list));
        return res;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Hash map string -> group index (open addressing). */
typedef struct { char* key; int group; int used; } GroupEntry;

static unsigned hash_str(const char* s) {
    unsigned h = 5381;
    while (*s) h = h * 33u + (unsigned char)*s++;   /* djb2 */
    return h;
}

static int cmp_char(const void* a, const void* b) {
    unsigned char x = *(const unsigned char*)a, y = *(const unsigned char*)b;
    return (x > y) - (x < y);
}

static char* dup_str(const char* s) {
    size_t n = strlen(s) + 1;
    char* c = malloc(n);
    memcpy(c, s, n);
    return c;
}

char*** groupAnagrams(char** strs, int strsSize, int* returnSize, int** returnColumnSizes) {
    *returnSize = 0;
    *returnColumnSizes = malloc(sizeof(int));
    if (strsSize == 0) return NULL;

    int cap = 16;
    while (cap < strsSize * 2) cap <<= 1;
    unsigned mask = (unsigned)cap - 1;
    GroupEntry* map = calloc((size_t)cap, sizeof(GroupEntry));

    char*** res = calloc((size_t)strsSize, sizeof(char**));
    int* col = calloc((size_t)strsSize, sizeof(int));
    int groups = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < strsSize; i++) {
        int len = (int)strlen(strs[i]);
        char* key = dup_str(strs[i]);
        qsort(key, (size_t)len, 1, cmp_char);      /* key = sorted letters */

        unsigned h = hash_str(key) & mask;
        while (map[h].used && strcmp(map[h].key, key) != 0) h = (h + 1u) & mask;

        int g;
        if (map[h].used) {
            g = map[h].group;
            free(key);
        } else {                                       /* new group */
            g = groups++;
            map[h].key = key;
            map[h].group = g;
            map[h].used = 1;
            res[g] = NULL;
        }
        col[g]++;
        res[g] = realloc(res[g], (size_t)col[g] * sizeof(char*));
        res[g][col[g] - 1] = dup_str(strs[i]);
    }
    free(map);
    *returnSize = groups;
    *returnColumnSizes = col;
    return res;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n·k) with the count-key (k = average string length); O(n·k log k) with the sort-key. Scanning every character of every word dominates in the count-key.
  • Space: O(n·k) — the hash map holds all strings (plus the keys).

Pitfalls

  • Return order is free — don’t waste time “preserving first-appearance order” in the hash map (unless the interviewer asks for it).
  • The canonical key must identify equality 1:1: “aab” and “aba” need the same key; “ab” and “aab” need different ones. Sort-key and count-key both guarantee this — keys that just concatenate letters don’t.
  • Count-key in Python: it must become a tuple (lists are not hashable); tuple(count) is the detail beginners forget.
  • In C: a freshly created group needs res[g] = NULL before the first realloc (otherwise realloc on garbage). And don’t rely on strdup (LeetCode doesn’t guarantee POSIX) — write your own dup_str.
  • Rust: entry(key).or_default().push(s) avoids the double lookup of an if let Some/else.

347. Top K Frequent Elements (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/top-k-frequent-elements/ · Topic: Arrays & Hashing

Problem (summary)

Given an array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. The answer may come in any order; k is always between 1 and the number of distinct elements.

nums = [1,1,1,2,2,3], k = 2  →  [1,2]
nums = [1],            k = 1  →  [1]

Pattern — what to memorize

Count frequencies → keep the top-k with a size-k heap. The heap holds at most k pairs (freq, num) ordered by frequency; when a more frequent element shows up than the heap’s smallest, it kicks the smallest out. Cost O(n log k) — with small k, nearly O(n). Classic alternative (the problem’s follow-up): bucket sort — an array of lists where position i holds the elements with frequency i; walk it back to front and collect k. Cost O(n) time and space. The clue in the statement: k most frequent elements → (frequency, element) pairs in a min-heap.

Python

from collections import Counter
import heapq

class Solution:
    def topKFrequent(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
        counts = Counter(nums)                      # {num: freq}
        # nsmallest sorts by -freq: the k with the highest frequency
        return [x for x, _ in heapq.nsmallest(k, counts.items(), key=lambda p: -p[1])]

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::{BinaryHeap, HashMap};

impl Solution {
    pub fn top_k_frequent(nums: Vec<i32>, k: i32) -> Vec<i32> {
        let mut counts: HashMap<i32, i32> = HashMap::new();
        for x in nums {
            *counts.entry(x).or_insert(0) += 1;
        }
        // BinaryHeap is a max-heap; Reverse turns it into a min-heap of (freq, num)
        let mut heap: BinaryHeap<Reverse<(i32, i32)>> = BinaryHeap::new();
        let k = k as usize;
        for (num, freq) in counts {
            heap.push(Reverse((freq, num)));
            if heap.len() > k {
                heap.pop();                            // evicts the least frequent
            }
        }
        heap.into_iter().map(|Reverse((_, num))| num).collect()
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <queue>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> topKFrequent(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
        unordered_map<int, int> counts;
        for (int x : nums) counts[x]++;
        // size-k min-heap ordered by (frequency, value)
        priority_queue<pair<int,int>, vector<pair<int,int>>, greater<pair<int,int>>> heap;
        for (auto& [num, freq] : counts) {
            heap.emplace(freq, num);
            if ((int)heap.size() > k) heap.pop();
        }
        vector<int> res;
        while (!heap.empty()) {
            res.push_back(heap.top().second);
            heap.pop();
        }
        return res;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

/* Counting int->int hash (open addressing) + hand-rolled min-heap of pairs. */
typedef struct { int key; int count; int used; } Count;
typedef struct { int freq; int num; } Pair;

static void heap_sift_up(Pair* h, int i) {
    while (i > 0) {
        int p = (i - 1) / 2;
        if (h[p].freq <= h[i].freq) break;
        Pair t = h[i]; h[i] = h[p]; h[p] = t;
        i = p;
    }
}

static void heap_sift_down(Pair* h, int n, int i) {
    for (;;) {
        int left = 2 * i + 1, right = left + 1, smallest = i;
        if (left < n && h[left].freq < h[smallest].freq) smallest = left;
        if (right < n && h[right].freq < h[smallest].freq) smallest = right;
        if (smallest == i) break;
        Pair t = h[i]; h[i] = h[smallest]; h[smallest] = t;
        i = smallest;
    }
}

int* topKFrequent(int* nums, int numsSize, int k, int* returnSize) {
    int cap = 16;
    while (cap < numsSize * 2) cap <<= 1;
    unsigned mask = (unsigned)cap - 1;
    Count* map = calloc((size_t)cap, sizeof(Count));
    for (int i = 0; i < numsSize; i++) {
        int x = nums[i];
        unsigned h = ((unsigned)x * 2654435761u) & mask;   /* Knuth multiplicative */
        while (map[h].used) {
            if (map[h].key == x) { map[h].count++; break; }
            h = (h + 1u) & mask;
        }
        if (!map[h].used) {
            map[h].key = x;
            map[h].count = 1;
            map[h].used = 1;
        }
    }
    Pair* heap = malloc((size_t)k * sizeof(Pair));
    int size = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < cap; i++) {
        if (!map[i].used) continue;
        Pair fresh = { map[i].count, map[i].key };
        if (size < k) {
            heap[size] = fresh;
            heap_sift_up(heap, size);
            size++;
        } else if (fresh.freq > heap[0].freq) {
            heap[0] = fresh;
            heap_sift_down(heap, k, 0);
        }
    }
    int* res = malloc((size_t)k * sizeof(int));
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) res[i] = heap[i].num;
    *returnSize = k;
    free(map);
    free(heap);
    return res;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n log k) — counting is O(n); each push/pop on the size-k heap is O(log k). (Bucket sort would do O(n) instead.)
  • Space: O(n + k) — the count map (O(n) worst case) + heap (O(k)).

Pitfalls

  • Heap direction: Python heapq is a min-heap (but we ask for nsmallest), Rust BinaryHeap is a max-heap and C++ priority_queue is a max-heap — that’s exactly the “negate / Reverse / greater<>” gotcha from the language guides. Draw the heap before coding.
  • k can equal the number of distinct elements: the heap never overflows.
  • Frequency ties: any element is correct — don’t worry about order among equals.
  • C: hashing a negative int — the cast to unsigned in (unsigned)x * 2654435761u handles it (same trick as Two Sum in this house).
  • Rust: iterating counts consuming the HashMap with for (num, freq) in counts sidesteps the borrow checker (the heap lives outside the loop).

238. Product of Array Except Self (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/product-of-array-except-self/ · Topic: Arrays & Hashing

Problem (summary)

Return an array where answer[i] is the product of all elements of nums except nums[i]. Without using division and in O(n) time; the follow-up asks for O(1) extra space (ignoring the output array).

nums = [1,2,3,4]       →  [24,12,8,6]
nums = [-1,1,0,-3,3]   →  [0,0,9,0,0]

Pattern — what to memorize

Prefix × suffix in two passes. Without division, the “except self” product at each position is the product of everything to its left (prefix) times everything to its right (suffix). First pass accumulates the prefixes; second pass walks back to front multiplying by the running suffix. The follow-up (O(1) extra) writes the prefix into the answer array itself and carries the suffix in a variable. This approach already handles zeros naturally — unlike the shortcut “total product divided by nums[i]”, which breaks on a zero divisor. Clue: no division + all except i → prefix/suffix.

Python

class Solution:
    def productExceptSelf(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        n = len(nums)
        res = [1] * n
        for i in range(1, n):          # pass 1: running prefix
            res[i] = res[i - 1] * nums[i - 1]
        suffix = 1
        for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): # pass 2: multiply by the suffix
            res[i] *= suffix
            suffix *= nums[i]
        return res

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn product_except_self(nums: Vec<i32>) -> Vec<i32> {
        let n = nums.len();
        let mut res = vec![1; n];
        for i in 1..n {                    // running prefix
            res[i] = res[i - 1] * nums[i - 1];
        }
        let mut suffix = 1;
        for i in (0..n).rev() {            // suffix walking back to front
            res[i] *= suffix;
            suffix *= nums[i];
        }
        res
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> productExceptSelf(vector<int>& nums) {
        int n = (int)nums.size();
        vector<int> res(n, 1);
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) res[i] = res[i - 1] * nums[i - 1];
        int suffix = 1;
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            res[i] *= suffix;
            suffix *= nums[i];
        }
        return res;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

int* productExceptSelf(int* nums, int numsSize, int* returnSize) {
    int* res = malloc((size_t)numsSize * sizeof(int));
    res[0] = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i < numsSize; i++) res[i] = res[i - 1] * nums[i - 1];
    int suffix = 1;
    for (int i = numsSize - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        res[i] *= suffix;
        suffix *= nums[i];
    }
    *returnSize = numsSize;
    return res;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — two passes (really 2n operations, one pass per side).
  • Space: O(1) extra beyond the output — the follow-up in the statement is this very solution; no auxiliary array other than res.

Pitfalls

  • “No division” is the problem’s thesis — the temptation is total_product / nums[i], which still explodes on a zero divisor (and on INT_MIN in C/C++). Don’t even mention division before the interviewer offers it.
  • Zeros are not a special case in prefix/suffix: [0,1,2,3] → [6,0,0,0] comes out on its own. (Senior curiosity: with division you’d need 3 cases — no zeros, one zero, two+ zeros.)
  • Large values: the product of i32s can overflow int (LeetCode constraints guarantee the final product fits in int, but 2·10⁹ is near the ceiling). In C/C++/Rust, if the constraints change, use long long.
  • Rust: the reverse loop (0..n).rev() — no i - 1 going down, so no usize panic; the prefix loop uses res[i - 1] with i starting at 1 (never 0 - 1).

128. Longest Consecutive Sequence (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-consecutive-sequence/ · Topic: Arrays & Hashing

Problem (summary)

Given an unsorted array of integers, return the length of the longest run of consecutive elements (e.g., 1,2,3,4). The solution must run in O(n) time — no sorting.

nums = [100,4,200,1,3,2]               →  4   (the sequence [1,2,3,4])
nums = [0,3,7,2,5,8,4,6,0,1]           →  9   ([0..8], duplicates ignored)

Pattern — what to memorize

HashSet + “only start from the head.” Put everything in a set; for each number, ask “am I the first of my sequence?” — if x - 1 is in the set, it already belongs to a longer sequence that started earlier, so skip it. If not, you’re the head: walk x+1, x+2, ... counting while it’s in the set. The cost magic: each element is visited at most twice (once as a candidate, once inside an expansion) — O(n) total, not O(n²). The set kills the “do I need to sort?” from the statement. Set “in” checks are amortized O(1).

Python

class Solution:
    def longestConsecutive(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        s = set(nums)
        best = 0
        for x in s:
            if x - 1 in s:        # not the head: someone else's sequence already counts me
                continue
            end = x
            length = 1
            while end + 1 in s:   # expand while consecutive
                end += 1
                length += 1
            best = max(best, length)
        return best

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashSet;

impl Solution {
    pub fn longest_consecutive(nums: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
        let s: HashSet<i32> = nums.into_iter().collect();
        let mut best = 0;
        for x in s.iter().copied() {
            // only start a sequence at its head (x-1 absent) — that's what ensures O(n)
            if s.contains(&(x - 1)) {
                continue;
            }
            let mut end = x;
            let mut length = 1;
            while s.contains(&(end + 1)) {
                end += 1;
                length += 1;
            }
            best = best.max(length);
        }
        best
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <unordered_set>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int longestConsecutive(vector<int>& nums) {
        unordered_set<int> s(nums.begin(), nums.end());
        int best = 0;
        for (int x : s) {
            if (s.count(x - 1)) continue;   // not the head
            int end = x, length = 1;
            while (s.count(end + 1)) { end++; length++; }
            best = max(best, length);
        }
        return best;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

/* Int hash set (open addressing); -1 = empty sentinel. */
static int contains(int* s, unsigned mask, int x) {
    unsigned h = ((unsigned)x * 2654435761u) & mask;
    while (s[h] != -1) {
        if (s[h] == x) return 1;
        h = (h + 1u) & mask;
    }
    return 0;
}

static void insert(int* s, unsigned mask, int x) {
    unsigned h = ((unsigned)x * 2654435761u) & mask;
    while (s[h] != -1) h = (h + 1u) & mask;
    s[h] = x;
}

int longestConsecutive(int* nums, int numsSize) {
    if (numsSize == 0) return 0;
    int cap = 16;
    while (cap < numsSize * 2) cap <<= 1;          /* load factor < 0.5 */
    unsigned mask = (unsigned)cap - 1;
    int* s = malloc((size_t)cap * sizeof(int));
    for (int i = 0; i < cap; i++) s[i] = -1;
    for (int i = 0; i < numsSize; i++) insert(s, mask, nums[i]);

    int best = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < cap; i++) {
        if (s[i] == -1) continue;
        int x = s[i];
        if (contains(s, mask, x - 1)) continue;       /* only from the head */
        int length = 1;
        while (contains(s, mask, x + 1)) { x++; length++; }
        if (length > best) best = length;
    }
    free(s);
    return best;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) amortized — expansion only happens at heads; each element enters an expansion at most once.
  • Space: O(n) — a set with all elements (in C, a hash array with capacity ≥ 2·n).

Pitfalls

  • The “naive solution” trap: set + expanding from every element (without the x-1 test) is O(n²) — each sequence gets re-walked by every one of its elements. The if x - 1 in s: continue IS the optimization.
  • Duplicates don’t count: [1,2,0,1] → 3 (the second 1 is absorbed by the set). Sorting and scanning would count wrong unless you handle equality.
  • Negative values work the same (the test is x-1, not 0).
  • C: the capacity must be a power of 2 (the cap - 1 mask with &) and ≥ 2·n for the load factor; hashing a negative int is handled by the cast to unsigned.
  • Rust: iterate s.iter().copied() (references to &i32) — x is an i32 by value; contains(&(x-1)) takes a reference.

271. Encode and Decode Strings (Medium · Premium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/encode-and-decode-strings/ · Topic: Arrays & Hashing (Design, Premium)

Problem (summary)

Premium problem: design a scheme to serialize a list of strings into a single string (encode) and revert it losslessly (decode). The challenge is that the strings may contain any character, including #, digits, and even the separator you pick.

["neet","code"]  →  encode  →  "4#neet4#code"  →  decode  →  ["neet","code"]
["a#b","c"]      →  encode  →  "2#a#b1#c"      →  decode  →  ["a#b","c"]

Pattern — what to memorize

Length-prefix (“explicit length”): each string becomes len + "#" + s, and everything is concatenated. The # is not a string separator — it’s a marker ending the numeric prefix. The length is read first, so decode knows exactly how many bytes to skip, even when the content has # or digits. It’s the same trick real protocols use (HTTP/2 HPACK, TLV, Redis buffers). Clue in the statement: any character possible in the string + a single string on output → each item must carry its own length.

Python

class Solution:
    def encode(self, strs: list[str]) -> str:
        return "".join(f"{len(s)}#{s}" for s in strs)   # "len#str" concatenated

    def decode(self, s: str) -> list[str]:
        res: list[str] = []
        i = 0
        while i < len(s):
            j = s.index("#", i)          # end of the numeric prefix
            length = int(s[i:j])
            i = j + 1                     # skip the '#'
            res.append(s[i:i + length])   # copy exactly length chars
            i += length
        return res

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn encode(strs: Vec<String>) -> String {
        let mut out = String::new();
        for s in strs {
            out.push_str(&s.len().to_string());
            out.push('#');
            out.push_str(&s);
        }
        out
    }

    pub fn decode(s: String) -> Vec<String> {
        let bytes = s.as_bytes();
        let mut res = Vec::new();
        let mut i = 0usize;
        while i < bytes.len() {
            let mut length = 0usize;
            while i < bytes.len() && bytes[i] != b'#' {
                length = length * 10 + (bytes[i] - b'0') as usize;
                i += 1;
            }
            i += 1;                                          // skip the '#'
            res.push(String::from_utf8(bytes[i..i + length].to_vec()).unwrap());
            i += length;
        }
        res
    }
}
}

C++

#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    string encode(vector<string>& strs) {
        string out;
        for (string& s : strs) {
            out += to_string(s.size()) + "#" + s;     // length-prefix
        }
        return out;
    }

    vector<string> decode(string s) {
        vector<string> res;
        size_t i = 0;
        while (i < s.size()) {
            size_t hash = s.find('#', i);
            int length = stoi(s.substr(i, hash - i));
            i = hash + 1;
            res.push_back(s.substr(i, (size_t)length));
            i += (size_t)length;
        }
        return res;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdio.h>

static char* dup_str(const char* s) {
    size_t n = strlen(s) + 1;
    char* c = malloc(n);
    memcpy(c, s, n);
    return c;
}

char* encode(char** strs, int strsSize) {
    long total = 1;                                  /* 1 for the trailing '\0' */
    for (int i = 0; i < strsSize; i++) {
        int len = (int)strlen(strs[i]);
        int d = 1, x = len;
        while (x >= 10) { x /= 10; d++; }            /* digits of len */
        total += len + d + 1;                        /* digits + '#' + body */
    }
    char* buf = malloc((size_t)total);
    int pos = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < strsSize; i++) {
        int len = (int)strlen(strs[i]);
        pos += sprintf(buf + pos, "%d#", len);
        memcpy(buf + pos, strs[i], (size_t)len);
        pos += len;
    }
    buf[pos] = '\0';
    return buf;
}

char** decode(char* s, int* returnSize) {
    /* pass 1: count how many strings there are */
    int n = 0, i = 0;
    while (s[i]) {
        int len = 0;
        while (s[i] && s[i] != '#') { len = len * 10 + (s[i] - '0'); i++; }
        i++;                       /* skip '#' */
        i += len;                  /* skip the body */
        n++;
    }
    /* pass 2: extract each string */
    char** res = calloc((size_t)(n > 0 ? n : 1), sizeof(char*));
    i = 0;
    n = 0;
    while (s[i]) {
        int len = 0;
        while (s[i] && s[i] != '#') { len = len * 10 + (s[i] - '0'); i++; }
        i++;
        res[n] = malloc((size_t)len + 1);
        memcpy(res[n], s + i, (size_t)len);
        res[n][len] = '\0';
        n++;
        i += len;
    }
    *returnSize = n;
    return res;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(total characters) — encode and decode walk each character once (C does two pass decode so it can size the output array).
  • Space: O(total characters) — the encoded string (and, on decode, the output array with copies).

Pitfalls

  • The ambiguous delimiter is the trap: separating by comma or by a bare # breaks when the content has that character. Length-prefix only breaks if you don’t read the length before the content.
  • Empty string: [""] → "0#" → [""] — the 0 in the prefix is the edge case the example pair must cover (and the C first loop would count 0 as a string).
  • Strings with digits and #: ["a#b","c"] → "2#a#b1#c" — decoding “2#a#…” means reading 2 as the length, not stopping at the inner #.
  • C: sprintf(buf + pos, "%d#", len) returns the number of bytes written — use the return value, not strlen, to accumulate pos.
  • Rust: String::from_utf8(...).unwrap() — encode only produces valid ASCII, so it’s safe; commenting why avoids a vague expect.

217. Contains Duplicate (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/contains-duplicate/ · Topic: Arrays & Hashing

Problem (summary)

Given an array nums, return true if any value appears more than once, false if all are distinct.

nums = [1,2,3,1]  →  true
nums = [1,2,3,4]  →  false

Pattern — what to memorize

One-pass hash set: for each x, the set holds what you’ve already seen; if x is already there, it’s the duplicate. The classic interview alternative when memory is tight: sort and compare neighbors — O(n log n) time and O(1) (in-place) space, at the cost of mutating the input array. Clue in the statement: repeated value (not pair, not index) → set of seen values; presence is the answer, not position.

Python

class Solution:
    def containsDuplicate(self, nums: list[int]) -> bool:
        seen: set[int] = set()
        for x in nums:
            if x in seen:
                return True
            seen.add(x)
        return False

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashSet;

impl Solution {
    pub fn contains_duplicate(nums: Vec<i32>) -> bool {
        let mut seen = HashSet::new();
        nums.iter().any(|&x| !seen.insert(x))
    }
}
}

C++

#include <unordered_set>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    bool containsDuplicate(vector<int>& nums) {
        unordered_set<int> seen;
        seen.reserve(nums.size());           // avoids rehash
        for (int x : nums) {
            if (seen.count(x)) return true;
            seen.insert(x);
        }
        return false;
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* comparator WITHOUT subtraction: (x > y) - (x < y) never overflows (INT_MIN) */
static int cmp_int(const void* a, const void* b) {
    int x = *(const int*)a, y = *(const int*)b;
    return (x > y) - (x < y);
}

bool containsDuplicate(int* nums, int numsSize) {
    qsort(nums, numsSize, sizeof(int), cmp_int);
    for (int i = 1; i < numsSize; i++) {
        if (nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one pass with amortized O(1) set lookups.
  • Space: O(n) — the set holds up to n elements. (Sorted version: O(n log n) time and O(1) space, if the statement allows mutating the array.)

Pitfalls

  • Empty or 1-element array → false (the C for i = 1 loop already covers it).
  • Negative numbers repeated are a normal duplicate ([-1,5,-1] → true).
  • The sorting version mutates the input array — mention this if the interviewer asks; 287 forbids mutation, here it doesn’t.
  • In C: the qsort comparator is the one from the languages page — (x > y) - (x < y), never x - y (overflow with INT_MIN).
  • In Rust: HashSet::insert returns false if the value already existed — !insert(x) is the duplicate, and .any() stops at the first true (doesn’t scan the whole array).

36. Valid Sudoku (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-sudoku/ · Topic: Arrays & Hashing

Problem (summary)

Check whether a 9×9 board is valid (row, column and 3×3 box rules), without caring whether it’s solvable. '.' cells are empty and ignored; digits may repeat, as long as not in the same row/column/box.

valid board (problem example)  →  true
(row 0 with two '5')           →  false

Pattern — what to memorize

3 families of 9 sets in a single pass: rows[r], cols[c] and boxes[box] are sets of the digits already seen; the box index is (r/3)*3 + c/3 (integer division groups the 3 rows/columns of each box). For each cell with a digit, if any of the three sets already contains it → invalid; otherwise insert into all three. Clue: validate (not solve) + fixed size 9 → count/bitmask per family; the board is small, so the complexity is O(1) “hidden” in O(81).

Python

class Solution:
    def isValidSudoku(self, board: list[list[str]]) -> bool:
        rows: list[set[str]] = [set() for _ in range(9)]
        cols: list[set[str]] = [set() for _ in range(9)]
        boxes: list[set[str]] = [set() for _ in range(9)]
        for r in range(9):
            for c in range(9):
                digit = board[r][c]
                if digit == ".":
                    continue
                box = (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3
                if (digit in rows[r] or digit in cols[c]
                        or digit in boxes[box]):
                    return False
                rows[r].add(digit)
                cols[c].add(digit)
                boxes[box].add(digit)
        return True

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashSet;

impl Solution {
    pub fn is_valid_sudoku(board: Vec<Vec<char>>) -> bool {
        let mut rows: [HashSet<char>; 9] = Default::default();
        let mut cols: [HashSet<char>; 9] = Default::default();
        let mut boxes: [HashSet<char>; 9] = Default::default();
        for r in 0..9 {
            for c in 0..9 {
                let digit = board[r][c];
                if digit == '.' {
                    continue;
                }
                let box = (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3;
                if rows[r].contains(&digit)
                    || cols[c].contains(&digit)
                    || boxes[box].contains(&digit)
                {
                    return false;
                }
                rows[r].insert(digit);
                cols[c].insert(digit);
                boxes[box].insert(digit);
            }
        }
        true
    }
}
}

C++

#include <unordered_set>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    bool isValidSudoku(vector<vector<char>>& board) {
        unordered_set<char> rows[9], cols[9], boxes[9];
        for (int r = 0; r < 9; ++r) {
            for (int c = 0; c < 9; ++c) {
                char d = board[r][c];
                if (d == '.') continue;
                int box = (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3;
                if (rows[r].count(d) || cols[c].count(d) || boxes[box].count(d))
                    return false;
                rows[r].insert(d);
                cols[c].insert(d);
                boxes[box].insert(d);
            }
        }
        return true;
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>

bool isValidSudoku(char** board, int boardSize, int* boardColSize) {
    (void)boardSize;
    (void)boardColSize;
    unsigned short rows[9] = {0}, cols[9] = {0}, boxes[9] = {0};
    for (int r = 0; r < 9; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < 9; c++) {
            char cell = board[r][c];
            if (cell == '.') continue;
            int bit = 1 << (cell - '1');       /* '1'..'9' -> bit 0..8 */
            int box = (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3;
            if ((rows[r] & bit) || (cols[c] & bit) || (boxes[box] & bit))
                return false;
            rows[r] |= bit;
            cols[c] |= bit;
            boxes[box] |= bit;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(81) = O(1) — one pass over the board; every set operation is O(1).
  • Space: O(1) — 27 sets of at most 9 digits (just bits in C).

Pitfalls

  • The box index is (r/3)*3 + c/3 — operation order matters: (r / 3) * 3, not r / (3 * 3).
  • Don’t validate solvability: a valid board can be unsolvable — the question is only about repeats within the families.
  • Digits are char, not int: in C, cell - '1' maps to bit 0..8; cell - '0' would give digit 0..9 and overflow 9 bits (and the box index).
  • Empty ('.') cells are ignored — don’t insert into the set (nor bump a count).
  • In C: unsigned short (16 bits) holds the 9 bits; int would work too — what matters is the |=/&.
  • In Rust: [HashSet<char>; 9] with Default::default() builds all 9 empty sets without a loop.

125. Valid Palindrome (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-palindrome/ · Topic: Two Pointers

Problem (summary)

Check whether a string is a palindrome ignoring spaces, punctuation and case: only letters and digits count, compared in lowercase.

"A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"  →  true
"race a car"                      →  false

Pattern — what to memorize

Two pointers converging: l at the left end, r at the right; each step, l skips everything non-alphanumeric, r the same, compare both in lowercase; if they differ, it’s not a palindrome. Clue in the statement: ignore non-alphanumeric characters + compare string with its reverse (without allocating) → two pointers. The trap of doing s[::-1] or copying the filtered string: O(n) memory and extra time — two pointers uses O(1) space.

Python

class Solution:
    def isPalindrome(self, s: str) -> bool:
        l, r = 0, len(s) - 1
        while l < r:
            while l < r and not s[l].isalnum():   # skip non-alphanumerics
                l += 1
            while l < r and not s[r].isalnum():
                r -= 1
            if s[l].lower() != s[r].lower():      # compare in lowercase
                return False
            l += 1
            r -= 1
        return True

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn is_palindrome(s: String) -> bool {
        let b = s.as_bytes();                       // ASCII per the statement
        let (mut l, mut r) = (0usize, b.len().wrapping_sub(1));
        while l < r {
            while l < r && !b[l].is_ascii_alphanumeric() {
                l += 1;
            }
            while l < r && !b[r].is_ascii_alphanumeric() {
                r -= 1;
            }
            if b[l].to_ascii_lowercase() != b[r].to_ascii_lowercase() {
                return false;
            }
            l += 1;
            r -= 1;
        }
        true
    }
}
}

C++

#include <string>
#include <cctype>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    bool isPalindrome(string s) {
        int l = 0, r = (int)s.size() - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            while (l < r && !isalnum((unsigned char)s[l])) l++;
            while (l < r && !isalnum((unsigned char)s[r])) r--;
            if (tolower((unsigned char)s[l]) != tolower((unsigned char)s[r])) return false;
            l++;
            r--;
        }
        return true;
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <ctype.h>
#include <string.h>

bool isPalindrome(char* s) {
    int l = 0, r = (int)strlen(s) - 1;
    while (l < r) {
        while (l < r && !isalnum((unsigned char)s[l])) l++;
        while (l < r && !isalnum((unsigned char)s[r])) r--;
        if (tolower((unsigned char)s[l]) != tolower((unsigned char)s[r])) return false;
        l++;
        r--;
    }
    return true;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each character is visited at most once per pointer.
  • Space: O(1) — just two indices; no filtered copy of the string.

Pitfalls

  • Mind the inner loop running off the string: always l < r inside the skip — otherwise l crosses the end (or r the start) and you compare garbage.
  • Case: "A" vs "a" are equal. Python lower(), C/C++ tolower((unsigned char)c).
  • 0P → false (digits count as alphanumeric, and '0' ≠ 'p').
  • “ “ (just a space) → true (no comparison happens — the loop ends because l == r).
  • In C/C++, isalnum/tolower take unsigned char (or EOF) — the cast avoids UB with negative (non-ASCII) characters.
  • Rust: as_bytes() assumes ASCII — the statement guarantees it (a-z, A-Z, 0-9); using chars() with unicode would be a different solution if you generalized.

167. Two Sum II (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/two-sum-ii-input-array-is-sorted/ · Topic: Two Pointers

Problem (summary)

Same as Two Sum, but the array is sorted in ascending order — and the answer is the 1-based indices of the two numbers that add up to target. There is exactly one solution.

numbers = [2,7,11,15], target = 9   →   [1,2]   (2 + 7 = 9, 1-based indices)
numbers = [2,3,4],     target = 6   →   [1,3]

Pattern — what to memorize

Two pointers converging — the advantage of being sorted. l at the start, r at the end: if numbers[l] + numbers[r] < target, the only way to raise the sum is l++; if > target, the only way to lower it is r--. Each step eliminates one candidate in O(1), so O(n) total. The classic Two Sum hash map still works (O(n) time, O(n) space), but the sorted array enables the O(1)-space version — that’s the improvement the interviewer wants to hear. Clue: sorted array + pair summing to a value → two pointers.

Python

class Solution:
    def twoSum(self, numbers: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
        l, r = 0, len(numbers) - 1
        while l < r:
            total = numbers[l] + numbers[r]
            if total == target:
                return [l + 1, r + 1]     # 1-based indices
            if total < target:
                l += 1                    # need a larger sum
            else:
                r -= 1                    # need a smaller sum
        return []                         # unreachable: there is always a solution

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn two_sum(numbers: Vec<i32>, target: i32) -> Vec<i32> {
        let (mut l, mut r) = (0usize, numbers.len() - 1);
        while l < r {
            let total = numbers[l] + numbers[r];
            if total == target {
                return vec![l as i32 + 1, r as i32 + 1];
            }
            if total < target {
                l += 1;
            } else {
                r -= 1;
            }
        }
        Vec::new()
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> twoSum(vector<int>& numbers, int target) {
        int l = 0, r = (int)numbers.size() - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            int total = numbers[l] + numbers[r];
            if (total == target) return {l + 1, r + 1};
            if (total < target) l++;
            else r--;
        }
        return {};
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

int* twoSum(int* numbers, int numbersSize, int target, int* returnSize) {
    int l = 0, r = numbersSize - 1;
    while (l < r) {
        int total = numbers[l] + numbers[r];
        if (total == target) {
            int* res = malloc(2 * sizeof(int));
            res[0] = l + 1;
            res[1] = r + 1;
            *returnSize = 2;
            return res;
        }
        if (total < target) l++;
        else r--;
    }
    *returnSize = 0;
    return NULL;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each pointer moves at most n steps, never back.
  • Space: O(1) — two indices (vs. the Two Sum hash map’s O(n)).

Pitfalls

  • 1-based indices! [1,2], not [0,1] — the most common mistake, and the statement’s example tests exactly that.
  • Empty/single-element array has no guaranteed solution — the while l < r loop never runs.
  • Negatives work normally: the sum can be smaller than both numbers ([-1,0], target -1 → [1,2]).
  • Can the sum overflow int? Typical constraints (±10³ per element) no; in C/C++, if values approach INT_MAX, the numbers[l] + numbers[r] computation before the comparison is where the overflow would live — use long long if the constraints ask for it (on LeetCode, they don’t).
  • Rust: numbers.len() - 1 on usize panics on an empty list — the problem guarantees a solution, but if numbers.len() < 2 { return vec![]; } keeps the function total (no unreachable!).

15. 3Sum (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/3sum/ · Topic: Two Pointers

Problem (summary)

Given an array of integers, return every triplet nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0 without repeats: i, j and k are distinct indices, and the same combination of values counts exactly once (the internal order of a triplet and the order of triplets is irrelevant — and duplicate values in the array don’t produce duplicate triplets).

nums = [-1,0,1,2,-1,-4]   →   [[-1,-1,2],[-1,0,1]]
nums = [0,0,0,0]          →   [[0,0,0]]        (not 4x the same)

Pattern — what to memorize

Sort → fix one → two pointers on the other two. With the array sorted, for each fixed i, l = i+1 and r = n-1 converge as in Two Sum II, adjusting the sum: less than 0 → l++; greater → r--; equal → record and move both. Dedup is pitfall #1 — and the heart of the problem: after sorting, equal values become neighbors, so you skip duplicates (1) on the fixed one: if i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue; and (2) on the sides after each find: skip nums[l] == nums[l-1] and nums[r] == nums[r+1]. Sorting costs O(n log n) and enables the two pointers — no crazy pair hash map.

Python

class Solution:
    def threeSum(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        nums.sort()
        res: list[list[int]] = []
        n = len(nums)
        for i in range(n - 2):
            if nums[i] > 0:               # sorted: the minimum sum from here is > 0
                break
            if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:   # dedup the fixed one
                continue
            l, r = i + 1, n - 1
            while l < r:
                total = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r]
                if total < 0:
                    l += 1
                elif total > 0:
                    r -= 1
                else:
                    res.append([nums[i], nums[l], nums[r]])
                    l += 1
                    r -= 1
                    while l < r and nums[l] == nums[l - 1]:   # dedup the pair
                        l += 1
                    while l < r and nums[r] == nums[r + 1]:
                        r -= 1
        return res

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn three_sum(mut nums: Vec<i32>) -> Vec<Vec<i32>> {
        nums.sort_unstable();
        let n = nums.len();
        let mut res = Vec::new();
        for i in 0..n {
            if nums[i] > 0 {
                break; // sorted: from here on the minimum sum is > 0
            }
            if i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1] {
                continue; // dedup the fixed one
            }
            let (mut l, mut r) = (i + 1, n - 1);
            while l < r {
                let total = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r];
                if total < 0 {
                    l += 1;
                } else if total > 0 {
                    r -= 1;
                } else {
                    res.push(vec![nums[i], nums[l], nums[r]]);
                    l += 1;
                    r -= 1;
                    while l < r && nums[l] == nums[l - 1] {
                        l += 1;
                    }
                    while l < r && nums[r] == nums[r + 1] {
                        r -= 1;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        res
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<vector<int>> threeSum(vector<int>& nums) {
        sort(nums.begin(), nums.end());
        int n = (int)nums.size();
        vector<vector<int>> res;
        for (int i = 0; i < n - 2; i++) {
            if (nums[i] > 0) break;
            if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) continue;   // dedup the fixed one
            int l = i + 1, r = n - 1;
            while (l < r) {
                long long total = (long long)nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r];
                if (total < 0) l++;
                else if (total > 0) r--;
                else {
                    res.push_back({nums[i], nums[l], nums[r]});
                    l++; r--;
                    while (l < r && nums[l] == nums[l - 1]) l++;   // dedup the pair
                    while (l < r && nums[r] == nums[r + 1]) r--;
                }
            }
        }
        return res;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

static int cmp_int(const void* a, const void* b) {
    int x = *(const int*)a, y = *(const int*)b;
    return (x > y) - (x < y);            /* never x - y (overflow) */
}

int** threeSum(int* nums, int numsSize, int* returnSize, int** returnColumnSizes) {
    qsort(nums, (size_t)numsSize, sizeof(int), cmp_int);
    /* capacity = max possible triplets C(n,3); computed in long long */
    long long cap_ll = (long long)numsSize * (numsSize - 1) * (numsSize - 2) / 6;
    int cap = (int)(cap_ll > 0 ? cap_ll : 1);
    int** res = malloc((size_t)cap * sizeof(int*));
    int* col = malloc((size_t)cap * sizeof(int));
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < numsSize - 2; i++) {
        if (nums[i] > 0) break;
        if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) continue;     /* dedup the fixed one */
        int l = i + 1, r = numsSize - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            long long total = (long long)nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r];
            if (total < 0) l++;
            else if (total > 0) r--;
            else {
                res[count] = malloc(3 * sizeof(int));
                res[count][0] = nums[i];
                res[count][1] = nums[l];
                res[count][2] = nums[r];
                col[count] = 3;
                count++;
                l++;
                r--;
                while (l < r && nums[l] == nums[l - 1]) l++; /* dedup the pair */
                while (l < r && nums[r] == nums[r + 1]) r--;
            }
        }
    }
    *returnSize = count;
    *returnColumnSizes = col;
    return res;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n²) — sorting O(n log n) + the fixed loop O(n), with the two pointers O(n) inside → O(n²) dominates.
  • Space: O(1) extra working (beyond the output; C allocates the theoretical ceiling of triplets C(n,3) up front — in practice the output is the worst case).

Pitfalls

  • Dedup IS the problem: without skipping nums[i] == nums[i-1] on the fixed one and nums[l] == nums[l-1]/nums[r] == nums[r+1] on the pair, you return repeats ([0,0,0,0] would become 4 triplets) and blow past the statement’s expectation. It’s the first thing the interviewer looks for.
  • Side dedup vs fixed dedup: the fixed one’s continue needs the i > 0 (otherwise i == 0 reads nums[-1]); the sides’ dedup runs after l++; r--, comparing against l-1/r+1 (the “old” values).
  • Sum of the three: in C/C++ the values can add up near 3·10⁴ under the typical constraints (no overflow), but the long long on the sum is the senior reflex (same for the C capacity computation — bare int would overflow).
  • nums[i] > 0 → break is the big optimization: with the array sorted, if the fixed element is already positive, the minimum three-sum is positive — there’s no solution after it.
  • Rust: sort_unstable() is faster than sort() and sufficient (duplicates don’t need stability — and equal neighbors are exactly what we want to skip).

11. Container With Most Water (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/container-with-most-water/ · Topic: Two Pointers

Problem (summary)

Given an array height where height[i] is the height of the wall at position i, find the two walls that form the container with the largest area. The water is bounded by the shorter wall (min(h[l], h[r])) and the width is the distance between them (r - l).

height = [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7]   →   49   (walls 8 at i=1 and 7 at i=8: 7 × 7)
height = [1,1]                 →    1

Pattern — what to memorize

Two pointers with the golden rule: move the SMALLER side. l = 0, r = n-1; the current area is min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l); update the max and move the pointer on the shorter wall. Why is it safe? The shorter wall is at its ceiling: any container inside this window that uses that wall will have a smaller width and height at most the wall’s height — it can never beat the current area. So that wall can be discarded in one move. Each pointer only moves inward, once — O(n), no sorting, no pair checking. Clue: two walls + largest area (not “the pair with the biggest sum”) → two pointers.

Python

class Solution:
    def maxArea(self, height: list[int]) -> int:
        l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
        best = 0
        while l < r:
            h = min(height[l], height[r])
            best = max(best, h * (r - l))   # area = shortest × width
            if height[l] < height[r]:
                l += 1                      # move the SMALLER side
            else:
                r -= 1
        return best

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn max_area(height: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
        let (mut l, mut r) = (0usize, height.len() - 1);
        let mut best = 0;
        while l < r {
            let h = height[l].min(height[r]);
            best = best.max(h * (r - l) as i32);
            // move the smaller side: that's what caps the current area
            if height[l] < height[r] {
                l += 1;
            } else {
                r -= 1;
            }
        }
        best
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int maxArea(vector<int>& height) {
        int l = 0, r = (int)height.size() - 1;
        int best = 0;
        while (l < r) {
            int h = min(height[l], height[r]);
            best = max(best, h * (r - l));
            if (height[l] < height[r]) l++;   // move the smaller side
            else r--;
        }
        return best;
    }
};

C

int maxArea(int* height, int heightSize) {
    int l = 0, r = heightSize - 1;
    int best = 0;
    while (l < r) {
        int h = height[l] < height[r] ? height[l] : height[r];
        int area = h * (r - l);
        if (area > best) best = area;
        if (height[l] < height[r]) l++;   /* move the smaller side */
        else r--;
    }
    return best;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each pointer walks the array exactly once; no iteration is revisited.
  • Space: O(1) — two indices and two variables.

Pitfalls

  • Height tie (height[l] == height[r]): moving either one is correct (the current area is the same both ways); the else moving r is an arbitrary choice that doesn’t lose a solution.
  • The “local optimum” trap: trying to “jump to the tallest wall” or comparing with a brute-force O(n²) pair check is the wrong direction — the two-pointers optimality proof comes from discarding the shorter wall, not from guessing promising pairs.
  • Area uses the shorter, not the taller — flipping the min is the classic bug.
  • Width matters: the (1, 100) container is tiny (1 × distance) — the [1,1] → 1 example tests exactly width × minimum height.
  • Typical constraints (n ≤ 10⁵, height ≤ 10⁴): max area ≈ 10⁹, fits in int (2.1·10⁹). If it blows up, long long.
  • Rust: (r - l) as i32 — subtract the usizes first (never negative, since l < r), then convert to multiply against i32.
