42. Trapping Rain Water (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/trapping-rain-water/ · Topic: Two Pointers

Problem (summary)

Given an array height (heights of histogram bars, width 1), compute how many units of water stay trapped between the bars after it rains. Bars at the edges don’t accumulate (water needs a wall on both sides).

height = [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1]  →  6
height = [4,2,0,3,2,5]              →  9

Pattern — what to memorize

The water at each position i is min(tallest bar left, tallest bar right) − height[i] (0 if negative). The problem is computing that in O(n) with O(1) space — which is where the two pointers with maxL/maxR lives:

The SMALLER side decides. We always advance the pointer sitting on the smaller bar (height[l] < height[r]). Since the other side already has a bar ≥ height[r] > height[l], the minimum ceiling for position l is guaranteed by the right side — so the effective ceiling at l is just maxL (the tallest seen on the left). We compute maxL = max(maxL, height[l]) and add maxL − height[l] (new max ⇒ adds 0), then advance l. Symmetric for r. We can never go wrong: the move is always on the side with the smaller bar, the side whose ceiling we already know.

Clues: water accumulating between bars + asks for the total volume → the right question is “only the lower of the two ceilings matters”. Equivalent alternatives (same phase): precomputation of maxL[i]/maxR[i] in two arrays (O(n) space, good for explaining the intuition) and a monotonic decreasing stack (O(n), the “valleys between rising bars” version — harder to reason through out loud).

Python

class Solution:
    def trap(self, height: list[int]) -> int:
        # two pointers: the SMALLER bar of the pair decides the ceiling of the processed side
        if len(height) < 3:
            return 0
        l, r = 0, len(height) - 1          # l and r walk toward the center
        maxL = maxR = total = 0            # tallest bars seen on the left/right
        while l < r:
            if height[l] < height[r]:
                # the water ceiling at l is ONLY maxL: on the other side there
                # is already a bar >= height[r] > height[l] guaranteeing the wall
                maxL = max(maxL, height[l])
                total += maxL - height[l]  # maxL >= height[l] (new max => 0)
                l += 1
            else:
                maxR = max(maxR, height[r])
                total += maxR - height[r]
                r -= 1
        return total

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn trap(height: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
        // two pointers: the SMALLER bar of the pair decides the ceiling of the processed side
        if height.len() < 3 {
            return 0;
        }
        let (mut l, mut r) = (0usize, height.len() - 1);
        let (mut max_l, mut max_r, mut total) = (0i32, 0i32, 0i32);
        while l < r {
            if height[l] < height[r] {
                max_l = max_l.max(height[l]);
                total += max_l - height[l]; // new max => adds 0
                l += 1;
            } else {
                max_r = max_r.max(height[r]);
                total += max_r - height[r];
                r -= 1;
            }
        }
        total
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int trap(vector<int>& height) {
        int n = (int)height.size();
        if (n < 3) return 0;
        int l = 0, r = n - 1, maxL = 0, maxR = 0, total = 0;
        while (l < r) {
            if (height[l] < height[r]) {
                maxL = max(maxL, height[l]);
                total += maxL - height[l];   // new maxL => adds 0
                ++l;
            } else {
                maxR = max(maxR, height[r]);
                total += maxR - height[r];
                --r;
            }
        }
        return total;
    }
};

C

int trap(int* height, int heightSize) {
    if (heightSize < 3) return 0;
    int l = 0, r = heightSize - 1;
    int maxL = 0, maxR = 0, total = 0;
    while (l < r) {
        if (height[l] < height[r]) {
            if (height[l] >= maxL) maxL = height[l];
            else total += maxL - height[l];
            l++;
        } else {
            if (height[r] >= maxR) maxR = height[r];
            else total += maxR - height[r];
            r--;
        }
    }
    return total;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one pass with l/r meeting in the middle; each position is visited exactly once.
  • Space: O(1) — just the maxL/maxR/total variables.

Pitfalls

  • n < 3 ⇒ answer 0: there’s no valley between bars (at least two walls needed).
  • Height tie height[l] == height[r] falls into the else — safe, since the right side’s ceiling now applies to r and the analogous invariant holds.
  • The sum uses maxL - height[l] after max(): if height[l] is a new max, the water is 0 — never negative.
  • In Rust: l/r as usize (no negatives) and r -= 1 only with l < r guaranteed — never underflows.
  • In Python: don’t slice height per iteration (O(n) per slice) — the two pointers work by index precisely to avoid allocating.

121. Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock/ · Topic: Sliding Window (two pointers)

Problem (summary)

Given an array prices (stock price per day), you may buy on one day and sell on a later day (one transaction only). Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profit is possible (prices only fall).

prices = [7,1,5,3,6,4]  →  5    (buy day 2 at 1, sell day 5 at 6)
prices = [7,6,4,3,1]    →  0    (only dropped — don't buy)

Pattern — what to memorize

Two pointers disguised as a sliding window: left is the best buy day seen so far (the lowest price), right scans the days. On each day the candidate profit is price − min_so_far; keep the running minimum and the max profit in a single pass. Clue in the statement: maximum profit over an ordered sequence + goes up and down → one-way sliding window, no hash, no DP table. The min walks on its own: when a new price is lower than the minimum, it becomes the new minimum (buying earlier is always better than any previous buy).

Python

class Solution:
    def maxProfit(self, prices: list[int]) -> int:
        minimo = float("inf")
        lucro = 0
        for p in prices:
            if p < minimo:
                minimo = p
            elif p - minimo > lucro:
                lucro = p - minimo
        return lucro

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn max_profit(prices: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
    let mut minimo = i32::MAX;
    let mut lucro = 0;
    for p in prices {
        minimo = minimo.min(p);
        lucro = lucro.max(p - minimo);
    }
    lucro
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int maxProfit(vector<int>& prices) {
        int minimo = INT_MAX, lucro = 0;
        for (int p : prices) {
            minimo = min(minimo, p);
            lucro = max(lucro, p - minimo);
        }
        return lucro;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

int maxProfit(int* prices, int pricesSize) {
    int minimo = prices[0]; /* pricesSize >= 1 guaranteed */
    int lucro = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < pricesSize; i++) {
        if (prices[i] < minimo) minimo = prices[i];
        int atual = prices[i] - minimo;
        if (atual > lucro) lucro = atual;
    }
    return lucro;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one scan; each day does two O(1) comparisons.
  • Space: O(1) — only two variables (minimo, lucro).

Pitfalls

  • Order matters: you can only sell on a day after the buy — fixing the minimum before computing the profit in the same loop guarantees that.
  • Constant or decreasing prices → 0, never negative (not buying is always an option).
  • In C, seeding the minimum with prices[0] is only safe because the problem guarantees pricesSize >= 1; in Rust/C++ the MAX sentinel makes that premise unnecessary on the first element.
  • Update minimo before computing lucro for the day (if you use the two-line form in another language) — reversing the order would sell on the same day.

3. Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-substring-without-repeating-characters/ · Topic: Sliding Window (hash set)

Problem (summary)

Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring with no repeating characters (substring = contiguous slice). Only the length matters, not the slice itself.

s = "abcabcbb"  →  3   ("abc")
s = "bbbbb"     →  1   ("b")
s = "pwwkew"    →  3   ("wke", not "pwke" which isn't contiguous)

Pattern — what to memorize

Sliding window with a hash set: two pointers l and r; r always grows, and for each new char, if it’s already in the set, shrink l by removing chars from the left until the duplicate is gone. The current window (r - l + 1) is a candidate for the max. Clue in the statement: longest contiguous substring with no repeats → “no repeats” = set, “contiguous” = window. The set is never cleared — each char enters once and leaves once: total O(n).

Python

class Solution:
    def lengthOfLongestSubstring(self, s: str) -> int:
        vistos: set[str] = set()
        esquerda = 0
        maior = 0
        for direita, c in enumerate(s):
            while c in vistos:
                vistos.remove(s[esquerda])
                esquerda += 1
            vistos.add(c)
            maior = max(maior, direita - esquerda + 1)
        return maior

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashSet;

pub fn length_of_longest_substring(s: String) -> i32 {
    let bytes = s.as_bytes();
    let mut vistos = HashSet::new();
    let (mut esquerda, mut maior) = (0, 0);
    for (direita, &c) in bytes.iter().enumerate() {
        while vistos.contains(&c) {
            vistos.remove(&bytes[esquerda]);
            esquerda += 1;
        }
        vistos.insert(c);
        maior = maior.max(direita - esquerda + 1);
    }
    maior as i32
}
}

C++

#include <string>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int lengthOfLongestSubstring(string s) {
        bool vistos[128] = {}; // ASCII-sized table for chars
        int esquerda = 0, maior = 0;
        for (int direita = 0; direita < (int)s.size(); ++direita) {
            char c = s[direita];
            while (vistos[(unsigned char)c]) {
                vistos[(unsigned char)s[esquerda]] = false;
                esquerda++;
            }
            vistos[(unsigned char)c] = true;
            maior = max(maior, direita - esquerda + 1);
        }
        return maior;
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <string.h>

int lengthOfLongestSubstring(char* s) {
    int n = strlen(s);
    bool vistos[256] = {false};
    int esquerda = 0, maior = 0;
    for (int direita = 0; direita < n; direita++) {
        unsigned char c = (unsigned char)s[direita];
        while (vistos[c]) {
            vistos[(unsigned char)s[esquerda]] = false;
            esquerda++;
        }
        vistos[c] = true;
        if (direita - esquerda + 1 > maior) maior = direita - esquerda + 1;
    }
    return maior;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each char enters and leaves the set at most once (the while shifts l O(n) times in total).
  • Space: O(min(n, alphabet)) — the set holds at most the window’s chars; with bool[128]/[256] it’s constant O(1) (fixed table).

Pitfalls

  • “Substring” ≠ subsequence: "pwke" doesn’t count in "pwwkew" — the window is contiguous; using a global set of repeated chars gets this wrong.
  • Empty string and 1-char string — trivial candidates of 0 and 1.
  • In C/C++, char can be signed: indexing a table with raw s[i] uses negative bytes for chars ≥ 0x80 — always cast to (unsigned char).
  • In Rust, s.as_bytes() is O(1) indexing (the statement is ASCII); calling s.chars().nth(i) would be O(n) and TLE.
  • The shrinking while keeps the invariant “window with no repeats” — if it becomes if, the duplicate stays and the max inflates.

424. Longest Repeating Character Replacement (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-repeating-character-replacement/ · Topic: Sliding Window (frequencies + max)

Problem (summary)

Given a string s of uppercase letters and an integer k, you may replace up to k characters with any other character. Return the length of the longest substring you can get with all identical characters.

s = "ABAB", k = 2     →  4   (replace both A's with B: "BBBB")
s = "AABABBA", k = 1  →  4   ("AABBBBA": the middle B becomes A)

Pattern — what to memorize

Sliding window + validity rule: a window is valid when size − frequency_of_most_frequent_char ≤ k (the rest of the window is what needs replacing). Golden rule: once invalid, shrink the left by 1 without touching max_freq — the historic max never goes down, so the window never shrinks again; the answer is len(s) − l at the end. Clue in the statement: limited replacements + longest substring → a window with frequency counts, and the final ingredient (max_freq) is what makes it O(n) instead of O(26·n).

Python

class Solution:
    def characterReplacement(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
        contagens: dict[str, int] = {}
        esquerda = 0
        maior = 0  # highest frequency of any char in the window
        for direita, c in enumerate(s):
            contagens[c] = contagens.get(c, 0) + 1
            maior = max(maior, contagens[c])
            largura = direita - esquerda + 1
            if largura - maior > k:
                contagens[s[esquerda]] -= 1
                esquerda += 1
        return len(s) - esquerda

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn character_replacement(s: String, k: i32) -> i32 {
    let bytes = s.as_bytes();
    let mut contagens = [0; 26];
    let (mut esquerda, mut maior_freq) = (0, 0);
    for (direita, &c) in bytes.iter().enumerate() {
        let i = (c - b'A') as usize;
        contagens[i] += 1;
        maior_freq = maior_freq.max(contagens[i]);
        let largura = direita - esquerda + 1;
        if largura as i32 - maior_freq > k {
            let j = (bytes[esquerda] - b'A') as usize;
            contagens[j] -= 1;
            esquerda += 1;
        }
    }
    (bytes.len() - esquerda) as i32
}
}

C++

#include <string>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int characterReplacement(string s, int k) {
        int contagens[26] = {};
        int esquerda = 0, maior_freq = 0, melhor = 0;
        for (int direita = 0; direita < (int)s.size(); ++direita) {
            int i = s[direita] - 'A';
            contagens[i]++;
            maior_freq = max(maior_freq, contagens[i]);
            int largura = direita - esquerda + 1;
            if (largura - maior_freq > k) {
                contagens[s[esquerda] - 'A']--;
                esquerda++;
            }
            melhor = max(melhor, direita - esquerda + 1);
        }
        return melhor;
    }
};

C

#include <string.h>

int characterReplacement(char* s, int k) {
    int n = strlen(s);
    int contagens[26] = {0};
    int esquerda = 0, maior_freq = 0, melhor = 0;
    for (int direita = 0; direita < n; direita++) {
        int i = s[direita] - 'A';
        contagens[i]++;
        if (contagens[i] > maior_freq) maior_freq = contagens[i];
        int largura = direita - esquerda + 1;
        if (largura - maior_freq > k) {
            contagens[s[esquerda] - 'A']--;
            esquerda++;
        }
        if (direita - esquerda + 1 > melhor) melhor = direita - esquerda + 1;
    }
    return melhor;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one scan; max_freq is updated in O(1) (we don’t re-scan for the max at every step — that’s the trick).
  • Space: O(1) — fixed 26-count table (Python: a dict with at most 26 keys).

Pitfalls

  • Never decrement max_freq: the max is “historic”. That’s correct because the window only grows or “walks” (shrink of 1) — decrementing would shrink the window and understate the result.
  • s is only uppercase: s[i] - 'A' assumes [0, 25]; if the statement accepted lowercase/mixed (interview variation), use a 128/256 table or a dict and adjust the indices.
  • k can be larger than the string length → answer = len(s) (works with no special case: the window grows to the end without ever becoming invalid).
  • The answer at the end is len(s) − esquerda, not a melhor variable (they converge, but the former skips the extra per-frame max).

76. Minimum Window Substring (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-window-substring/ · Topic: Sliding Window (frequency counts)

Problem (summary)

Given strings s and t, return the smallest substring of s that contains every letter of t (counting repetitions — if t = "AABC", you need two A’s, one B, one C). If none exists, return "".

s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC"  →  "BANC"
s = "a", t = "a"                →  "a"
s = "a", t = "aa"               →  ""   (only one 'a' available)

Pattern — what to memorize

Sliding window with a “missing” counter: count the letters of t in a map; always expand right, and for each char present in the map, decrement its count (and drop missing only when the count was still ≥ 0). When missing == 0 the window covers t — then shrink left while it stays valid, recording the best (start, size) pair at each shrink. Clue in the statement: smallest window + all letters of another string → sliding window with two maps/counts and the missing variable instead of recomparing entire maps (that’s what kills the O(26·n) factor).

Python

class Solution:
    def minWindow(self, s: str, t: str) -> str:
        if len(s) < len(t):
            return ""
        falta = len(t)
        contagens: dict[str, int] = {}
        for c in t:
            contagens[c] = contagens.get(c, 0) + 1
        esquerda = 0
        melhor = (0, len(s) + 1)  # (start, size) — sentinel size
        for direita, c in enumerate(s):
            if c in contagens:
                contagens[c] -= 1
                if contagens[c] >= 0:
                    falta -= 1
            while falta == 0:
                if direita - esquerda + 1 < melhor[1]:
                    melhor = (esquerda, direita - esquerda + 1)
                e = s[esquerda]
                if e in contagens:
                    contagens[e] += 1
                    if contagens[e] > 0:
                        falta += 1
                esquerda += 1
        inicio, tamanho = melhor
        return s[inicio:inicio + tamanho] if tamanho <= len(s) else ""

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashMap;

pub fn min_window(s: String, t: String) -> String {
    if s.len() < t.len() {
        return String::new();
    }
    let sb = s.as_bytes();
    let mut contagens: HashMap<u8, i32> = HashMap::new();
    for &c in t.as_bytes() {
        *contagens.entry(c).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }
    let mut falta = t.len() as i32;
    let (mut esquerda, mut melhor_inicio, mut melhor_tam) = (0, 0, usize::MAX);
    for (direita, &c) in sb.iter().enumerate() {
        if let Some(n) = contagens.get_mut(&c) {
            *n -= 1;
            if *n >= 0 {
                falta -= 1;
            }
        }
        while falta == 0 {
            let largura = direita - esquerda + 1;
            if largura < melhor_tam {
                melhor_inicio = esquerda;
                melhor_tam = largura;
            }
            let e = sb[esquerda];
            if let Some(n) = contagens.get_mut(&e) {
                *n += 1;
                if *n > 0 {
                    falta += 1;
                }
            }
            esquerda += 1;
        }
    }
    if melhor_tam == usize::MAX {
        String::new()
    } else {
        s[melhor_inicio..melhor_inicio + melhor_tam].to_string()
    }
}
}

C++

#include <string>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    string minWindow(string s, string t) {
        if (s.size() < t.size()) return "";
        int contagens[128] = {};
        for (char c : t) contagens[(unsigned char)c]++;
        int falta = (int)t.size();
        int esquerda = 0, melhor_inicio = 0, melhor_tam = INT_MAX;
        for (int direita = 0; direita < (int)s.size(); ++direita) {
            int c = (unsigned char)s[direita];
            if (--contagens[c] >= 0) falta--;
            while (falta == 0) {
                int largura = direita - esquerda + 1;
                if (largura < melhor_tam) {
                    melhor_inicio = esquerda;
                    melhor_tam = largura;
                }
                int e = (unsigned char)s[esquerda];
                if (++contagens[e] > 0) falta++;
                esquerda++;
            }
        }
        return melhor_tam == INT_MAX ? "" : s.substr(melhor_inicio, melhor_tam);
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

char* minWindow(char* s, char* t) {
    int ns = strlen(s), nt = strlen(t);
    if (ns < nt) {
        char* vazio = malloc(1);
        vazio[0] = '\0';
        return vazio;
    }
    int contagens[128] = {0};
    for (int i = 0; i < nt; i++) contagens[(unsigned char)t[i]]++;
    int falta = nt;
    int esquerda = 0, melhor_inicio = 0, melhor_tam = 2147483647 /* INT_MAX */;
    for (int direita = 0; direita < ns; direita++) {
        if (--contagens[(unsigned char)s[direita]] >= 0) falta--;
        while (falta == 0) {
            int largura = direita - esquerda + 1;
            if (largura < melhor_tam) {
                melhor_inicio = esquerda;
                melhor_tam = largura;
            }
            if (++contagens[(unsigned char)s[esquerda]] > 0) falta++;
            esquerda++;
        }
    }
    if (melhor_tam == 2147483647) {
        char* vazio = malloc(1);
        vazio[0] = '\0';
        return vazio;
    }
    char* resp = malloc((melhor_tam + 1) * sizeof(char));
    memcpy(resp, s + melhor_inicio, (size_t)melhor_tam);
    resp[melhor_tam] = '\0';
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — s is scanned twice in total (expansion + contraction; each char visits both ends at most once); map lookups are O(1) average (in C/C++ a fixed table, absolute O(1)).
  • Space: O(|t|) for the counts (C/C++: O(128) = O(1); Rust: a map with at most |t| keys).

Pitfalls

  • Repetitions count: t = "aa" requires two a’s — that’s why we decrement the count and falta only drops while the char’s count ≥ 0 (an extra a in a right step doesn’t reduce falta further).
  • Chars outside t are also scanned and ignored (they don’t touch falta), but the shrink must check the outgoing char — only restore the count if it was in the map.
  • Tied windows: either works — return the first found (compare with <, not <=).
  • In Rust, the final slice uses byte indices; the statement is ASCII (upper/lowercase), so byte = char.
  • In C/C++: without the (unsigned char) casts, high-byte chars would become negative indices into contagens[128].

239. Sliding Window Maximum (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/sliding-window-maximum/ · Topic: Sliding Window (monotonic deque)

Problem (summary)

Given an array nums and a size k, slide a window of size k from left to right and return an array with the maximum of each window.

nums = [1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7], k = 3  →  [3,3,5,5,6,7]
nums = [1], k = 1                  →  [1]

Pattern — what to memorize

Monotonically decreasing deque of indices: the front of the deque is always the max of the window. At each i: (1) pop from the tail every index whose value is ≤ nums[i] (they can never be the max while i exists); (2) push i; (3) pop from the front if it left the window (front + k <= i); (4) from i >= k−1 on, the front is the answer. Clue in the statement: max of every fixed-size window → the classic “I have a window, I need the dynamic max” — a heap works but the deque is O(1) amortized per element and respects eviction order (the heap doesn’t know when an element leaves the window). <= (not <) in the tail pruning is the detail: ties keep the newest index at the front, which leaves the window later.

Python

from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def maxSlidingWindow(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
        dq: deque[int] = deque()  # indices; values decreasing
        resp: list[int] = []
        for i, x in enumerate(nums):
            while dq and nums[dq[-1]] <= x:  # drop smaller/equal from the tail
                dq.pop()
            dq.append(i)
            if dq[0] <= i - k:  # left the window through the left edge
                dq.popleft()
            if i >= k - 1:
                resp.append(nums[dq[0]])
        return resp

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::VecDeque;

pub fn max_sliding_window(nums: Vec<i32>, k: i32) -> Vec<i32> {
    let k = k as usize;
    let mut dq: VecDeque<usize> = VecDeque::new();
    let mut resp = Vec::new();
    for (i, &x) in nums.iter().enumerate() {
        while let Some(&ultimo) = dq.back() {
            if nums[ultimo] <= x {
                dq.pop_back();
            } else {
                break;
            }
        }
        dq.push_back(i);
        if let Some(&frente) = dq.front() {
            if frente + k <= i {
                dq.pop_front();
            }
        }
        if i + 1 >= k {
            resp.push(nums[dq[0]]);
        }
    }
    resp
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <deque>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> maxSlidingWindow(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
        deque<int> dq; // indices; values decreasing
        vector<int> resp;
        for (int i = 0; i < (int)nums.size(); ++i) {
            while (!dq.empty() && nums[dq.back()] <= nums[i]) dq.pop_back();
            dq.push_back(i);
            if (dq.front() + k <= i) dq.pop_front();
            if (i + 1 >= k) resp.push_back(nums[dq.front()]);
        }
        return resp;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

/* Hand-rolled circular deque (C has no native one): queue with front/back
   over a circular array holding INDICES; never holds more than numsSize. */
typedef struct {
    int* dados;
    int frente, tras, tam, capacidade;
} Deque;

static void deque_init(Deque* dq, int capacidade) {
    dq->dados = malloc((size_t)capacidade * sizeof(int));
    dq->frente = 0; dq->tras = 0; dq->tam = 0; dq->capacidade = capacidade;
}
static void deque_push_back(Deque* dq, int v) {
    dq->dados[dq->tras] = v;
    dq->tras = (dq->tras + 1) % dq->capacidade;
    dq->tam++;
}
static int deque_back(Deque* dq) {
    return dq->dados[(dq->tras - 1 + dq->capacidade) % dq->capacidade];
}
static void deque_pop_back(Deque* dq) {
    dq->tras = (dq->tras - 1 + dq->capacidade) % dq->capacidade;
    dq->tam--;
}
static int deque_front(Deque* dq) { return dq->dados[dq->frente]; }
static void deque_pop_front(Deque* dq) {
    dq->frente = (dq->frente + 1) % dq->capacidade;
    dq->tam--;
}
static void deque_free(Deque* dq) { free(dq->dados); }

int* maxSlidingWindow(int* nums, int numsSize, int k, int* returnSize) {
    *returnSize = numsSize - k + 1;
    int* resp = malloc((size_t)(*returnSize) * sizeof(int));
    Deque dq;
    deque_init(&dq, numsSize);
    int saida = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < numsSize; i++) {
        while (dq.tam > 0 && nums[deque_back(&dq)] <= nums[i]) deque_pop_back(&dq);
        deque_push_back(&dq, i);
        if (deque_front(&dq) + k <= i) deque_pop_front(&dq);
        if (i + 1 >= k) resp[saida++] = nums[deque_front(&dq)];
    }
    deque_free(&dq);
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each index enters and leaves the deque exactly once (amortized); the pruning while runs O(n) times in total.
  • Space: O(k) — the deque holds at most k indices (with a fixed n capacity in C for simplicity, which needs O(n) worst-case allocation).

Pitfalls

  • The deque stores indices, never values — without the index you can’t tell when the element leaves the window (the front + k <= i test).
  • Tail pruning with <=: with [..., x] tied to the new x, the old one goes; the new one is “preferable” because it lasts more windows.
  • Step order: prune tail → push → evict front → answer. Swapping the order breaks the k = 1 case (the front would be evicted before answering) and the case of a freshly pushed already-obsolete element.
  • In C: the circular array uses (idx - 1 + cap) % cap for back — the + cap avoids modular arithmetic with a negative number (UB in C).
  • Edge output: when numsSize < k there is no window — the statement guarantees k <= numsSize.

567. Permutation in String (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/permutation-in-string/ · Topic: Sliding Window

Problem (summary)

Given s1 and s2, return true if some permutation of s1 is a substring (contiguous window) of s2. Only lowercase letters.

s1 = "ab", s2 = "eidbaooo"  →  true   (window "ba" at positions 3-4)
s1 = "ab", s2 = "eidboaoo"  →  false

Pattern — what to memorize

Fixed window of size len(s1) sliding over s2, with 26-letter counters and the matches trick: the window is a permutation of s1 when the 26 counters match. Recounting all 26 letters on every slide would be O(26·n);

matches tracks how many positions the window agrees with s1 and is only updated on the 2 letters that change (the one leaving, the one entering) — reaching 26 is the answer. Clue: contiguous + multiset of letters → fixed 26-count; fixed size → a window that walks 1 by 1, not the shrink while.

Python

class Solution:
    def checkInclusion(self, s1: str, s2: str) -> bool:
        n, m = len(s1), len(s2)
        if n > m:
            return False

        alvo = [0] * 26
        janela = [0] * 26
        for ch in s1:
            alvo[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1
        for ch in s2[:n]:
            janela[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1

        # matches = on how many of the 26 letter counters the window agrees
        # with the target; reaching 26 means the window IS a permutation of s1.
        matches = sum(1 for i in range(26) if alvo[i] == janela[i])
        if matches == 26:
            return True

        for i in range(n, m):
            sai = ord(s2[i - n]) - ord("a")
            entra = ord(s2[i]) - ord("a")
            if alvo[sai] == janela[sai]:
                matches -= 1
            janela[sai] -= 1
            if alvo[sai] == janela[sai]:
                matches += 1
            if alvo[entra] == janela[entra]:
                matches -= 1
            janela[entra] += 1
            if alvo[entra] == janela[entra]:
                matches += 1
            if matches == 26:
                return True
        return False

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn check_inclusion(s1: String, s2: String) -> bool {
        let alvo = s1.as_bytes();
        let base = s2.as_bytes();
        let n = alvo.len();
        if n > base.len() {
            return false;
        }
        let mut contagem_alvo = [0i32; 26];
        let mut contagem_janela = [0i32; 26];
        for &ch in alvo {
            contagem_alvo[(ch - b'a') as usize] += 1;
        }
        for &ch in &base[..n] {
            contagem_janela[(ch - b'a') as usize] += 1;
        }
        // on how many of the 26 counters does the window agree? 26 => permutation
        let mut matches = (0..26)
            .filter(|&i| contagem_alvo[i] == contagem_janela[i])
            .count() as i32;
        if matches == 26 {
            return true;
        }
        for i in n..base.len() {
            let sai = (base[i - n] - b'a') as usize;
            let entra = (base[i] - b'a') as usize;
            if contagem_alvo[sai] == contagem_janela[sai] {
                matches -= 1;
            }
            contagem_janela[sai] -= 1;
            if contagem_alvo[sai] == contagem_janela[sai] {
                matches += 1;
            }
            if contagem_alvo[entra] == contagem_janela[entra] {
                matches -= 1;
            }
            contagem_janela[entra] += 1;
            if contagem_alvo[entra] == contagem_janela[entra] {
                matches += 1;
            }
            if matches == 26 {
                return true;
            }
        }
        false
    }
}
}

C++

#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    bool checkInclusion(string s1, string s2) {
        int n = (int)s1.size(), m = (int)s2.size();
        if (n > m) return false;
        vector<int> alvo(26, 0), janela(26, 0);
        for (char ch : s1) alvo[ch - 'a']++;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) janela[s2[i] - 'a']++;

        int matches = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 26; ++i) if (alvo[i] == janela[i]) ++matches;
        if (matches == 26) return true;

        for (int i = n; i < m; ++i) {
            int sai = s2[i - n] - 'a', entra = s2[i] - 'a';
            if (alvo[sai] == janela[sai]) --matches;
            --janela[sai];
            if (alvo[sai] == janela[sai]) ++matches;
            if (alvo[entra] == janela[entra]) --matches;
            ++janela[entra];
            if (alvo[entra] == janela[entra]) ++matches;
            if (matches == 26) return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <string.h>

bool checkInclusion(char* s1, char* s2) {
    int n = (int)strlen(s1), m = (int)strlen(s2);
    if (n > m) return false;
    int alvo[26] = {0}, janela[26] = {0};
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) alvo[s1[i] - 'a']++;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) janela[s2[i] - 'a']++;

    int matches = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 26; i++) if (alvo[i] == janela[i]) matches++;
    if (matches == 26) return true;

    for (int i = n; i < m; i++) {
        int sai = s2[i - n] - 'a', entra = s2[i] - 'a';
        if (alvo[sai] == janela[sai]) matches--;
        janela[sai]--;
        if (alvo[sai] == janela[sai]) matches++;
        if (alvo[entra] == janela[entra]) matches--;
        janela[entra]++;
        if (alvo[entra] == janela[entra]) matches++;
        if (matches == 26) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n + m) — build the counters in O(n) and slide the window in O(m); each step updates only the 2 affected letters (O(1)).
  • Space: O(1) — two fixed 26-element vectors.

Pitfalls

  • The naive alternative (comparing all 26 counters on every slide) is O(26·m) — correct, but the incremental matches is the differentiator interviewers ask for.
  • Order of matches updates: adjust before mutating the counter (compares old counts) and after mutating (new counts) — reversing the order breaks the count by 1.
  • matches counts equal positions, not summed letters: if one letter is in excess and another is short in the same window, matches doesn’t magically cancel out — each letter is updated independently.
  • s1 longer than s2 → false at the door (no window possible).
  • Only lowercase: the byte offset - 'a' (97) maps to 0..25; in Rust the bytes of a String are accessible and safe here precisely for that reason.

20. Valid Parentheses (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/valid-parentheses/ · Topic: Stack

Problem (summary)

Given a string s with only (, ), [, ], {, }, check whether the parentheses are balanced: every opener closes with the same type, in the correct order (nesting) and nothing is left over.

s = "()[]{}"  →  true
s = "(]"      →  false
s = "([)]"    →  false   (the ')' closes out of order)
s = ""        →  true

Pattern — what to memorize

Stack of openers: every opening char pushes; every closing char must match the top (the most recent) and destroy it. Closing on an empty stack or with a mismatched top → invalid. At the end the stack must be empty. Clue in the statement: delimiter balancing + constant nesting → LIFO = stack. This is the “hello world” of stacks: if you can’t write the no-template version mid-interview, review before the next one.

Python

class Solution:
    def isValid(self, s: str) -> bool:
        pilha: list[str] = []
        pares = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
        for c in s:
            if c in pares:
                if not pilha or pilha[-1] != pares[c]:
                    return False
                pilha.pop()
            else:
                pilha.append(c)
        return not pilha

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn is_valid(s: String) -> bool {
    let mut pilha: Vec<char> = Vec::new();
    for c in s.chars() {
        match c {
            '(' | '[' | '{' => pilha.push(c),
            ')' => {
                if pilha.pop() != Some('(') {
                    return false;
                }
            }
            ']' => {
                if pilha.pop() != Some('[') {
                    return false;
                }
            }
            '}' => {
                if pilha.pop() != Some('{') {
                    return false;
                }
            }
            _ => return false,
        }
    }
    pilha.is_empty()
}
}

C++

#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    bool isValid(string s) {
        vector<char> pilha;
        for (char c : s) {
            if (c == '(' || c == '[' || c == '{') {
                pilha.push_back(c);
            } else {
                if (pilha.empty()) return false;
                char topo = pilha.back();
                if ((c == ')' && topo != '(') ||
                    (c == ']' && topo != '[') ||
                    (c == '}' && topo != '{')) {
                    return false;
                }
                pilha.pop_back();
            }
        }
        return pilha.empty();
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

bool isValid(char* s) {
    int n = strlen(s);
    int* pilha = malloc((size_t)n * sizeof(int));
    int topo = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        char c = s[i];
        if (c == '(' || c == '[' || c == '{') {
            pilha[topo++] = c;
        } else {
            if (topo == 0 || (c == ')' && pilha[topo - 1] != '(') ||
                (c == ']' && pilha[topo - 1] != '[') ||
                (c == '}' && pilha[topo - 1] != '{')) {
                free(pilha);
                return false;
            }
            topo--;
        }
    }
    free(pilha);
    return topo == 0;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each char pushes or destroys one stack entry, an O(1) operation.
  • Space: O(n) worst case — a string of only openers ("((((...").

Pitfalls

  • Closing on an empty stack is invalid (")("); an unmatched opener at the end is too ("()(") — both checks are required.
  • "([)]" is the teaching case for order: the ) doesn’t match the top [ — anyone who only counts occurrences (like a balance counter) gets it wrong.
  • In C: the top check happens before topo-- — reading pilha[topo-1] with topo == 0 is an out-of-bounds read (UB); the topo == 0 test comes first.
  • In Rust, pilha.pop() != Some(c) does “pop-and-compare” in one line: an empty stack returns None and already fails — no index access.

22. Generate Parentheses (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/generate-parentheses/ · Topic: Backtracking

Problem (summary)

Given n pairs of parentheses, generate every valid (well-formed) string of length 2n. “Valid” = every ) has a matching ( to its left.

n = 3  →  ["((()))","(()())","(())()","()(())","()()()"]
n = 1  →  ["()"]

Pattern — what to memorize

Backtracking with two counters: open and closed. The path is the string under construction; the only choices per position are adding ( or ), and the statement boils down to two simple conditions:

  • you may open while abertos < n;
  • you may close while fechados < abertos (never let closed exceed open — that alone guarantees well-formedness with no extra validation).

When the path reaches 2n chars, it is a valid solution — no pruning beyond that (the number of solutions is the Catalan number C_n = C(2n,n)/(n+1)). Clue in the statement: “all combinations” + a pairing constraint → backtrack over the partial prefix; the rule “closing requires a pending open” is the heart.

Python

class Solution:
    def generateParenthesis(self, n: int) -> list[str]:
        resp: list[str] = []

        def voltar(abertos: int, fechados: int, atual: list[str]) -> None:
            if len(atual) == 2 * n:                # parentheses complete
                resp.append("".join(atual))
                return
            if abertos < n:                        # may OPEN up to n times
                atual.append("(")
                voltar(abertos + 1, fechados, atual)
                atual.pop()
            if fechados < abertos:                 # closing needs a pending open
                atual.append(")")
                voltar(abertos, fechados + 1, atual)
                atual.pop()

        voltar(0, 0, [])
        return resp

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn generate_parenthesis(n: i32) -> Vec<String> {
        fn voltar(n: usize, abertos: usize, fechados: usize, atual: &mut Vec<char>, resp: &mut Vec<String>) {
            if atual.len() == 2 * n {              // parentheses complete
                resp.push(atual.iter().collect());
                return;
            }
            if abertos < n {                       // may OPEN up to n times
                atual.push('(');
                voltar(n, abertos + 1, fechados, atual, resp);
                atual.pop();
            }
            if fechados < abertos {                // closing needs a pending open
                atual.push(')');
                voltar(n, abertos, fechados + 1, atual, resp);
                atual.pop();
            }
        }
        let mut resp = Vec::new();
        voltar(n as usize, 0, 0, &mut Vec::new(), &mut resp);
        resp
    }
}
}

C++

#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<string> generateParenthesis(int n) {
        vector<string> resp;
        string atual;
        voltar(n, 0, 0, atual, resp);
        return resp;
    }

private:
    void voltar(int n, int abertos, int fechados, string& atual, vector<string>& resp) {
        if ((int)atual.size() == 2 * n) {          // parentheses complete
            resp.push_back(atual);
            return;
        }
        if (abertos < n) {                         // may OPEN up to n times
            atual.push_back('(');
            voltar(n, abertos + 1, fechados, atual, resp);
            atual.pop_back();
        }
        if (fechados < abertos) {                  // closing needs a pending open
            atual.push_back(')');
            voltar(n, abertos, fechados + 1, atual, resp);
            atual.pop_back();
        }
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

static void voltar(int n, int abertos, int fechados, char* atual, int pos,
                   char** resp, int* tam) {
    if (pos == 2 * n) {                            // parentheses complete
        resp[*tam] = malloc((2 * n + 1) * sizeof(char));
        memcpy(resp[*tam], atual, 2 * n);
        resp[(*tam)++][2 * n] = '\0';
        return;
    }
    if (abertos < n) {                             // may OPEN up to n times
        atual[pos] = '(';
        voltar(n, abertos + 1, fechados, atual, pos + 1, resp, tam);
    }
    if (fechados < abertos) {                      // closing needs a pending open
        atual[pos] = ')';
        voltar(n, abertos, fechados + 1, atual, pos + 1, resp, tam);
    }
}

char** generateParenthesis(int n, int* returnSize) {
    /* Number of strings = Catalan C(n) = C(2n, n) / (n + 1) */
    long catalan = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) catalan = catalan * 2 * (2 * i - 1) / (i + 1);
    char** resp = malloc(catalan * sizeof(char*));
    char* atual = malloc((2 * n + 1) * sizeof(char));
    int tam = 0;
    voltar(n, 0, 0, atual, 0, resp, &tam);
    free(atual);
    *returnSize = tam;
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(C_n · n) — we generate the C_n Catalan strings and spend O(n) materializing each (push/collect). Always better than the 2^(2n) raw combinations.
  • Space: O(n) recursion/stack depth (2n), excluding the output.

Pitfalls

  • Output order: LeetCode accepts any order; the canonical one (always try ( first) is what interviewers expect against the test cases.
  • n = 0 ⇒ [""] (one empty string), not [] — worth testing.
  • Counters are plain ints; the rule “close when abertos > fechados” is equivalent to “fechados < abertos” — don’t invert it.
  • In C: string size is 2n + 1 because of the \0; the number of strings is the Catalan number — allocating comb(2n,n)/(n+1) exactly avoids realloc.
  • In Rust: the nested voltar takes &mut Vec<char> and &mut Vec<String>; the pop() after each call is the backtracking “undo”; atual.iter().collect() turns it into a String.
  • Python: join with "".join(atual) per solution, never + in a loop.

155. Min Stack (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/min-stack/ · Topic: Stack (design)

Problem (summary)

Design a stack that supports push, pop, top and getMin (the smallest element in the stack) — all in O(1). Example of operations:

push(-2); push(0); push(-3)
getMin() → -3
pop()
top()    → 0
getMin() → -2

Pattern — what to memorize

Stack of (value, min-so-far) pairs: each entry stores the value and the smallest value pushed up to it. getMin reads the second field of the top — O(1) at any height, no scanning. On pop, the pair comes out together and the min restores itself (the valid min is the one on the pair left at the top). Clue in the statement: all operations O(1) + min under arbitrary pops → store the min per layer next to the value. There’s no way to keep the min in a single variable, because pop wouldn’t know how to restore it.

Python

class MinStack:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._pilha: list[tuple[int, int]] = []  # (value, min so far)

    def push(self, val: int) -> None:
        minimo = val if not self._pilha else min(val, self._pilha[-1][1])
        self._pilha.append((val, minimo))

    def pop(self) -> None:
        self._pilha.pop()

    def top(self) -> int:
        return self._pilha[-1][0]

    def getMin(self) -> int:
        return self._pilha[-1][1]

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub struct MinStack {
    pilha: Vec<(i32, i32)>, // (value, min so far)
}

impl MinStack {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self { pilha: Vec::new() }
    }

    pub fn push(&mut self, val: i32) {
        let minimo = self.pilha.last().map_or(val, |&(_, m)| m.min(val));
        self.pilha.push((val, minimo));
    }

    pub fn pop(&mut self) {
        self.pilha.pop();
    }

    pub fn top(&self) -> i32 {
        self.pilha.last().unwrap().0
    }

    pub fn get_min(&self) -> i32 {
        self.pilha.last().unwrap().1
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <utility>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class MinStack {
    vector<pair<int, int>> pilha; // (value, min so far)
public:
    MinStack() {}

    void push(int val) {
        int minimo = pilha.empty() ? val : min(val, pilha.back().second);
        pilha.emplace_back(val, minimo);
    }

    void pop() { pilha.pop_back(); }

    int top() { return pilha.back().first; }

    int getMin() { return pilha.back().second; }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

/* Two parallel stacks: values + mins so far (pair-less struct version,
   identical math). */
typedef struct {
    int* valores;
    int* minimos;
    int tam;
    int cap;
} MinStack;

MinStack* minStackCreate(void) {
    MinStack* ms = malloc(sizeof(MinStack));
    ms->cap = 8;
    ms->tam = 0;
    ms->valores = malloc((size_t)ms->cap * sizeof(int));
    ms->minimos = malloc((size_t)ms->cap * sizeof(int));
    return ms;
}

void minStackPush(MinStack* ms, int val) {
    if (ms->tam == ms->cap) {
        ms->cap *= 2;
        ms->valores = realloc(ms->valores, (size_t)ms->cap * sizeof(int));
        ms->minimos = realloc(ms->minimos, (size_t)ms->cap * sizeof(int));
    }
    int minimo = (ms->tam == 0)
                     ? val
                     : (val < ms->minimos[ms->tam - 1] ? val : ms->minimos[ms->tam - 1]);
    ms->valores[ms->tam] = val;
    ms->minimos[ms->tam] = minimo;
    ms->tam++;
}

void minStackPop(MinStack* ms) {
    if (ms->tam > 0) ms->tam--;
}

int minStackTop(MinStack* ms) {
    return ms->valores[ms->tam - 1];
}

int minStackGetMin(MinStack* ms) {
    return ms->minimos[ms->tam - 1];
}

void minStackFree(MinStack* ms) {
    free(ms->valores);
    free(ms->minimos);
    free(ms);
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(1) in every operation — push compares with the top, the others just read the last pair.
  • Space: O(n) — one pair (or two stacks) per element; it’s the extra transient memory that buys the O(1) getMin.

Pitfalls

  • Never keep only the min in a variable: pop couldn’t undo it; the min must be per layer (pair at the top or a parallel stack).
  • Values equal to the min (push -3 twice) don’t break anything: the pair compares with implicit <= — the second -3 also stores -3 as the min, and a single pop keeps the other -3 intact in the min.
  • In C: growth uses realloc on both arrays (values and mins) — missing one leaves the pair desynced; minStackFree releases both plus the struct.
  • In Rust, top()/get_min() use last().unwrap() — the operations are only defined with a non-empty stack per the problem’s contract; in production code this would be an Option.
  • C++ push via emplace_back(val, minimo): constructs the pair in place, no extra copy (a detail that shows sharp STL).

150. Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/evaluate-reverse-polish-notation/ · Topic: Stack

Problem (summary)

Given an array tokens in reverse Polish notation (RPN — the operator comes after the operands), evaluate it and return the integer result. Division truncates toward zero (not floor, not rounding).

["2","1","+","3","*"]                  → 9    ((2+1)*3)
["4","13","5","/","+"]                 → 6    (4 + 13/5 = 4 + 2)
["10","6","9","3","+","-11","*","/","*","17","+","5","+"] → 22

Pattern — what to memorize

Stack of operands: number → push; operator → pop b and a (in that order! a is the first operand), apply a op b and push the result. At the end the stack has a single element. RPN is the historical reason stacks exist (HP calculators): the LIFO order is the built-in precedence. Clue in the statement: operators between already-ordered operands → stack; the deterministic gotcha is division with negatives (truncate toward zero, not round down).

Python

class Solution:
    def evalRPN(self, tokens: list[str]) -> int:
        pilha: list[int] = []
        for t in tokens:
            if t in {"+", "-", "*", "/"}:
                b = pilha.pop()
                a = pilha.pop()
                if t == "+":
                    pilha.append(a + b)
                elif t == "-":
                    pilha.append(a - b)
                elif t == "*":
                    pilha.append(a * b)
                else:
                    pilha.append(int(a / b))  # truncates toward zero, like C
            else:
                pilha.append(int(t))
        return pilha[0]

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn eval_rpn(tokens: Vec<String>) -> i32 {
    let mut pilha: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();
    for t in &tokens {
        match t.as_str() {
            "+" => {
                let b = pilha.pop().unwrap();
                let a = pilha.pop().unwrap();
                pilha.push(a + b);
            }
            "-" => {
                let b = pilha.pop().unwrap();
                let a = pilha.pop().unwrap();
                pilha.push(a - b);
            }
            "*" => {
                let b = pilha.pop().unwrap();
                let a = pilha.pop().unwrap();
                pilha.push(a * b);
            }
            "/" => {
                let b = pilha.pop().unwrap();
                let a = pilha.pop().unwrap();
                pilha.push(a / b); // Rust truncates toward zero natively
            }
            _ => pilha.push(t.parse::<i32>().unwrap()),
        }
    }
    pilha[0]
}
}

C++

#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int evalRPN(vector<string>& tokens) {
        vector<long long> pilha; // long long: division/negatives without overflow
        for (const string& t : tokens) {
            if (t == "+" || t == "-" || t == "*" || t == "/") {
                long long b = pilha.back(); pilha.pop_back();
                long long a = pilha.back(); pilha.pop_back();
                if (t == "+") pilha.push_back(a + b);
                else if (t == "-") pilha.push_back(a - b);
                else if (t == "*") pilha.push_back(a * b);
                else pilha.push_back(a / b); // truncates toward zero in C++
            } else {
                pilha.push_back(stoll(t));
            }
        }
        return (int)pilha.back();
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

int evalRPN(char** tokens, int tokensSize) {
    long long* pilha = malloc((size_t)tokensSize * sizeof(long long));
    int topo = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < tokensSize; i++) {
        char* t = tokens[i];
        /* operator = "+", "-", "*", "/" — a negative number "-11" is NOT */
        int operador = (t[0] == '+' || t[0] == '*' || t[0] == '/') ||
                       (t[0] == '-' && t[1] == '\0');
        if (operador) {
            long long b = pilha[--topo];
            long long a = pilha[--topo];
            char op = t[0];
            if (op == '+') pilha[topo++] = a + b;
            else if (op == '-') pilha[topo++] = a - b;
            else if (op == '*') pilha[topo++] = a * b;
            else pilha[topo++] = a / b; /* C truncates toward zero natively */
        } else {
            pilha[topo++] = strtoll(t, NULL, 10);
        }
    }
    int resp = (int)pilha[0];
    free(pilha);
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — every token is processed once, with O(1) stack operations.
  • Space: O(n) worst case (all numbers before the operators).

Pitfalls

  • Division with negatives truncates toward zero: 6 / -132 = 0 (not -1!). Python // is floor — it needs int(a / b); Rust, C++ and C already do the right thing natively.
  • Operand order: pop b after a — a - b and a / b don’t commute (["3","-7","/"] is 3 / -7, never -7 / 3).
  • The token "-11" is not the - operator: distinguish by length ("-" alone is the operator; C checks t[1] == '\0').
  • Operands can be negative and may not fit in atoi/int because they are large mid-calculation numbers — in C/C++ a long long stack (strtoll) is the habit against overflow; in Rust i32 suffices because the problem guarantees intermediates fit in 32 bits.
  • No division by zero in the statement (the expression is always valid), so unwrap()/direct top reads are safe.

739. Daily Temperatures (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/daily-temperatures/ · Topic: Monotonic stack

Problem (summary)

Given an array temperatures (per day), return an array where answer[i] is the number of days until the next warmer temperature than i’s (0 if none exists).

temperatures = [73,74,75,71,69,72,76,73]  →  [1,1,4,2,1,1,0,0]
temperatures = [30,40,50,60]              →  [1,1,1,0]
temperatures = [90,80,70]                 →  [0,0,0]   (only cools off)

Pattern — what to memorize

Monotonic (decreasing) stack of indices: the stack holds indices whose temperatures are in strictly decreasing order. When day i is warmer than the top, the top has found its answer (i - top) and leaves — every index resolves exactly once, and the stack turns an O(n²) double loop into O(n). Clue in the statement: next greater to the right (distance version) → this is the fundamental monotonic stack template; the same spine solves Largest Rectangle (width) and Car Fleet (arrival times).

Python

class Solution:
    def dailyTemperatures(self, temperatures: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        n = len(temperatures)
        resp = [0] * n
        pilha: list[int] = []  # indices with decreasing temperature
        for i, t in enumerate(temperatures):
            while pilha and temperatures[pilha[-1]] < t:
                j = pilha.pop()
                resp[j] = i - j
            pilha.append(i)
        return resp

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn daily_temperatures(temperatures: Vec<i32>) -> Vec<i32> {
    let n = temperatures.len();
    let mut resp = vec![0; n];
    let mut pilha: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
    for (i, &t) in temperatures.iter().enumerate() {
        while let Some(&j) = pilha.last() {
            if temperatures[j] < t {
                pilha.pop();
                resp[j] = (i - j) as i32;
            } else {
                break;
            }
        }
        pilha.push(i);
    }
    resp
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> dailyTemperatures(vector<int>& temperatures) {
        int n = (int)temperatures.size();
        vector<int> resp(n, 0);
        vector<int> pilha; // indices with decreasing temperature
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
            while (!pilha.empty() && temperatures[pilha.back()] < temperatures[i]) {
                int j = pilha.back();
                pilha.pop_back();
                resp[j] = i - j;
            }
            pilha.push_back(i);
        }
        return resp;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

int* dailyTemperatures(int* temperatures, int temperaturesSize, int* returnSize) {
    int* resp = calloc((size_t)temperaturesSize, sizeof(int));
    int* pilha = malloc((size_t)temperaturesSize * sizeof(int));
    int topo = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < temperaturesSize; i++) {
        while (topo > 0 && temperatures[pilha[topo - 1]] < temperatures[i]) {
            int j = pilha[--topo];
            resp[j] = i - j;
        }
        pilha[topo++] = i;
    }
    free(pilha);
    *returnSize = temperaturesSize;
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each index enters and leaves the stack exactly once (amortized); the inner while runs O(n) times in total.
  • Space: O(n) — the stack can hold n indices (temperatures decreasing end to end) and the answer has size n.

Pitfalls

  • Compare with < (strictly warmer): an equal day does not resolve the top ([70,70] → [0,0], not [1,0]).
  • The answer array must be zero-initialized — days with no warmer day to the right stay 0 (in C, calloc; in Rust/C++, vec![0; n]).
  • The stack holds indices, not values — the answer is the distance i - j, which only exists with the top’s index.
  • In an interview variation (“greater or equal”), swap < for <= — nothing else changes; knowing that lever shows mastery of the pattern.

853. Car Fleet (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/car-fleet/ · Topic: Stack + Sorting

Problem (summary)

n cars drive to a target on a highway: each car has position[i] and speed[i]. Cars never overtake — the one behind catches up and caravans with the one ahead (they form a fleet, which moves at the speed of the slowest). Cars that start together are also a fleet. Return the number of fleets.

target = 12, position = [10,8,0,5,3], speed = [2,4,1,1,3]  →  3
target = 10, position = [3], speed = [3]                   →  1
target = 100, position = [0,2,4], speed = [4,2,1]          →  1

Pattern — what to memorize

Arrival time + stack of leaders: for each car, the time (target − pos) / speed (how long it takes to arrive alone). Processing from the frontmost car to the rearmost: if its time is greater than the current leader’s, it won’t catch anyone — it becomes a new fleet (and the new leader); if it’s less or equal, it catches the leader and joins the fleet (doesn’t count). Clue in the statement: cars in a line that merge + fleet speed = the slowest’s → sort by position and compare arrival times; the “stack” here is just the last leader’s time (a one-element stack — the full interview statement becomes a real stack when you track the sequence).

Python

class Solution:
    def carFleet(self, target: int, position: list[int], speed: list[int]) -> int:
        carros = sorted(zip(position, speed), reverse=True)
        frota = 0
        tempo_chegada = 0.0  # arrival time of the slowest fleet ahead
        for pos, vel in carros:
            t = (target - pos) / vel
            if t > tempo_chegada:
                frota += 1
                tempo_chegada = t
        return frota

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn car_fleet(target: i32, position: Vec<i32>, speed: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
    let mut carros: Vec<(i32, i32)> = position.into_iter().zip(speed).collect();
    carros.sort_unstable_by(|a, b| b.0.cmp(&a.0)); // frontmost to rearmost
    let mut frotas = 0;
    let mut tempo_chefe = -1.0f64; // arrival time of the slowest fleet ahead
    for (pos, vel) in carros {
        let t = (target - pos) as f64 / vel as f64;
        if t > tempo_chefe {
            frotas += 1;
            tempo_chefe = t;
        }
    }
    frotas
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <utility>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int carFleet(int target, vector<int>& position, vector<int>& speed) {
        vector<pair<int, int>> carros;
        int n = (int)position.size();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) carros.emplace_back(position[i], speed[i]);
        sort(carros.begin(), carros.end(), greater<pair<int, int>>());
        int frotas = 0;
        double tempo_chefe = -1.0;
        for (auto& [pos, vel] : carros) {
            double t = (double)(target - pos) / vel;
            if (t > tempo_chefe) {
                frotas++;
                tempo_chefe = t;
            }
        }
        return frotas;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

typedef struct {
    int pos;
    int vel;
} Carro;

static int cmp_carro(const void* a, const void* b) {
    const Carro* x = (const Carro*)a;
    const Carro* y = (const Carro*)b;
    return (y->pos > x->pos) - (y->pos < x->pos); /* descending, no "x - y" */
}

int carFleet(int target, int* position, int positionSize, int* speed, int speedSize) {
    Carro* carros = malloc((size_t)positionSize * sizeof(Carro));
    for (int i = 0; i < positionSize; i++) {
        carros[i].pos = position[i];
        carros[i].vel = speed[i];
    }
    qsort(carros, (size_t)positionSize, sizeof(Carro), cmp_carro);
    int frotas = 0;
    double tempo_chefe = -1.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < positionSize; i++) {
        double t = (double)(target - carros[i].pos) / carros[i].vel;
        if (t > tempo_chefe) {
            frotas++;
            tempo_chefe = t;
        }
    }
    free(carros);
    return frotas;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n log n) — the sort by position dominates; the following scan is O(n).
  • Space: O(n) — the array of pairs (sorted cars) in all 4 languages.

Pitfalls

  • Processing order: from the closest to the target to the farthest — sort by position descending. Processing in the given order mixes leaders and followers.
  • Compare times, not speeds: losing to a faster car only matters if it catches up before the target; only the arrival time decides.
  • Exact tie (t == tempo_chefe) = catches up at the target → same fleet — that’s why the condition is > and not >=.
  • C qsort comparator without subtraction ((y > x) - (y < x)) — x - y overflows with INT_MIN (the C page’s detail).
  • Float is sufficient and idiomatic here (simple ratio comparisons) — precision drift doesn’t change the result; for total exactness you can compare (target - pos) * speed_other cross-multiplied.

84. Largest Rectangle in Histogram (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/largest-rectangle-in-histogram/ · Topic: Monotonic stack

Problem (summary)

A histogram is an array heights where each bar is 1 unit wide. Return the area of the largest rectangle that fits entirely inside the bars (the base can spread across several contiguous bars, but the height is capped by the shortest of them).

heights = [2,1,5,6,2,3]  →  10   (rectangle 5×2: bars 5 and 6, height 5)
heights = [2,4]          →  4    (the height-4 bar alone)

Pattern — what to memorize

Monotonically increasing stack of indices + sentinel: the stack keeps indices in increasing height order. When heights[i] is lower than the top, the bar at the top has just found its bounds (the left one is the new stack top, the right one is i) — pop and compute height × (i − left_bound − 1), repeating until the top fits. A 0 sentinel at the end forces the stack to empty completely (0 is lower than everyone). Clue in the statement: largest contiguous area + height capped by the shortest bar → for each bar, “how far is it the shortest?” — exactly a monotonic stack; it’s the same skeleton as Daily Temperatures, turned into “next smaller to the left and to the right” in a single pass.

Python

class Solution:
    def largestRectangleArea(self, heights: list[int]) -> int:
        pilha: list[int] = []  # indices, increasing heights
        melhor = 0
        for i, h in enumerate(heights + [0]):  # 0 sentinel empties the stack
            while pilha and heights[pilha[-1]] >= h:
                altura = heights[pilha.pop()]
                largura = i if not pilha else i - pilha[-1] - 1
                melhor = max(melhor, altura * largura)
            pilha.append(i)
        return melhor

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn largest_rectangle_area(heights: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
    let n = heights.len();
    let mut pilha: Vec<usize> = Vec::new();
    let mut melhor: i64 = 0;
    for i in 0..=n {
        let h = if i < n { heights[i] } else { 0 }; // sentinel
        while let Some(&topo) = pilha.last() {
            if heights[topo] < h {
                break;
            }
            pilha.pop();
            let altura = heights[topo] as i64;
            let largura = (i - pilha.last().map_or(0, |&j| j + 1)) as i64;
            melhor = melhor.max(altura * largura);
        }
        pilha.push(i);
    }
    melhor as i32
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int largestRectangleArea(vector<int>& heights) {
        int n = (int)heights.size();
        vector<int> pilha;
        int melhor = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i) {
            long long h = (i < n) ? heights[i] : 0; // sentinel
            while (!pilha.empty() && heights[pilha.back()] >= h) {
                long long altura = heights[pilha.back()];
                pilha.pop_back();
                long long largura = pilha.empty() ? i : i - pilha.back() - 1;
                melhor = max(melhor, (int)(altura * largura));
            }
            pilha.push_back(i);
        }
        return melhor;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

int largestRectangleArea(int* heights, int heightsSize) {
    int* pilha = malloc((size_t)(heightsSize + 1) * sizeof(int));
    int topo = 0;
    long melhor = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i <= heightsSize; i++) {
        long h = (i < heightsSize) ? heights[i] : 0; /* sentinel */
        while (topo > 0 && heights[pilha[topo - 1]] >= h) {
            long altura = heights[pilha[topo - 1]];
            topo--;
            long largura = (topo == 0) ? i : i - pilha[topo - 1] - 1;
            long area = altura * largura;
            if (area > melhor) melhor = area;
        }
        pilha[topo++] = i;
    }
    free(pilha);
    return (int)melhor;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each index enters and leaves the stack once (amortized); the inner while runs O(n) in total.
  • Space: O(n) — the stack holds up to n indices (heights increasing end to end).

Pitfalls

  • The width uses the new stack top, not the index that left: after the pop, the left bound is the remaining top (i - pilha[-1] - 1); if the stack emptied, the bar reaches the start (largura = i).
  • 0 sentinel: without it the last group of bars is never drained; the i <= n loop (or heights + [0] in Python) is mandatory, not a detail.
  • Equal heights: using >= for the pop resolves correctly (the last of a group of equals computes the full width); with > the result is the same but takes one extra pop.
  • Area overflow: height × width reaches 10⁴ × 10⁵ = 10⁹, near INT_MAX — in Rust and C++ the math runs in i64/long long (in C, long is 64 bits on macOS/Linux) and only the final result becomes int.
  • In Rust, pilha.last().map_or(0, |&j| j + 1) encodes the “left bound or -1” the borrow-checker-safe way: j + 1 is the first valid index after the top (or 0 when empty).

704. Binary Search (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-search/ · Topic: Binary Search

Problem (summary)

Given a sorted (ascending) integer array nums and a target, return the index of target in nums, or -1 if it does not exist. LeetCode’s acceptance criteria require O(log n) complexity.

nums = [-1,0,3,5,9,12], target = 9 → 4
nums = [-1,0,3,5,9,12], target = 2 → -1

Pattern — what to memorize

Classic binary search with the inclusive [l, r] invariant: while l <= r, the middle candidate m = l + (r - l) / 2 splits the space: if nums[m] < target the target is to the right (l = m + 1); if greater, to the left (r = m - 1). Two clues in the statement: sorted array + return an index → binary search.

Senior detail: use m = l + (r - l) / 2 (not (l + r) / 2) — it avoids l + r overflow with large indices (a 32-bit usize/int won’t overflow here, but a 64-bit huge array would).

Python

class Solution:
    def search(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
        l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
        while l <= r:
            m = (l + r) // 2
            if nums[m] == target:
                return m
            if nums[m] < target:
                l = m + 1
            else:
                r = m - 1
        return -1

Python integers never overflow, and (l + r) // 2 gives the same result; writing l + (r - l) // 2 just carries the same defensive habit as the other languages.

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn search(nums: Vec<i32>, target: i32) -> i32 {
        // (l, r) as i32 so r can go to -1 in the "empty" case; `len` casts to i32.
        let (mut l, mut r) = (0i32, nums.len() as i32 - 1);
        while l <= r {
            let m = l + (r - l) / 2; // avoids (l + r) overflow
            match nums[m as usize].cmp(&target) {
                std::cmp::Ordering::Equal => return m,
                std::cmp::Ordering::Less => l = m + 1,
                std::cmp::Ordering::Greater => r = m - 1,
            }
        }
        -1
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    int search(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
        int l = 0, r = (int)nums.size() - 1; /* cast: size_t is unsigned */
        while (l <= r) {
            int m = l + (r - l) / 2; /* avoids (l+r) overflow */
            if (nums[m] == target) return m;
            if (nums[m] < target) l = m + 1;
            else r = m - 1;
        }
        return -1;
    }
};

C

int search(int* nums, int numsSize, int target) {
    int l = 0, r = numsSize - 1;
    while (l <= r) {
        int m = l + (r - l) / 2; /* avoids (l+r) overflow */
        if (nums[m] == target) return m;
        if (nums[m] < target) l = m + 1;
        else r = m - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(log n) — the search space halves every iteration.
  • Space: O(1) — indices only; no auxiliary structure.

Pitfalls

  • Empty array: initial r = -1 → the l <= r loop never runs and it returns -1. But numsSize is size_t/usize in C/Rust — subtracting 1 from 0 yields a huge number. In C++, cast (int)nums.size(); in Rust, start r as i32 and it just works.
  • Loop termination: with the inclusive l <= r invariant, the not-found case ends with l > r — that’s the final return -1. Don’t switch to < without also changing the l/r moves.
  • l + r overflow: in 32-bit languages with huge arrays, (l + r) can overflow; l + (r - l) / 2 never does.
  • Single element [5]: the loop runs once with m = 0 — works, but it’s the case that catches most off-by-one bugs in binary search.

74. Search a 2D Matrix (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/search-a-2d-matrix/ · Topic: Array · Binary Search · Matrix

Problem (summary)

An m × n matrix where every row is sorted ascending and the first element of each row is greater than the last element of the previous row (basically a sorted array that was “flattened”). Given target, return whether it exists in the matrix.

matrix = [[1,3,5,7],[10,11,16,20],[23,30,34,60]], target = 3  → true
matrix = [[1,3,5,7],[10,11,16,20],[23,30,34,60]], target = 13 → false

Pattern — what to memorize

Linearized binary search: the matrix invariant (sorted rows and columns, with the 1st of each row greater than the last of the previous one) guarantees that reading in row-major order is an ascending array of m*n elements. So pretend it’s an array: indices 0..m*n, and the element at position k is matrix[k / n][k % n]. One single binary search in O(log(m·n)) — no need to find the row first.

Clue in the statement: matrix sorted in chained rows and columns → treat it as 1D. The inverse gotcha: if the rows were only sorted among themselves (not chained), then you’d need two binary searches (column 0 first, then the row).

Python

class Solution:
    def searchMatrix(self, matrix: list[list[int]], target: int) -> bool:
        m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        l, r = 0, m * n - 1
        while l <= r:
            mid = (l + r) // 2
            v = matrix[mid // n][mid % n]
            if v == target:
                return True
            if v < target:
                l = mid + 1
            else:
                r = mid - 1
        return False

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn search_matrix(matrix: Vec<Vec<i32>>, target: i32) -> bool {
        let m = matrix.len();
        let n = matrix[0].len();
        // Search with an EXCLUSIVE upper bound [l, r): `r = mid` never needs
        // `mid - 1`, so usize cannot underflow when mid = 0.
        let (mut l, mut r) = (0usize, m * n);
        while l < r {
            let mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
            let v = matrix[mid / n][mid % n];
            if v == target {
                return true;
            }
            if v < target {
                l = mid + 1;
            } else {
                r = mid;
            }
        }
        false
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    bool searchMatrix(vector<vector<int>>& matrix, int target) {
        int m = (int)matrix.size(), n = (int)matrix[0].size();
        int l = 0, r = m * n - 1;
        while (l <= r) {
            int mid = l + (r - l) / 2;
            int v = matrix[mid / n][mid % n];
            if (v == target) return true;
            if (v < target) l = mid + 1;
            else r = mid - 1;
        }
        return false;
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>

bool searchMatrix(int** matrix, int matrixSize, int* matrixColSize, int target) {
    int n = matrixColSize[0];
    int l = 0, r = matrixSize * n - 1;
    while (l <= r) {
        int m = l + (r - l) / 2;
        int v = matrix[m / n][m % n];
        if (v == target) return true;
        if (v < target) l = m + 1;
        else r = m - 1;
    }
    return false;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(log(m·n)) — the binary search runs over m*n “virtual” positions; each matrix access is O(1).
  • Space: O(1) — indices only.

Pitfalls

  • Empty matrix: the constraints guarantee m, n >= 1, but if the code ever ran on an empty matrix, matrix[0]/matrix[0].size() already breaks before the search — handle m == 0 first if you want to be defensive (senior interviews mention this out loud).
  • r = m * n - 1 in usize: if m*n == 0 (empty matrix), it underflows. That’s why the Rust version uses the exclusive [l, r) range — it never does mid - 1, and the C/C++ versions rely on the guaranteed m*n >= 1.
  • Consecutive elements across rows: it’s matrix[1][0] > matrix[0][n-1] that makes the linearization valid; without it the algorithm breaks (and the target = 60 test — the last element — covers the last-row boundary).
  • mid % n and mid / n with n coming from matrixColSize[0] in C: it’s the width, not the row count — swapping them indexes out of bounds.
