875. Koko Eating Bananas (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/koko-eating-bananas/ · Topic: Array · Binary Search

Problem (summary)

Koko eats piles of bananas; each hour she eats from one pile at a constant speed k bananas/hour (if the pile has fewer than k, she finishes it and the hour does not “carry over” to another pile). Given h hours and the pile sizes, find the smallest k that lets her eat everything within h hours.

piles = [3,6,7,11], h = 8        → 4
piles = [30,11,23,4,20], h = 5   → 30
piles = [30,11,23,4,20], h = 6   → 23

Pattern — what to memorize

Binary search on the ANSWER (over the value range, not indices). The candidate is k ∈ [1, max(piles)] (eating faster than the largest pile is pointless). For a given k, the total time is Σ ceil(pile / k) = Σ (pile + k - 1) / k — a monotonically decreasing function of k (faster → fewer hours). With monotonicity, everything that’s feasible lies to the right of the boundary: classic “first value that satisfies the condition” binary search.

Clue in the statement: smallest value k + clearly monotone feasible function → binary search on the answer. It’s easy to misread as two piles per hour — but the statement says ONE pile per hour, and that’s what the ceil models.

Python

class Solution:
    def minEatingSpeed(self, piles: list[int], h: int) -> int:
        def horas(k: int) -> int:
            return sum((p + k - 1) // k for p in piles)

        l, r = 1, max(piles)
        while l < r:
            k = (l + r) // 2
            if horas(k) <= h:
                r = k          # k is feasible: try a smaller one
            else:
                l = k + 1      # k not feasible: must eat faster
        return l

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn min_eating_speed(piles: Vec<i32>, h: i32) -> i32 {
        let mut l = 1i64;
        let mut r = *piles.iter().max().unwrap() as i64;
        while l < r {
            let k = (l + r) / 2;
            let horas: i64 = piles.iter().map(|&p| (p as i64 + k - 1) / k).sum();
            if horas <= h as i64 {
                r = k; // k is feasible: try a smaller one
            } else {
                l = k + 1;
            }
        }
        l as i32
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    int minEatingSpeed(vector<int>& piles, int h) {
        long long l = 1, r = *max_element(piles.begin(), piles.end());
        while (l < r) {
            long long k = (l + r) / 2;
            long long horas = 0;
            for (int p : piles)
                horas += ((long long)p + k - 1) / k; /* ceil: p/k rounded up */
            if (horas <= h) r = k;
            else l = k + 1;
        }
        return (int)l;
    }
};

C

static long long horas_com(long long k, int* piles, int pilesSize) {
    long long h = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < pilesSize; i++)
        h += (piles[i] + k - 1) / k; /* ceiling of the division */
    return h;
}

int minEatingSpeed(int* piles, int pilesSize, int h) {
    long long l = 1, r = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < pilesSize; i++)
        if (piles[i] > r) r = piles[i];
    while (l < r) {
        long long k = (l + r) / 2;
        if (horas_com(k, piles, pilesSize) <= h) r = k;
        else l = k + 1;
    }
    return (int)l;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n · log max(piles)) — each candidate k costs O(n) (summing the ceil over all piles), and the binary search tries O(log max(piles)) candidates.
  • Space: O(1) — variables only.

Pitfalls

  • Integer division ceiling: (p + k - 1) / k is the ceil; the + k - 1 avoids floating point (and the mental “0.5 hour” problem).
  • accumulate(..., 0) truncates: in C++, sum into a long long (the 0LL idiom); p can reach 10⁹ and n 10⁴ — the total won’t overflow an int exactly, but p + k needs long long to be safe.
  • k smaller than max(piles) is possible when h > n (e.g. [5], h=3 → k=2): that’s why the lower bound is 1, not the max, and r is the max.
  • The function is monotonically DECREASING: when k fails (hours > h), the only way is to raise k → l = k + 1; when it passes, r = k looks for the smallest feasible. Swapping the sides returns 1 (wrong).
  • h >= n always (the statement guarantees it: each pile needs at least 1 hour), otherwise there’d be no solution — the binary search would still terminate at max(piles).

153. Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array/ · Topic: Array · Binary Search

Problem (summary)

An ascending array of distinct integers was rotated at some pivot (e.g. [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] became [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]). Find the minimum in O(log n). Distinct values are part of the problem’s contract.

nums = [3,4,5,1,2]           → 1
nums = [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]       → 0
nums = [11,13,15,17]         → 11   (not rotated)

Pattern — what to memorize

Binary search comparing nums[m] with nums[r] — the “signature” of the minimum is the first element less than or equal to the last (nums[0] > nums[last] in any real rotation; if nums[0] <= nums[last], no rotation happened and the first element is the minimum). Invariant:

  • nums[m] > nums[r] → the turn is to the right of m (m is on the “climbing” part) → l = m + 1.
  • otherwise → nums[r] and its neighbors are in order (the sorted part); the minimum may be m itself or something to its left → r = m.

The l < r loop with r = m (never m - 1) converges with l == r at the minimum.

Clue in the statement: rotated + minimum → binary search comparing against the right end. Equivalent alternative: look for the first nums[i] with nums[i] <= nums[last].

Python

class Solution:
    def findMin(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
        while l < r:
            m = (l + r) // 2
            if nums[m] > nums[r]:
                l = m + 1  # minimum is to the right of m
            else:
                r = m
        return nums[l]

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn find_min(nums: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
        // usize has no negative: r never "passes" behind 0 because the
        // l < r invariant guarantees r >= 1 before r = m.
        let (mut l, mut r) = (0usize, nums.len() - 1);
        while l < r {
            let m = l + (r - l) / 2;
            if nums[m] > nums[r] {
                l = m + 1; // m is on the rotated part: minimum to the right
            } else {
                r = m; // sorted part: minimum may be m itself
            }
        }
        nums[l]
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    int findMin(vector<int>& nums) {
        int l = 0, r = (int)nums.size() - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            int m = l + (r - l) / 2;
            if (nums[m] > nums[r]) l = m + 1;
            else r = m;
        }
        return nums[l];
    }
};

C

int findMin(int* nums, int numsSize) {
    int l = 0, r = numsSize - 1;
    while (l < r) {
        int m = l + (r - l) / 2;
        if (nums[m] > nums[r])
            l = m + 1; /* m is on the rotated half: minimum to the right */
        else
            r = m; /* m is on the sorted part: minimum may be m itself */
    }
    return nums[l];
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(log n) — one comparison per iteration, space halved each time.
  • Space: O(1).

Pitfalls

  • Unrotated array [11,13,15,17]: nums[m] <= nums[r] always → r walks toward 0 → returns the first element. The problem allows a rotation of 0 positions.
  • r = m instead of r = m - 1: since the minimum can be m itself (when nums[m] <= nums[r]), excluding m makes you LOSE the answer — the classic off-by-one of this variant. The loop stops when l == r.
  • In Rust, nums.len() - 1 underflows on an empty vector; the l < r invariant guarantees r > 0 before any access, and nums.len() is >= 1 per the statement (1 <= n <= 5000).
  • Case [2,1]: m = 0, nums[0] > nums[1] → l = 1 → returns 1. It’s the test that separates who used >= instead of >.

33. Search in Rotated Sorted Array (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/search-in-rotated-sorted-array/ · Topic: Array · Binary Search

Problem (summary)

An ascending array of distinct integers was rotated at an unknown pivot (e.g. [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] → [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]). Given target, return its index, or -1. Distinct values are part of the contract (with duplicates the problem becomes #81 and the binary search degrades to O(n)).

nums = [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], target = 0 → 4
nums = [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], target = 3 → -1

Pattern — what to memorize

A single binary search that checks which half is in order. At each step, mid splits the array in two; since there is only ONE rotation point, at least one half is perfectly sorted:

  • if nums[l] <= nums[m] → left half sorted: does the target belong to it? (nums[l] <= target < nums[m] → discard the right) otherwise go right;
  • otherwise → right half sorted: analogous with nums[m] < target <= nums[r].

Getting the <=/< on the right ends is the difference between working and an infinite loop. It runs in O(log n) without finding the pivot first (finding the pivot = problem 153, then two searches — also valid, just the longer version).

Clue in the statement: sorted but rotated + search a value → binary search that identifies the sorted half.

Python

class Solution:
    def search(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
        l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
        while l <= r:
            m = (l + r) // 2
            if nums[m] == target:
                return m
            if nums[l] <= nums[m]:          # left half is sorted
                if nums[l] <= target < nums[m]:
                    r = m - 1
                else:
                    l = m + 1
            else:                           # right half is sorted
                if nums[m] < target <= nums[r]:
                    l = m + 1
                else:
                    r = m - 1
        return -1

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn search(nums: Vec<i32>, target: i32) -> i32 {
        let (mut l, mut r) = (0i32, nums.len() as i32 - 1);
        while l <= r {
            let m = l + (r - l) / 2;
            if nums[m as usize] == target {
                return m;
            }
            if nums[l as usize] <= nums[m as usize] {
                // left half is sorted: does the target belong to it?
                if nums[l as usize] <= target && target < nums[m as usize] {
                    r = m - 1;
                } else {
                    l = m + 1;
                }
            } else {
                // right half is sorted
                if nums[m as usize] < target && target <= nums[r as usize] {
                    l = m + 1;
                } else {
                    r = m - 1;
                }
            }
        }
        -1
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    int search(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
        int l = 0, r = (int)nums.size() - 1;
        while (l <= r) {
            int m = l + (r - l) / 2;
            if (nums[m] == target) return m;
            if (nums[l] <= nums[m]) {          /* left half is sorted */
                if (nums[l] <= target && target < nums[m]) r = m - 1;
                else l = m + 1;
            } else {                           /* right half is sorted */
                if (nums[m] < target && target <= nums[r]) l = m + 1;
                else r = m - 1;
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
};

C

int search(int* nums, int numsSize, int target) {
    int l = 0, r = numsSize - 1;
    while (l <= r) {
        int m = l + (r - l) / 2;
        if (nums[m] == target) return m;
        if (nums[l] <= nums[m]) {          /* left half is sorted */
            if (nums[l] <= target && target < nums[m])
                r = m - 1;
            else
                l = m + 1;
        } else {                           /* right half is sorted */
            if (nums[m] < target && target <= nums[r])
                l = m + 1;
            else
                r = m - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(log n) — one half is discarded every iteration.
  • Space: O(1).

Pitfalls

  • Endpoint comparison < vs <=: target < nums[m] on the left (the m itself was already tested by ==), but target <= nums[r] on the right (r has NOT been tested yet). Flipping either to the wrong side breaks cases like [3,1], target=1.
  • nums[l] <= nums[m] identifies the sorted half, but with an unrotated array the “left” half always looks sorted and the algorithm still works — and the single-element case ([1]) hits the == right away.
  • With duplicates the <= breaks (e.g. [1,0,1,1,1]): if the statement doesn’t say “distinct”, do problem 81 instead (same idea + l += 1 when nums[l] == nums[m] == nums[r]).
  • Cast (int)nums.size() in C++ / as i32 in Rust: 0..size-1 on an empty vector becomes SIZE_MAX/a giant usize — this problem guarantees n >= 1, but the habit (and the [1] test) prevents surprises.

981. Time Based Key-Value Store (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/time-based-key-value-store/ · Topic: Design · Hash Table · Binary Search · String

Problem (summary)

Implement a structure with two operations: set(key, value, timestamp) stores a value with its instant; get(key, timestamp) returns the value associated with the largest timestamp ≤ the request for that key (or "" if none exists). Problem guarantee: the timestamps of the SAME key are strictly increasing across set calls.

set("foo","bar",1); get("foo",1)="bar"; get("foo",3)="bar";
set("foo","bar2",4); get("foo",4)="bar2"; get("foo",5)="bar2"; get("foo",0)=""

Pattern — what to memorize

Hash map of key → (timestamp, value) vector + binary search on the vector. Two observations that solve the problem:

  1. Since a key’s timestamps arrive increasing (append), each key’s vector is born sorted — set is amortized O(1) and the order never needs to be redone.
  2. get is “find the last element with ts ≤ request”: a binary search that keeps the best candidate whenever regs[m].ts <= timestamp and keeps looking to the right (i.e., lower_bound/partition_point, then decrement, or the “last ≤ x” search).

Clue in the statement: key → multiple values over time + ts increasing → per-key sorted vector + binary search. Without timestamp monotonicity you’d have to sort (O(k log k)) or use a TreeMap with floorEntry.

Python

class TimeMap:
    def __init__(self):
        self.dados: dict[str, list[tuple[int, str]]] = {}

    def set(self, key: str, value: str, timestamp: int) -> None:
        self.dados.setdefault(key, []).append((timestamp, value))

    def get(self, key: str, timestamp: int) -> str:
        vals = self.dados.get(key, [])
        l, r = 0, len(vals) - 1
        resp = ""
        while l <= r:
            m = (l + r) // 2
            if vals[m][0] <= timestamp:
                resp = vals[m][1]  # candidate: a newer one may exist
                l = m + 1
            else:
                r = m - 1
        return resp

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashMap;

pub struct TimeMap {
    dados: HashMap<String, Vec<(i32, String)>>, // timestamps increasing per key
}

impl TimeMap {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self { dados: HashMap::new() }
    }

    pub fn set(&mut self, key: String, value: String, timestamp: i32) {
        self.dados.entry(key).or_default().push((timestamp, value));
    }

    pub fn get(&self, key: String, timestamp: i32) -> String {
        // partition_point: count of records with ts <= timestamp; the last one
        // (index i-1) is the answer. Does not insert a missing key.
        let Some(regs) = self.dados.get(&key) else { return String::new() };
        let i = regs.partition_point(|&(ts, _)| ts <= timestamp);
        if i == 0 { String::new() } else { regs[i - 1].1.clone() }
    }
}
}

C++

class TimeMap {
    unordered_map<string, vector<pair<int, string>>> dados;

public:
    void set(string key, string value, int timestamp) {
        dados[key].emplace_back(timestamp, std::move(value)); /* ts increasing */
    }

    string get(string key, int timestamp) {
        auto it = dados.find(key); /* find: don't insert a missing key on get */
        if (it == dados.end()) return "";
        auto& regs = it->second;
        int l = 0, r = (int)regs.size() - 1;
        string melhor;
        while (l <= r) {
            int m = l + (r - l) / 2;
            if (regs[m].first <= timestamp) {
                melhor = regs[m].second; /* candidate; a newer one may exist */
                l = m + 1;
            } else {
                r = m - 1;
            }
        }
        return melhor;
    }
};

C

LeetCode has no C signature for this design problem; here’s the API as a struct. Keys are looked up with a linear scan (small key count in the tests; for production, swap in a string hash) and each key’s records live in a dynamic vector sorted by timestamp, queried with binary search.

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

typedef struct { long ts; char* valor; } Registro;

typedef struct {
    char* chave;
    Registro* regs; /* sorted by ts (append) */
    int n, cap;
} Entrada;

typedef struct { Entrada* entradas; int n, cap; } TimeMap;

static Entrada* achar_ou_criar(TimeMap* tm, const char* chave) {
    for (int i = 0; i < tm->n; i++)
        if (strcmp(tm->entradas[i].chave, chave) == 0) return &tm->entradas[i];
    if (tm->n == tm->cap) {
        tm->cap = tm->cap ? tm->cap * 2 : 4;
        tm->entradas = realloc(tm->entradas, (size_t)tm->cap * sizeof(Entrada));
    }
    Entrada* e = &tm->entradas[tm->n++];
    memset(e, 0, sizeof(*e));
    e->chave = strdup(chave);
    return e;
}

TimeMap* tm_novo(void) { return calloc(1, sizeof(TimeMap)); }

void tm_libera(TimeMap* tm) {
    for (int i = 0; i < tm->n; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < tm->entradas[i].n; j++)
            free(tm->entradas[i].regs[j].valor);
        free(tm->entradas[i].regs);
        free(tm->entradas[i].chave);
    }
    free(tm->entradas);
    free(tm);
}

void tm_set(TimeMap* tm, const char* chave, const char* valor, int ts) {
    Entrada* e = achar_ou_criar(tm, chave);
    if (e->n == e->cap) {
        e->cap = e->cap ? e->cap * 2 : 4;
        e->regs = realloc(e->regs, (size_t)e->cap * sizeof(Registro));
    }
    e->regs[e->n].ts = ts;
    e->regs[e->n].valor = strdup(valor);
    e->n++;
}

/* returns a pointer to an INTERNAL string (valid until the next set on the
 * SAME key); empty string when no record has ts <= timestamp. */
const char* tm_get(TimeMap* tm, const char* chave, int ts) {
    static const char* VAZIA = "";
    for (int i = 0; i < tm->n; i++) {
        if (strcmp(tm->entradas[i].chave, chave) != 0) continue;
        Registro* regs = tm->entradas[i].regs;
        int l = 0, r = tm->entradas[i].n - 1;
        const char* melhor = VAZIA;
        while (l <= r) {
            int m = l + (r - l) / 2;
            if (regs[m].ts <= ts) { melhor = regs[m].valor; l = m + 1; }
            else r = m - 1;
        }
        return melhor;
    }
    return VAZIA;
}

Complexity

  • set: O(1) amortized — append at the end of the key’s vector (hash O(1)).
  • get: O(log k) with k = record count of that key (binary search), plus O(1) for the key hash. In C, the key lookup is linear in the key count (documented decision; a string hash would make it O(1)).
  • Space: O(K × R) — K keys, R records per key (timestamps are never overwritten; every set adds memory).

Pitfalls

  • get must NOT insert the key: dados[key] in get would create an empty entry (side effect); use get/find/dados.get(&key).
  • Requested timestamp smaller than the first one: get("foo", 0) when the 1st set had ts=1 → the search never updates the candidate → returns "". Initializing resp/melhor as empty is what guarantees it.
  • Rust’s partition_point returns the count of elements ≤ ts; the right value is at i - 1 (and i == 0 means “none”).
  • “Last ≤ ts”, not “match ==”: if set("k","a",1) and set("k","b",4), then get("k",3) must return "a" — that’s why the search keeps going right even after finding a candidate.
  • Manual memory in C: every strdup/realloc has its free in tm_libera; returning an internal pointer (not a copy) is the struct contract’s documented decision.

4. Median of Two Sorted Arrays (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/median-of-two-sorted-arrays/ · Topic: Array · Binary Search · Divide and Conquer

Problem (summary)

Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2 (sizes m and n), return the median of their union, in O(log(m+n)) time. The median is the middle element if the total is odd, or the average of the two central ones if even.

nums1 = [1,3], nums2 = [2]    → 2.0
nums1 = [1,2], nums2 = [3,4]  → 2.5
nums1 = [],    nums2 = [1]    → 1.0

Pattern — what to memorize

Binary partitioning on the SMALLER array (the cut technique). The median splits the union into two halves of sizes (m+n+1)/2 (left) and the rest (right). The idea: pick corte_a (how much of the left half comes from A) and corte_b = metade - corte_a (how much comes from B) such that:

  • esq_a <= dir_b and esq_b <= dir_a → the partition is correct: the median is max(esq_a, esq_b) (odd) or the average with min(dir_a, dir_b) (even);
  • esq_a > dir_b → A’s left side is “too big” → cut less in A;
  • otherwise → cut more in A.

The only way to guarantee the cut satisfies the condition is binary search on the smaller array (O(log min(m,n))) — searching both is O(log(m+n)) in practice, but the min is the tight bound and avoids a search on the larger array being O(log m + log n).

Clue in the statement: two sorted + median + O(log) → a pair of cuts with the “entire left ≤ entire right” invariant. What makes it Hard: the edge cases at the ends (± infinity) and the cut bookkeeping.

Python

class Solution:
    def findMedianSortedArrays(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int]) -> float:
        a, b = nums1, nums2
        if len(a) > len(b):
            a, b = b, a          # search the smaller one; the other is the complement
        m, n = len(a), len(b)
        lo, hi = 0, m
        metade = (m + n + 1) // 2
        INF = float("inf")
        while lo <= hi:
            corte_a = (lo + hi) // 2
            corte_b = metade - corte_a
            esq_a = a[corte_a - 1] if corte_a > 0 else -INF
            esq_b = b[corte_b - 1] if corte_b > 0 else -INF
            dir_a = a[corte_a] if corte_a < m else INF
            dir_b = b[corte_b] if corte_b < n else INF
            if esq_a <= dir_b and esq_b <= dir_a:   # correct partition
                if (m + n) % 2 == 1:
                    return max(esq_a, esq_b)
                return (max(esq_a, esq_b) + min(dir_a, dir_b)) / 2.0
            if esq_a > dir_b:
                hi = corte_a - 1   # a's left side is "too big"
            else:
                lo = corte_a + 1
        return 0.0  # unreachable

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn find_median_sorted_arrays(nums1: Vec<i32>, nums2: Vec<i32>) -> f64 {
        // Independent references: a = smaller array, b = larger (no copy).
        let (a, b) = if nums1.len() > nums2.len() {
            (&nums2, &nums1)
        } else {
            (&nums1, &nums2)
        };
        let (m, n) = (a.len(), b.len());
        let metade = (m + n + 1) / 2; // elements in the left partition
        let (mut lo, mut hi) = (0usize, m); // hi INCLUSIVE here (cut can be m)
        while lo <= hi {
            let corte_a = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
            let corte_b = metade - corte_a;
            let esq_a = if corte_a > 0 { a[corte_a - 1] } else { i32::MIN };
            let esq_b = if corte_b > 0 { b[corte_b - 1] } else { i32::MIN };
            let dir_a = if corte_a < m { a[corte_a] } else { i32::MAX };
            let dir_b = if corte_b < n { b[corte_b] } else { i32::MAX };
            if esq_a <= dir_b && esq_b <= dir_a {
                let max_esq = esq_a.max(esq_b);
                if (m + n) % 2 == 1 {
                    return max_esq as f64;
                }
                return (max_esq + dir_a.min(dir_b)) as f64 / 2.0;
            }
            if esq_a > dir_b {
                hi = corte_a - 1; // a's left side too big
            } else {
                lo = corte_a + 1;
            }
        }
        0.0 // unreachable with valid inputs
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    double findMedianSortedArrays(vector<int>& a, vector<int>& b) {
        /* You can't "re-point" references: the swap is a call with the
         * arguments flipped (without mutating the caller's vectors). */
        if (a.size() > b.size()) return findMedianSortedArrays(b, a);
        int m = (int)a.size(), n = (int)b.size();
        const int NEG_INF = INT_MIN, POS_INF = INT_MAX;
        int lo = 0, hi = m;
        int metade = (m + n + 1) / 2; /* elements in the left partition */
        while (lo <= hi) {
            int corte_a = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
            int corte_b = metade - corte_a;
            int esq_a = corte_a > 0 ? a[corte_a - 1] : NEG_INF;
            int esq_b = corte_b > 0 ? b[corte_b - 1] : NEG_INF;
            int dir_a = corte_a < m ? a[corte_a] : POS_INF;
            int dir_b = corte_b < n ? b[corte_b] : POS_INF;
            if (esq_a <= dir_b && esq_b <= dir_a) { /* correct partition */
                int max_esq = max(esq_a, esq_b);
                if ((m + n) % 2 == 1) return max_esq;
                return (max_esq + min(dir_a, dir_b)) / 2.0;
            }
            if (esq_a > dir_b) hi = corte_a - 1; /* a's left side too big */
            else lo = corte_a + 1;
        }
        return 0.0; /* unreachable */
    }
};

C

#include <stdint.h>

#define NEG_INF (-2147483647 - 1) /* INT_MIN without overflowing the literal */
#define POS_INF 2147483647

double findMedianSortedArrays(int* nums1, int nums1Size,
                              int* nums2, int nums2Size) {
    int* a = nums1; int m = nums1Size;
    int* b = nums2; int n = nums2Size;
    if (m > n) { int* t = a; a = b; b = t; int s = m; m = n; n = s; }

    int lo = 0, hi = m;
    int metade = (m + n + 1) / 2;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int corte_a = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        int corte_b = metade - corte_a;
        int esq_a = corte_a > 0 ? a[corte_a - 1] : NEG_INF;
        int esq_b = corte_b > 0 ? b[corte_b - 1] : NEG_INF;
        int dir_a = corte_a < m ? a[corte_a]     : POS_INF;
        int dir_b = corte_b < n ? b[corte_b]     : POS_INF;
        if (esq_a <= dir_b && esq_b <= dir_a) {
            int max_esq = esq_a > esq_b ? esq_a : esq_b;
            if ((m + n) % 2 == 1) return (double)max_esq;
            int min_dir = dir_a < dir_b ? dir_a : dir_b;
            return (max_esq + min_dir) / 2.0;
        }
        if (esq_a > dir_b) hi = corte_a - 1; /* a's left side too big */
        else lo = corte_a + 1;
    }
    return 0.0; /* unreachable with valid inputs */
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(log(min(m, n))) — the binary search only walks the smaller array; the other is the cut’s complement (an O(1)-per-iteration step).
  • Space: O(1) — indices only (Python/Rust/C++ don’t copy the arrays; in C, pointer swap).

Pitfalls

  • Sentinel at the ends: when the cut hits a boundary (corte_a == 0), esq_a doesn’t exist — using -INF/INT_MIN/i32::MIN keeps the “left ≤ right” condition true. Forgetting this is mistake #1.
  • metade = (m+n+1)/2 counts the left partition; the +1 makes the cut consistent for odd totals (median on the left) and even (two central values split between the halves).
  • Even average: (max_esq + min_dir) / 2.0 — division by 2.0 (f64), not integer // 2 (which would truncate).
  • Overflow of l+r and a + b: m*n fits in 32 bits, but l + r near INT_MAX can overflow — lo + (hi - lo) / 2 avoids it (as always).
  • C++ swap(a, b) mutates the caller: with references, swapping the contents changes the original vectors and breaks the test sequence; the recursive call with flipped arguments is the idiom (and m = n in C swaps the pointers).
  • Case [] and a single element: [],[1] → sentinels on both sides; corte_b must stay within [0, n] — the m <= n guarantee is what keeps corte_b in range.

206. Reverse Linked List (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/reverse-linked-list/ · Topic: Linked List

Problem (summary)

Reverse a singly linked list (iteratively or recursively) and return the new head. The list can have 0 to 5000 nodes.

head = [1,2,3,4,5]  →  [5,4,3,2,1]
head = [1,2]        →  [2,1]
head = []           →  []

Pattern — what to memorize

Three pointers walking: anterior (prev), atual (cur), proximo (next). For each node, save proximo, point atual->next back to anterior, then advance both. The list is one-directional — you are the one who remembers the node behind. Clue in the statement: reverse + single linked list → walk with a previous pointer. A recursive version exists, but the iterative one is the interview answer (O(1) space, no risk of blowing the stack on long lists).

Python

def reverseList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    anterior, atual = None, head
    while atual:
        proximo = atual.next       # save before cutting
        atual.next = anterior      # flip the pointer
        anterior = atual
        atual = proximo
    return anterior                # anterior is the new head

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn reverse_list(head: Option<Box<ListNode>>) -> Option<Box<ListNode>> {
    let mut anterior = None;      // the reversed head (starts empty)
    let mut atual = head;
    while let Some(mut no) = atual {
        let proximo = no.next.take(); // take ownership of the rest
        no.next = anterior;           // point backwards
        anterior = Some(no);
        atual = proximo;
    }
    anterior
}
}

C++

ListNode* reverseList(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode* anterior = nullptr;
    ListNode* atual = head;
    while (atual) {
        ListNode* proximo = atual->next;
        atual->next = anterior;   // flip the pointer
        anterior = atual;
        atual = proximo;
    }
    return anterior;
}

C

struct ListNode* reverseList(struct ListNode* head) {
    struct ListNode* anterior = NULL;
    struct ListNode* atual = head;
    while (atual) {
        struct ListNode* proximo = atual->next;
        atual->next = anterior;   /* flip the pointer */
        anterior = atual;
        atual = proximo;
    }
    return anterior;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one pass over the n nodes.
  • Space: O(1) — just three pointers; the recursive version would cost O(n) of stack (depth = list length).

Pitfalls

  • Save proximo BEFORE overwriting atual->next — the classic bug is losing the rest of the list.
  • Empty and single-node cases: the loop never runs and anterior is already the right answer (None / the node itself).
  • In C: returning atual at the end returns NULL (the “empty list” bug) — the answer is anterior.
  • In Rust: no.next.take() is the idiom — without it the borrow checker won’t let you move the next field out of the Box.

21. Merge Two Sorted Lists (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/merge-two-sorted-lists/ · Topic: Linked List

Problem (summary)

Given two ascending linked lists, interleave them into ONE ascending list (reusing the existing nodes, without creating new ones) and return the head. Lists can be empty.

list1 = [1,2,4], list2 = [1,3,4]  →  [1,1,2,3,4,4]
list1 = [], list2 = []            →  []
list1 = [], list2 = [0]           →  [0]

Pattern — what to memorize

Sentinel (dummy head) + walk with the smaller of the two: a disposable ghost node removes the “first insertion” special case; at each step the smaller of the two heads goes into the answer. When one list runs out, the rest of the other is attached whole. Clue: two sorted structures + merge → the same skeleton as the Merge Sort merge.

Python

def mergeTwoLists(self, list1: Optional[ListNode], list2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    sentinela = ListNode()               # ghost node: kills the empty case
    cur = sentinela
    while list1 and list2:
        if list1.val <= list2.val:
            cur.next = list1
            list1 = list1.next
        else:
            cur.next = list2
            list2 = list2.next
        cur = cur.next
    cur.next = list1 or list2            # leftover of one of the lists
    return sentinela.next

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn merge_two_lists(
    list1: Option<Box<ListNode>>,
    list2: Option<Box<ListNode>>,
) -> Option<Box<ListNode>> {
    match (list1, list2) {
        (None, restante) => restante,
        (restante, None) => restante,
        (Some(mut a), Some(mut b)) => {
            // the smaller becomes the head; attach the rest recursively
            if a.val <= b.val {
                a.next = Self::merge_two_lists(a.next.take(), Some(b));
                Some(a)
            } else {
                b.next = Self::merge_two_lists(Some(a), b.next.take());
                Some(b)
            }
        }
    }
}
}

C++

ListNode* mergeTwoLists(ListNode* list1, ListNode* list2) {
    ListNode sentinela;              // on the stack — disposable, avoids empty checks
    ListNode* cur = &sentinela;
    while (list1 && list2) {
        if (list1->val <= list2->val) {
            cur->next = list1;
            list1 = list1->next;
        } else {
            cur->next = list2;
            list2 = list2->next;
        }
        cur = cur->next;
    }
    cur->next = list1 ? list1 : list2; // leftover of one of the lists
    return sentinela.next;
}

C

struct ListNode* mergeTwoLists(struct ListNode* list1, struct ListNode* list2) {
    struct ListNode sentinela;       /* disposable head: avoids empty checks */
    struct ListNode* cur = &sentinela;
    sentinela.next = NULL;
    while (list1 && list2) {
        if (list1->val <= list2->val) {
            cur->next = list1;
            list1 = list1->next;
        } else {
            cur->next = list2;
            list2 = list2->next;
        }
        cur = cur->next;
    }
    cur->next = list1 ? list1 : list2;  /* leftover of one of the lists */
    return sentinela.next;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n + m) — one pass over each list (n and m = sizes).
  • Space: O(1) (iterative, sentinel on the stack). The Rust recursion uses O(n + m) of call stack — acceptable, but the iterative version is the reference.

Pitfalls

  • Use <= (less-or-equal) so the order stays stable (list1 nodes before equal list2 nodes — preserves the ordering asked for).
  • Both empty → sentinela.next = NULL (the sentinel is what saves you from this if).
  • After the loop one list may be entirely left over: cur->next = list1 or list2.
  • In C++: a sentinel on the stack is safe because the problem reuses the existing nodes (nothing deletes it).
  • In Rust: recursion inside match is the natural idiom with Box (owner of the list); an iterative version would need a mutable tail pointer — more verbose.

141. Linked List Cycle (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/linked-list-cycle/ · Topic: Linked List · Two Pointers

Problem (summary)

Determine whether a linked list has a cycle (some next points back to an earlier node). The answer is just a bool; pos is zero-based and only given in the statement to make the example clear — it is not an input to the function.

head = [3,2,0,-4], pos = 1  →  true   (the -4 points back to the 2)
head = [1,2], pos = 0       →  true   (the 2 points to the 1)
head = [1], pos = -1        →  false  (no cycle)

Pattern — what to memorize

Floyd’s cycle detection (tortoise & hare): two pointers, one moves 1 node per step and the other 2. With a cycle, the fast one “laps around” and catches the slow one (in at most O(cycle) steps); without one, the fast pointer hits NULL first. Clue: detect cycle in a linked list → two pointers at different speeds. Worst case the list has just 1 node pointing to itself — the fast pointer must check rapido->next before taking its second step.

Python

def hasCycle(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> bool:
    lento = rapido = head
    while rapido and rapido.next:
        lento = lento.next          # moves 1
        rapido = rapido.next.next   # moves 2
        if lento is rapido:         # they meet: cycle
            return True
    return False

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn has_cycle(head: Option<Rc<RefCell<ListNode>>>) -> bool {
    // Floyd: slow moves 1, fast moves 2; if they meet, there is a cycle.
    let mut lento = head.clone();
    let mut rapido = head;
    while let Some(r) = rapido {
        let passo = match r.borrow().next.clone() {
            Some(p) => p,
            None => return false, // fast reached the end: no cycle
        };
        rapido = passo.borrow().next.clone();
        lento = match lento {
            Some(l) => l.borrow().next.clone(),
            None => return false,
        };
        if let (Some(a), Some(b)) = (&lento, &rapido) {
            if Rc::ptr_eq(a, b) {
                return true;
            }
        }
    }
    false
}
}

C++

bool hasCycle(ListNode* head) {
    // Floyd: slow moves 1, fast moves 2; if they meet, there is a cycle.
    ListNode* lento = head;
    ListNode* rapido = head;
    while (rapido && rapido->next) {
        lento = lento->next;
        rapido = rapido->next->next;
        if (lento == rapido) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

C

bool hasCycle(struct ListNode* head) {
    struct ListNode* lento = head;
    struct ListNode* rapido = head;
    while (rapido && rapido->next) {
        lento = lento->next;
        rapido = rapido->next->next;
        if (lento == rapido) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — without a cycle, rapido walks the list once; with a cycle, they meet after O(n) total steps (not O(n²)).
  • Space: O(1) — two pointers. (A hash set of visited nodes is O(n): it works, but the interview expects Floyd.)

Pitfalls

  • Compare pointers (lento is rapido / ==), not values — two nodes can hold the same val without being the same node.
  • Empty list and 1 node → false; but 1 node with next to itself → true (check rapido->next->next without dereferencing NULL).
  • In C/C++ the && order in the while protects the rapido->next->next access.
  • In Rust this problem uses Rc<RefCell<ListNode>> on LeetCode (the node definition needs reference counting for a cycle to exist); node comparison is Rc::ptr_eq, never == on the values.

143. Reorder List (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/reorder-list/ · Topic: Linked List · Two Pointers

Problem (summary)

Reorder the list in-place in the zig-zag pattern L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 → L2 → Ln-2 → … (return nothing; each node’s val stays put, only the pointers change).

head = [1,2,3,4]    →  [1,4,2,3]
head = [1,2,3,4,5]  →  [1,5,2,4,3]
head = [1]          →  [1]

Pattern — what to memorize

Three steps with tools you already know: (1) find the middle with slow/fast; (2) reverse the second half (Reverse Linked List); (3) interleave the two halves. The middle is ceil(n/2) counting the first half — for odd n the first half keeps the middle node, which ends up last in the answer. Clue: reorder in zig-zag = reversed second half + alternating merge.

Python

def reorderList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
    if not head:
        return
    # 1) middle: slow moves 1, fast moves 2
    lento = rapido = head
    while rapido.next and rapido.next.next:
        lento = lento.next
        rapido = rapido.next.next
    # 2) cut and reverse the second half
    segunda = lento.next
    lento.next = None
    anterior = None
    while segunda:
        proximo = segunda.next
        segunda.next = anterior
        anterior = segunda
        segunda = proximo
    # 3) interleave: A0, B0, A1, B1...
    primeira = head
    segunda = anterior
    while segunda:
        n1, n2 = primeira.next, segunda.next
        primeira.next = segunda
        segunda.next = n1
        primeira, segunda = n1, n2

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn reorder_list(head: &mut Option<Box<ListNode>>) {
    // 1) length
    let mut n = 0usize;
    {
        let mut no = head.as_ref();
        while let Some(x) = no {
            n += 1;
            no = x.next.as_ref();
        }
    }
    if n < 3 {
        return; // 1 or 2 nodes: nothing to reorder
    }
    // 2) cut at the middle: the first half keeps the middle node
    let meio = (n + 1) / 2;
    let mut segundo = None;
    {
        let mut atual: Option<&mut Box<ListNode>> = head.as_mut();
        for _ in 0..meio - 1 {
            atual = atual.and_then(|x| x.next.as_mut());
        }
        if let Some(x) = atual {
            segundo = x.next.take();
        }
    }
    // 3) reverse the second half
    let mut rev = None;
    let mut no = segundo;
    while let Some(mut x) = no {
        let proximo = x.next.take();
        x.next = rev;
        rev = Some(x);
        no = proximo;
    }
    // 4) interleave A0, B0, A1, B1, ...
    let mut a = head.take();
    let mut b = rev;
    let mut saida = None;
    let mut cauda = &mut saida;
    loop {
        match a.take() {
            Some(mut no) => {
                a = no.next.take();
                cauda = Self::anexar(cauda, Some(no));
            }
            None => break,
        }
        match b.take() {
            Some(mut no) => {
                b = no.next.take();
                cauda = Self::anexar(cauda, Some(no));
            }
            None => break,
        }
    }
    *head = saida;
}
}

anexar (append) reuses the &mut tail between iterations (the borrow checker won’t let two &muts to the same node be alive at once):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn anexar<'a>(cauda: &'a mut Option<Box<ListNode>>, no: Option<Box<ListNode>>)
    -> &'a mut Option<Box<ListNode>> {
    *cauda = no;
    &mut cauda.as_mut().unwrap().next
}
}

C++

void reorderList(ListNode* head) {
    if (!head) return;
    // 1) middle with slow/fast
    ListNode* lento = head;
    ListNode* rapido = head;
    while (rapido->next && rapido->next->next) {
        lento = lento->next;
        rapido = rapido->next->next;
    }
    // 2) cut and reverse the second half
    ListNode* segunda = lento->next;
    lento->next = nullptr;
    ListNode* anterior = nullptr;
    while (segunda) {
        ListNode* proximo = segunda->next;
        segunda->next = anterior;
        anterior = segunda;
        segunda = proximo;
    }
    // 3) interleave A0, B0, A1, B1...
    ListNode* primeira = head;
    segunda = anterior;
    while (segunda) {
        ListNode *n1 = primeira->next, *n2 = segunda->next;
        primeira->next = segunda;
        segunda->next = n1;
        primeira = n1;
        segunda = n2;
    }
}

C

void reorderList(struct ListNode* head) {
    if (!head) return;
    struct ListNode* lento = head;
    struct ListNode* rapido = head;
    while (rapido->next && rapido->next->next) {
        lento = lento->next;
        rapido = rapido->next->next;
    }
    struct ListNode* segunda = lento->next;
    lento->next = NULL;
    struct ListNode* anterior = NULL;
    while (segunda) {
        struct ListNode* proximo = segunda->next;
        segunda->next = anterior;
        anterior = segunda;
        segunda = proximo;
    }
    struct ListNode* primeira = head;
    segunda = anterior;
    while (segunda) {
        struct ListNode* n1 = primeira->next;
        struct ListNode* n2 = segunda->next;
        primeira->next = segunda;
        segunda->next = n1;
        primeira = n1;
        segunda = n2;
    }
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — find the middle (n/2), reverse (n/2), interleave (n).
  • Space: O(1) — local pointers. (An array of nodes would solve it with O(n); the interview asks for the in-place one.)

Pitfalls

  • Cut the list in two (lento.next = None) before reversing — without the cut, the reversal leaks into the first half.
  • Odd n: the middle node is the last node of the answer; the while segunda stops before flipping the order (the first half has one extra node).
  • In C++/C rapido->next->next can only be read when rapido->next is not NULL (the while condition already guarantees it).
  • In Rust: without anexar re-borrowing the tail, the interleave turns into a fight with the borrow checker — the &mut cauda.as_mut().unwrap().next pattern is what advances the tail without holding two borrows.

19. Remove Nth Node From End of List (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list/ · Topic: Linked List · Two Pointers

Problem (summary)

Remove the n-th node from the end of a linked list (in one pass, without knowing the size) and return the head (which may change if the removed node is the first). n is always valid (1 ≤ n ≤ size).

head = [1,2,3,4,5], n = 2  →  [1,2,3,5]
head = [1], n = 1          →  []
head = [1,2], n = 2        →  [2]   (removes the head)

Pattern — what to memorize

Two-pointer window with a sentinel: l and r start at the sentinel; r advances n steps; then both walk together until r reaches the end. At that point l sits exactly before the node to remove — “skip” the node. The sentinel kills the special case of removing the head. Clue: n-th from the end + one pass → keep a distance of n with two pointers.

Python

def removeNthFromEnd(self, head: Optional[ListNode], n: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
    sentinela = ListNode(0, head)
    l = r = sentinela
    for _ in range(n):
        r = r.next                     # open the window of n
    while r.next:                      # push until the end
        r = r.next
        l = l.next
    l.next = l.next.next               # "skip" the node
    return sentinela.next

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn remove_nth_from_end(mut head: Option<Box<ListNode>>, n: i32) -> Option<Box<ListNode>> {
    // Box gives single ownership, so two pointers advancing together won't
    // compile: find the index from the length and remove by position.
    let mut tamanho = 0usize;
    {
        let mut no = head.as_ref();
        while let Some(x) = no {
            tamanho += 1;
            no = x.next.as_ref();
        }
    }
    let alvo = tamanho - n as usize; // 0-based index of the node to remove
    if alvo == 0 {
        return head.and_then(|x| x.next); // removes the head itself
    }
    // walk to the node BEFORE the target
    let mut cursor: Option<&mut Box<ListNode>> = head.as_mut();
    for _ in 0..alvo - 1 {
        cursor = cursor.and_then(|x| x.next.as_mut());
    }
    if let Some(x) = cursor {
        let saltado = x.next.take();
        x.next = saltado.and_then(|no| no.next);
    }
    head
}
}

C++

ListNode* removeNthFromEnd(ListNode* head, int n) {
    // dummy: removes the head without a special case
    ListNode* dummy = new ListNode(0, head);
    ListNode *l = dummy, *r = dummy;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) r = r->next;   // open the window of n
    while (r->next) {                            // push until the end
        r = r->next;
        l = l->next;
    }
    ListNode* alvo = l->next;
    l->next = l->next->next;                     // "skip" the node
    delete alvo;
    ListNode* resp = dummy->next;
    delete dummy;
    return resp;
}

C

struct ListNode* removeNthFromEnd(struct ListNode* head, int n) {
    struct ListNode sentinela;  /* on the stack: removes the head without a special case */
    sentinela.next = head;
    struct ListNode *l = &sentinela, *r = &sentinela;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) r = r->next;   /* open the window of n */
    while (r->next) {                           /* push until the end */
        r = r->next;
        l = l->next;
    }
    struct ListNode* alvo = l->next;
    l->next = l->next->next;                    /* "skip" the node */
    free(alvo);
    return sentinela.next;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — the r pointer crosses the list once in total (n opening steps + (size − n) pushing steps).
  • Space: O(1) — two pointers (+ the sentinel).

Pitfalls

  • N-th from the end = index tamanho - n (0-based) — the sentinel + window avoids computing the size (in the “one pass” version).
  • Removing the head: without a sentinel you need a special case (head = head.next).
  • The window opens with n steps from the sentinel: for n = 1 ([1,2], ends as [1]), r stops at the last node and l lands on the node before the target.
  • In C++ the dummy is allocated and must be freed (intentionally here) — the removed node too; LeetCode frees what you return.
  • In Rust, with Box the “two pointers” won’t compile (two owners): compute the length and walk a &mut cursor — same O(n) order of magnitude.

138. Copy List with Random Pointer (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/copy-list-with-random-pointer/ · Topic: Linked List · Hash Table

Problem (summary)

A linked list where each node has val, next and random (a pointer to any node — or null). Return a deep copy: NEW nodes, with the same next and random structure (a copy node’s random must point to the corresponding copy node, never to an original).

head = [[7,null],[13,0],[11,4],[10,2],[1,0]]  →  [[7,null],[13,0],[11,4],[10,2],[1,0]]
head = []  →  []

Pattern — what to memorize

Two strategies in your pocket:

  1. HashMap (easiest to reason about): first pass creates the new nodes in a original → copy map; second pass wires next/random by translating through the map. O(n) space.
  2. Interleaving (O(1) space, the LeetCode “classic”): create each copy node RIGHT AFTER its original (A → A' → B → B'); the copy’s random = original’s random → next; then split the two lists apart. No map — the list layout itself is the translation table.

Clue: deep copy + random pointer → translating pointers between the two worlds is the essence.

Python

def copyRandomList(self, head: "Optional[Node]") -> "Optional[Node]":
    if not head:
        return None
    # 1) interleave copies: A -> A' -> B -> B'
    cur = head
    while cur:
        copia = Node(cur.val, cur.next)
        cur.next = copia
        cur = copia.next
    # 2) copies' random point to the copy of the target
    cur = head
    while cur:
        if cur.random:
            cur.next.random = cur.random.next
        cur = cur.next.next
    # 3) split apart (restore the original and chain the copies)
    sentinela = Node(0)
    copia_cur = sentinela
    cur = head
    while cur:
        copia = cur.next
        copia_cur.next = copia
        cur.next = copia.next
        cur = cur.next
        copia_cur = copia_cur.next
    return sentinela.next

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub fn copy_random_list(head: Option<Rc<RefCell<Node>>>) -> Option<Rc<RefCell<Node>>> {
    // HashMap origin -> copy approach (O(n) space): the natural one in Rust,
    // since the "interleaved" version (O(1) space) requires mutating the
    // original list in the middle — awkward with Rc.
    //
    // Rc<RefCell<Node>> does not implement Hash/Eq (recursive struct), so the
    // map key is the RAW POINTER `Rc::as_ptr(&no)` — safe because the
    // original nodes outlive the whole call.
    let mut mapa: HashMap<*const RefCell<Node>, Rc<RefCell<Node>>> = HashMap::new();

    let mut atual = head.clone();
    while let Some(no) = atual {
        let copia = Rc::new(RefCell::new(Node {
            val: no.borrow().val,
            next: None,
            random: None,
        }));
        mapa.insert(Rc::as_ptr(&no), copia);
        atual = no.borrow().next.clone();
    }
    let mut atual = head.clone();
    while let Some(no) = atual {
        let original = no.borrow();
        let copia = &mapa[&Rc::as_ptr(&no)];
        copia.borrow_mut().next = original
            .next
            .as_ref()
            .map(|n| mapa[&Rc::as_ptr(n)].clone());
        copia.borrow_mut().random = original
            .random
            .as_ref()
            .map(|r| mapa[&Rc::as_ptr(r)].clone());
        atual = original.next.clone();
    }
    head.as_ref().map(|h| mapa[&Rc::as_ptr(h)].clone())
}
}

C++

Node* copyRandomList(Node* head) {
    if (!head) return nullptr;
    unordered_map<Node*, Node*> mapa;   // original node -> copy
    Node* cur = head;
    while (cur) {
        mapa[cur] = new Node(cur->val); // 1) create disconnected copies
        cur = cur->next;
    }
    cur = head;
    auto copia = [&](Node* n) -> Node* { return n ? mapa[n] : nullptr; };
    while (cur) {                       // 2) wire next and random
        mapa[cur]->next = copia(cur->next);
        mapa[cur]->random = copia(cur->random);
        cur = cur->next;
    }
    return mapa[head];
}

C

struct Node* copyRandomList(struct Node* head) {
    if (!head) return NULL;
    /* 1) interleave copies: A -> A' -> B -> B' */
    struct Node* cur = head;
    while (cur) {
        struct Node* copia = (struct Node*)malloc(sizeof(struct Node));
        copia->val = cur->val;
        copia->next = cur->next;
        copia->random = NULL; /* filled in step 2 */
        cur->next = copia;
        cur = copia->next;
    }
    /* 2) copy's random = copy of the original's random (cur->random->next) */
    cur = head;
    while (cur) {
        struct Node* copia = cur->next;
        if (cur->random) copia->random = cur->random->next;
        cur = copia->next;
    }
    /* 3) split apart: restore the original and chain the copies */
    struct Node* sentinela = (struct Node*)malloc(sizeof(struct Node));
    struct Node* copia_cur = sentinela;
    cur = head;
    while (cur) {
        struct Node* copia = cur->next;
        copia_cur->next = copia;
        cur->next = copia->next;
        cur = cur->next;
        copia_cur = copia_cur->next;
    }
    copia_cur->next = NULL;
    struct Node* resp = sentinela->next;
    free(sentinela);
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — two (interleaving) or three (map) linear passes.
  • Space: O(1) with interleaving (just pointers); O(n) with the HashMap (n entries). Interviews usually expect both — offer the O(1) as the “senior” one and the map as the “safe” one.

Pitfalls

  • Copying the node is not enough: the random must be translated into the copy world (never point to an original — otherwise it’s not a deep copy).
  • random can be null — interleaving’s step 2 checks before reading cur->random->next.
  • Step 3 (splitting) is where most slip: each original node must point back to the next ORIGINAL (not the copy), and the copies must stay chained to each other, ending in NULL.
  • In C++/C (interleaving): the original is mutated in the middle — if the judge checks the original list afterwards (some cases do), step 3 restores it.
  • In Rust (map): mapa[cur] with nullable cur — the copia lambda wraps the null-safe translation; Rc::as_ptr is only safe because the originals are not dropped during the function.

146. LRU Cache (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/lru-cache/ · Topic: Design · Linked List · Hash Table

Problem (summary)

Design a Least Recently Used cache with two operations: get(key) returns the value (or −1) and put(key, value) inserts/updates — both O(1) on average. When capacity overflows, the item that has gone unused longest is evicted. A get or put on an existing key counts as “use”.

["LRUCache","put","put","get","put","get","put","get","get","get"]
[[2],[1,1],[2,2],[1],[3,3],[2],[4,4],[1],[3],[4]]
→ [null,null,null,1,null,-1,null,-1,3,4]

Pattern — what to memorize

HashMap + doubly linked list: the map gives O(1) key access; the list gives the usage order (most recent at the front, LRU at the back) with O(1) removal/insertion at any position (that’s why it’s doubly linked). Every operation follows the ritual: found → unlink the node from the list (remove) and relink at the front (insert); overflow → throw away the tail node. Depending on who asks, mentioning collections.OrderedDict in Python is worth it — but the educational version (the interview one) is the hand-rolled list. Clue: cache with age-based eviction → the structure that “remembers order” is the linked list.

Python

class NoLRU:
    __slots__ = ("chave", "valor", "ant", "prox")
    def __init__(self, chave=0, valor=0):
        self.chave = chave
        self.valor = valor
        self.ant = self.prox = None

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.mapa: dict[int, NoLRU] = {}
        self.cabeca = NoLRU()  # sentinel on the most-recent (MRU) side
        self.cauda = NoLRU()   # sentinel on the oldest (LRU) side
        self.cabeca.prox = self.cauda
        self.cauda.ant = self.cabeca

    def _remover(self, no: NoLRU) -> None:
        no.ant.prox = no.prox
        no.prox.ant = no.ant

    def _inserir_inicio(self, no: NoLRU) -> None:
        no.prox = self.cabeca.prox
        no.ant = self.cabeca
        self.cabeca.prox.ant = no
        self.cabeca.prox = no

    def get(self, key: int) -> int:
        no = self.mapa.get(key)
        if no is None:
            return -1
        self._remover(no)
        self._inserir_inicio(no)
        return no.valor

    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
        if key in self.mapa:
            no = self.mapa[key]
            no.valor = value
            self._remover(no)
            self._inserir_inicio(no)
            return
        if len(self.mapa) == self.cap:
            # remove the LRU (the real node right before the tail sentinel)
            lru = self.cauda.ant
            self._remover(lru)
            del self.mapa[lru.chave]
        novo = NoLRU(key, value)
        self.mapa[key] = novo
        self._inserir_inicio(novo)

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::rc::{Rc, Weak};

struct No {
    chave: i32,
    valor: i32,
    anterior: Option<Weak<RefCell<No>>>, // Weak avoids a reference cycle
    proximo: Option<Rc<RefCell<No>>>,
}
impl No {
    fn novo(chave: i32, valor: i32) -> Rc<RefCell<No>> {
        Rc::new(RefCell::new(No { chave, valor, anterior: None, proximo: None }))
    }
}

pub struct LRUCache {
    capacidade: usize,
    mapa: HashMap<i32, Rc<RefCell<No>>>,
    // Head sentinel: most-recent (MRU) side; tail sentinel: oldest (LRU) side.
    cabeca: Rc<RefCell<No>>,
    cauda: Rc<RefCell<No>>,
}

impl LRUCache {
    pub fn new(capacity: i32) -> Self {
        let cabeca = No::novo(0, 0);
        let cauda = No::novo(0, 0);
        cabeca.borrow_mut().proximo = Some(cauda.clone());
        cauda.borrow_mut().anterior = Some(Rc::downgrade(&cabeca));
        LRUCache { capacidade: capacity as usize, mapa: HashMap::new(), cabeca, cauda }
    }

    fn remover(&self, no: &Rc<RefCell<No>>) {
        let ant = no.borrow().anterior.as_ref().and_then(Weak::upgrade).expect("node without previous");
        let prox = no.borrow().proximo.clone().expect("node without next");
        ant.borrow_mut().proximo = Some(prox.clone());
        prox.borrow_mut().anterior = Some(Rc::downgrade(&ant));
    }

    fn inserir_inicio(&self, no: &Rc<RefCell<No>>) {
        let proximo_atual = self.cabeca.borrow().proximo.clone().expect("head always has a next");
        no.borrow_mut().anterior = Some(Rc::downgrade(&self.cabeca));
        no.borrow_mut().proximo = Some(proximo_atual.clone());
        proximo_atual.borrow_mut().anterior = Some(Rc::downgrade(no));
        self.cabeca.borrow_mut().proximo = Some(no.clone());
    }

    pub fn get(&mut self, chave: i32) -> i32 {
        match self.mapa.get(&chave) {
            Some(no) => {
                let no = no.clone();
                self.remover(&no);
                self.inserir_inicio(&no);
                // stash the value in a local: the temporary Ref must die
                // before the block ends (the local `no` drops together)
                let valor = no.borrow().valor;
                valor
            }
            None => -1,
        }
    }

    pub fn put(&mut self, chave: i32, valor: i32) {
        if let Some(no) = self.mapa.get(&chave) {
            let no = no.clone();
            no.borrow_mut().valor = valor;
            self.remover(&no);
            self.inserir_inicio(&no);
            return;
        }
        if self.mapa.len() == self.capacidade {
            // LRU is the real node right before the tail sentinel
            let lru = self.cauda.borrow().anterior.as_ref().and_then(Weak::upgrade)
                .expect("cache full without an LRU");
            let chave_lru = lru.borrow().chave;
            self.remover(&lru);
            self.mapa.remove(&chave_lru);
        }
        let no = No::novo(chave, valor);
        self.inserir_inicio(&no);
        self.mapa.insert(chave, no);
    }
}
}

C++

class LRUCache {
    int cap;
    list<pair<int, int>> cache; // MRU at the front, LRU at the back
    unordered_map<int, list<pair<int, int>>::iterator> mapa;
public:
    LRUCache(int capacity) : cap(capacity) {}

    int get(int key) {
        auto it = mapa.find(key);
        if (it == mapa.end()) return -1;
        // splice moves the node to the front WITHOUT allocating (O(1))
        cache.splice(cache.begin(), cache, it->second);
        return it->second->second;
    }

    void put(int key, int value) {
        auto it = mapa.find(key);
        if (it != mapa.end()) {
            it->second->second = value; // update the value
            cache.splice(cache.begin(), cache, it->second);
            return;
        }
        if ((int)cache.size() == cap) {
            auto [chave_lru, _] = cache.back(); // structured binding
            mapa.erase(chave_lru);
            cache.pop_back();
        }
        cache.emplace_front(key, value);
        mapa[key] = cache.begin();
    }
};

C

/* Documented simplification: indexed arrays (nodes in 0..cap-1, sentinels
 * head=cap and tail=cap+1) instead of pointers — cache-friendly and no
 * malloc/free per operation, a common pattern among top C answers.
 * Hash: power-of-2 open addressing (linear probing, with EMPTY/ACTIVE/
 * TOMBSTONE states so removal doesn't break the probe chain).
 */
typedef struct {
    int capacidade;
    int tamanho;
    int* chave; /* per slot 0..capacidade+1 (the last 2 are the sentinels) */
    int* valor;
    int* ant;
    int* prox;
    unsigned hash_cap; /* power of 2 */
    int* hash_chave;
    int* hash_slot;
    char* hash_estado; /* 0=EMPTY, 1=ACTIVE, 2=TOMBSTONE */
    int* livres;       /* stack of free slots */
    int topo_livres;
    int cabeca; /* index of the MRU-side sentinel */
    int cauda;  /* index of the LRU-side sentinel */
} LRUCache;

static unsigned hash_int(int chave, unsigned cap) {
    return ((unsigned)chave * 2654435761u) & (cap - 1); /* Knuth multiplicative */
}

static int achar(LRUCache* c, int chave) {
    unsigned i = hash_int(chave, c->hash_cap);
    while (c->hash_estado[i] != 0) {
        if (c->hash_estado[i] == 1 && c->hash_chave[i] == chave) return c->hash_slot[i];
        i = (i + 1) & (c->hash_cap - 1);
    }
    return -1;
}

static void inserir_hash(LRUCache* c, int chave, int slot) {
    unsigned i = hash_int(chave, c->hash_cap);
    while (c->hash_estado[i] == 1) i = (i + 1) & (c->hash_cap - 1);
    c->hash_chave[i] = chave;
    c->hash_slot[i] = slot;
    c->hash_estado[i] = 1;
}

static void remover_hash(LRUCache* c, int chave) {
    unsigned i = hash_int(chave, c->hash_cap);
    while (c->hash_estado[i] != 0) {
        if (c->hash_estado[i] == 1 && c->hash_chave[i] == chave) {
            c->hash_estado[i] = 2; /* TOMBSTONE: marks the entry without breaking the chain */
            return;
        }
        i = (i + 1) & (c->hash_cap - 1);
    }
}

static void remover_no(LRUCache* c, int no) {
    c->prox[c->ant[no]] = c->prox[no];
    c->ant[c->prox[no]] = c->ant[no];
}

static void inserir_inicio(LRUCache* c, int no) {
    int primeiro = c->prox[c->cabeca];
    c->prox[no] = primeiro;
    c->ant[no] = c->cabeca;
    c->prox[c->cabeca] = no;
    c->ant[primeiro] = no;
}

LRUCache* lruCacheCreate(int capacity) {
    LRUCache* c = (LRUCache*)calloc(1, sizeof(LRUCache));
    int total = capacity + 2;
    c->capacidade = capacity;
    c->chave = (int*)malloc(total * sizeof(int));
    c->valor = (int*)malloc(total * sizeof(int));
    c->ant = (int*)malloc(total * sizeof(int));
    c->prox = (int*)malloc(total * sizeof(int));
    c->livres = (int*)malloc(capacity * sizeof(int));
    for (int i = 0; i < capacity; i++) c->livres[i] = capacity - 1 - i; /* top = 0 */
    c->topo_livres = capacity;
    c->cabeca = capacity;
    c->cauda = capacity + 1;
    c->prox[c->cabeca] = c->cauda;
    c->ant[c->cauda] = c->cabeca;
    /* hash: power of 2 >= 4*cap (holds ACTIVE+TOMBSTONE without filling up) */
    unsigned cap = 16;
    while (cap < (unsigned)capacity * 4) cap <<= 1;
    c->hash_cap = cap;
    c->hash_chave = (int*)malloc(cap * sizeof(int));
    c->hash_slot = (int*)malloc(cap * sizeof(int));
    c->hash_estado = (char*)calloc(cap, 1);
    return c;
}

int lruCacheGet(LRUCache* obj, int key) {
    int slot = achar(obj, key);
    if (slot == -1) return -1;
    remover_no(obj, slot);
    inserir_inicio(obj, slot);
    return obj->valor[slot];
}

void lruCachePut(LRUCache* obj, int key, int value) {
    int slot = achar(obj, key);
    if (slot != -1) {
        obj->valor[slot] = value;
        remover_no(obj, slot);
        inserir_inicio(obj, slot);
        return;
    }
    if (obj->tamanho == obj->capacidade) {
        int lru = obj->ant[obj->cauda];
        remover_no(obj, lru);
        remover_hash(obj, obj->chave[lru]);
        obj->livres[obj->topo_livres++] = lru; /* return the slot to the stack */
        obj->tamanho--;
    }
    int novo = obj->livres[--obj->topo_livres];
    obj->chave[novo] = key;
    obj->valor[novo] = value;
    inserir_hash(obj, key, novo);
    inserir_inicio(obj, novo);
    obj->tamanho++;
}

void lruCacheFree(LRUCache* obj) {
    free(obj->chave); free(obj->valor); free(obj->ant); free(obj->prox);
    free(obj->livres); free(obj->hash_chave); free(obj->hash_slot);
    free(obj->hash_estado); free(obj);
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(1) amortized for get and put — O(1) hash + O(1) removal/insertion of the doubly linked list (C++’s splice and the ant/prox pointers in the others).
  • Space: O(capacity) — the map + the nodes = at most capacity live entries.

Pitfalls

  • put on an existing key updates the value AND moves it to “most recent” (does not count as a new insertion, does not evict anything).
  • The sentinels (head/tail) simplify things: without them, “remove the LRU when the list has 1 node” becomes an extra if.
  • The evicted node is the real node before the tail — the tail itself never leaves the list.
  • In Python: the official shortcut is collections.OrderedDict (move_to_end + popitem(last=False)) — show the hand-rolled version first and mention the shortcut.
  • In Rust: Weak for the backward pointer avoids the reference cycle (Rc ↔ Rc is never dropped); RefCell borrows must die before the end of the block (hence let valor = no.borrow().valor;).
  • In C: removal in a linear-probing hash needs the TOMBSTONE state (otherwise future probe chains “die” in a hole); say the indexed-array simplification out loud: “same doubly linked list, but with indices instead of pointers”.

2. Add Two Numbers (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/add-two-numbers/ · Topic: Linked List

Problem (summary)

Two linked lists represent non-negative numbers with the digits in reverse order (each node is 0..9; no leading zeros except the number 0 itself). Add the two numbers and return the sum in the same representation (reversed digits).

l1 = [2,4,3] (342), l2 = [5,6,4] (465)  →  [7,0,8] (807)
l1 = [9,9,9,9,9,9,9], l2 = [9,9,9,9]    →  [8,9,9,9,0,0,0,1]

Pattern — what to memorize

Dummy head + carry, always adding the same digit in front of both lists: because the representation is reversed, the first node is the units — the sum comes out naturally left to right. The carry comes from the division by 10 and the new node from the remainder; the loop continues while l1, l2 or carry remains — this condition covers the edge of a final carry becoming an extra node (99 + 1 = 100). Clue: digit sum + carry → the same skeleton as pencil-and-paper addition; reversed representation → no stack, nothing to reverse.

Python

class Solution:
    def addTwoNumbers(self, l1: Optional[ListNode], l2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        sentinela = ListNode()                 # disposable head
        cur = sentinela
        carry = 0
        while l1 or l2 or carry:
            soma = carry
            if l1:
                soma += l1.val
                l1 = l1.next
            if l2:
                soma += l2.val
                l2 = l2.next
            cur.next = ListNode(soma % 10)
            cur = cur.next
            carry = soma // 10
        return sentinela.next

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn add_two_numbers(
        mut l1: Option<Box<ListNode>>,
        mut l2: Option<Box<ListNode>>,
    ) -> Option<Box<ListNode>> {
        // "Leaked" dummy: a Box the owner discards at the end while the tail
        // grows through &mut — the idiom for building a linked list by hand.
        let mut dummy = Box::new(ListNode::new(0));
        let mut cauda = &mut *dummy;
        let mut carry = 0;
        while l1.is_some() || l2.is_some() || carry != 0 {
            let mut soma = carry;
            if let Some(no) = l1 {
                soma += no.val;
                l1 = no.next;
            }
            if let Some(no) = l2 {
                soma += no.val;
                l2 = no.next;
            }
            carry = soma / 10;
            cauda.next = Some(Box::new(ListNode::new(soma % 10)));
            cauda = cauda.next.as_mut().unwrap(); // we just allocated it
        }
        dummy.next
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* addTwoNumbers(ListNode* l1, ListNode* l2) {
        ListNode sentinela(0);          // disposable head
        ListNode* cur = &sentinela;
        int carry = 0;
        while (l1 || l2 || carry) {
            int soma = carry;
            if (l1) { soma += l1->val; l1 = l1->next; }
            if (l2) { soma += l2->val; l2 = l2->next; }
            cur->next = new ListNode(soma % 10);
            cur = cur->next;
            carry = soma / 10;
        }
        return sentinela.next;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

struct ListNode* addTwoNumbers(struct ListNode* l1, struct ListNode* l2) {
    struct ListNode sentinela;          /* disposable head on the stack */
    sentinela.next = NULL;
    struct ListNode* cur = &sentinela;
    int carry = 0;
    while (l1 || l2 || carry) {
        int soma = carry;
        if (l1) { soma += l1->val; l1 = l1->next; }
        if (l2) { soma += l2->val; l2 = l2->next; }
        cur->next = (struct ListNode*)malloc(sizeof(struct ListNode));
        cur->next->val = soma % 10;
        cur->next->next = NULL;
        cur = cur->next;
        carry = soma / 10;
    }
    return sentinela.next;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(max(n, m)) — one pass over the nodes of both lists, plus the carry tail at the end.
  • Space: O(max(n, m)) — the output list, plus O(1) auxiliary (the dummy and the carry). No input list is modified or copied.

Pitfalls

  • Trailing carry: [9,9] + [1] → [0,0,1] — the while ... || carry is what creates the extra node; forgetting || carry is the classic mistake.
  • The shorter list ends first: the if l1: ... condition zeroes its contribution without stalling the sum.
  • soma % 10 goes into the node and soma / 10 becomes the carry — in that order; using soma after the division corrupts the digit.
  • The sum of two digits ≤ 9 + carry ≤ 1 never exceeds 19 → no int overflow (but the digit is still soma % 10).
  • In Rust: the “leaked dummy” pattern (Box + cauda = &mut *dummy) compiles with NLL; the Rc<RefCell> alternative is unnecessary — the nodes are Box, single ownership.
  • In C: each malloc must set the new node’s next = NULL — the cur->next = malloc; ...; cur = cur->next sequence is what doesn’t lose the allocated node.

287. Find the Duplicate Number (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/find-the-duplicate-number/ · Topic: Linked List

Problem (summary)

Array of n+1 integers with values in [1, n]; exactly one number repeats (it can repeat 2+ times). Find it without modifying the array and with O(1) extra space.

nums = [1,3,4,2,2]  →  2
nums = [3,1,3,4,2]  →  3

Pattern — what to memorize

Floyd (tortoise and hare) on the functional graph i → nums[i]: because the values are in [1, n] and the array has n+1 positions, nums[i] always indexes a valid position — so the jump chain starts at index 0 (which no value points to, since no value is 0) and enters a cycle. The cycle exists because there are more nodes than distinct values; the cycle’s entry point is the duplicate (the only value with two predecessors: one from outside and one from inside the cycle). Draw the graph of [1,3,4,2,2] and memorize it. The statement’s constraints forbid sorting, using a set and mutating the array — that’s what pushes you to the pointer cycle. Citable alternative: binary search over the value (count how many elements are ≤ mid).

Python

class Solution:
    def findDuplicate(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        # "i -> nums[i]" is a functional graph: values in 1..n index the array.
        # Phase 1: the tortoise and the hare meet inside the cycle.
        lenta = nums[0]
        rapida = nums[nums[0]]
        while lenta != rapida:
            lenta = nums[lenta]
            rapida = nums[nums[rapida]]
        # Phase 2: same speed from index 0 finds the cycle ENTRY — the only
        # node with two predecessors, which is the duplicate.
        lenta = 0
        while lenta != rapida:
            lenta = nums[lenta]
            rapida = nums[rapida]
        return lenta

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn find_duplicate(nums: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
        // "i -> nums[i]" forms a functional graph with a cycle.
        let mut lenta = nums[0];
        let mut rapida = nums[nums[0] as usize];
        while lenta != rapida {
            lenta = nums[lenta as usize];
            rapida = nums[nums[rapida as usize] as usize];
        }
        // phase 2: cycle entry = the duplicate (the only node with 2 parents)
        lenta = 0;
        while lenta != rapida {
            lenta = nums[lenta as usize];
            rapida = nums[rapida as usize];
        }
        lenta
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int findDuplicate(vector<int>& nums) {
        int lenta = nums[0];
        int rapida = nums[nums[0]];
        while (lenta != rapida) {
            lenta = nums[lenta];
            rapida = nums[nums[rapida]];
        }
        lenta = 0;
        while (lenta != rapida) {
            lenta = nums[lenta];
            rapida = nums[rapida];
        }
        return lenta;
    }
};

C

int findDuplicate(int* nums, int numsSize) {
    (void)numsSize;   /* the size is irrelevant: the cycle is guaranteed */
    int lenta = nums[0];
    int rapida = nums[nums[0]];
    while (lenta != rapida) {
        lenta = nums[lenta];
        rapida = nums[nums[rapida]];
    }
    lenta = 0;
    while (lenta != rapida) {
        lenta = nums[lenta];
        rapida = nums[rapida];
    }
    return lenta;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — both Floyd phases are linear in the chain + cycle.
  • Space: O(1) — just two pointers/indices; the array is not modified (satisfies the constraints: no sort, no set, no mutation).

Pitfalls

  • The answer is the cycle entry, not phase 1’s meeting point — phase 2 (two walkers at the same speed, one starting from 0) is what finds it.
  • Start at nums[0] (index 0): it’s the only node no value points to (values go from 1 to n), so it sits outside the cycle — the entry is never 0.
  • The duplicated value can be at the start or end of the cycle — the algorithm doesn’t care; [2,2,2,2,2] and [1,1] are valid cases (and pass).
  • Don’t index nums[rapida] without checking the index: in Python/C++ the value IS the position (the indices are the values themselves); in Rust the as usize before indexing is mandatory.
  • “I can’t sort or use a set” is the pattern clue: say the prohibitions out loud before drawing the graph.
  • Alternative to mention: binary search over the value (not the index) — count from mid down and narrow the range — O(n log n), O(1).
