23. Merge k Sorted Lists (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/merge-k-sorted-lists/ · Topic: Linked List

Problem (summary)

An array of k ascending linked lists (some may be empty, and k = 0 is allowed). Merge into ONE ascending list reusing the existing nodes (without allocating new ones). The order must be stable with respect to equal values across lists (no tie-break rule beyond the values themselves).

lists = [[1,4,5],[1,3,4],[2,6]]  →  [1,1,2,3,4,4,5,6]
lists = []                       →  []

Pattern — what to memorize

Min-heap of the k heads, O(N log k): at each step the smallest live node (the heap holds the k current heads) comes out and the next node of its list comes in — picking the minimum among k candidates becomes O(log k) instead of O(k). Clue: several sorted structures → the natural extension of the two-list merge (the Merge Two Sorted Lists skeleton) with the heap in place of the if <=. Heap-free alternative: pairwise merge in rounds (divide and conquer, Merge Sort style): merge 2-by-2 until one remains — same O(N log k), O(1) space.

Python

class Solution:
    def mergeKLists(self, lists: list[Optional[ListNode]]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        sentinela = ListNode()
        cur = sentinela
        # min-heap of heads: (value, index, node) — the index breaks ties
        # between equal values without comparing the nodes themselves.
        heap = [(no.val, i, no) for i, no in enumerate(lists) if no]
        heapq.heapify(heap)
        while heap:
            _, i, no = heapq.heappop(heap)
            cur.next = no
            cur = cur.next
            if no.next:
                heapq.heappush(heap, (no.next.val, i, no.next))
        return sentinela.next

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cmp::Ordering;
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

// BinaryHeap is a max-heap; this wrapper inverts the order and compares
// only the value. The whole node (Box) travels in the heap — no Rc/RefCell
// or external index needed.
struct NoMenor(Box<ListNode>);

impl PartialEq for NoMenor {
    fn eq(&self, outro: &Self) -> bool {
        self.0.val == outro.0.val
    }
}
impl Eq for NoMenor {}
impl PartialOrd for NoMenor {
    fn partial_cmp(&self, outro: &Self) -> Option<Ordering> {
        Some(self.cmp(outro))
    }
}
impl Ord for NoMenor {
    fn cmp(&self, outro: &Self) -> Ordering {
        // inverted: the smallest value becomes the "maximum" of the
        // max-heap (comes out first)
        outro.0.val.cmp(&self.0.val)
    }
}

impl Solution {
    pub fn merge_k_lists(lists: Vec<Option<Box<ListNode>>>) -> Option<Box<ListNode>> {
        let mut heap = BinaryHeap::new();
        for lista in lists {
            if let Some(no) = lista {
                heap.push(NoMenor(no));
            }
        }
        let mut dummy = Box::new(ListNode::new(0));
        let mut cauda = &mut *dummy;
        while let Some(NoMenor(menor)) = heap.pop() {
            cauda.next = Some(menor);
            cauda = cauda.next.as_mut().unwrap();
            let resto = cauda.next.take(); // the tail of the node that just came out
            if let Some(proximo) = resto {
                heap.push(NoMenor(proximo));
            }
        }
        dummy.next
    }
}
}

C++

#include <queue>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

// min-heap of heads: inverts the priority_queue order (which is a max-heap)
struct Cmp {
    bool operator()(ListNode* a, ListNode* b) const { return a->val > b->val; }
};

class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* mergeKLists(vector<ListNode*>& lists) {
        priority_queue<ListNode*, vector<ListNode*>, Cmp> heap;
        for (ListNode* no : lists) if (no) heap.push(no);

        ListNode sentinela(0);
        ListNode* cur = &sentinela;
        while (!heap.empty()) {
            ListNode* menor = heap.top();
            heap.pop();
            cur->next = menor;
            cur = cur->next;
            if (menor->next) heap.push(menor->next);
        }
        return sentinela.next;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

/* merge of two sorted lists (same skeleton as Merge Two Sorted Lists) */
static struct ListNode* fundir(struct ListNode* a, struct ListNode* b) {
    struct ListNode sentinela;
    sentinela.next = NULL;
    struct ListNode* cur = &sentinela;
    while (a && b) {
        if (a->val <= b->val) { cur->next = a; a = a->next; }
        else { cur->next = b; b = b->next; }
        cur = cur->next;
    }
    cur->next = a ? a : b;
    return sentinela.next;
}

struct ListNode* mergeKLists(struct ListNode** lists, int listsSize) {
    if (listsSize == 0) return NULL;
    /* pairwise (divide and conquer): merge in rounds until 1 list remains */
    while (listsSize > 1) {
        int escrita = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i + 1 < listsSize; i += 2)
            lists[escrita++] = fundir(lists[i], lists[i + 1]);
        if (listsSize % 2 == 1)
            lists[escrita++] = lists[listsSize - 1];
        listsSize = escrita;
    }
    return lists[0];
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(N log k) — N = total nodes; each push/pop is O(log k), and each node enters and leaves once. The C pairwise version costs the same (log k rounds).
  • Space: O(k) — the heap holds up to k heads (plus the dummy). The pairwise version is O(1) extra (works on the lists array itself).

Pitfalls

  • k = 0 and k empty lists: the heap starts empty and the dummy returns NULL — no extra special case (only C needs the if (listsSize == 0)).
  • Each list emits the same node object (no new/clone): when you connect cur->next = menor, the rest of its list stays alive — that’s where the next push comes from.
  • In Python the heap tuple needs the index to break ties between equal values ((val, idx, no)) — without it Python tries to compare the ListNodes.
  • In Rust BinaryHeap is a max-heap, so the key is inverting the cmp; the hand-written Ord compares only val (nodes with equal values compare equal — valid, and it doesn’t break the heap). Alternative that also compiles: heap of (val, index) keeping the heads in a separate Vec.
  • In C++ the priority_queue comparator returns a->val > b->val — the queue’s “largest” is the smallest value. Cmp must live outside the class (the template parameter can’t access a private member).
  • Rust’s take() is C’s /= next: it detaches the tail after the step completes, so cauda.next.as_mut() points to the node that just came out.

25. Reverse Nodes in k-Group (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/reverse-nodes-in-k-group/ · Topic: Linked List

Problem (summary)

Given a linked list, reverse the nodes in groups of k; a final group with fewer than k nodes stays untouched (no partial reversal). Only the existing nodes — no new ones.

head = [1,2,3,4,5], k = 2  →  [2,1,4,3,5]
head = [1,2,3,4,5], k = 3  →  [3,2,1,4,5]

Pattern — what to memorize

Iterative with prev pointing just before the group: each round, (1) check that k nodes remain ahead — otherwise return the finished head — and (2) reverse the group by shifting, k-1 times, the first pending node to right after the group’s end. prev advances to the tail of the reversed group (the original first node), which is where the next group starts. Checking the k nodes before reversing is what separates a full group from the short final one. Alternative: recursion that reverses the first k and chains reverseKGroup(rest) — shorter and very quotable in an interview.

Python

class Solution:
    def reverseKGroup(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        sentinela = ListNode(0, head)
        prev = sentinela
        while True:
            # are there k nodes ahead? if not, the answer is ready
            fim = prev
            for _ in range(k):
                fim = fim.next
                if fim is None:
                    return sentinela.next
            # reverse the group: k-1 times, shift the first pending node
            # to right after `fim` (which becomes the group's new head)
            inicio = prev.next              # will be the reversed group's tail
            for _ in range(k - 1):
                mover = prev.next
                prev.next = mover.next
                mover.next = fim.next
                fim.next = mover
            prev = inicio

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn reverse_k_group(head: Option<Box<ListNode>>, k: i32) -> Option<Box<ListNode>> {
        let k = k as usize;
        // are there k nodes left? if not, return the list as is (short final group)
        let mut cursor = &head;
        for _ in 0..k {
            match cursor {
                Some(no) => cursor = &no.next,
                None => return head,
            }
        }
        // reverse the first k nodes without touching the rest
        let mut prev = None;
        let mut atual = head;
        for _ in 0..k {
            let mut no = atual.unwrap(); // guaranteed by the check above
            let proximo = no.next.take();
            no.next = prev;
            prev = Some(no);
            atual = proximo;
        }
        // attach the rest (recursively) to the reversed group's tail
        let resto = Self::reverse_k_group(atual, k as i32);
        let mut fim = &mut prev;
        while let Some(ref mut no) = fim {
            fim = &mut no.next;
        }
        *fim = resto;
        prev
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* reverseKGroup(ListNode* head, int k) {
        ListNode sentinela(0, head);
        ListNode* prev = &sentinela;
        while (true) {
            ListNode* fim = prev;
            for (int i = 0; i < k; ++i) {       // are there k nodes ahead?
                fim = fim->next;
                if (!fim) return sentinela.next;
            }
            ListNode* inicio = prev->next;      // will be the group's tail
            for (int i = 0; i < k - 1; ++i) {   // attach the first pending node
                ListNode* mover = prev->next;
                prev->next = mover->next;
                mover->next = fim->next;
                fim->next = mover;
            }
            prev = inicio;
        }
    }
};

C

struct ListNode* reverseKGroup(struct ListNode* head, int k) {
    struct ListNode sentinela;          /* disposable head */
    sentinela.val = 0;
    sentinela.next = head;
    struct ListNode* prev = &sentinela;
    for (;;) {
        struct ListNode* fim = prev;
        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {      /* are there k nodes ahead? */
            fim = fim->next;
            if (!fim) return sentinela.next;   /* no: answer ready */
        }
        struct ListNode* inicio = prev->next;  /* will be the group's tail */
        for (int i = 0; i < k - 1; i++) {      /* attach the first pending node */
            struct ListNode* mover = prev->next;
            prev->next = mover->next;
            mover->next = fim->next;
            fim->next = mover;
        }
        prev = inicio;
    }
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each node of a full group is shifted k-1 times; in total each node takes part in exactly one reversal (O(1) per node).
  • Space: O(1) — just pointers (iterative). The recursion uses O(n/k) of call stack; the iterative version is the reference.

Pitfalls

  • Check the k nodes BEFORE reversing: reversing a partial group and only finding out later that a node was missing is the most common mistake; the check is a separate loop at the very start of each round.
  • prev advances to inicio (the reversed group’s tail — what used to be the group’s first node), not to fim/the new head — otherwise the next group is detected from the wrong place.
  • k = 1 → no reversal happens and the whole list comes out unchanged (the k - 1 = 0 loop runs zero times) — a good on-the-spot test case.
  • n not a multiple of k: does the last (shorter) group come out reversed back to original order? No — it stays intact: the check fails and the finished head is returned without touching it.
  • In Rust take() detaches next before reconnecting — that’s mover->next = fim->next with ownership; the recursion avoids the iterative loop with two simultaneous mutable pointers (which the borrow checker would reject).
  • In C/C++ the stack sentinel needs the next field initialized — forgetting sentinela.next = head loses the whole list.

226. Invert Binary Tree (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/invert-binary-tree/ · Topic: Trees (DFS)

Problem (summary)

Given the root of a binary tree, mirror the tree: at every node, the left and right children swap places (recursively). Return the root.

[4,2,7,1,3,6,9]  →  [4,7,2,9,6,3,1]
[]               →  []

Pattern — what to memorize

DFS in any order works: at each node, swap(left, right) and recurse into the children. It’s the simplest tree problem on LeetCode — the interview tests whether you don’t overcomplicate it. Clue: “invert/mirror”

  • recursive structure → swap the children at every node, pre- or post-order, doesn’t matter (the swap is self-contained per node).

Python

class Solution:
    def invertTree(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> TreeNode | None:
        if root is None:
            return None
        root.left, root.right = root.right, root.left  # swap without a temp
        self.invertTree(root.left)
        self.invertTree(root.right)
        return root

Iterative version (avoids recursion on a skewed tree): explicit node stack, while stack: node = stack.pop(); swap; push the children.

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn invert_tree(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>> {
        if let Some(no) = &root {
            let mut no = no.borrow_mut();
            // sequential take(): two `&mut` through the same RefMut don't
            // split the borrow — mem::swap(a, b) doesn't compile here.
            let inv = no.left.take();
            no.left = no.right.take();
            no.right = inv;
            let esq = no.left.clone(); // pragmatic clone: drop the borrow
            let dir = no.right.clone(); // before recursing (Rc only counts refs)
            drop(no);
            Self::invert_tree(esq);
            Self::invert_tree(dir);
        }
        root
    }
}
}

C++

#include <algorithm>
#include <utility> // std::swap
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    TreeNode* invertTree(TreeNode* root) {
        if (!root) return nullptr;
        swap(root->left, root->right); // std::swap swaps the pointers
        invertTree(root->left);
        invertTree(root->right);
        return root;
    }
};

C

#include <stddef.h> /* NULL */

struct TreeNode* invertTree(struct TreeNode* root) {
    if (!root) return NULL;
    struct TreeNode* tmp = root->left;
    root->left = root->right;
    root->right = tmp;
    invertTree(root->left);
    invertTree(root->right);
    return root;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — visits each node once; the swap is O(1) per node.
  • Space: O(h) recursion stack (h = height; worst case O(n) on a skewed tree). The iterative version with an explicit stack is O(h) of heap.

Pitfalls

  • The swap destroys the reference to the children: clone them (Rust) or stash them in a temp (C) BEFORE overwriting — in Python a, b = b, a already handles it.
  • Skewed tree (h = n): recursion in Python can blow the frame limit — when in doubt, use the iterative stack version.
  • Leaf and empty tree are valid cases; a leaf inverts into itself.
  • Rust: borrow_mut() can’t be alive when you recurse — clone and drop first (see code).

104. Maximum Depth of Binary Tree (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-depth-of-binary-tree/ · Topic: Trees (DFS)

Problem (summary)

Given the root of a binary tree, return its height (the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf). A null root is 0.

[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]  →  3   (path 3→20→15)
[1,null,2]               →  2
[]                       →  0

Pattern — what to memorize

Post-order that returns height: 1 + max(height(left), height(right)). A node’s height depends only on its children — the base case (null → 0) seals the recursion. Clue: “maximum level” / “depth” → simple recurrence with a base case, no global state.

Python

class Solution:
    def maxDepth(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> int:
        if root is None:
            return 0
        return 1 + max(self.maxDepth(root.left), self.maxDepth(root.right))

Rust

Version with the real LeetCode signature (Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn max_depth(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> i32 {
        if let Some(no) = &root {
            let no = no.borrow();
            1 + Self::max_depth(no.left.clone()).max(Self::max_depth(no.right.clone()))
        } else {
            0
        }
    }
}
}

The same logic on pure borrows (&TreeNode) — not available on LeetCode but instructive — note how as_deref() converts Option<Rc<RefCell<T>>> into Option<&T>:

#![allow(unused)]

C++

#include <algorithm> // max
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int maxDepth(TreeNode* root) {
        if (!root) return 0;
        return 1 + max(maxDepth(root->left), maxDepth(root->right));
    }
};

C

int maxDepth(struct TreeNode* root) {
    if (!root) return 0;
    int esq = maxDepth(root->left);
    int dir = maxDepth(root->right);
    return 1 + (esq > dir ? esq : dir);
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each node is visited exactly once.
  • Space: O(h) recursion stack (h = height; worst case O(n) on a skewed tree). Iterative BFS (queue) is O(n) in the worst case of memory.

Pitfalls

  • Base case null → 0 (not -1): height in nodes, not edges.
  • max in C is not a native function: compare esq > dir ? esq : dir (as above) or write a helper.
  • Python: recursion on a skewed tree with n > 1000 blows the frame limit — the alternative is iterative BFS with a deque counting levels.
  • Rust: must borrow() drop before the recursive call? No — clone left/right in the same expression and the temporary Ref dies at the end of the line.

100. Same Tree (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/same-tree/ · Topic: Trees (DFS)

Problem (summary)

Given the roots p and q of two binary trees, tell whether they are the SAME tree: same structure and same value at each corresponding position.

p = [1,2,3], q = [1,2,3]  →  true
p = [1,2],   q = [1,null,2] → false   (structure differs)

Pattern — what to memorize

Parallel recursion comparing node by node: if one of the two is null, both must be; if the values diverge, false; otherwise compare (left, left) and (right, right). It’s the parent cell of Subtree of Another Tree (572) — memorize the match form over the two Options once and it shows up everywhere.

Python

class Solution:
    def isSameTree(self, p: TreeNode | None, q: TreeNode | None) -> bool:
        if p is None or q is None:
            return p is q          # one null: true only if BOTH are null
        if p.val != q.val:
            return False
        return self.isSameTree(p.left, q.left) and self.isSameTree(p.right, q.right)

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn is_same_tree(
        p: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,
        q: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,
    ) -> bool {
        match (p, q) {
            (None, None) => true,
            (Some(_), None) | (None, Some(_)) => false,
            (Some(a), Some(b)) => {
                let a = a.borrow();
                let b = b.borrow();
                a.val == b.val
                    && Self::is_same_tree(a.left.clone(), b.left.clone())
                    && Self::is_same_tree(a.right.clone(), b.right.clone())
            }
        }
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    bool isSameTree(TreeNode* p, TreeNode* q) {
        if (!p || !q) return p == q;
        if (p->val != q->val) return false;
        return isSameTree(p->left, q->left) && isSameTree(p->right, q->right);
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>

bool isSameTree(struct TreeNode* p, struct TreeNode* q) {
    if (!p || !q) return p == q; /* one null: true only if both are null */
    if (p->val != q->val) return false;
    return isSameTree(p->left, q->left) && isSameTree(p->right, q->right);
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — in the worst case (equal trees) visits both entirely; on early divergence it stops sooner.
  • Space: O(h) recursion stack.

Pitfalls

  • p == q when one is null is not enough: it must be p is q/p == q (both null). The form if (!p || !q) return p == q; covers all three null cases at once.
  • Structure ≠ values: [1,2,1] vs [1,1,2] have the same values but are different trees — the order of the &&s guarantees positional comparison.
  • Rust: the match on (p, q) moves both roots — exactly what the signature allows (they’re consumed); no need to clone here.
  • C/C++: empty trees (NULL/nullptr) are equal to each other — base case.

572. Subtree of Another Tree (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/subtree-of-another-tree/ · Topic: Trees (DFS)

Problem (summary)

Given the roots root and subRoot, tell whether subRoot is a subtree of root: there exists a node of root whose entire tree (structure + values) equals subRoot.

root = [3,4,5,1,2], subRoot = [4,1,2]        →  true
root = [3,4,5,1,2,null,null,null,null,0], subRoot = [4,1,2]  →  false

Pattern — what to memorize

Two steps on top of the Same Tree (100) cell: for every node of root, ask “from here down, is it equal to subRoot?”. If not, descend into the children (DFS). Clean brute force: O(n · m) worst case — usually accepted; the senior alternative is serializing both trees and searching for a substring (string matching), O(n + m) with hashing.

Python

class Solution:
    def isSubtree(self, root: TreeNode | None, subRoot: TreeNode | None) -> bool:
        if root is None:
            return False                        # subRoot is non-null (guaranteed)
        if self.igual(root, subRoot):
            return True
        return self.isSubtree(root.left, subRoot) or self.isSubtree(root.right, subRoot)

    def igual(self, a: TreeNode | None, b: TreeNode | None) -> bool:
        if a is None or b is None:
            return a is b
        if a.val != b.val:
            return False
        return self.igual(a.left, b.left) and self.igual(a.right, b.right)

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn is_subtree(
        root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,
        sub_root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,
    ) -> bool {
        if root.is_none() {
            return false;
        }
        if Self::mesmas_arvores(&root, &sub_root) {
            return true;
        }
        // clone the children and drop the borrow before recursing
        let no = root.unwrap();
        let (esq, dir) = {
            let n = no.borrow();
            (n.left.clone(), n.right.clone())
        };
        Self::is_subtree(esq, sub_root.clone()) || Self::is_subtree(dir, sub_root)
    }

    fn mesmas_arvores(
        a: &Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,
        b: &Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,
    ) -> bool {
        match (a, b) {
            (None, None) => true,
            (Some(_), None) | (None, Some(_)) => false,
            (Some(u), Some(v)) => {
                let u = u.borrow();
                let v = v.borrow();
                u.val == v.val
                    && Self::mesmas_arvores(&u.left, &v.left)
                    && Self::mesmas_arvores(&u.right, &v.right)
            }
        }
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    bool isSubtree(TreeNode* root, TreeNode* subRoot) {
        if (!root) return false;
        if (mesmas_arvores(root, subRoot)) return true;
        return isSubtree(root->left, subRoot) || isSubtree(root->right, subRoot);
    }
private:
    static bool mesmas_arvores(TreeNode* a, TreeNode* b) {
        if (!a || !b) return a == b;
        return a->val == b->val && mesmas_arvores(a->left, b->left) &&
               mesmas_arvores(a->right, b->right);
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>

static bool mesmas_arvores(struct TreeNode* a, struct TreeNode* b) {
    if (!a || !b) return a == b;
    return a->val == b->val && mesmas_arvores(a->left, b->left) &&
           mesmas_arvores(a->right, b->right);
}

bool isSubtree(struct TreeNode* root, struct TreeNode* subRoot) {
    if (!root) return false; /* subRoot is non-null (guaranteed) */
    if (mesmas_arvores(root, subRoot)) return true;
    return isSubtree(root->left, subRoot) || isSubtree(root->right, subRoot);
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n · m) in the worst case — for each of the n nodes of root, mesmas_arvores may walk up to m nodes (e.g., a whole tree with the same value and an almost-equal subRoot). The string-matching alternative (serialization prefix) is O(n + m) with hashing.
  • Space: O(h₁ + h₂) from the two recursion stacks (plus the combined depth of the two nested DFS passes).

Pitfalls

  • The comparison is structural at the anchor point: [4,1,2] is NOT a subtree of a tree whose node 4 has an extra 0 child — those are different trees.
  • Empty root with non-empty subRoot → false (the problem guarantees subRoot non-null; if it came null, it would be a subtree of anything).
  • The order of the ||s matters for performance: the “anchored and equal” case returns before descending.
  • Rust: root.unwrap() after is_none() — safe, or use if let Some(no) = &root; cloning the children before recursing avoids a live Ref spanning calls.

235. Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-bst/ · Topic: Trees (BST)

Problem (summary)

Given a BST and two nodes p and q (distinct, both exist in the tree), return the lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that is an ancestor of both (a node is an ancestor of itself).

root = [6,2,8,0,4,7,9,null,null,3,5]
p=2, q=8 → 6        p=2, q=4 → 2

Pattern — what to memorize

The BST property decides the path with no ancestor search at all: walk down from the root while p and q are on the SAME side (both < val → left; both > val → right). The first node where they diverge (or where one of them IS the current node) is the LCA. No stack, no parent visits — it’s the most direct tree problem in the BST list.

Python

class Solution:
    def lowestCommonAncestor(self, root: 'TreeNode', p: 'TreeNode', q: 'TreeNode') -> 'TreeNode':
        no = root
        while no is not None:
            if p.val < no.val and q.val < no.val:
                no = no.left
            elif p.val > no.val and q.val > no.val:
                no = no.right
            else:
                return no
        return None          # unreachable: p and q exist

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn lowest_common_ancestor(
        root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,
        p: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,
        q: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,
    ) -> Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>> {
        let (pv, qv) = {
            let p = p.as_ref().expect("p exists").borrow();
            let q = q.as_ref().expect("q exists").borrow();
            (p.val, q.val)
        };
        let mut no = root;
        while let Some(rc) = no.as_ref() {
            let val = rc.borrow().val;
            if pv < val && qv < val {
                let esq = rc.borrow().left.clone(); // last borrow use
                no = esq;                          // → assignment released (NLL)
            } else if pv > val && qv > val {
                let dir = rc.borrow().right.clone();
                no = dir;
            } else {
                return Some(rc.clone()); // avoids moving still-borrowed `no`
            }
        }
        None
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    TreeNode* lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode* root, TreeNode* p, TreeNode* q) {
        TreeNode* no = root;
        while (no) {
            if (p->val < no->val && q->val < no->val) no = no->left;
            else if (p->val > no->val && q->val > no->val) no = no->right;
            else return no;
        }
        return nullptr; // unreachable
    }
};

C

#include <stddef.h> /* NULL */

struct TreeNode* lowestCommonAncestor(struct TreeNode* root, struct TreeNode* p,
                                      struct TreeNode* q) {
    struct TreeNode* no = root;
    while (no) {
        if (p->val < no->val && q->val < no->val) {
            no = no->left;
        } else if (p->val > no->val && q->val > no->val) {
            no = no->right;
        } else {
            return no;
        }
    }
    return NULL; /* unreachable: p and q exist */
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(h) — worst case walks from the root to the deepest leaf (O(n) on a skewed tree, O(log n) on a balanced one).
  • Space: O(1) — just the no pointer (the recursive version would use O(h) of stack; the iterative one is preferable in the interview).

Pitfalls

  • The comparison is on values, not node identity: the “p is an ancestor of q” case falls naturally into the else (p.val == no.val).
  • p == q also works: the current node is valid for both.
  • Flipping the signs (p->val > no->val && q->val > no->val → right) is the classic mistake of someone rote-memorizing code — re-derive from the BST invariant.
  • Can a BST have equal values? Not in this problem (LC BST constraints are strict); if it could, the binary descent would break.

102. Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-tree-level-order-traversal/ · Topic: Trees (BFS)

Problem (summary)

Given the root of a binary tree, return its values level by level, left to right, top to bottom, as a list of lists.

[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]  →  [[3],[9,20],[15,7]]
[]                       →  []

Pattern — what to memorize

Level-by-level BFS: the queue while processes exactly one level per iteration — tam = len(queue) up front, then for _ in range(tam) drains the level while enqueueing the next level’s children. The tell is the output shape (a list per level), which is the signature of a “layered” BFS — no depth recursion here.

Python

from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def levelOrder(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> list[list[int]]:
        resp = []
        if root is None:
            return resp
        fila = deque([root])
        while fila:
            nivel = []
            for _ in range(len(fila)):   # freezes the current level size
                no = fila.popleft()
                nivel.append(no.val)     # O(1) at both ends
                if no.left is not None:
                    fila.append(no.left)
                if no.right is not None:
                    fila.append(no.right)
            resp.append(nivel)
        return resp

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::collections::VecDeque;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn level_order(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> Vec<Vec<i32>> {
        let mut resp: Vec<Vec<i32>> = Vec::new();
        if root.is_none() {
            return resp;
        }
        let mut fila: VecDeque<Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>> = VecDeque::new();
        fila.push_back(root);
        while !fila.is_empty() {
            let tam = fila.len(); // nodes of this level
            let mut nivel = Vec::with_capacity(tam);
            for _ in 0..tam {
                if let Some(no) = fila.pop_front().expect("we only enqueue Some") {
                    let no = no.borrow();
                    nivel.push(no.val);
                    if no.left.is_some() {
                        fila.push_back(no.left.clone());
                    }
                    if no.right.is_some() {
                        fila.push_back(no.right.clone());
                    }
                }
            }
            resp.push(nivel);
        }
        resp
    }
}
}

C++

#include <queue>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<vector<int>> levelOrder(TreeNode* root) {
        vector<vector<int>> resp;
        if (!root) return resp;
        queue<TreeNode*> fila;
        fila.push(root);
        while (!fila.empty()) {
            int tam = (int)fila.size(); // freezes the current level
            vector<int> nivel;
            while (tam--) {
                TreeNode* no = fila.front();
                fila.pop();
                nivel.push_back(no->val);
                if (no->left) fila.push(no->left);
                if (no->right) fila.push(no->right);
            }
            resp.push_back(nivel);
        }
        return resp;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

static int contar_nos(struct TreeNode* raiz) {
    if (!raiz) return 0;
    return 1 + contar_nos(raiz->left) + contar_nos(raiz->right);
}

/**
 * Return an array of arrays of size *returnSize.
 * The sizes of the arrays are returned as *returnColumnSizes array.
 */
int** levelOrder(struct TreeNode* root, int* returnSize, int** returnColumnSizes) {
    *returnSize = 0;
    if (!root) {
        *returnColumnSizes = NULL;
        return NULL;
    }
    int n = contar_nos(root);
    struct TreeNode** fila = (struct TreeNode**)malloc(n * sizeof(struct TreeNode*));

    int** resp = (int**)malloc(n * sizeof(int*));
    int* colunas = (int*)malloc(n * sizeof(int));

    int frente = 0, tras = 0, nivel = 0;
    fila[tras++] = root;
    while (frente < tras) {
        int tam = tras - frente; /* nodes of this level */
        resp[nivel] = (int*)malloc(tam * sizeof(int));
        colunas[nivel] = tam;
        for (int i = 0; i < tam; i++) {
            struct TreeNode* no = fila[frente++];
            resp[nivel][i] = no->val;
            if (no->left) fila[tras++] = no->left;
            if (no->right) fila[tras++] = no->right;
        }
        nivel++;
    }
    free(fila);
    *returnSize = nivel;
    *returnColumnSizes = colunas;
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each node enters and leaves the queue once; building each level is O(its nodes).
  • Space: O(n) — the queue holds at most the tree’s width (a full last level ≈ n/2) plus the n output lists.

Pitfalls

  • Freeze tam BEFORE the inner loop: for _ in range(len(fila)) captures the size at call time; if you use len(fila) as a dynamic condition, the level “leaks” into the next iteration.
  • Empty tree → return an empty list (not [[]]).
  • C: the contract requires returnColumnSizes filled (1 int per level) and returnSize = number of levels; the judge frees resp/columns, but the temporary fila is yours (free it before returning).
  • Rust: fila.len() and the index inside the for act on the SAME queue — does the borrow() of the current node drop before the sibling’s push_back? No: the push uses no.left.clone() with the Ref alive — allowed because the clone touches neither the queue nor mutates the node.

199. Binary Tree Right Side View (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-tree-right-side-view/ · Topic: Trees (BFS)

Problem (summary)

Given the root of a binary tree, return, top to bottom, the value of the rightmost node of each level — the view of someone looking at the tree from the right side (nodes hidden behind a right sibling don’t show).

[1,2,3,null,5,null,4]  →  [1,3,4]
[1,null,3]             →  [1,3]
[]                     →  []

Pattern — what to memorize

Two approaches are worth knowing; the code implements BFS:

  • Layer-by-layer BFS (implemented): process the whole level in one iteration (for _ in range(len(queue))) and, by the end of the level, no is the last node dequeued — the rightmost one. Push each child in left→right order.
  • DFS root → right → left: tracking depth, the FIRST visit of each depth is its rightmost node — if the answer list has profundidade elements, the current node is new and goes in (if len(resp) == prof: resp.append(val)). Also O(n), memory O(h) — no queue.

Clue: “per level / lateral” → BFS counting levels; the DFS version is the mental shortcut for any “first of each layer” (top view likewise).

Python

from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def rightSideView(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> list[int]:
        if root is None:
            return []
        resp = []
        fila = deque([root])
        while fila:
            for _ in range(len(fila)):      # processes the whole level
                no = fila.popleft()
                if no.left:
                    fila.append(no.left)
                if no.right:
                    fila.append(no.right)
            resp.append(no.val)             # no is the level's last = rightmost
        return resp

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::collections::VecDeque;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn right_side_view(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> Vec<i32> {
        let mut resp = Vec::new();
        let mut fila = VecDeque::new();
        if let Some(raiz) = root {
            fila.push_back(raiz);
        }
        while !fila.is_empty() {
            let tamanho = fila.len();
            let mut ultimo = 0;
            for _ in 0..tamanho {
                let no = fila.pop_front().expect("queue not empty");
                let no = no.borrow();
                ultimo = no.val;
                if let Some(esq) = &no.left {
                    fila.push_back(esq.clone());
                }
                if let Some(dir) = &no.right {
                    fila.push_back(dir.clone());
                }
            }
            resp.push(ultimo); // the level's last dequeued = rightmost
        }
        resp
    }
}
}

C++

#include <deque>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> rightSideView(TreeNode* root) {
        vector<int> resp;
        if (!root) return resp;
        deque<TreeNode*> fila = {root};
        while (!fila.empty()) {
            int tamanho = (int)fila.size();
            int ultimo = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < tamanho; i++) {
                TreeNode* no = fila.front();
                fila.pop_front();
                ultimo = no->val; // at level end, it's the rightmost
                if (no->left) fila.push_back(no->left);
                if (no->right) fila.push_back(no->right);
            }
            resp.push_back(ultimo);
        }
        return resp;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

static int contar_nos(struct TreeNode* no) {
    if (!no) return 0;
    return 1 + contar_nos(no->left) + contar_nos(no->right);
}

int* rightSideView(struct TreeNode* root, int* returnSize) {
    *returnSize = 0;
    if (!root) return NULL;
    int n = contar_nos(root);
    struct TreeNode** fila = (struct TreeNode**)malloc(n * sizeof(struct TreeNode*));
    int* resp = (int*)malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    int ini = 0, fim = 0;
    fila[fim++] = root;
    while (ini < fim) {
        int tamanho = fim - ini; /* current level */
        int ultimo = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < tamanho; i++) {
            struct TreeNode* no = fila[ini++];
            ultimo = no->val; /* at level end: the rightmost */
            if (no->left) fila[fim++] = no->left;
            if (no->right) fila[fim++] = no->right;
        }
        resp[(*returnSize)++] = ultimo;
    }
    free(fila);
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — BFS visits each node exactly once (likewise DFS).
  • Space: O(n) — the queue holds at most one full layer (O(n) on a complete tree); the DFS alternative uses O(h) of stack.

Pitfalls

  • Null root → [], not [0] or a crash (C: returnSize = 0 and NULL).
  • The answer is NOT the max value of each level, it’s level order: a node only disappears if another is literally to its right on the SAME level.
  • BFS: freeze the level size (tamanho = fila.len()) before the for — children pushed during the level must not be processed in the same layer.
  • Python: deque.popleft() is O(1); fila.pop(0) would be O(n) — the classic BFS trap.
  • DFS alternative (note): the len(resp) == profundidade condition marks the first node seen of each layer — it works because the root→right→left order visits the rightmost first.

1448. Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/count-good-nodes-in-binary-tree/ · Topic: Trees (DFS)

Problem (summary)

A node is good if no node with a greater value exists on the path from the root down to it (equal values count as good). Return the total number of good nodes in the tree.

[3,1,4,3,null,1,5]           →  4   (3, 3, 4, 5)
[3,3,null,4,2]               →  3   (3, 3, 4)
[1]                          →  1

Pattern — what to memorize

DFS carrying the path’s max (not the node — the MAX). At each node, ask: val >= max_so_far? — if so, count one good. Then update the max for the children (max(maximo, val)) and descend. The root is always good (no ancestors). Clue: “path from root to X” is the signature of a DFS with accumulated state going down — the recursion parameter carries the max, not a global accumulator.

Python

class Solution:
    def goodNodes(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> int:
        def contar(no: TreeNode | None, maximo: int) -> int:
            if no is None:
                return 0
            novo_max = max(maximo, no.val)
            bom = 1 if no.val >= maximo else 0   # >=: equal is good too
            return bom + contar(no.left, novo_max) + contar(no.right, novo_max)
        return contar(root, float("-inf"))

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn good_nodes(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> i32 {
        fn contar(no: &Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>, maximo: i32) -> i32 {
            let Some(rc) = no else { return 0; };
            let no = rc.borrow();
            let novo_max = maximo.max(no.val);
            let bom = i32::from(no.val >= maximo); // >= counts equal too
            bom + contar(&no.left, novo_max) + contar(&no.right, novo_max)
        }
        contar(&root, i32::MIN)
    }
}
}

C++

#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int goodNodes(TreeNode* root) {
        return contar(root, INT_MIN);
    }
private:
    static int contar(TreeNode* no, int maximo) {
        if (!no) return 0;
        int novo_max = max(maximo, no->val);
        int bom = no->val >= maximo ? 1 : 0; // >= counts equal too
        return bom + contar(no->left, novo_max) + contar(no->right, novo_max);
    }
};

C

#include <limits.h>

static int conta_good(struct TreeNode* no, int maximo) {
    if (!no) return 0;
    int novo_max = no->val > maximo ? no->val : maximo;
    int bom = no->val >= maximo ? 1 : 0; /* >= counts equal too */
    return bom + conta_good(no->left, novo_max) + conta_good(no->right, novo_max);
}

int goodNodes(struct TreeNode* root) {
    return conta_good(root, INT_MIN);
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each node is visited exactly once.
  • Space: O(h) recursion stack (worst case O(n) on a skewed tree).

Pitfalls

  • The comparison is against the ANCESTORS’ max, and the node enters the count before the max is updated with it — the order bom = val >= maximo; novo_max = max(...) is the heart of the problem.
  • Equal counts: >=, not >. A node with the same value as the path’s max is good ([3,3,null,4,2] → 3, not 2).
  • The root is always good: initialize the max with INT_MIN/-inf, never with the root’s value in the external call… actually maximo = val_da_raiz also works (val >= val is true), but -inf is cleaner and covers a null root (defensive).
  • Rust: i32::from(bool) converts cleanly; the borrow() coexists with the recursive calls because contar receives &no.left (borrowed), not the moved Rc.

110. Balanced Binary Tree (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/balanced-binary-tree/ · Topic: Trees (DFS)

Problem (summary)

A binary tree is height-balanced if, for EVERY node, the heights of the two subtrees differ by at most 1. Return true/false. (Height definition: distance in edges to the deepest leaf — a lone root has height 0.)

[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]              →  true
[1,2,2,3,3,null,null,4,4]            →  false   (subtree 2-3-4 unbalanced)
[]                                   →  true

Pattern — what to memorize

One height with an error sentinel: the altura(node) helper returns the height in nodes, or -1 if the subtree is already unbalanced. Every node checks |esq - dir| > 1 and propagates the children’s -1 (if esq == -1: return -1) — the early exit cuts recursion as soon as the first imbalance shows, instead of computing “real” heights and comparing separately. Clue: “for every node” is the call to split and test each node; the -1 sentinel avoids passing the whole tree twice (once for height, once to check).

Python

class Solution:
    def isBalanced(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> bool:
        def altura(no: TreeNode | None) -> int:
            if no is None:
                return 0
            esq = altura(no.left)
            if esq == -1:
                return -1                          # child already unbalanced: cut
            dir_ = altura(no.right)
            if dir_ == -1 or abs(esq - dir_) > 1:
                return -1                          # unbalanced sentinel
            return 1 + max(esq, dir_)
        return altura(root) != -1

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn is_balanced(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> bool {
        fn altura(no: &Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> i32 {
            let Some(rc) = no else { return 0; };
            let no = rc.borrow();
            let esq = altura(&no.left);
            if esq == -1 {
                return -1; // child already unbalanced: cut
            }
            let dir = altura(&no.right);
            if dir == -1 || (esq - dir).abs() > 1 {
                return -1; // unbalanced sentinel
            }
            1 + esq.max(dir)
        }
        altura(&root) != -1
    }
}
}

C++

#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    bool isBalanced(TreeNode* root) {
        return altura(root) != -1;
    }
private:
    static int altura(TreeNode* no) {
        if (!no) return 0;
        int esq = altura(no->left);
        if (esq == -1) return -1;       // child already unbalanced: cut
        int dir = altura(no->right);
        if (dir == -1 || abs(esq - dir) > 1) return -1; // sentinel
        return 1 + max(esq, dir);
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>

static int altura_bal(struct TreeNode* no) {
    if (!no) return 0;
    int esq = altura_bal(no->left);
    if (esq == -1) return -1;      /* child already unbalanced: cut */
    int dir = altura_bal(no->right);
    int dif = esq > dir ? esq - dir : dir - esq;
    if (dir == -1 || dif > 1) return -1; /* unbalanced sentinel */
    return 1 + (esq > dir ? esq : dir);
}

bool isBalanced(struct TreeNode* root) {
    return altura_bal(root) != -1;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each node is visited once; worst case (balanced) computes all heights, an unbalanced one cuts early.
  • Space: O(h) recursion stack (worst case O(n) on a skewed tree).

Pitfalls

  • The sentinel must propagate: if esq == -1, return -1 BEFORE computing dir (and before using esq in any math) — the cut is the win.
  • Height base 0 vs 1: using nodes (1 + max) and comparing with 1 is consistent; what you CANNOT do is mix conventions mid-way through the abs math.
  • Skewed tree ([1,2,null,3,null]) is the edge case that sinks the naive solution (it computes two passes without early exit and still gets it wrong node by node).
  • C: abs of int comes from <stdlib.h> — the sum esq + dir without abs won’t do here; the ternary avoids including <stdlib.h> just for that.

543. Diameter of Binary Tree (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/diameter-of-binary-tree/ · Topic: Trees (DFS, tree DP)

Problem (summary)

Return the tree’s diameter: the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. The path may or may not pass through the root.

[1,2,3,4,5]                                       →  3   (4→2→1→3)
[1,2]                                             →  1
[1]                                               →  0

Pattern — what to memorize

“Return the height, update an accumulator with the sum” — the most reused pattern in tree DP. altura(node) returns the height in NODES of the subtree; for each node, the longest path that “bends” at it has esq + dir edges (see the math in Pitfalls), so we compare that with the global best and climb up 1 + max(esq, dir). The answer is the accumulator, not the root’s height. Clue: “path between two NODES, no direction” → the optimal path has a bend point; this problem IS the base of 124. Maximum Path Sum — there the accumulator sums val + g_esq + g_dir with branches cut at 0, here it’s just heights (no zeros).

Python

class Solution:
    def diameterOfBinaryTree(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> int:
        melhor = 0
        def altura(no: TreeNode | None) -> int:
            nonlocal melhor
            if no is None:
                return 0
            esq = altura(no.left)
            dir_ = altura(no.right)
            melhor = max(melhor, esq + dir_)       # path that "bends" here
            return 1 + max(esq, dir_)              # height that climbs to the parent
        altura(root)
        return melhor

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn diameter_of_binary_tree(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> i32 {
        fn altura(no: &Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>, melhor: &mut i32) -> i32 {
            let Some(rc) = no else { return 0; };
            let no = rc.borrow();
            let esq = altura(&no.left, melhor);
            let dir = altura(&no.right, melhor);
            *melhor = (*melhor).max(esq + dir); // path that "bends" here
            1 + esq.max(dir)                     // height that climbs to the parent
        }
        let mut melhor = 0;
        altura(&root, &mut melhor);
        melhor
    }
}
}

C++

#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int diameterOfBinaryTree(TreeNode* root) {
        int melhor = 0;
        altura(root, melhor);
        return melhor;
    }
private:
    static int altura(TreeNode* no, int& melhor) {
        if (!no) return 0;
        int esq = altura(no->left, melhor);
        int dir = altura(no->right, melhor);
        melhor = max(melhor, esq + dir); // path that "bends" here
        return 1 + max(esq, dir);        // height that climbs to the parent
    }
};

C

static int altura_diam(struct TreeNode* no, int* melhor) {
    if (!no) return 0;
    int esq = altura_diam(no->left, melhor);
    int dir = altura_diam(no->right, melhor);
    int soma = esq + dir;
    if (soma > *melhor) *melhor = soma; /* path that "bends" here */
    return 1 + (esq > dir ? esq : dir); /* height that climbs */
}

int diameterOfBinaryTree(struct TreeNode* root) {
    int melhor = 0;
    altura_diam(root, &melhor);
    return melhor;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — post-order visits each node once.
  • Space: O(h) recursion stack (worst case O(n) on a skewed tree).

Pitfalls

  • The answer is in EDGES; altura() in nodes. The math closes because the height in nodes of ONE child is exactly the edge distance from the parent to that side’s deepest leaf: esq + dir at a node = number of edges in the path through it. Mental model: leaf → 0, [1,2] → 1, [1,2,3,4,5] → 3 (4→2→1→3).
  • The diameter doesn’t need to pass through the root — that’s why the accumulator is global and every node is a candidate; returning altura(root) would be a mistake.
  • Single-node tree → 0; null root → 0 (guard the base case before accessing).
  • Rust: the accumulator goes down as &mut i32 (no global — a global would leak between judge calls); the esq + dir read of the accumulator coexists with the write because the update is a max after both.
  • Base of 124 (Maximum Path Sum): swap esq + dir for val + ganho_esq + ganho_dir with max(ganho, 0) per branch — the skeleton is identical.

98. Validate Binary Search Tree (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/validate-binary-search-tree/ · Topic: Trees (BST)

Problem (summary)

Given the root, tell whether the tree is a valid BST: for EVERY node, the left subtree holds only values smaller and the right only values greater (strictly) than it — this holds for ALL descendants, not just the immediate children.

[2,1,3]                  →  true
[5,1,4,null,null,3,6]    →  false   (3 is right of 5 but < 4)

Pattern — what to memorize

Inherited bounds (min/max) in DFS: each node receives the allowed value range — descending left, the ceiling becomes the parent’s value; right, the floor. The classic mistake is comparing ONLY with the parent (no->left < no && no->right > no), which wrongly passes [5,4,6,null,null,3,7]. Swap “compare with the parent” for “pass down the bound you descended through” and the problem dies.

Python

class Solution:
    def isValidBST(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> bool:
        def valida(no: TreeNode | None, lo: float, hi: float) -> bool:
            if no is None:
                return True
            if not (lo < no.val < hi):
                return False
            return valida(no.left, lo, no.val) and valida(no.right, no.val, hi)

        return valida(root, float("-inf"), float("inf"))

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn is_valid_bst(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> bool {
        // i64 sentinel: covers ANY i32 without an "infinity" that collides
        // (i32::MIN/MAX are legitimate tree values).
        fn valida(no: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>, lo: i64, hi: i64) -> bool {
            match no {
                None => true,
                Some(no) => {
                    let no = no.borrow();
                    let v = no.val as i64;
                    lo < v
                        && v < hi
                        && valida(no.left.clone(), lo, v)
                        && valida(no.right.clone(), v, hi)
                }
            }
        }
        valida(root, i64::MIN, i64::MAX)
    }
}
}

C++

#include <climits>

class Solution {
public:
    bool isValidBST(TreeNode* root) {
        return valida(root, LLONG_MIN, LLONG_MAX);
    }
private:
    static bool valida(TreeNode* no, long long lo, long long hi) {
        if (!no) return true;
        if (no->val <= lo || no->val >= hi) return false;
        return valida(no->left, lo, no->val) && valida(no->right, no->val, hi);
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <limits.h>

static bool valida(struct TreeNode* no, long long lo, long long hi) {
    if (!no) return true;
    if (no->val <= lo || no->val >= hi) return false;
    return valida(no->left, lo, no->val) && valida(no->right, no->val, hi);
}

bool isValidBST(struct TreeNode* root) {
    return valida(root, LLONG_MIN, LLONG_MAX);
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each node is visited once.
  • Space: O(h) recursion stack. The in-order alternative (compare previous < current during an inorder walk) is also O(n)/O(h) and can be iterative with an explicit stack.

Pitfalls

  • Inherited bounds, never just the parent — [5,4,6,null,null,3,7] is the classic trap: 3 < 5, but it sits in 5’s right subtree.
  • Duplicates are invalid: it must be strictly greater/smaller (no->val <= lo returns false) — [2,2,2] is not a BST.
  • “Infinity” sentinel in C/C++: the value can be INT_MAX/INT_MIN, so the bounds must fit beyond the domain — long long (LLONG_MIN/MAX). In Python, float("inf") handles it; in Rust, i64.
  • Inorder alternative: in a BST the in-order walk is strictly increasing — but mind the “previous” on the first node (use None/nullopt as state, not a value).
  • In C the int is promoted to long long in the comparison — no overflow; same in C++ (no->val <= lo).

230. Kth Smallest Element in a BST (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/kth-smallest-element-in-a-bst/ · Topic: Trees (BST)

Problem (summary)

Given the root of a BST (unique values, left child < node < right child) and an integer k (1-indexed), return the k-th smallest value in the tree without building the entire sorted list.

[3,1,4,null,2], k=1                  →  1
[5,3,6,2,4,null,null,1], k=3         →  3
[1], k=1                             →  1

Pattern — what to memorize

ITERATIVE inorder with early stop: in a BST, the inorder walk (left → node → right) visits values in increasing order. The iterative version with an explicit stack always descends left, pops (visits), counts, and goes right — stopping as soon as k == 0. Cost O(H + k): descending to the smallest (the leftmost) costs H, and each following pop is one inorder step — it never walks the whole tree. Clue: “k-th smallest” + BST → inorder; the phrase “without building everything” suggests the iterative/early stop.

Python

class Solution:
    def kthSmallest(self, root: TreeNode | None, k: int) -> int:
        pilha = []
        no = root
        while pilha or no:
            while no:                             # always descend left
                pilha.append(no)
                no = no.left
            no = pilha.pop()                      # inorder: visit the pop
            k -= 1
            if k == 0:
                return no.val
            no = no.right                         # then the right branch
        return -1                                 # unreachable (k valid)

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn kth_smallest(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>, k: i32) -> i32 {
        let mut pilha: Vec<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>> = Vec::new();
        let mut no = root;
        let mut restante = k;
        loop {
            while let Some(rc) = no.clone() {
                pilha.push(rc.clone()); // always descend left
                no = rc.borrow().left.clone();
            }
            let Some(atual) = pilha.pop() else { break; };
            restante -= 1; // inorder: the pop is the next smallest
            if restante == 0 {
                return atual.borrow().val;
            }
            no = atual.borrow().right.clone();
        }
        -1 // unreachable (k is valid)
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int kthSmallest(TreeNode* root, int k) {
        vector<TreeNode*> pilha;
        TreeNode* no = root;
        while (!pilha.empty() || no) {
            while (no) { pilha.push_back(no); no = no->left; } // descend left
            no = pilha.back();
            pilha.pop_back();
            if (--k == 0) return no->val; // inorder: the pop is the next smallest
            no = no->right;
        }
        return -1; // unreachable (k valid)
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

static int contar_nos(struct TreeNode* no) {
    if (!no) return 0;
    return 1 + contar_nos(no->left) + contar_nos(no->right);
}

int kthSmallest(struct TreeNode* root, int k) {
    int n = contar_nos(root);
    struct TreeNode** pilha = (struct TreeNode**)malloc((n ? n : 1) * sizeof(struct TreeNode*));
    int topo = 0;
    struct TreeNode* no = root;
    while (topo > 0 || no) {
        while (no) { pilha[topo++] = no; no = no->left; } /* descend left */
        no = pilha[--topo];
        if (--k == 0) { /* inorder: the pop is the next smallest */
            int resp = no->val;
            free(pilha);
            return resp;
        }
        no = no->right;
    }
    free(pilha);
    return -1; /* unreachable (k valid) */
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(H + k), H = tree height — descending to the smallest (O(H)) plus k pops. Balanced: O(log n + k); skewed: O(n + k).
  • Space: O(H) stack (maximum stacked ancestors).

Pitfalls

  • k is 1-indexed: decrement and return when k == 0 (not k == 1 before decrementing, no k == k confusions).
  • No “building everything”: the full recursive inorder (or collecting a list) is O(n) time AND O(n) memory — loses both points of the question.
  • The iterative exists because the recursive stack can’t “stop early” cleanly without an exception — knowing the while pilha or no shape plus descending left by heart is the differentiator.
  • Rust: no.clone() in the while let decouples the Rc from the no borrow — assigning no = rc.borrow().left.clone() (a new Rc) doesn’t conflict with a while let Some(atual) = &no loop, which would borrow no (error E0506).
  • C: you need n to allocate the stack — a counting pass up front (O(n) extra, no asymptotic impact) or realloc-based allocation.

105. Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/construct-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-inorder/ · Topic: Trees (Divide & Conquer)

Problem (summary)

Given the preorder and inorder traversals of a binary tree (unique values), rebuild and return the root of the original tree.

preorder = [3,9,20,15,7], inorder = [9,3,15,20,7]
→ [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]

Pattern — what to memorize

Preorder hands you the root; inorder tells you what goes left and right. Take the next preorder value (root of the current range), find its position k in inorder (precomputed in a value→index map) and recurse: construir(left of k) and construir(right of k). The preorder pointer only moves forward; the inorder ranges (indices) cut the recursion. Clue: “rebuild a tree” + two orders → divide by the root.

Python

class Solution:
    def buildTree(self, preorder: list[int], inorder: list[int]) -> TreeNode | None:
        pos = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}   # value → index, O(1)
        self.pre_i = 0

        def constroi(ini: int, fim: int) -> TreeNode | None:
            if ini > fim:
                return None
            val = preorder[self.pre_i]      # next root from preorder
            self.pre_i += 1
            no = TreeNode(val)
            k = pos[val]                    # everything before k goes left
            no.left = constroi(ini, k - 1)
            no.right = constroi(k + 1, fim)
            return no

        return constroi(0, len(inorder) - 1)

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn build_tree(preorder: Vec<i32>, inorder: Vec<i32>) -> Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>> {
        // Ranges in i32: `k - 1` with k = 0 becomes -1 → ini(0) > fim(-1) → null,
        // no usize underflow.
        fn constroi(
            pre: &[i32],
            pre_i: &mut usize,
            pos: &HashMap<i32, usize>,
            ini: i32,
            fim: i32,
        ) -> Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>> {
            if ini > fim {
                return None;
            }
            let val = pre[*pre_i];
            *pre_i += 1; // preorder delivers each range's root in order
            let no = Rc::new(RefCell::new(TreeNode::new(val)));
            let k = pos[&val] as i32;
            no.borrow_mut().left = constroi(pre, pre_i, pos, ini, k - 1);
            no.borrow_mut().right = constroi(pre, pre_i, pos, k + 1, fim);
            Some(no)
        }

        if inorder.is_empty() {
            return None;
        }
        let pos: HashMap<i32, usize> = inorder.iter().enumerate().map(|(i, &v)| (v, i)).collect();
        let mut pre_i = 0;
        constroi(&preorder, &mut pre_i, &pos, 0, inorder.len() as i32 - 1)
    }
}
}

C++

#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    TreeNode* buildTree(vector<int>& preorder, vector<int>& inorder) {
        int n = (int)inorder.size();
        pos.clear();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) pos[inorder[i]] = i;
        pre_i = 0;
        return constroi(preorder, 0, n - 1);
    }

private:
    unordered_map<int, int> pos; // value → inorder index (unique values)
    int pre_i = 0;

    TreeNode* constroi(vector<int>& pre, int ini, int fim) {
        if (ini > fim) return nullptr;
        int val = pre[pre_i++]; // next in preorder = root of the range
        TreeNode* no = new TreeNode(val);
        int k = pos[val]; // everything before k in inorder goes left
        no->left = constroi(pre, ini, k - 1);
        no->right = constroi(pre, k + 1, fim);
        return no;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

/* Value → index map in open addressing (house pattern, see two-sum). */
typedef struct {
    int chave;
    int indice;
    int usado;
} Entrada;

static unsigned hash_chave(int chave, unsigned mask) {
    return ((unsigned)chave * 2654435761u) & mask; /* Knuth multiplicative */
}

static int procurar(Entrada* pos, unsigned mask, int chave) {
    unsigned h = hash_chave(chave, mask);
    while (pos[h].usado) {
        if (pos[h].chave == chave) return pos[h].indice;
        h = (h + 1) & mask; /* linear probing */
    }
    return -1; /* never happens: values are unique */
}

/* Creates a tree node (LeetCode provides the struct, not the factory). */
static struct TreeNode* novo_no(int val) {
    struct TreeNode* no = (struct TreeNode*)malloc(sizeof(struct TreeNode));
    no->val = val;
    no->left = NULL;
    no->right = NULL;
    return no;
}

static struct TreeNode* constroi(int* pre, int* pre_i, Entrada* pos, unsigned mask, int ini,
                                 int fim) {
    if (ini > fim) return NULL;
    int val = pre[(*pre_i)++]; /* next in preorder = root of the range */
    struct TreeNode* no = novo_no(val);
    int k = procurar(pos, mask, val);
    no->left = constroi(pre, pre_i, pos, mask, ini, k - 1);
    no->right = constroi(pre, pre_i, pos, mask, k + 1, fim);
    return no;
}

struct TreeNode* buildTree(int* preorder, int preorderSize, int* inorder, int inorderSize) {
    (void)preorderSize;
    if (inorderSize == 0) return NULL;

    unsigned cap = 16;
    while (cap < (unsigned)inorderSize * 2u) cap <<= 1; /* load factor < 0.5 */
    Entrada* pos = (Entrada*)calloc(cap, sizeof(Entrada));
    unsigned mask = cap - 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < inorderSize; i++) {
        unsigned h = hash_chave(inorder[i], mask);
        while (pos[h].usado) h = (h + 1) & mask;
        pos[h].chave = inorder[i];
        pos[h].indice = i;
        pos[h].usado = 1;
    }

    int pre_i = 0;
    struct TreeNode* raiz = constroi(preorder, &pre_i, pos, mask, 0, inorderSize - 1);
    free(pos);
    return raiz;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each preorder value is read once and each k is an O(1) map lookup (C with open-addressing hash).
  • Space: O(n) for the map + O(h) recursion (worst case O(n) on a skewed tree).

Pitfalls

  • Unique values are the contract: without them the value→index map breaks.
  • The preorder pointer moves only forward (even inside left-subtree calls) — a pre_i by reference (or class member) is mandatory; each call creates novo_no with the next value.
  • Inorder ranges: k-1 on the left side — with k = 0 it becomes -1; in Rust use i32 for the ranges (usize would underflow); in C/C++ int already covers it.
  • C: preorderSize is ignored (the real size comes from inorder) — the compiler warns about the unused parameter; (void)preorderSize silences it.
  • C: negative values work in the hash ((unsigned)chave before the multiplication), as in two-sum.
  • Postorder + inorder is the same pattern, only pre_i becomes a pointer that walks from the END to the start.

124. Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/binary-tree-maximum-path-sum/ · Topic: Trees (DFS, tree DP)

Problem (summary)

Given the root, return the maximum sum of any path in the tree: a sequence of connected nodes where each node appears at most once, allowed to start and end at any node — the path may pass through the root, consist of a single node, or never touch the root.

[1,2,3]                     →  6   (2 + 1 + 3)
[-10,9,20,null,null,15,7]   →  42  (15 + 20 + 7 — CANNOT go up and down)

Pattern — what to memorize

Post-order returning “gain” + a global accumulator. Each node returns the best path that DESCENDS into it (max(gain(left), gain(right), 0) + val) — the max(..., 0) cuts negative branches at node level — and the maximum path that PASSES through it is val + gain_left + gain_right, compared with the global best. The optimal path “bends” at exactly one node; each candidate’s height is captured when it’s the vertex. Clue: “maximum path” → ask “what’s the best leg that climbs up from this node?”.

Python

class Solution:
    def maxPathSum(self, root: TreeNode | None) -> int:
        melhor = float("-inf")

        def ganho(no: TreeNode | None) -> int:
            nonlocal melhor
            if no is None:
                return 0
            g_esq = max(ganho(no.left), 0)   # discard a negative branch
            g_dir = max(ganho(no.right), 0)
            melhor = max(melhor, no.val + g_esq + g_dir)  # passes through here
            return no.val + max(g_esq, g_dir)             # climbs to the parent

        ganho(root)
        return melhor

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

impl Solution {
    pub fn max_path_sum(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> i32 {
        fn ganho(no: &Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>, melhor: &mut i32) -> i32 {
            let Some(rc) = no else {
                return 0;
            };
            let no = rc.borrow();
            let g_esq = ganho(&no.left, melhor).max(0); // cuts a negative branch
            let g_dir = ganho(&no.right, melhor).max(0);
            *melhor = (*melhor).max(no.val + g_esq + g_dir); // passes through here
            no.val + g_esq.max(g_dir) // climbs to the parent
        }
        let mut melhor = i32::MIN;
        ganho(&root, &mut melhor);
        melhor
    }
}
}

C++

#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int maxPathSum(TreeNode* root) {
        int melhor = INT_MIN;
        ganho(root, melhor);
        return melhor;
    }
private:
    static int ganho(TreeNode* no, int& melhor) {
        if (!no) return 0;
        int g_esq = max(ganho(no->left, melhor), 0); // discard negatives
        int g_dir = max(ganho(no->right, melhor), 0);
        melhor = max(melhor, no->val + g_esq + g_dir); // path that passes here
        return no->val + max(g_esq, g_dir); // what climbs to the parent
    }
};

C

#include <limits.h>

static int ganho(struct TreeNode* no, int* melhor) {
    if (!no) return 0;
    int g_esq = ganho(no->left, melhor);
    if (g_esq < 0) g_esq = 0;
    int g_dir = ganho(no->right, melhor);
    if (g_dir < 0) g_dir = 0;

    int passando = no->val + g_esq + g_dir;
    if (passando > *melhor) *melhor = passando; /* accumulator by reference */

    int volta = no->val + (g_esq > g_dir ? g_esq : g_dir);
    return volta;
}

int maxPathSum(struct TreeNode* root) {
    int melhor = INT_MIN;
    ganho(root, &melhor);
    return melhor;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — each node is visited once (post-order).
  • Space: O(h) recursion stack (worst case O(n) on a skewed tree).

Pitfalls

  • The max(ganho(x), 0) is double duty: it cuts negative branches FROM THE PATH that passes through the node AND keeps the child out of the gain that climbs — but a lone node is never cut: val + g_esq + g_dir with both zeroed = val.
  • All-negative tree: [-3] → -3 (not 0). The accumulator must start at INT_MIN/-inf and the node is always a candidate.
  • The path CANNOT “go up and down”: 15 → 20 → 7 works, 9 → -10 → 20 doesn’t climb more than once — that’s why each node returns ONE leg and the sum of TWO only counts at the bend point.
  • C/C++: use INT_MIN from <limits.h>/<climits> and pass the accumulator by reference/pointer (no global — a global leaks between judge calls).
  • Rust: the accumulator is &mut i32; the node borrow() coexists with the recursive calls because ganho reads &no.left (borrowed), never moves.

297. Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree/ · Topic: Design (tree serialization)

Problem (summary)

Design two functions: serialize turns a binary tree into a string and deserialize rebuilds the SAME tree from it — the format is free but must be unambiguous (arbitrary design choice, which makes it an interview classic).

[1,2,3,null,null,4,5]  →  "1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#"  (this page's format)
[]                     →  "#"

Pattern — what to memorize

Preorder with a null marker (#) separated by commas and deserialization that rebuilds in the same order. The string stores the pre-order walk where every null becomes #; to deserialize, read one token at a time: # → null node, number → create the node and recurse (left, right). The format is unambiguous because preorder with nulls reconstitutes the whole tree and both sides share the order. Clue: “serialize” + tree → preorder + null marker (BFS with nulls also works, but forces you to handle "null" at the fringe).

Python

class Codec:
    def serialize(self, root):
        partes = []

        def pre(no):
            if no is None:
                partes.append("#")
                return
            partes.append(str(no.val))
            pre(no.left)
            pre(no.right)

        pre(root)
        return ",".join(partes)

    def deserialize(self, data):
        def constroi(it):
            v = next(it)
            if v == "#":
                return None
            no = TreeNode(int(v))
            no.left = constroi(it)
            no.right = constroi(it)
            return no

        return constroi(iter(data.split(",")))

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

struct Codec {}

impl Codec {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Codec {}
    }

    fn serialize(&self, root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> String {
        fn pre(no: &Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>, partes: &mut Vec<String>) {
            match no {
                None => partes.push("#".to_string()),
                Some(rc) => {
                    let no = rc.borrow();
                    partes.push(no.val.to_string());
                    pre(&no.left, partes);
                    pre(&no.right, partes);
                }
            }
        }
        let mut partes = Vec::new();
        pre(&root, &mut partes);
        partes.join(",")
    }

    fn deserialize(&self, data: String) -> Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>> {
        fn constroi(it: &mut dyn Iterator<Item = &str>) -> Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>> {
            match it.next() {
                None | Some("#") => None,
                Some(v) => {
                    let no = Rc::new(RefCell::new(TreeNode::new(v.parse().unwrap())));
                    {
                        let mut m = no.borrow_mut();
                        m.left = constroi(it);
                        m.right = constroi(it);
                    } // the RefMut dies here — safe to return the Rc
                    Some(no)
                }
            }
        }
        constroi(&mut data.split(','))
    }
}
}

C++

#include <sstream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

class Codec {
public:
    string serialize(TreeNode* root) {
        if (!root) return "#";
        return to_string(root->val) + "," + serialize(root->left) + "," + serialize(root->right);
    }

    TreeNode* deserialize(string data) {
        istringstream iss(data);
        return constroi(iss);
    }

private:
    TreeNode* constroi(istringstream& iss) {
        string tok;
        if (!getline(iss, tok, ',')) return nullptr; // end of string
        if (tok == "#") return nullptr;
        TreeNode* no = new TreeNode(stoi(tok));
        no->left = constroi(iss);
        no->right = constroi(iss);
        return no;
    }
};

C

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Creates a node (LeetCode provides the struct, not the factory). */
static struct TreeNode* novo_no(int val) {
    struct TreeNode* no = (struct TreeNode*)malloc(sizeof(struct TreeNode));
    no->val = val;
    no->left = NULL;
    no->right = NULL;
    return no;
}

/* Serialize: two passes — count nodes+nulls, allocate, fill. */
static int contar(struct TreeNode* no) { /* nodes + null markers */
    if (!no) return 1;
    return 1 + contar(no->left) + contar(no->right);
}

static int preencher(struct TreeNode* no, char* saida, int pos) {
    if (!no) {
        saida[pos] = '#';
        saida[pos + 1] = ',';
        return pos + 2;
    }
    pos += sprintf(saida + pos, "%d,", no->val);
    pos = preencher(no->left, saida, pos);
    pos = preencher(no->right, saida, pos);
    return pos;
}

char* serialize(struct TreeNode* root) {
    int m = contar(root);
    /* each node: "−2147483648," (12 bytes) — extra room; null: "#," (2 bytes) */
    char* saida = (char*)malloc((size_t)m * 12 + 1);
    int pos = preencher(root, saida, 0);
    saida[pos - 1] = '\0'; /* drop the trailing comma */
    return saida;
}

/* Deserialize: index-based parser — EVERY token consumes its own separator. */
static struct TreeNode* construir(const char* d, int* p) {
    if (d[*p] == '\0' || d[*p] == ',') return NULL; /* end or loose separator */
    if (d[*p] == '#') {
        *p += 1;
        if (d[*p] == ',') *p += 1; /* the '#' also swallows its comma */
        return NULL;
    }
    int val, consumidos;
    sscanf(d + *p, "%d%n", &val, &consumidos);
    *p += consumidos;
    if (d[*p] == ',') *p += 1;

    struct TreeNode* no = novo_no(val);
    no->left = construir(d, p);
    no->right = construir(d, p);
    return no;
}

struct TreeNode* deserialize(char* data) {
    int pos = 0;
    return construir(data, &pos);
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — serialize walks the tree once; deserialize reads each token once.
  • Space: O(n) — the string has ~2n tokens (# per null), + O(h) recursion in both directions.

Pitfalls

  • The preorder-with-# format is unambiguous; post/level order also work, but need the same null on both sides — the comma is mandatory in C/C++/Rust (Python’s join/split already embeds it).
  • Negative numbers: sprintf("%d,") (C) and stoi/parse handle them; the C parser needs %n to know how many characters it consumed.
  • C — the separator is each token’s own duty: a # branch that advances only 1 (leaving the comma to the next call) desyncs the recursion — advance past '#' and then its comma (see construir).
  • C++: getline(iss, tok, ',') returns false at the end of the string — the last token needs no comma; an empty iss.str() can’t happen if the string came from our serialize.
  • Rust: no.borrow_mut().left = ... followed by ...right = ... — two statements; drop the RefMut (a { } block or chained assignments) before returning the Rc.
  • Recursion vs depth: on a skewed tree recursion uses O(n) of stack — Python can blow the frame limit at n > 1000; in the interview, mention the iterative version with an explicit stack.
