286. Walls and Gates (Medium · Premium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/walls-and-gates/ · Topic: Multi-source BFS (Premium)

Problem (summary)

An m x n grid with -1 = wall, 0 = gate, 2147483647 (INF) = empty room. Fill each room with the minimum distance to the nearest gate (in orthogonal steps). Unreachable rooms stay INF. (Note: Premium problem — solve it through knowledge.)

INF INF 0   INF     3 -1 0  1
INF INF INF -1   2  2 1 -1
INF -1  INF -1  →  1 -1 2 -1
0   -1  INF INF    0 -1 3  4

Pattern — what to memorize

Multi-source BFS from ALL gates at once. When the queue starts with every gate (distance 0), the first time BFS touches a room it is from the nearest source — so rooms[room] = rooms[current] + 1 is already that room’s final answer. Every cell is visited exactly once.

Contrast with DFS-per-cell: the naive temptation is, for each room, to run a DFS/BFS looking for a gate — O((m·n)²) and re-exploring the same paths; the multi-source approach flips the question upside down (“for each gate, who is in the wave front?”) and costs O(m·n). Tell: “distance to the nearest of a set of sources” ⇒ reversed source: BFS leaving the sources, not the targets. Same pattern as Rotting Oranges — the difference is we record distance instead of time, and we mark rooms with the == INF test.

Python

class Solution:
    def wallsAndGates(self, rooms: list[list[int]]) -> None:
        from collections import deque
        if not rooms:
            return
        m, n = len(rooms), len(rooms[0])
        fila = deque()
        for i in range(m):
            for j in range(n):
                if rooms[i][j] == 0:
                    fila.append((i, j))            # MULTI-SOURCE BFS: all gates
        direcoes = ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1))
        while fila:
            r, c = fila.popleft()
            for dr, dc in direcoes:
                nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
                if 0 <= nr < m and 0 <= nc < n and rooms[nr][nc] == 2**31 - 1:
                    rooms[nr][nc] = rooms[r][c] + 1  # distance = BFS level
                    fila.append((nr, nc))

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn walls_and_gates(rooms: &mut Vec<Vec<i32>>) {
        use std::collections::VecDeque;
        let (m, n) = (rooms.len(), rooms[0].len());
        let mut fila: VecDeque<(usize, usize)> = VecDeque::new();
        for i in 0..m {
            for j in 0..n {
                if rooms[i][j] == 0 {
                    fila.push_back((i, j)); // MULTI-SOURCE BFS: all gates
                }
            }
        }
        let direcoes = [(1isize, 0isize), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)];
        while let Some((r, c)) = fila.pop_front() {
            for (dr, dc) in direcoes {
                let (nr, nc) = (r as isize + dr, c as isize + dc);
                if nr >= 0 && nr < m as isize && nc >= 0 && nc < n as isize {
                    let (nr, nc) = (nr as usize, nc as usize);
                    if rooms[nr][nc] == i32::MAX {
                        rooms[nr][nc] = rooms[r][c] + 1; // distance = BFS level
                        fila.push_back((nr, nc));
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
}

C++

#include <climits>
#include <queue>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    void wallsAndGates(vector<vector<int>>& rooms) {
        int m = (int)rooms.size(), n = (int)rooms[0].size();
        queue<pair<int, int>> fila;
        for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i)
            for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j)
                if (rooms[i][j] == 0) fila.push({i, j}); // MULTI-SOURCE BFS: all
        int dirs[4][2] = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
        while (!fila.empty()) {
            auto [r, c] = fila.front();
            fila.pop();
            for (auto& d : dirs) {
                int nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1];
                if (nr >= 0 && nr < m && nc >= 0 && nc < n && rooms[nr][nc] == INT_MAX) {
                    rooms[nr][nc] = rooms[r][c] + 1;   // distance = BFS level
                    fila.push({nr, nc});
                }
            }
        }
    }
};

C

#include <limits.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

void wallsAndGates(int** rooms, int roomsSize, int* roomsColSize) {
    if (roomsSize == 0) return;
    int cols = roomsColSize[0];
    int* fila = malloc((size_t)roomsSize * cols * sizeof(int));
    int frente = 0, tras = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < roomsSize; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < cols; j++)
            if (rooms[i][j] == 0) fila[tras++] = i * cols + j; /* MULTI-SOURCE BFS */
    int dirs[4][2] = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
    while (frente < tras) {
        int pos = fila[frente++];
        int r = pos / cols, c = pos % cols;
        for (int d = 0; d < 4; d++) {
            int nr = r + dirs[d][0], nc = c + dirs[d][1];
            if (nr >= 0 && nr < roomsSize && nc >= 0 && nc < cols
                && rooms[nr][nc] == INT_MAX) {
                rooms[nr][nc] = rooms[r][c] + 1;   /* distance = BFS level */
                fila[tras++] = nr * cols + nc;
            }
        }
    }
    free(fila);
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(m·n) — each room enters the queue at most once, marked on first visit.
  • Space: O(m·n) — the queue in the worst case; everything in place (mutates the input).

Pitfalls

  • The “unvisited” test is rooms[nr][nc] == INF — mark with +1 over the current value and push to the queue at the same time (otherwise it gets re-enqueued).
  • Don’t use a separate visited[]: INF is the natural marker; gates (0) and walls (-1) are never overwritten.
  • Grid with no gates ⇒ nothing changes (queue empty from the start).
  • C: INT_MAX (2147483647) comes from <limits.h> — roomsColSize[0] must be passed (it isn’t optional like in problems without a 2D grid).
  • Rust/C++: could rooms[r][c] + 1 reach 2^31 − 1 + 1? No — reachable cells only get values ≤ m·n, far below INT_MAX; the == i32::MAX guard prevents writing into already marked cells.

261. Graph Valid Tree (Medium · Premium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/graph-valid-tree/ · Topic: Union-Find (Premium)

Problem (summary)

Given n nodes labeled 0..n-1 and a list of edges (an UNDIRECTED graph), say whether the graph is a valid tree: connected AND acyclic (a tree with n nodes has exactly n−1 edges). (Note: Premium problem — solve it through knowledge.)

n = 5, edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[0,3],[1,4]]   →  true
n = 5, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[1,3],[1,4]]  →  false (cycle 1-2-3-1)
n = 4, edges = [[0,1],[2,3]]               →  false (disconnected)

Pattern — what to memorize

Union-Find with cycle detection + a components == 1 check. Two separate, independent conditions:

  1. Cycle: when uniting a and b, if encontrar(a) == encontrar(b) both were already in the same component ⇒ the edge closes a cycle ⇒ not a tree.
  2. Connectivity: after processing everything, with componentes starting at n and decrementing on every real union, require componentes == 1.

Alternative (DFS/BFS): a single connected component with one visited AND edges == n - 1 — it works because “tree” is exactly “1 component and n−1 edges”. Union-find is preferable because it’s iterative (no recursion stack) and costs O(α(n)) per operation. Tell: validating graph structure on a big sample → union-find; I also want the component count → the counter in the union.

Python

class Solution:
    def validTree(self, n: int, edges: list[list[int]]) -> bool:
        pai = list(range(n))                     # union-find: each node is its root
        tam = [1] * n                            # size for union by size

        def encontrar(x: int) -> int:
            while pai[x] != x:                   # iterative path compression
                pai[x] = pai[pai[x]]
                x = pai[x]
            return x

        componentes = n
        for a, b in edges:
            ra, rb = encontrar(a), encontrar(b)
            if ra == rb:
                return False                     # edge joins ALREADY-connected nodes = cycle
            if tam[ra] < tam[rb]:
                ra, rb = rb, ra
            pai[rb] = ra
            tam[ra] += tam[rb]
            componentes -= 1
        return componentes == 1                  # tree: 1 component and no cycle

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn valid_tree(n: i32, edges: Vec<Vec<i32>>) -> bool {
        fn encontrar(pai: &mut Vec<usize>, x: usize) -> usize {
            if pai[x] != x {
                pai[x] = encontrar(pai, pai[x]); // path compression
            }
            pai[x]
        }
        let n = n as usize;
        let mut pai: Vec<usize> = (0..n).collect();
        let mut tam = vec![1usize; n];           // union by size
        let mut componentes = n;
        for e in &edges {
            let a = encontrar(&mut pai, e[0] as usize);
            let b = encontrar(&mut pai, e[1] as usize);
            if a == b {
                return false; // edge joins ALREADY-connected nodes = cycle
            }
            let (a, b) = if tam[a] < tam[b] { (b, a) } else { (a, b) };
            pai[b] = a;
            tam[a] += tam[b];
            componentes -= 1;
        }
        componentes == 1 // tree: 1 component and no cycle
    }
}
}

C++

#include <numeric>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    bool validTree(int n, vector<vector<int>>& edges) {
        pai.resize(n);
        iota(pai.begin(), pai.end(), 0);        // union-find: each node its root
        tam.assign(n, 1);
        int componentes = n;
        for (auto& e : edges) {
            int a = encontrar(e[0]);
            int b = encontrar(e[1]);
            if (a == b) return false;           // edge joins ALREADY-connected nodes = cycle
            if (tam[a] < tam[b]) swap(a, b);    // union by size
            pai[b] = a;
            tam[a] += tam[b];
            --componentes;
        }
        return componentes == 1;                // tree: 1 component and no cycle
    }

private:
    vector<int> pai, tam;

    int encontrar(int x) {
        if (pai[x] != x) pai[x] = encontrar(pai[x]); // path compression
        return pai[x];
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

static int encontrar(int* pai, int x) {
    int raiz = x;
    while (pai[raiz] != raiz) raiz = pai[raiz];   /* climb to the root */
    while (pai[x] != x) {                         /* iterative path compression */
        int prox = pai[x];
        pai[x] = raiz;
        x = prox;
    }
    return raiz;
}

bool validTree(int n, int** edges, int edgesSize, int* edgesColSize) {
    (void)edgesColSize;
    int* pai = malloc((size_t)n * sizeof(int));
    int* tam = malloc((size_t)n * sizeof(int));   /* union by size */
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { pai[i] = i; tam[i] = 1; }
    int componentes = n;
    bool valido = true;
    for (int i = 0; i < edgesSize && valido; i++) {
        int a = encontrar(pai, edges[i][0]);
        int b = encontrar(pai, edges[i][1]);
        if (a == b) {
            valido = false;                       /* edge joins ALREADY-connected nodes = cycle */
        } else {
            if (tam[a] < tam[b]) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; }
            pai[b] = a;
            tam[a] += tam[b];
            componentes--;
        }
    }
    free(pai);
    free(tam);
    return valido && componentes == 1;            /* tree: 1 component, no cycle */
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n + α(n)·E) ≈ O(n + E) in practice — each encontrar is near-O(1) with path compression + union by size.
  • Space: O(n) — the pai and tam arrays.

Pitfalls

  • n = 1 with 0 edges is a tree (true). The statement guarantees n ≥ 1.
  • Don’t mix up the two conditions: a cyclic graph can have 1 component (components==1 alone isn’t enough); a disconnected graph can be acyclic (cycle detection alone isn’t enough). The order of checks doesn’t matter, but a return false mid-loop means condition 2 needs all edges processed.
  • Duplicate edges (a,b) and (b,a): union-find handles them naturally (the second one is a cycle) — correct, not a bug.
  • Rust: recursive encontrar with classic path compression (pai[x] = encontrar(...)) in a nested fn that takes &mut pai — no closure capturing the environment.
  • C++: iota(pai.begin(), pai.end(), 0) is the idiom to initialize 0,1,2,...; swap(a, b) for union by size.
  • C: two-step iterative path compression (climb to root, then flatten) avoids deep recursion on degenerate trees.

127. Word Ladder (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/word-ladder/ · Topic: Graphs · BFS (minimum steps)

Problem (summary)

Given beginWord, endWord, and a word list, transform beginWord into endWord by changing one letter per step, with every intermediate word in the list. Return the total number of words in the shortest path (including the start and end), or 0 if no path exists.

beginWord = "hit", endWord = "cog",
wordList = ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log","cog"]
→ 5  ("hit" → "hot" → "dot" → "dog" → "cog")

Pattern — what to memorize

BFS on an implicit graph: each word is a node; two nodes are neighbors if they differ in 1 character. “Shortest path from A to B in an unweighted graph” is layered BFS — the level at which endWord is first discovered is the answer. Generate neighbors by character substitution (26×L candidates per word) instead of comparing against the whole list (N comparisons). BFS guarantees the minimum because it explores by level.

Bidirectional (interview bonus): run BFS from BOTH ends (start and goal) and stop when the fronts meet — it halves the search space: the number of visited states drops from b^d to 2·b^(d/2). The required solution here is plain BFS; bidirectional is the natural upgrade to mention.

Python

from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def ladderLength(self, beginWord: str, endWord: str, wordList: list[str]) -> int:
        palavras = set(wordList)
        if endWord not in palavras:
            return 0
        fila = deque([(beginWord, 1)])
        while fila:
            atual, passo = fila.popleft()
            if atual == endWord:
                return passo
            for i in range(len(atual)):
                for c in "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz":
                    if c == atual[i]:
                        continue
                    nova = atual[:i] + c + atual[i + 1:]
                    if nova in palavras:
                        palavras.remove(nova)     # mark visited in the set
                        fila.append((nova, passo + 1))
        return 0

Removing from the set IS the visited mark: a discovered word can’t be rediscovered at a deeper level (BFS discovers at the minimum level). String slicing atual[:i] + c + atual[i+1:] is the Python way to swap one char (strings are immutable).

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::{HashSet, VecDeque};

impl Solution {
    pub fn ladder_length(begin_word: String, end_word: String, word_list: Vec<String>) -> i32 {
        let mut palavras: HashSet<String> = word_list.into_iter().collect();
        if !palavras.contains(&end_word) {
            return 0; // goal not in the list
        }
        let mut fila: VecDeque<(String, i32)> = VecDeque::new();
        fila.push_back((begin_word, 1));
        while let Some((atual, passo)) = fila.pop_front() {
            if atual == end_word {
                return passo;
            }
            let mut bytes: Vec<u8> = atual.bytes().collect();
            for i in 0..bytes.len() {
                let original = bytes[i];
                for c in b'a'..=b'z' {
                    if c == original {
                        continue;
                    }
                    bytes[i] = c; // generate the neighbor
                    let nova = String::from_utf8(bytes.clone()).unwrap();
                    if palavras.remove(&nova) { // mark visited
                        fila.push_back((nova, passo + 1));
                    }
                }
                bytes[i] = original; // restore
            }
        }
        0 // unreachable goal
    }
}
}

C++

#include <queue>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_set>
#include <utility>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int ladderLength(string beginWord, string endWord, vector<string>& wordList) {
        unordered_set<string> palavras(wordList.begin(), wordList.end());
        if (!palavras.count(endWord)) return 0;  // goal not in the list
        queue<pair<string, int>> fila;
        fila.push({beginWord, 1});
        while (!fila.empty()) {
            auto [atual, passo] = fila.front();
            fila.pop();
            if (atual == endWord) return passo;
            for (int i = 0; i < (int)atual.size(); ++i) {
                char original = atual[i];
                for (char c = 'a'; c <= 'z'; ++c) {
                    if (c == original) continue;
                    atual[i] = c;                     // generate the neighbor
                    if (palavras.count(atual)) {
                        palavras.erase(atual);        // mark visited
                        fila.push({atual, passo + 1});
                    }
                }
                atual[i] = original;                  // restore
            }
        }
        return 0;                                     // unreachable goal
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

typedef struct { const char* palavra; int nivel; } ItemFila;

int ladderLength(char* beginWord, char* endWord, char** wordList, int wordListSize) {
    int tamanho = (int)strlen(beginWord);
    int fim = -1;
    for (int i = 0; i < wordListSize; i++)
        if (strcmp(wordList[i], endWord) == 0) { fim = i; break; }
    if (fim == -1) return 0;                         /* the goal is not on the list */

    int* visitado = calloc(wordListSize, sizeof(int));
    for (int i = 0; i < wordListSize; i++)
        if (strcmp(wordList[i], beginWord) == 0) visitado[i] = 1;

    ItemFila* fila = malloc((wordListSize + 1) * sizeof(ItemFila));
    int frente = 0, tras = 0;
    fila[tras].palavra = beginWord;
    fila[tras].nivel = 1;
    tras++;

    while (frente < tras) {
        ItemFila atual = fila[frente++];
        if (strcmp(atual.palavra, endWord) == 0) {
            free(visitado);
            free(fila);
            return atual.nivel;
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < wordListSize; i++) {
            if (visitado[i]) continue;
            int difs = 0;                            /* count char differences */
            for (int c = 0; c < tamanho && difs <= 1; c++)
                if (wordList[i][c] != atual.palavra[c]) difs++;
            if (difs == 1) {
                visitado[i] = 1;
                fila[tras].palavra = wordList[i];
                fila[tras].nivel = atual.nivel + 1;
                tras++;
            }
        }
    }
    free(visitado);
    free(fila);
    return 0;                                        /* unreachable goal */
}

With no free mutable strings, C generates neighbors differently: scan the list comparing char by char (counting differences) — an implicit graph by checking rather than generating. visitado[] plays the role of the set; the queue points into the list’s own strings (no copies).

Complexity

  • Time: O(N·L·26), with N = words and L = length — each word is discovered once and generates 26·L candidates (in practice each generation costs O(L) of string → O(N·L²) counting the strings; the C diff-counting version is O(N·L) per pop).
  • Space: O(N·L) — the word set plus the queue in the worst case.

Pitfalls

  • endWord outside the list → immediate 0 (check before the BFS).
  • Mark visited at discovery time (not at pop): otherwise the same word enters the queue many times, exploding the BFS.
  • Words have fixed length; the substitution respects position — never remove/insert characters.
  • beginWord may not be in the list — BFS starts from it anyway (what matters is marking the list’s words). If beginWord == endWord and both are in the list, answer 1 (the initial level).
  • Rust: String::from_utf8(...).unwrap() is safe because only one ASCII byte is mutated; with real Unicode, build a Vec<char>.
  • C: difs <= 1 in the loop cuts the counting early — a legitimate micro-optimization, but keep the difs == 1 logic in the decision.

130. Surrounded Regions (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/surrounded-regions/ · Topic: Graphs

Problem (summary)

An m×n board of 'X' and 'O': capture every region of 'O' fully surrounded by 'X' (flip to 'X'). An 'O' that touches a border — or connects to a border 'O' — is not surrounded and stays.

X X X X      X X X X
X O O X  →   X X X X
X X O X      X X X X
X O X X      X O X X      ← the O at (3,1) touches the border and stays

Pattern — what to memorize

Mark the SAFE ones (connected to the border), not the capturable ones. It’s tempting to scan and flip every 'O' whose 4 neighbors are 'X' — but the decision is global, not local: an interior 'O' can reach the border through a path, and the only way to know is to propagate from the border. Worse: if you flip 'O'→'X' mid-scan, a border 'O' already flipped becomes a “wall” and hides the interior cells that depended on it. Recipe: (1) multi-source — push every border 'O' marked 'E' (escaped); (2) flood fill (BFS/DFS) from the 'E's into neighboring 'O's; (3) final scan: 'E'→'O', 'O'→'X'. Flood fill iterative with an explicit stack — recursion overflows on large boards.

Python

class Solution:
    def solve(self, board: list[list[str]]) -> None:
        """Mutates board in place: only interior O's are flipped."""
        m, n = len(board), len(board[0])

        # Multi-source: every border 'O' is safe (not capturable).
        pilha = []
        for i in range(m):
            for j in range(n):
                if (i == 0 or i == m - 1 or j == 0 or j == n - 1) and board[i][j] == "O":
                    board[i][j] = "E"  # E = escaped (safe)
                    pilha.append((i, j))

        # Iterative flood fill starting from the borders.
        while pilha:
            i, j = pilha.pop()
            for di, dj in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
                ni, nj = i + di, j + dj
                if 0 <= ni < m and 0 <= nj < n and board[ni][nj] == "O":
                    board[ni][nj] = "E"
                    pilha.append((ni, nj))

        # Final: safe flips back to 'O'; everything else becomes 'X'.
        for i in range(m):
            for j in range(n):
                if board[i][j] == "E":
                    board[i][j] = "O"
                elif board[i][j] == "O":
                    board[i][j] = "X"

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn solve(board: &mut Vec<Vec<char>>) {
        let (m, n) = (board.len(), board[0].len());
        let mut pilha: Vec<(usize, usize)> = Vec::new();

        // Multi-source: every border 'O' is safe ('E' = escaped).
        for i in 0..m {
            for j in 0..n {
                if (i == 0 || i == m - 1 || j == 0 || j == n - 1) && board[i][j] == 'O' {
                    board[i][j] = 'E';
                    pilha.push((i, j));
                }
            }
        }

        // Iterative flood fill (explicit stack: no deep recursion).
        while let Some((i, j)) = pilha.pop() {
            for (di, dj) in [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)] {
                let (ni, nj) = (i as isize + di, j as isize + dj);
                if ni >= 0 && nj >= 0 && (ni as usize) < m && (nj as usize) < n {
                    let (ni, nj) = (ni as usize, nj as usize);
                    if board[ni][nj] == 'O' {
                        board[ni][nj] = 'E';
                        pilha.push((ni, nj));
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        // Final: safe flips back to 'O'; everything else becomes 'X'.
        for linha in board.iter_mut() {
            for celula in linha.iter_mut() {
                if *celula == 'E' {
                    *celula = 'O';
                } else if *celula == 'O' {
                    *celula = 'X';
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <utility>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    void solve(vector<vector<char>>& board) {
        int m = board.size(), n = board[0].size();
        vector<pair<int, int>> pilha;

        // Multi-source: every border 'O' is safe ('E' = escaped).
        for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i)
            for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j)
                if ((i == 0 || i == m - 1 || j == 0 || j == n - 1) && board[i][j] == 'O') {
                    board[i][j] = 'E';
                    pilha.emplace_back(i, j);
                }

        // Iterative flood fill (explicit stack: no deep recursion).
        int d[5] = {1, 0, -1, 0, 1};
        while (!pilha.empty()) {
            auto [i, j] = pilha.back();
            pilha.pop_back();
            for (int k = 0; k < 4; ++k) {
                int ni = i + d[k], nj = j + d[k + 1];
                if (ni >= 0 && ni < m && nj >= 0 && nj < n && board[ni][nj] == 'O') {
                    board[ni][nj] = 'E';
                    pilha.emplace_back(ni, nj);
                }
            }
        }

        // Final: safe flips back to 'O'; everything else becomes 'X'.
        for (auto& linha : board)
            for (char& c : linha)
                if (c == 'E')
                    c = 'O';
                else if (c == 'O')
                    c = 'X';
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

void solve(char** board, int boardSize, int* boardColSize) {
    if (boardSize == 0) return;
    int colunas = boardColSize[0];

    /* Explicit stack for the flood fill (large boards don't recurse). */
    int* pilha_i = (int*)malloc((size_t)boardSize * colunas * sizeof(int));
    int* pilha_j = (int*)malloc((size_t)boardSize * colunas * sizeof(int));
    int topo = 0;

    /* Multi-source: every border 'O' is safe ('E' = escaped). */
    for (int i = 0; i < boardSize; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < colunas; j++) {
            if ((i == 0 || i == boardSize - 1 || j == 0 || j == colunas - 1)
                && board[i][j] == 'O') {
                board[i][j] = 'E';
                pilha_i[topo] = i; pilha_j[topo] = j; topo++;
            }
        }
    }

    int d[5] = {1, 0, -1, 0, 1};
    while (topo > 0) {
        topo--;
        int i = pilha_i[topo], j = pilha_j[topo];
        for (int k = 0; k < 4; k++) {
            int ni = i + d[k], nj = j + d[k + 1];
            if (ni >= 0 && ni < boardSize && nj >= 0 && nj < colunas
                && board[ni][nj] == 'O') {
                board[ni][nj] = 'E';
                pilha_i[topo] = ni; pilha_j[topo] = nj; topo++;
            }
        }
    }

    /* Final: safe flips back to 'O'; everything else becomes 'X'. */
    for (int i = 0; i < boardSize; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < colunas; j++) {
            if (board[i][j] == 'E') board[i][j] = 'O';
            else if (board[i][j] == 'O') board[i][j] = 'X';
        }

    free(pilha_i);
    free(pilha_j);
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(m·n) — each cell enters the flood fill at most once, plus the final scan.
  • Space: O(m·n) worst case (the stack can hold an entire region).

Pitfalls

  • The central trap is marking capturable instead of safe — explained in the Pattern; the tell you got it wrong: a border-linked 'O' turned into 'X'.
  • 1×1 board and 100% 'O' borders: nothing changes (everything is safe).
  • Python: deep recursion in the flood fill → use the explicit stack (~1000-frame limit).
  • Rust: i as usize panics on negatives — neighbors go through isize with the >= 0 test before the cast (the code above already does it).
  • C++: auto [i, j] = pilha.back() (structured binding, C++17) — mind declaring pilha as vector<pair<int,int>>.
  • C: the stacks live on the heap (malloc) — a 1000×1000 int grid on the call stack overflows; free before returning (void, LeetCode won’t free for you).

743. Network Delay Time (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/network-delay-time/ · Topic: Dijkstra (weighted graphs)

Problem (summary)

Network of n nodes (1..n) with directed edges times = [u, v, w] (w in ms). A signal starts at node k and propagates in parallel; return the minimum time for all nodes to receive the signal, or -1 if some node is unreachable.

times = [[2,1,1],[2,3,1],[3,4,1]], n = 4, k = 2  →  2   (2→1 in 1 ms; 2→3→4 in 2 ms)
times = [[1,2,1]], n = 2, k = 2                  →  -1  (the edge points into the source; node 1 never receives)

Pattern — what to memorize

Dijkstra with a min-heap: weights ≥ 0, and the signal leaves the source over all edges at the same time — exactly “shortest path from k”. Every relaxed edge pushes (distance, node) into the heap; anything that pops with a cost larger than the recorded one is a stale entry (classic pruning).

Two ideas the prompt begs you to verbalize:

  1. Why the answer is max of the distances, not “the last one”: the slowest node is what defines when the whole network received the signal. (Do not be confused: Dijkstra relaxes distance from the source; the naive “last one” is neither the last heap pop nor the largest id.)
  2. Heap vs O(V²): in a sparse graph (E ≪ V²) the heap wins (O(E log V)); in a dense one (E ~ V²), the linear selection per iteration (V iterations × O(V)) is just as good and without the log factor — that is the C version below, which has no heap in the stdlib and does not need one: n ≤ 100 here.

Python

import heapq

class Solution:
    def networkDelayTime(self, times: list[list[int]], n: int, k: int) -> int:
        grafo = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
        for u, v, w in times:
            grafo[u].append((v, w))

        dist = [float("inf")] * (n + 1)
        dist[k] = 0
        fila = [(0, k)]                             # (cost, node) — min-heap
        while fila:
            custo, u = heapq.heappop(fila)
            if custo > dist[u]:
                continue                            # stale entry
            for v, w in grafo[u]:
                if custo + w < dist[v]:
                    dist[v] = custo + w
                    heapq.heappush(fila, (dist[v], v))

        atraso = max(dist[1:])
        return atraso if atraso < float("inf") else -1

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

impl Solution {
    pub fn network_delay_time(times: Vec<Vec<i32>>, n: i32, k: i32) -> i32 {
        let n = n as usize;
        let mut grafo = vec![vec![]; n + 1];
        for t in &times {
            let (u, v, w) = (t[0] as usize, t[1] as usize, t[2]);
            grafo[u].push((v, w));
        }

        let mut dist = vec![i32::MAX; n + 1];
        dist[k as usize] = 0;
        // BinaryHeap is a MAX-heap: Reverse turns it into a min-heap (linguagens/rust.md).
        let mut fila = BinaryHeap::new();
        fila.push(Reverse((0, k as usize)));
        while let Some(Reverse((custo, u))) = fila.pop() {
            if custo > dist[u] {
                continue; // stale entry
            }
            for &(v, w) in &grafo[u] {
                if custo + w < dist[v] {
                    dist[v] = custo + w;
                    fila.push(Reverse((dist[v], v)));
                }
            }
        }

        let atraso = dist[1..].iter().copied().max().unwrap_or(i32::MAX);
        if atraso == i32::MAX {
            -1
        } else {
            atraso
        }
    }
}
}

C++

#include <queue>
#include <vector>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int networkDelayTime(vector<vector<int>>& times, int n, int k) {
        vector<vector<pair<int, int>>> grafo(n + 1);
        for (auto& t : times) {
            grafo[t[0]].emplace_back(t[1], t[2]);
        }
        vector<int> dist(n + 1, INT_MAX);
        dist[k] = 0;
        priority_queue<pair<int, int>, vector<pair<int, int>>, greater<>> fila;
        fila.emplace(0, k);
        while (!fila.empty()) {
            auto [custo, u] = fila.top();
            fila.pop();
            if (custo > dist[u]) continue; // stale entry
            for (auto [v, w] : grafo[u]) {
                if (custo + w < dist[v]) {
                    dist[v] = custo + w;
                    fila.emplace(dist[v], v);
                }
            }
        }
        int atraso = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) atraso = max(atraso, dist[i]);
        return atraso == INT_MAX ? -1 : atraso;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <limits.h>

/* Dijkstra O(V²) — no heap in C; on a dense graph (E ~ V²) this beats the
   O(E log V) heap: linear minimum selection per iteration = V×O(V) of
   selection + V×average_degree of relaxation. Vertex index = id (1..n). */
int networkDelayTime(int** times, int timesSize, int* timesColSize,
                     int n, int k) {
    (void)timesColSize;
    const int INF = INT_MAX / 2;
    int tam = n + 1;
    int* mat = malloc((size_t)tam * tam * sizeof(int));
    int* dist = malloc((size_t)tam * sizeof(int));
    int* visitado = malloc((size_t)tam * sizeof(int));

    for (int i = 0; i < tam; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < tam; j++) mat[i * tam + j] = INF;
        dist[i] = INF;
        visitado[i] = 0;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < timesSize; i++) {
        int u = times[i][0], v = times[i][1], w = times[i][2];
        if (w < mat[u * tam + v]) mat[u * tam + v] = w; // multi-edge: keep the smallest
    }
    dist[k] = 0;

    for (int passo = 0; passo < n; passo++) {
        int u = -1;
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
            if (!visitado[i] && (u == -1 || dist[i] < dist[u])) u = i;
        if (u == -1 || dist[u] == INF) break; // the rest is unreachable
        visitado[u] = 1;
        for (int v = 1; v <= n; v++)
            if (!visitado[v] && mat[u * tam + v] != INF &&
                dist[u] + mat[u * tam + v] < dist[v])
                dist[v] = dist[u] + mat[u * tam + v];
    }

    int atraso = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
        if (dist[i] > atraso) atraso = dist[i];
    free(mat);
    free(dist);
    free(visitado);
    return atraso >= INF ? -1 : atraso;
}

Complexity

  • Heap (Python/Rust/C++): time O(E log V) — every edge relaxes at most once, each push/pop is O(log V); space O(V + E) (adjacency list).
  • O(V²) (C): time O(V²) — n iterations, each with O(V) selection and O(V) relaxation; space O(V²) (matrix) + O(V).

Pitfalls

  • Nodes are 1-indexed: arrays of size n + 1 and ignore index 0.
  • If max(dist) is infinite, some node never received → -1 (not “0” nor the largest finite value).
  • Repeated u→v edges: keep the smallest weight (in the matrix, only overwrite if smaller — in the adjacency list, relax and the min resolves).
  • Stale entry in the heap (cost larger than the recorded one): continue — without it you only pay an extra log, but with it the code reads “interview-grade”.
  • C: the INT_MAX / 2 sentinel keeps dist[u] + w from ever overflowing.

787. Cheapest Flights Within K Stops (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/cheapest-flights-within-k-stops/ · Topic: Bellman-Ford (graphs with a stop limit)

Problem (summary)

n cities connected by flights flights = [from, to, price] (directed). Find the cheapest price from src to dst using at most k stops (a stop = intermediate city; k stops = up to k+1 flights), or -1 if there is no route within the limit.

n = 3, flights = [[0,1,100],[1,2,100],[0,2,500]], src = 0, dst = 2
k = 1  →  200   (0→1→2, with 1 stop)
k = 0  →  500   (only the direct flight 0→2)

Pattern — what to memorize

Bellman-Ford with a bubble of k+1 iterations is the natural tool for “path with a cost AND an edge-count limit”: each round relaxes all edges, and the number of rounds is exactly the edge cap on the path.

The detail that separates the ones who know from the ones who memorize: the per-round snapshot. If you relax using dist that was already updated in the same round, Bellman-Ford chains edges and “spends” more than k+1 stops without noticing — the classic case is 0→1→2→3 with k = 1 (needs 3 edges → should be -1, but the in-place version returns a price). So: copy dist at the start of each round and relax only from the copy.

And why not Dijkstra right away? Textbook Dijkstra chases the cheapest cost and prunes the node once visited — then a more expensive path with fewer stops, which would be the only viable one within the limit, dies before its time. That trap shows up precisely in this problem. Two honest ways out:

  • BFS/Dijkstra with the state (city, stops) instead of (city) — dist[node][stops] does not prune the same node with different stop counts;
  • Bellman-Ford with k+1 rounds (the one in all 4 languages here).

Python

class Solution:
    def findCheapestPrice(self, n: int, flights: list[list[int]],
                          src: int, dst: int, k: int) -> int:
        INF = float("inf")
        dist = [INF] * n
        dist[src] = 0
        # k stops => at most k+1 edges => k+1 relaxation rounds.
        for _ in range(k + 1):
            anterior = dist[:]          # SNAPSHOT: forbids chaining edges
            for u, v, p in flights:     # in the SAME round (k+2-stop cost)
                if anterior[u] != INF and anterior[u] + p < dist[v]:
                    dist[v] = anterior[u] + p
        return dist[dst] if dist[dst] != INF else -1

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn find_cheapest_price(n: i32, flights: Vec<Vec<i32>>, src: i32, dst: i32, k: i32) -> i32 {
        const INF: i32 = i32::MAX / 2;
        let n = n as usize;
        let mut dist = vec![INF; n];
        dist[src as usize] = 0;

        // k stops => at most k+1 edges => k+1 relaxation rounds.
        for _ in 0..=k {
            let anterior = dist.clone(); // SNAPSHOT: forbids chaining edges
            for f in &flights {          // in the SAME round (k+2-stop cost)
                let (u, v, p) = (f[0] as usize, f[1] as usize, f[2]);
                if anterior[u] != INF && anterior[u] + p < dist[v] {
                    dist[v] = anterior[u] + p;
                }
            }
        }
        let resp = dist[dst as usize];
        if resp == INF {
            -1
        } else {
            resp
        }
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int findCheapestPrice(int n, vector<vector<int>>& flights,
                          int src, int dst, int k) {
        const int INF = INT_MAX / 2;
        vector<int> dist(n, INF);
        dist[src] = 0;

        // k stops => at most k+1 edges => k+1 relaxation rounds.
        for (int r = 0; r <= k; ++r) {
            vector<int> anterior = dist; // SNAPSHOT: forbids chaining edges
            for (auto& f : flights) {    // in the SAME round (k+2-stop cost)
                int u = f[0], v = f[1], p = f[2];
                if (anterior[u] != INF && anterior[u] + p < dist[v])
                    dist[v] = anterior[u] + p;
            }
        }
        return dist[dst] == INF ? -1 : dist[dst];
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <limits.h>

/* Bellman-Ford with a stop limit: k+1 rounds, each relaxing ALL edges from
   the SNAPSHOT of the previous round — forbidding in-round chaining is what
   guarantees "at most k+1 edges". */
int findCheapestPrice(int n, int** flights, int flightsSize, int* flightsColSize,
                      int src, int dst, int k) {
    (void)flightsColSize;
    const int INF = INT_MAX / 2;
    int* dist = malloc((size_t)n * sizeof(int));
    int* anterior = malloc((size_t)n * sizeof(int));
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) dist[i] = INF;
    dist[src] = 0;

    for (int r = 0; r <= k; r++) {
        memcpy(anterior, dist, (size_t)n * sizeof(int));
        for (int i = 0; i < flightsSize; i++) {
            int u = flights[i][0], v = flights[i][1], p = flights[i][2];
            if (anterior[u] != INF && anterior[u] + p < dist[v])
                dist[v] = anterior[u] + p;
        }
    }
    int resp = dist[dst];
    free(anterior);
    free(dist);
    return resp >= INF ? -1 : resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(k·E) — k+1 rounds, each scanning every edge. (It is NOT O(V·E) because the cap is k, not V.)
  • Space: O(V) — dist + the round snapshot.

Pitfalls

  • Snapshot is mandatory per round — without it the “k+2-stop cost” leaks and the 0→1→2→3 case with k = 1 answers a price instead of -1 (a covered test on the page; write that case in the interview).
  • Stop counting: k stops = k+1 flights — the loop is for r in 0..=k.
  • -1 when dist[dst] is still infinite: no route or every route blows the stop limit.
  • Plain Dijkstra without the stop limit is too cheap to be used here: that is the question the interviewer asks when you say “Dijkstra” — answer with the (city, stops) state.
  • C: the INT_MAX / 2 sentinel prevents overflow in anterior[u] + p.

1584. Min Cost to Connect All Points (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/min-cost-to-connect-all-points/ · Topic: MST — Prim / Kruskal (complete graph)

Problem (summary)

points[i] = [xi, yi]. The cost of connecting two points is the Manhattan distance |x1-x2| + |y1-y2|. Return the minimum cost to connect all points (one single network — a minimum spanning tree).

[[0,0],[2,2],[3,10],[5,2],[7,0]]               →  20
[[3,12],[-2,5],[-4,1]]                         →  18

Pattern — what to memorize

The problem is a MST in disguise: the graph is complete (n(n-1)/2 edges), and that is exactly where the algorithm choice becomes interview conversation.

  • Dense Prim O(n²) (the one implemented in all 4 languages): grows the tree one vertex at a time, always via the out-of-tree neighbor with the cheapest connection cost. The linear selection per iteration (O(n)) totals O(n²) — no heap, no edge list to build: the Manhattan distance is computed on the fly, during relaxation. For a complete graph, O(n²) is optimal.
  • Kruskal + union-find (the alternative, explained): generates the ~n² edges, sorts by cost (O(E log E) = O(n² log n)) and unions with DSU (path compression) until n-1 edges are in. It wins on graphs that are not complete; here, just the sorting already ties the whole of Prim.

Clue in the prompt: connect all points with minimum cost → MST; and Manhattan (not Euclidean) only changes the edge cost computation, not the algorithm.

Python

class Solution:
    def minCostConnectPoints(self, points: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(points)
        if n <= 1:
            return 0
        na_arvore = [False] * n
        menor = [float("inf")] * n
        menor[0] = 0                                # start from point 0
        custo_total = 0
        for _ in range(n):
            # pick the cheapest out-of-tree point to connect
            u = min((i for i in range(n) if not na_arvore[i]),
                    key=lambda i: menor[i])
            na_arvore[u] = True
            custo_total += menor[u]
            x0, y0 = points[u]
            for v in range(n):
                if not na_arvore[v]:
                    custo = abs(x0 - points[v][0]) + abs(y0 - points[v][1])
                    if custo < menor[v]:
                        menor[v] = custo
        return custo_total

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn min_cost_connect_points(points: Vec<Vec<i32>>) -> i32 {
        let n = points.len();
        if n <= 1 {
            return 0;
        }
        let mut na_arvore = vec![false; n];
        let mut menor = vec![i64::MAX; n];
        menor[0] = 0; // start from point 0
        let mut custo_total: i64 = 0;
        for _ in 0..n {
            // pick the out-of-tree point with the cheapest connection cost
            let u = (0..n)
                .filter(|&i| !na_arvore[i])
                .min_by_key(|&i| menor[i])
                .expect("there is always an out-of-tree point");
            na_arvore[u] = true;
            custo_total += menor[u];
            for v in 0..n {
                if !na_arvore[v] {
                    let custo = (points[u][0] - points[v][0]).abs() as i64
                        + (points[u][1] - points[v][1]).abs() as i64;
                    if custo < menor[v] {
                        menor[v] = custo;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        custo_total as i32
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <climits>
#include <cstdlib>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int minCostConnectPoints(vector<vector<int>>& points) {
        int n = points.size();
        if (n <= 1) return 0;
        vector<char> naArvore(n, 0);
        vector<long long> menor(n, LLONG_MAX);
        menor[0] = 0; // start from point 0
        long long custoTotal = 0;
        for (int passo = 0; passo < n; ++passo) {
            int u = -1;
            for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
                if (!naArvore[i] && (u == -1 || menor[i] < menor[u])) u = i;
            naArvore[u] = 1;
            custoTotal += menor[u];
            for (int v = 0; v < n; ++v) {
                if (!naArvore[v]) {
                    long long custo = (long long)abs(points[u][0] - points[v][0])
                                    + abs(points[u][1] - points[v][1]);
                    if (custo < menor[v]) menor[v] = custo;
                }
            }
        }
        return (int)custoTotal;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdint.h>

/* Prim O(V²) — the graph is complete (K_n): E = n(n-1)/2, so the linear
   minimum selection per iteration (O(V) × V iterations) is optimal; Kruskal
   would pay O(E log E) = O(n² log n) just on sorting the edges. */
int minCostConnectPoints(int** points, int pointsSize, int* pointsColSize) {
    (void)pointsColSize;
    int n = pointsSize;
    if (n <= 1) return 0;

    bool* na_arvore = calloc((size_t)n, sizeof(bool));
    int64_t* menor = malloc((size_t)n * sizeof(int64_t));
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) menor[i] = INT64_MAX;
    menor[0] = 0; // start from point 0
    int64_t custo_total = 0;

    for (int passo = 0; passo < n; passo++) {
        int u = -1;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            if (!na_arvore[i] && (u == -1 || menor[i] < menor[u])) u = i;
        na_arvore[u] = true;
        custo_total += menor[u];
        for (int v = 0; v < n; v++) {
            if (!na_arvore[v]) {
                int64_t d1 = points[u][0] - points[v][0];
                int64_t d2 = points[u][1] - points[v][1];
                int64_t custo = (d1 < 0 ? -d1 : d1) + (d2 < 0 ? -d2 : d2);
                if (custo < menor[v]) menor[v] = custo;
            }
        }
    }
    free(na_arvore);
    free(menor);
    return (int)custo_total;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n²) — n iterations × (O(n) minimum selection + O(n) relaxation). Complete graph, so E ~ n² and the heap (O(E log V) = O(n² log n)) only makes it worse; that is why dense O(n²) is the “interview optimum” here.
  • Space: O(n) — only the menor vector and the na_arvore marker (the Manhattan distance is computed on the fly; edges are never materialized).

Pitfalls

  • Does the accumulator overflow? The total cost can get close to 2×10⁹ (n = 1000 × edges of up to 2×10⁶): in Rust/C++/C use i64/long long/ int64_t for the accumulator — i32/int is a silent bug near the limit.
  • n = 1 → cost 0 (empty tree), before any selection.
  • Negative coordinates in Manhattan: abs of the difference, not of the sum.
  • Prim never materializes edges: the memory footprint stays O(n) even on a complete graph — fill menor with INF and relax straight from the array.
  • C: INT64_MAX sentinel and safe linear selection with the initial u == -1.

Review card

  • R1 (+1d) · [ ] R2 (+3d) · [ ] R3 (+7d, another language) · [ ] R4 (+21d) · [ ] R5 (+60d)

778. Swim in Rising Water (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/swim-in-rising-water/ · Topic: Dijkstra with “max along the path” (grid)

Problem (summary)

n×n grid; at time t the water covers the cells with grid[i][j] ≤ t. Starting from (0,0) — only navigable in the 4 directions — return the smallest t at which you can reach (n-1, n-1). Each cell’s value is the height the water must rise for you to enter it.

[[0,2],[1,3]]                                              →  3
[[0,1,2,3,4],[24,23,22,21,5],[12,13,14,15,16],
 [11,17,18,19,20],[10,9,8,7,6]]                            →  16

Pattern — what to memorize

Reframe as a shortest path with a different “sum”: the cost of a path is the maximum of the cell values, not the sum. We want the minimum over all paths of max(cells on the path) — and Dijkstra works with any monotone semigroup (sum, max, xor…): the relaxation at a neighbor becomes novo = max(atual, grid[ni][nj]) and the heap orders by that value. The first time (n-1,n-1) pops out of the heap is the answer (Dijkstra property: the minimum pop is final).

An alternative worth mentioning: binary search on t + BFS — “navigability” is monotone (if it works at t, it works for any t' > t), so for t { BFS over cells ≤ t } becomes binary search (0..n²) + BFS, O(n² log n) without a heap.

Python

import heapq

class Solution:
    def swimInRisingWater(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(grid)
        melhor = [[float("inf")] * n for _ in range(n)]
        melhor[0][0] = grid[0][0]
        fila = [(grid[0][0], 0, 0)]                  # (max so far, i, j)
        while fila:
            t, i, j = heapq.heappop(fila)
            if t > melhor[i][j]:
                continue                             # stale entry
            if i == n - 1 and j == n - 1:
                return t                             # 1st pop of the target is optimal
            for di, dj in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
                ni, nj = i + di, j + dj
                if 0 <= ni < n and 0 <= nj < n:
                    novo = max(t, grid[ni][nj])      # cost = max along the path
                    if novo < melhor[ni][nj]:
                        melhor[ni][nj] = novo
                        heapq.heappush(fila, (novo, ni, nj))
        return -1                                    # unreachable (never happens)

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::cmp::Reverse;
use std::collections::BinaryHeap;

impl Solution {
    pub fn swim_in_rising_water(grid: Vec<Vec<i32>>) -> i32 {
        let n = grid.len();
        let mut melhor = vec![vec![i32::MAX; n]; n];
        melhor[0][0] = grid[0][0];
        let mut fila = BinaryHeap::new();
        fila.push(Reverse((grid[0][0], 0usize, 0usize)));
        while let Some(Reverse((t, i, j))) = fila.pop() {
            if t > melhor[i][j] {
                continue; // stale entry
            }
            if i == n - 1 && j == n - 1 {
                return t; // 1st pop of the target is the optimal one (Dijkstra)
            }
            for (di, dj) in [(1i32, 0i32), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)] {
                let (ni, nj) = (i as i32 + di, j as i32 + dj);
                if ni < 0 || nj < 0 || ni as usize >= n || nj as usize >= n {
                    continue;
                }
                let (ni, nj) = (ni as usize, nj as usize);
                let novo = t.max(grid[ni][nj]); // cost = max along the path
                if novo < melhor[ni][nj] {
                    melhor[ni][nj] = novo;
                    fila.push(Reverse((novo, ni, nj)));
                }
            }
        }
        unreachable!("the problem guarantees a path to (n-1, n-1)")
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <queue>
#include <tuple>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int swimInRisingWater(vector<vector<int>>& grid) {
        int n = grid.size();
        vector<vector<int>> melhor(n, vector<int>(n, INT_MAX));
        melhor[0][0] = grid[0][0];
        priority_queue<tuple<int, int, int>, vector<tuple<int, int, int>>,
                       greater<>>
            fila; // (max so far, i, j) — min-heap
        fila.emplace(grid[0][0], 0, 0);
        int dirs[4][2] = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
        while (!fila.empty()) {
            auto [t, i, j] = fila.top();
            fila.pop();
            if (t > melhor[i][j]) continue; // stale entry
            if (i == n - 1 && j == n - 1) return t; // 1st pop of the target is optimal
            for (auto& d : dirs) {
                int ni = i + d[0], nj = j + d[1];
                if (ni < 0 || nj < 0 || ni >= n || nj >= n) continue;
                int novo = max(t, grid[ni][nj]); // cost = max along the path
                if (novo < melhor[ni][nj]) {
                    melhor[ni][nj] = novo;
                    fila.emplace(novo, ni, nj);
                }
            }
        }
        return -1; // unreachable (never happens)
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <limits.h>

/* Dijkstra O(V²) with no heap (C). V = n² ≤ 2500 → ~6M operations, plenty.
   The cost of a cell is the MAXIMUM grid value on the path to it. */
int swimInRisingWater(int** grid, int gridSize, int* gridColSize) {
    (void)gridColSize;
    int n = gridSize;
    if (n == 1) return grid[0][0];

    int* melhor = malloc((size_t)n * n * sizeof(int));
    bool* visitado = calloc((size_t)n * n, sizeof(bool));
    for (int i = 0; i < n * n; i++) melhor[i] = INT_MAX / 2;
    melhor[0] = grid[0][0];

    for (int passo = 0; passo < n * n; passo++) {
        int alvo = -1, valor = INT_MAX / 2;
        for (int i = 0; i < n * n; i++)
            if (!visitado[i] && melhor[i] < valor) { valor = melhor[i]; alvo = i; }
        if (alvo == -1) break;
        visitado[alvo] = true;
        if (alvo == n * n - 1) {
            free(melhor);
            free(visitado);
            return valor; // 1st selection of the target is the optimal one
        }
        int i = alvo / n, j = alvo % n;
        int viz[4][2] = {{i - 1, j}, {i + 1, j}, {i, j - 1}, {i, j + 1}};
        for (int d = 0; d < 4; d++) {
            int ni = viz[d][0], nj = viz[d][1];
            if (ni < 0 || nj < 0 || ni >= n || nj >= n) continue;
            int k = ni * n + nj;
            if (visitado[k]) continue;
            int novo = valor > grid[ni][nj] ? valor : grid[ni][nj];
            if (novo < melhor[k]) melhor[k] = novo;
        }
    }
    free(melhor);
    free(visitado);
    return -1; // unreachable (never happens)
}

Complexity

  • Heap (Python/Rust/C++): time O(V log V) with V = n² cells — each cell enters/leaves the heap in O(log V), each edge is visited 4 times; space O(n²) (melhor matrix + heap).
  • O(V²) (C): time O(V²) = O(n⁴) in the worst shape — each iteration scans all cells to find the minimum. With n ≤ 50 that is ~6M operations, trivial. Space O(n²).

Pitfalls

  • The cost is max, not sum: novo = max(t, grid[ni][nj]) — summing turns this into a completely different (and wrong) problem.
  • The heap state is (t, i, j); t is the largest cell value so far, not the accumulated time.
  • The grid is always square (n×n) — do not build a 1×k test case.
  • The target’s 1st pop answers: stopping there is Dijkstra’s canonical “early exit” (and it holds even in C, which returns on the 1st selection).
  • C: no heap in the stdlib; the melhor matrix keeps the min-max and visitado keeps a cell from being relaxed twice.

269. Alien Dictionary (Hard · Premium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/alien-dictionary/ · Topic: Topological sort (Kahn) + cycle detection

Problem (summary)

A list of words is sorted in the alien alphabet. Figure out the order of the letters (the alien lexicographic order) from that sequencing, or "" if the data is inconsistent (cycle or mis-ordered prefix). Any valid order is accepted.

words = ["wrt","wrf","er","ett","rftt"]            →  "wertf"
words = ["z","x",   "z"]     (cycle z < x < z)     →  ""
words = ["abc","ab"]  (longer word before its prefix) → ""

Pattern — what to memorize

Compare adjacent pairs and extract the first differing character — only that one carries ordering information (wrf vs wrt says f < t; wrf vs er says w < e). Each difference becomes an edge x → y (“x comes before y”) of a digraph; Kahn (indegree) returns the topological order and the cycle is detected at the end: len(ordem) != len(letras) → "".

Two invalid cases the prompt hides:

  1. Prefix: ["abc","ab"] — abc comes before ab, but in a lexicographic society the shorter prefix comes first. A length difference with zero differing characters = invalid.
  2. Cycle: a→b and b→a from different pairs — Kahn ends with letters stuck (their degree never reaches zero).

Output detail: the problem accepts any valid order; picking the smallest available letter at each step (heap/ordered set) gives a deterministic output that is guaranteed “accepted”.

Python

import heapq
from collections import defaultdict

class Solution:
    def alienOrder(self, words: list[str]) -> str:
        letras = set("".join(words))
        grafo = defaultdict(set)
        indeg = {c: 0 for c in letras}

        for a, b in zip(words, words[1:]):
            for x, y in zip(a, b):
                if x != y:
                    if y not in grafo[x]:            # edge x → y
                        grafo[x].add(y)
                        indeg[y] += 1
                    break
            else:
                # one is a prefix of the other: invalid if the longer one comes first
                if len(a) > len(b):
                    return ""

        # Kahn with a heap: smallest available letter (indeg 0) first —
        # deterministic output, and any valid topological order works.
        fila = [c for c in letras if indeg[c] == 0]
        heapq.heapify(fila)
        ordem = []
        while fila:
            c = heapq.heappop(fila)
            ordem.append(c)
            for viz in sorted(grafo[c]):
                indeg[viz] -= 1
                if indeg[viz] == 0:
                    heapq.heappush(fila, viz)

        return "".join(ordem) if len(ordem) == len(letras) else ""

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::{BTreeSet, HashMap, HashSet};

impl Solution {
    pub fn alien_order(words: Vec<String>) -> String {
        let mut letras: HashSet<char> = HashSet::new();
        for w in &words {
            for c in w.chars() {
                letras.insert(c);
            }
        }

        let mut grafo: HashMap<char, HashSet<char>> = HashMap::new();
        let mut indeg: HashMap<char, usize> = letras.iter().map(|&c| (c, 0)).collect();

        'par: for par in words.windows(2) {
            let (a, b) = (&par[0], &par[1]);
            for (x, y) in a.chars().zip(b.chars()) {
                if x != y {
                    // edge x → y (only the 1st differing char decides)
                    if grafo.entry(x).or_default().insert(y) {
                        *indeg.entry(y).or_default() += 1;
                    }
                    continue 'par;
                }
            }
            // one is a prefix of the other: invalid if the "longer" comes first
            if a.len() > b.len() {
                return String::new();
            }
        }

        // Kahn with a BTreeSet: pop_first() always gives the smallest available letter.
        let mut disponiveis: BTreeSet<char> = letras
            .iter()
            .copied()
            .filter(|c| indeg[c] == 0)
            .collect();
        let mut ordem = String::new();
        while let Some(c) = disponiveis.pop_first() {
            ordem.push(c);
            if let Some(vizinhos) = grafo.get(&c) {
                let vizinhos: Vec<char> = vizinhos.iter().copied().collect();
                for v in vizinhos {
                    let d = indeg.get_mut(&v).expect("node with an edge must exist");
                    *d -= 1;
                    if *d == 0 {
                        disponiveis.insert(v);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        if ordem.len() != letras.len() {
            return String::new(); // cycle → no valid order
        }
        ordem
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <unordered_set>
#include <set>
#include <algorithm> // min for size_t on the prefixes
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    string alienOrder(vector<string>& words) {
        unordered_set<char> letras;
        for (auto& w : words)
            for (char c : w) letras.insert(c);

        unordered_map<char, unordered_set<char>> grafo;
        unordered_map<char, int> indeg;
        for (char c : letras) indeg[c] = 0;

        for (int i = 0; i + 1 < (int)words.size(); ++i) {
            const string& a = words[i];
            const string& b = words[i + 1];
            size_t n = min(a.size(), b.size());
            bool achou = false;
            for (size_t j = 0; j < n; ++j) {
                if (a[j] != b[j]) {
                    if (grafo[a[j]].insert(b[j]).second) ++indeg[b[j]];
                    achou = true;
                    break;
                }
            }
            // one is a prefix of the other: invalid if the "longer" comes first
            if (!achou && a.size() > b.size()) return "";
        }

        set<char> disponiveis; // ordered set: the smallest available letter always
        for (auto& [c, d] : indeg)
            if (d == 0) disponiveis.insert(c);

        string ordem;
        while (!disponiveis.empty()) {
            char c = *disponiveis.begin();
            disponiveis.erase(disponiveis.begin());
            ordem += c;
            for (char v : grafo[c]) {
                if (--indeg[v] == 0) disponiveis.insert(v);
            }
        }
        return ordem.size() == letras.size() ? ordem : ""; // cycle → invalid
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Kahn with a fixed 26-lowercase-letter alphabet. Deterministic: at each
   step it picks the SMALLEST letter with indegree 0 (scanning the alphabet
   in order). */
char* alienOrder(char** words, int wordsSize) {
    int presente[26] = {0}, indeg[26] = {0}, grafo[26][26] = {{0}};

    for (int i = 0; i < wordsSize; i++)
        for (int j = 0; words[i][j]; j++) presente[words[i][j] - 'a'] = 1;

    for (int i = 0; i + 1 < wordsSize; i++) {
        const char* a = words[i];
        const char* b = words[i + 1];
        int achou = 0;
        for (int j = 0; a[j] && b[j]; j++) {
            if (a[j] != b[j]) {
                int x = a[j] - 'a', y = b[j] - 'a';
                if (!grafo[x][y]) {      // edge x → y, no duplicate
                    grafo[x][y] = 1;
                    indeg[y]++;
                }
                achou = 1;
                break;
            }
        }
        if (!achou && strlen(a) > strlen(b)) { // invalid prefix ('abc','ab')
            char* vazio = malloc(1);
            vazio[0] = '\0';
            return vazio;
        }
    }

    char* ordem = malloc(27 * sizeof(char));
    int preenchido = 0;
    for (int passo = 0; passo < 26; passo++) {
        int melhor = -1;
        for (int c = 0; c < 26; c++)
            if (presente[c] && indeg[c] == 0) { melhor = c; break; }
        if (melhor == -1) break;
        indeg[melhor] = -1;              // mark as processed
        ordem[preenchido++] = (char)('a' + melhor);
        for (int v = 0; v < 26; v++)
            if (grafo[melhor][v]) indeg[v]--;
    }
    ordem[preenchido] = '\0';

    int total = 0;
    for (int c = 0; c < 26; c++) total += presente[c];
    if (preenchido != total) {           // cycle → no valid order
        free(ordem);
        char* vazio = malloc(1);
        vazio[0] = '\0';
        return vazio;
    }
    return ordem;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(C) — C = total characters across all words (the pair comparison spends at most the compared characters; Kahn is O(26 + E) with E ≤ 26×25, a constant).
  • Space: O(1) in practice — the graph has at most 26 vertices (lowercase alphabet); C keeps everything in arrays of 26.

Pitfalls

  • Only the 1st differing character of each pair creates an edge — equal characters in the same prefix say nothing.
  • Invalid prefix (abc before ab) is an "" condition along with cycle — the pair generates no edge at all, so Kahn alone does not detect it.
  • “Loose” letters (appear once): enter the answer with indegree 0. Repeated words (["a","a"]) generate neither an edge nor an error.
  • A cycle is only discovered at the end of Kahn — the check is len(ordem) != letras.
  • C: a word’s char is indexed by words[i][j] - 'a'; the -1 in indeg marks “already processed” so it is not re-selected.

332. Reconstruct Itinerary (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/reconstruct-itinerary/ · Topic: Eulerian path (Hierholzer) + lexical min-heap

Problem (summary)

List of tickets tickets = [from, to] (there may be several between the same two airports). Reconstruct the itinerary that starts at "JFK" and uses every ticket exactly once, with the smallest lexicographic order possible. At least one valid route always exists.

[["MUC","LHR"],["JFK","MUC"],["SFO","SJC"],["LHR","SFO"]]
  →  ["JFK","MUC","LHR","SFO","SJC"]

[["JFK","SFO"],["JFK","ATL"],["SFO","ATL"],["ATL","JFK"],["ATL","SFO"]]
  →  ["JFK","ATL","JFK","SFO","ATL","SFO"]

Pattern — what to memorize

This is an Eulerian path (traverse every edge of the digraph exactly once) — and the fix is Hierholzer with post-order:

  1. Adjacency list with destinations in lexicographic order (in code, sorted descending so that pop() takes the smallest);
  2. DFS from "JFK": while there is an edge, consume the smallest and go down; when it runs out, push the airport (post-order);
  3. At the end, reverse the stack.

Why the naive greedy (always take the smallest lexically and record in pre-order) fails: tickets can get “stuck” in a loop — JFK→KUL + JFK→NRT + NRT→JFK: if you go JFK→KUL first (smallest lexically), you die at KUL with two tickets unused. Hierholzer’s post-order solves it because the segment that returns to the airport is discovered and “stitched” in the right place: the DFS only pushes a node when it has no outgoing edges left, so the loop enters the route at the re-entry point (JFK→NRT→JFK→KUL).

Python

from collections import defaultdict

class Solution:
    def findItinerary(self, tickets: list[list[str]]) -> list[str]:
        grafo = defaultdict(list)
        for origem, destino in tickets:
            grafo[origem].append(destino)
        for origem in grafo:
            grafo[origem].sort(reverse=True)   # pop() takes the SMALLEST (lex)

        rota = []                              # post-order (Hierholzer)
        def visitar(aeroporto: str) -> None:
            while grafo[aeroporto]:
                visitar(grafo[aeroporto].pop())
            rota.append(aeroporto)             # exhausted: push at the end

        visitar("JFK")
        return rota[::-1] if len(rota) == len(tickets) + 1 else []

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashMap;

impl Solution {
    pub fn find_itinerary(tickets: Vec<Vec<String>>) -> Vec<String> {
        let mut grafo: HashMap<String, Vec<String>> = HashMap::new();
        for t in &tickets {
            grafo.entry(t[0].clone()).or_default().push(t[1].clone());
        }
        for destino in grafo.values_mut() {
            destino.sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a)); // desc: pop() takes the SMALLEST (lex)
        }

        let mut rota: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
        fn visitar(
            aeroporto: String,
            grafo: &mut HashMap<String, Vec<String>>,
            rota: &mut Vec<String>,
        ) {
            loop {
                let proximo = grafo.get_mut(&aeroporto).and_then(|v| v.pop());
                match proximo {
                    Some(destino) => visitar(destino, grafo, rota),
                    None => break,
                }
            }
            rota.push(aeroporto); // post-order (Hierholzer)
        }

        visitar("JFK".to_string(), &mut grafo, &mut rota);
        if rota.len() == tickets.len() + 1 {
            rota.reverse();
            rota
        } else {
            Vec::new()
        }
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <string>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <functional>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<string> findItinerary(vector<vector<string>>& tickets) {
        unordered_map<string, vector<string>> grafo;
        for (auto& t : tickets) grafo[t[0]].push_back(t[1]);
        for (auto& [_, destinos] : grafo)
            sort(destinos.rbegin(), destinos.rend()); // pop_back: SMALLEST (lex)

        vector<string> rota;
        function<void(const string&)> visitar = [&](const string& aeroporto) {
            while (!grafo[aeroporto].empty()) {
                string proximo = grafo[aeroporto].back();
                grafo[aeroporto].pop_back();
                visitar(proximo);
            }
            rota.push_back(aeroporto); // post-order (Hierholzer)
        };
        visitar("JFK");
        reverse(rota.begin(), rota.end());
        return rota.size() == tickets.size() + 1 ? rota : vector<string>{};
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Hierholzer/Eulerian path in C: map (string → id) via linear search +
   per-node out list, sorted ASC by name and consumed from the START
   (always the smallest available lexically). Post-order + reversal as in
   the other languages. Ceiling: 305 nodes / 305 out-edges per node —
   tickets ≤ 300. */
#define MAX_N 305
#define MAX_OUT 305

static char nomes[MAX_N][4];
static int saidas[MAX_N][MAX_OUT];
static int tam_saida[MAX_N];
static int inicio_saida[MAX_N];
static int contagem;
static int itinerario[MAX_N]; /* post-order (ids), reversed when assembling */
static int pos_ordem;

static int id_de(const char* nome) {
    for (int i = 0; i < contagem; i++)
        if (strcmp(nomes[i], nome) == 0) return i;
    strcpy(nomes[contagem], nome);
    return contagem++;
}

static int cmp_saida(const void* a, const void* b) {
    int x = *(const int*)a, y = *(const int*)b;
    int cmp = strcmp(nomes[x], nomes[y]);
    return (cmp > 0) - (cmp < 0); /* a string can never overflow this */
}

static void visitar(int u) {
    while (inicio_saida[u] < tam_saida[u]) {
        int v = saidas[u][inicio_saida[u]++];
        visitar(v);
    }
    itinerario[pos_ordem++] = u; /* post-order (Hierholzer) */
}

char** findItinerary(char*** tickets, int ticketsSize, int* ticketsColSize,
                     int* returnSize) {
    (void)ticketsColSize;
    contagem = 0;
    pos_ordem = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < MAX_N; i++) {
        tam_saida[i] = 0;
        inicio_saida[i] = 0;
        nomes[i][0] = '\0';
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < ticketsSize; i++) {
        int u = id_de(tickets[i][0]);
        int v = id_de(tickets[i][1]);
        saidas[u][tam_saida[u]++] = v;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < contagem; i++)
        qsort(saidas[i], (size_t)tam_saida[i], sizeof(int), cmp_saida);

    visitar(id_de("JFK"));

    if (pos_ordem != ticketsSize + 1) {
        *returnSize = 0;
        return NULL; /* the problem guarantees a valid route; this is armor */
    }
    char** resp = malloc((size_t)pos_ordem * sizeof(char*));
    for (int i = 0; i < pos_ordem; i++) {
        int u = itinerario[pos_ordem - 1 - i]; /* reverse the post-order */
        resp[i] = malloc(4 * sizeof(char));
        strcpy(resp[i], nomes[u]);
    }
    *returnSize = pos_ordem;
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(E log E) — sorting each node’s destination list (the sum of degrees = E), then every edge is walked once in the DFS; accessing the smallest is O(1) per pop. Space: O(E) — graphs + route.

Pitfalls

  • Lexicographic order of strings, not numeric: "ATL" < "SFO"; the descending sort exists only so that pop() (off the vector end) hands out the smallest — in C (no mid-pop), sort ascending and consume from the start.
  • Multiple tickets between the same two airports: the adjacency list with duplicates (not a set) handles it — each edge is a ticket.
  • The post-order must be reversed; without the reversal the route comes out backwards.
  • The size guard (tickets + 1) protects against input with no route — the problem guarantees one, but the guard turns it into an empty answer instead of a bug.
  • Rust: edges consumed by pop() inside the recursion — get_mut + and_then resolves the borrow (the list empties before the next node).

70. Climbing Stairs (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/climbing-stairs/ · Topic: 1D DP

Problem (summary)

Climbing a staircase of n steps, you can only take 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways are there to reach the top?

n = 2 → 2   (1+1, 2)
n = 3 → 3   (1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1)

Pattern — what to memorize

Hidden Fibonacci: the only way to reach step i is from i-1 (a 1-step) or from i-2 (a 2-step). Hence dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2], with dp[0] = dp[1] = 1. Clue in the prompt: “can climb 1 OR 2 steps” — each state depends on the two previous ones = a linear recurrence, and since only the last two values matter, the DP runs on two variables (O(1) space), not an array.

Python

class Solution:
    def climbStairs(self, n: int) -> int:
        # fib(n+1): dp[0] = 1, dp[1] = 1
        a, b = 1, 1
        for _ in range(2, n + 1):
            a, b = b, a + b
        return b

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn climb_stairs(n: i32) -> i32 {
        let (mut a, mut b) = (1i64, 1i64);
        for _ in 2..=n {
            let t = a + b;
            a = b;
            b = t;
        }
        b as i32
    }
}
}

C++


class Solution {
public:
    int climbStairs(int n) {
        long long a = 1, b = 1;
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; ++i) {
            long long t = a + b;
            a = b;
            b = t;
        }
        return (int)b;
    }
};

C

int climbStairs(int n) {
    long long a = 1, b = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; ++i) {
        long long t = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = t;
    }
    return (int)b;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — a single loop from 2 to n; each iteration is O(1).
  • Space: O(1) — only the two variables a and b (a dp array version would be O(n), unnecessary here).

Pitfalls

  • Not the textbook Fibonacci with fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1: here dp[0]=1 (1 way to climb nothing) and dp[1]=1 are the seeds, so climbStairs(n) = fib(n+1) in the classic indexing.
  • n = 1 doesn’t need a special case: the 2..=1 loop doesn’t run and returns b = 1.
  • n = 45 (problem limit): the result is 1,836,311,903 — fits in a 32-bit int, but only just (max 2,147,483,647). If the prompt ever grows, use long long (as here) and cast at the end.
  • Python has no overflow (arbitrary-precision integers) — the concern is only for C/C++/Rust.

746. Min Cost Climbing Stairs (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/min-cost-climbing-stairs/ · Topic: 1D DP

Problem (summary)

You start for free at step 0 or step 1; you pay cost[i] only when you step on step i. Each move goes up 1 or 2 steps. Minimum cost to reach the top (the position past the last step)?

cost = [10,15,20]               → 15   (start at 1, pay 15, top)
cost = [1,100,1,1,1,100,1,1,100,1] → 6  (alternating 1s)

Pattern — what to memorize

Two-value DP with a “stepping” bias: dp[i] = minimum cost to reach step i paying cost[i], so dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]) (you either came from i-1 or jumped from i-2). The top is past the last step, so the answer is min(dp[n-1], dp[n-2]) — not dp[n]. Since the recurrence only looks at the two previous values, it runs on two variables (O(1) space). Clue in the prompt: cost per step + 1-or-2 step moves → same skeleton as Climbing Stairs (LC 70), swapping counting for minimizing.

Python

class Solution:
    def minCostClimbingStairs(self, cost: list[int]) -> int:
        # dp[i] = min cost to REACH step i, paying cost[i];
        # only the last two values matter (1- or 2-step moves).
        # Answer = min(dp[-1], dp[-2]) — the top is PAST the last step.
        um, dois = cost[0], cost[1]  # um = dp[i-2], dois = dp[i-1]
        for c in cost[2:]:
            um, dois = dois, c + min(um, dois)
        return min(um, dois)

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn min_cost_climbing_stairs(cost: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
        // dp[i] = min cost to REACH step i, paying cost[i];
        // only the last two values matter (1- or 2-step moves).
        // Answer = min(dp[-1], dp[-2]) — the top is PAST the last one.
        let (mut um, mut dois) = (cost[0], cost[1]); // um = dp[i-2], dois = dp[i-1]
        for &c in cost[2..].iter() {
            let atual = c + um.min(dois);
            um = dois;
            dois = atual;
        }
        um.min(dois)
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int minCostClimbingStairs(vector<int>& cost) {
        // dp[i] = min cost to REACH step i, paying cost[i];
        // answer = min(dp[n-1], dp[n-2]) — the top is PAST the last one.
        int um = cost[0], dois = cost[1]; // um = dp[i-2], dois = dp[i-1]
        for (int i = 2; i < (int)cost.size(); ++i) {
            int atual = cost[i] + min(um, dois);
            um = dois;
            dois = atual;
        }
        return min(um, dois);
    }
};

C

/* dp[i] = min cost to REACH step i, paying cost[i];
 * answer = min(dp[n-2], dp[n-1]) — the top is PAST the last step.  */
int minCostClimbingStairs(int* cost, int costSize) {
    int um = cost[0], dois = cost[1]; /* um = dp[i-2], dois = dp[i-1] */
    for (int i = 2; i < costSize; i++) {
        int atual = cost[i] + (um < dois ? um : dois);
        um = dois;
        dois = atual;
    }
    return um < dois ? um : dois;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one loop over cost[2:], each iteration O(1).
  • Space: O(1) — only the two variables um/dois (a dp array version would be O(n), unnecessary).

Pitfalls

  • Starting for free at 0 OR 1: there’s no “entry” dp[0] — the cost starts only when you step. That’s why the seeds are cost[0] and cost[1].
  • Top ≠ last step: the answer is the min of the last two, not the last one. [10,15,20] → 15 (ignores the 10: start at 1, pay 15, exit). If it were dp[n], you’d try to “pay” for a step that doesn’t exist.
  • Unlike LC 70 (which counts ways and sums paths): here it’s minimizing — min, not +, between states.
  • n = 2 is the minimum: the loop doesn’t run and the min of the two is the direct answer.
  • Overflows are practically impossible (cost[i] ≤ 999, n ≤ 1000 → total < 10⁶): in C/Rust, int/i32 suffice; Python doesn’t have the problem.
