115. Distinct Subsequences (Hard)

https://leetcode.com/problems/distinct-subsequences/ · Topic: 2D DP (strings) — counting

Problem (summary)

Given s and t, return how many subsequences of s equal t — subsequences distinct by position: different ways of choosing indices count separately, even if the resulting text is the same.

s = "rabbbit", t = "rabbit" → 3
s = "babgbag", t = "bag"    → 5

Pattern — what to memorize

Count with “skip or use”: let dp[i][j] = number of subsequences of s[0..i) forming t[0..j).

base:      dp[i][0] = 1            (the empty subsequence exists from every prefix)
if s[i-1] == t[j-1]:
       dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]       (skip s[i-1]...)
                + dp[i-1][j-1]     (...or use it: matches t[j-1])
else:
       dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]       (only skipping is possible)

It’s the “LCS of counting”: instead of max, you add the two decisions when characters match. Implemented 1D version (only the previous row matters), with j decreasing — the diagonal dp[i-1][j-1] comes from the previous row, so going up would overwrite the value still needed (the 0/1 knapsack rule). Problem tells: “number of distinct subsequences” + two strings → counting with the same silhouette as LCS.

Python

class Solution:
    def numDistinct(self, s: str, t: str) -> int:
        n = len(t)
        dp = [0] * (n + 1)
        dp[0] = 1  # empty subsequence of every prefix of s
        for ch in s:
            for j in range(n, 0, -1):     # decreasing: uses dp[j-1] from the previous row
                if ch == t[j - 1]:
                    dp[j] += dp[j - 1]
        return dp[n]

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn num_distinct(s: String, t: String) -> i32 {
        let (a, b) = (s.as_bytes(), t.as_bytes());
        let n = b.len();
        let mut dp = vec![0u64; n + 1]; // u64: intermediate sums
        dp[0] = 1;
        for &x in a {
            for j in (1..=n).rev() { // decreasing: uses dp[j-1] from the previous row
                if x == b[j - 1] {
                    dp[j] += dp[j - 1];
                }
            }
        }
        dp[n] as i32 // the statement guarantees a 32-bit answer
    }
}
}

C++

#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int numDistinct(string s, string t) {
        int n = (int)t.size();
        vector<unsigned long long> dp(n + 1, 0); // u64: intermediate sums
        dp[0] = 1;
        for (char x : s)
            for (int j = n; j >= 1; --j)          // decreasing: uses dp[j-1] from the previous row
                if (x == t[j - 1]) dp[j] += dp[j - 1];
        return (int)dp[n]; // the statement guarantees a 32-bit answer
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
int numDistinct(char* s, char* t) {
    int n = (int)strlen(t);
    /* unsigned long long: intermediate sums may exceed int;
       the statement guarantees the final answer fits in 32 bits. */
    unsigned long long* dp = calloc((size_t)n + 1, sizeof(unsigned long long));
    dp[0] = 1; /* empty subsequence of every prefix of s */
    for (int i = 0; s[i]; ++i)
        for (int j = n; j >= 1; --j)           /* decreasing: uses dp[j-1] from the previous row */
            if (s[i] == t[j-1]) dp[j] += dp[j-1];
    int resp = (int)dp[n];
    free(dp);
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(m × n) — for each character of s, scans all of t (the for j goes down from n to 1).
  • Space: O(n) — the 1D array of n + 1; the 2D matrix would be O(m × n).

Pitfalls

  • “Distinct” is by POSITION, not by text: s = "aaa", t = "aa" → 3 (pick any pair of positions), not 1. It’s a count of paths, not of unique substrings.
  • dp[0] = 1: the empty subsequence exists in every prefix (including empty s) — that’s why s = "abc", t = "" → 1. And s = "", t = "a" → 0 (nothing forms a non-empty subsequence).
  • The decreasing loop is mandatory (unlike LCS, which goes up): the transition reads dp[j-1] from the PREVIOUS row. Going up, dp[j-1] would already carry the current row’s contribution and the number would inflate.
  • long/u64 for intermediates: the largest table value can be big (with s = "aaaa...", t = "aa..." the answer is a binomial); the statement guarantees the final answer fits a signed 32-bit integer, so the final cast is safe — but add in u64/long long (never int) for the intermediate steps.
  • In C, dp is calloc of u64 — calloc already zeroes; dp[0] = 1 separately.
  • Rust: s.as_bytes() for positional indexing (the statement uses English letters, ASCII); don’t use chars().nth(i) (O(n)).
  • s.length, t.length ≤ 1000 → O(10⁶) cells, easily fine for O(m×n).

53. Maximum Subarray (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-subarray/ · Topic: Greedy (Kadane)

Problem (summary)

Given nums (with negatives), find the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray (at least one element) and return that sum.

[-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4] → 6   (subarray [4,-1,2,1])
[1]                      → 1
[-3,-1,-2]               → -1  (a one-element subarray is mandatory)

Pattern — what to memorize

Kadane: keep accumulating while the running sum is useful, reset when it becomes a loss. Walk keeping atual = max(atual, 0) + x — if the running sum so far is negative, the best subarray starting at the current position is just x (the earlier accumulation only hurts). melhor tracks the largest atual seen. This is a 1-state greedy/DP: the “continue or reset” decision is local and optimal. For extra depth: divide & conquer (left part, right part, or crossing the middle) in O(n log n) — mention it, don’t implement it in the interview.

Python

class Solution:
    def maxSubArray(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        melhor = float("-inf")
        atual = 0
        for x in nums:
            atual = max(atual, 0) + x   # negative running sum = reset
            melhor = max(melhor, atual)
        return melhor

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn max_sub_array(nums: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
        let mut melhor = i32::MIN;
        let mut atual = 0i64;
        for &x in &nums {
            atual = atual.max(0) + x as i64; // negative running sum = reset
            melhor = melhor.max(atual as i32);
        }
        melhor
    }
}
}

C++

#include <climits>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int maxSubArray(vector<int>& nums) {
        int melhor = INT_MIN, atual = 0;
        for (int x : nums) {
            atual = max(atual, 0) + x;   // negative running sum = reset
            melhor = max(melhor, atual);
        }
        return melhor;
    }
};

C

#include <limits.h>
int maxSubArray(int* nums, int numsSize) {
    int melhor = INT_MIN, atual = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < numsSize; ++i) {
        atual = (atual > 0 ? atual : 0) + nums[i];  /* Kadane */
        if (atual > melhor) melhor = atual;
    }
    return melhor;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — a single pass.
  • Space: O(1) — two variables (atual and melhor).

Pitfalls

  • All negatives: [−3,−1,−2] → −1. Kadane with max(atual, 0) + x returns the largest element (we reset to 0 and add the negative — the first element becomes melhor). Don’t “fix” it to 0: the answer here is NEVER 0, because the subarray must have ≥ 1 element.
  • INT_MIN/-inf sentinel: if nums were empty the max would break (the problem guarantees ≥ 1 element, but the sentinel is already the defensive pattern).
  • Sum overflow: atual + x — use long long/i64 when values are large (a subarray sum can exceed int).
  • Classic interview variant: “return the subarray INDICES” (same logic, keeping track of where the reset happens).
  • Divide & conquer is O(n log n); only cite it to show you know the alternative, and remember the “crossing the middle” case is the delicate part.

55. Jump Game (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/jump-game/ · Topic: Greedy (reachability)

Problem (summary)

You start at index 0 of nums; at each position i you can advance up to nums[i] steps. Return true if you can reach the last index.

[2,3,1,1,4] → true    (jump 1 → 1, then 3 → end)
[3,2,1,0,4] → false   (every path dies on the 0 at index 3)

Pattern — what to memorize

Keep the maximum reach and advance: alcance = max(alcance, i + nums[i]). If at some i the reach doesn’t cover i (i > alcance), you’re stuck → false. Tell: “can you get there?” with forward jumps → what matters is the reachable FRONTIER, not the path. It’s greedy because picking the largest extension at each step is dominant — never worse. Don’t confuse with Jump Game II: here it only asks “can you reach?”.

Python

class Solution:
    def canJump(self, nums: list[int]) -> bool:
        alcance = 0
        for i, passos in enumerate(nums):
            if i > alcance:
                return False
            alcance = max(alcance, i + passos)
        return True

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn can_jump(nums: Vec<i32>) -> bool {
        let mut alcance = 0usize;
        for (i, &passos) in nums.iter().enumerate() {
            if i > alcance {
                return false;
            }
            alcance = alcance.max(i + passos as usize);
        }
        true
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>

using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    bool canJump(vector<int>& nums) {
        int alcance = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < (int)nums.size(); ++i) {
            if (i > alcance) return false;
            alcance = max(alcance, i + nums[i]);
        }
        return true;
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>
bool canJump(int* nums, int numsSize) {
    int alcance = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < numsSize; ++i) {
        if (i > alcance) return false;
        int candidato = i + nums[i];
        if (candidato > alcance) alcance = candidato;
    }
    return true;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — a single pass.
  • Space: O(1) — one variable.

Pitfalls

  • [0] → true: we’re already at the last index; the loop runs i=0, 0 > 0 is false, and it returns true naturally — no special case.
  • The i > alcance check must come BEFORE the update: if you extend the reach first, [3,2,1,0,4] slips through (the middle 0 never gets caught at the right time — testing i > alcance after the update still works here, but would break a variant that requires early return).
  • In Rust, i + passos as usize needs passos >= 0 (the contract guarantees it); the initial 0usize already answers [0].
  • The “greedy” reading of why: if from position i you reach j, then you reach ANY k between i and j (you can stop earlier) — that’s why tracking only the max works, with no jump simulation.
  • Notice the last index never needs to “reach itself” — the condition already checks each position individually all the way to the end.

45. Jump Game II (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/jump-game-ii/ · Topic: Greedy (BFS by levels)

Problem (summary)

Same rule as Jump Game (at i you advance up to nums[i]), but now the end is guaranteed reachable — return the minimum number of jumps to get to the last index.

[2,3,1,1,4] → 2   (jump to 1, then 3 → end)
[2,3,0,1,4] → 2   (jump to 1, then 3 → end)

Pattern — what to memorize

Think BFS in “layers” (jump levels), without a queue: fim_da_camada = where the current layer ends (the indices reachable with saltos jumps); fronteira = the farthest reachable from the current layer. Scan i: extend fronteira; when i crosses fim_da_camada, the layer closed → saltos++ and the next layer runs up to fronteira. Tell: minimum movements + always jump forward → count layers. Greedy because extending maximally within the layer is dominant (same dominance reasoning as Jump Game).

Python

class Solution:
    def jump(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        n = len(nums)
        saltos = fim_da_camada = fronteira = 0
        for i in range(n - 1):              # the last index doesn't "jump"
            fronteira = max(fronteira, i + nums[i])
            if i == fim_da_camada:          # layer closed: +1 jump
                saltos += 1
                fim_da_camada = fronteira
        return saltos

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn jump(nums: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
        let n = nums.len();
        let (mut saltos, mut fim_camada, mut fronteira) = (0i32, 0usize, 0usize);
        for i in 0..n - 1 {
            fronteira = fronteira.max(i + nums[i] as usize);
            if i == fim_camada {
                saltos += 1;
                fim_camada = fronteira;
            }
        }
        saltos
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>

using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int jump(vector<int>& nums) {
        int n = (int)nums.size();
        int saltos = 0, fim = 0, novoFim = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; ++i) {
            novoFim = max(novoFim, i + nums[i]);
            if (i == fim) { ++saltos; fim = novoFim; }
        }
        return saltos;
    }
};

C

int jump(int* nums, int numsSize) {
    int saltos = 0, fim = 0, novoFim = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < numsSize - 1; ++i) {
        int candidato = i + nums[i];
        if (candidato > novoFim) novoFim = candidato;
        if (i == fim) { ++saltos; fim = novoFim; }
    }
    return saltos;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — a single pass, each index visited once.
  • Space: O(1) — three variables.

Pitfalls

  • n == 1 → 0: the 0..n-1 loop (empty) returns 0 — no special case needed, but don’t do numsSize - 1 in size_t with n == 0 (the problem guarantees n >= 1).
  • The last index never “jumps”: the loop runs up to n-2. If you include the last one, you may count one jump too many (the frontier already reached the end before).
  • Order matters inside the loop: first extend fronteira, THEN check i == fim_da_camada. If the current index has nums[i] == 0 and already is the layer end, we still close the layer (the jump counts the transition to the next frontier, which already absorbed the jumps of the WHOLE layer).
  • Compare with Jump Game I: there the question is a boolean reachability; here it’s the minimum count. The same “frontier” serves, but with layer counting.
  • Simulate on paper: [1,2,3] → layer 0 = {0}; process 0 → frontier = 1, layer closes → jump 1, layer 1 = up to 1; process 1 → frontier = 3, closes → jump 2. Answer 2 ✓.

134. Gas Station (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/gas-station/ · Topic: Greedy (unique candidate)

Problem (summary)

A circular circuit has gas[i] fuel at pump i and cost[i] gas to go from i to i+1. You start with an empty tank — return the index of the pump where you should start to complete the circuit (a full lap), or -1 if impossible. If a solution exists, it is unique.

gas = [1,2,3,4,5], cost = [3,4,5,1,2] → 3   (start at pump 3)
gas = [2,3,4],     cost = [3,4,3]     → -1  (total gas < total cost)

Pattern — what to memorize

Two observations that kill the problem:

  1. If sum(gas) < sum(cost), it’s impossible (otherwise the total fuel can’t cover the lap) → -1.
  2. If the total is ≥ 0, there is a unique start: the candidate is the index right after the first point where the running gas - cost goes negative. Starting from the candidate, the running sum never dips below zero (the “deficit” was left behind). Scan once keeping atual; when atual < 0, the current start is dead → try i+1 and reset the accumulator. Tell: circular circuit + unique solution → sweep with a discardable candidate, no O(n²) check of every start.

Python

class Solution:
    def canCompleteCircuit(self, gas: list[int], cost: list[int]) -> int:
        total = atual = 0
        inicio = 0
        for i, (g, c) in enumerate(zip(gas, cost)):
            diff = g - c
            total += diff
            atual += diff
            if atual < 0:               # current start never closes: try next
                inicio = i + 1
                atual = 0
        return inicio if total >= 0 else -1

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn can_complete_circuit(gas: Vec<i32>, cost: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
        let (mut total, mut atual) = (0i64, 0i64);
        let mut inicio = 0i32;
        for i in 0..gas.len() {
            let diff = gas[i] as i64 - cost[i] as i64;
            total += diff;
            atual += diff;
            if atual < 0 {
                inicio = i as i32 + 1;
                atual = 0;
            }
        }
        if total >= 0 { inicio } else { -1 }
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>

using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int canCompleteCircuit(vector<int>& gas, vector<int>& cost) {
        long long total = 0, atual = 0;
        int inicio = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < (int)gas.size(); ++i) {
            long long diff = (long long)gas[i] - cost[i];
            total += diff;
            atual += diff;
            if (atual < 0) { inicio = i + 1; atual = 0; }
        }
        return total >= 0 ? inicio : -1;
    }
};

C

int canCompleteCircuit(int* gas, int gasSize, int* cost, int costSize) {
    (void)costSize;
    long long total = 0, atual = 0;
    int inicio = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < gasSize; ++i) {
        long long diff = (long long)gas[i] - cost[i];
        total += diff;
        atual += diff;
        if (atual < 0) { inicio = i + 1; atual = 0; }
    }
    return total >= 0 ? inicio : -1;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — a single pass.
  • Space: O(1) — three variables.

Pitfalls

  • total == 0 is not impossible: with a zero sum, if you can “survive” the whole stretch, a solution exists; the test is total >= 0 (not > 0). Case [1,2]/[1,2] → net zero at each pump → answer 0.
  • The total >= 0 check at the END is mandatory: the atual accumulator alone doesn’t decide the impossible case — for example [2,4]/[3,4] sinks in atual, but the final test is what answers -1.
  • In C: the LeetCode signature also receives costSize — use (void) or simply ignore it; the real count is gasSize.
  • The uniqueness proof: when the candidate i fails, no start between the previous one and i can work — the deficit accumulated since the previous candidate would be even worse for them. That’s why discarding and restarting at i+1 without looking back is correct.
  • It often shows up as an “intuitively O(1)” problem — don’t fall for the brute force of testing every start (O(n²)).

846. Hand of Straights (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/hand-of-straights/ · Topic: Greedy + counting

Problem (summary)

Given a group of cards hand (values may repeat) and a groupSize, say whether the hand can be split into groups of groupSize consecutive cards (value increases by 1 within the group).

hand = [1,2,3,6,2,3,4,7,8], groupSize = 3 → true   ([1,2,3], [2,3,4], [6,7,8])
hand = [1,2,3,4,5],          groupSize = 4 → false  (5 cards don't split into groups of 4)

Pattern — what to memorize

Greedy on the smallest element: if the hand is valid, the smallest remaining value must be the start of a group (there is no smaller value to fit it in the middle of another). So: count the cards, walk the cards in increasing order and, for each one still having “pieces”, try to consume card, card+1, …, card+groupSize-1 — if any is missing right away, it’s false. Tell: consecutive + split into groups → the smallest decides; greedy with counting (hashmap) avoids the O(n log n) sort over repeated values.

Python

from collections import Counter

class Solution:
    def isNStraightHand(self, hand: list[int], groupSize: int) -> bool:
        if len(hand) % groupSize != 0:
            return False
        contagem = Counter(hand)
        for carta in sorted(contagem):
            while contagem[carta] > 0:
                for k in range(groupSize):
                    c = carta + k
                    if contagem.get(c, 0) == 0:
                        return False
                    contagem[c] -= 1
        return True

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashMap;

impl Solution {
    pub fn is_n_straight_hand(hand: Vec<i32>, group_size: i32) -> bool {
        if hand.len() % group_size as usize != 0 {
            return false;
        }
        let mut contagem: HashMap<i32, i32> = HashMap::new();
        for &c in &hand {
            *contagem.entry(c).or_insert(0) += 1;
        }
        let mut cartas: Vec<i32> = contagem.keys().copied().collect();
        cartas.sort_unstable();
        for carta in cartas {
            while contagem[&carta] > 0 {
                for k in 0..group_size {
                    let c = carta + k;
                    let entrada = contagem.entry(c).or_insert(0);
                    if *entrada == 0 {
                        return false;
                    }
                    *entrada -= 1;
                }
            }
        }
        true
    }
}
}

C++

#include <map>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    bool isNStraightHand(vector<int>& hand, int groupSize) {
        int n = (int)hand.size();
        if (n % groupSize != 0) return false;
        map<int, int> contagem;
        for (int c : hand) contagem[c]++;
        for (auto& [carta, qtd] : contagem) {
            while (qtd > 0) {
                for (int k = 0; k < groupSize; ++k) {
                    auto it = contagem.find(carta + k);
                    if (it == contagem.end() || it->second == 0) return false;
                    it->second--;
                }
            }
        }
        return true;
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
static int cmp_int(const void* a, const void* b) {
    int x = *(const int*)a, y = *(const int*)b;
    return (x > y) - (x < y);   /* NEVER "x - y": overflows at the extremes */
}

bool isNStraightHand(int* hand, int handSize, int groupSize) {
    if (handSize % groupSize != 0) return false;
    qsort(hand, (size_t)handSize, sizeof(int), cmp_int);
    bool* usado = calloc((size_t)handSize, sizeof(bool));
    for (int i = 0; i < handSize; ++i) {
        if (usado[i]) continue;
        int grupo = 1;
        int anterior = hand[i];
        usado[i] = true;
        /* grab the next groupSize-1 consecutive ones (sorted array) */
        for (int j = i + 1; j < handSize && grupo < groupSize; ++j) {
            if (usado[j]) continue;
            if (hand[j] == anterior + 1) {
                usado[j] = true;
                anterior = hand[j];
                ++grupo;
            } else if (hand[j] > anterior + 1) {
                break;   /* sorted: the next ones won't fit either */
            }
        }
        if (grupo < groupSize) { free(usado); return false; }
    }
    free(usado);
    return true;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n log n) — the sort dominates (the two group-building passes are O(n) in amortized total: each card is consumed once).
  • Space: O(n) — the count (Python/Rust/C++) or the usado array (C).

Pitfalls

  • len(hand) % groupSize != 0 → false right away: 5 cards with groups of 4 have no way out; exact divisibility is a precondition.
  • groupSize == 1 → always true (groups of 1 card never fail): the inner loop of k in 0..1 consumes 1 card per remaining value.
  • Repeated values: they can’t be in the SAME group (consecutive) — the while contagem[carta] > 0 guarantees each copy starts/joins its own group on the right turn.
  • In Python, contagem[c] == 0 with missing c raises KeyError — use contagem.get(c, 0).
  • In C++, don’t use contagem[c] directly in the loop: operator[] INSERTS a 0 when the key is missing, and inserting while iterating the map invalidates the range-for. Check with find first (that’s why C++/Rust use entry/find).
  • In C there’s no native hashmap: this house’s trick is sort + mark used with the same greedy (the smallest available always starts a group).
  • This problem is identical to 846 “Straight Hand”; the 1296 variation (“Divide Array in Sets of K Consecutive Numbers”) is the SAME solution with groupSize called k — learning one solves both.

1899. Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/merge-triplets-to-form-target-triplet/ · Topic: Greedy

Problem (summary)

A list of triplets (3 numbers) and a target triplet. A “merge” of two triplets A and B produces [max(A[0],B[0]), max(A[1],B[1]), max(A[2],B[2])]. Using as many merges as you want (including with intermediate merge results), can you reach exactly target? Return true/false.

triplets = [[2,5,3],[1,8,4],[1,7,5]], target = [2,7,5]  →  true
triplets = [[1,3,4],[2,5,8]],         target = [2,5,8]  →  true
triplets = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]],         target = [3,4,5]  →  false

Pattern — what to memorize

Filter the dominated triplets and OR component by component. Merging only ever increases (component-wise, it’s the max). So:

  1. A triplet with any component > the target’s is useless: merging never reduces, so it could only overshoot the target — discard it.
  2. Of the ones left (all components ≤ target), the question becomes: is there a triplet with component 0 == target, one with component 1 == target and one with component 2 == target? The max of all of them is exactly the target.

Why boolean OR? Because max(a set touching the target on each axis) = target. A single triplet [a,b,c] with a=target[0], b=target[1], c=target[2] also satisfies it — the algorithm doesn’t require the three numbers in the SAME triplet, it just covers each axis somewhere (the merge joins everything). Dominance is the insight: instead of simulating merges (which explode exponentially), notice that a triplet with a component > target can never join.

Python

class Solution:
    def mergeTriplets(self, triplets: list[list[int]], target: list[int]) -> bool:
        possivel = [False, False, False]
        for t in triplets:
            # dominated triplet: some component > target => max() would overshoot
            if t[0] <= target[0] and t[1] <= target[1] and t[2] <= target[2]:
                for i in range(3):
                    possivel[i] |= t[i] == target[i]  # OR component by component
        return all(possivel)

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn merge_triplets(triplets: Vec<Vec<i32>>, target: Vec<i32>) -> bool {
        let mut possivel = [false; 3];
        for t in &triplets {
            // dominated triplet: some component > target => max() would overshoot
            if t[0] <= target[0] && t[1] <= target[1] && t[2] <= target[2] {
                for i in 0..3 {
                    possivel[i] |= t[i] == target[i]; // OR component by component
                }
            }
        }
        possivel[0] && possivel[1] && possivel[2]
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    bool mergeTriplets(vector<vector<int>>& triplets, vector<int>& target) {
        bool possivel[3] = {false, false, false};
        for (auto& t : triplets) {
            // dominated triplet: some component > target => max() would overshoot
            if (t[0] <= target[0] && t[1] <= target[1] && t[2] <= target[2]) {
                for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i)
                    possivel[i] = possivel[i] || (t[i] == target[i]); // OR component
            }
        }
        return possivel[0] && possivel[1] && possivel[2];
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>

bool mergeTriplets(int** triplets, int tripletsSize, int* tripletsColSize,
                   int* target, int targetSize) {
    (void)tripletsColSize;
    (void)targetSize;
    bool possivel[3] = {false, false, false};
    for (int i = 0; i < tripletsSize; i++) {
        int* t = triplets[i];
        /* dominated triplet: some component > target => max() would overshoot */
        if (t[0] <= target[0] && t[1] <= target[1] && t[2] <= target[2]) {
            possivel[0] = possivel[0] || (t[0] == target[0]);
            possivel[1] = possivel[1] || (t[1] == target[1]);
            possivel[2] = possivel[2] || (t[2] == target[2]);
        }
    }
    return possivel[0] && possivel[1] && possivel[2];
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one pass, three comparisons per triplet plus three booleans.
  • Space: O(1) — three flags (or an array of 3).

Pitfalls

  • A triplet with a component equal to the target BUT another component bigger is discarded — you can’t “use the good part and drop the bad part”: the merge is component-wise, but the whole triplet participates.
  • Merge order doesn’t matter (max is commutative/associative) — don’t simulate the sequence.
  • Triplets that already have ALL components ≤ target never overshoot — including them in the OR is always safe.
  • Edge: target exact in a single triplet ⇒ true; a single triplet that’s dominated on another component ⇒ false (test both).
  • In C++/Rust/C, compare each component against the indexed target — note that targetSize/tripletsColSize are always 3 (don’t assume positions).

763. Partition Labels (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/partition-labels/ · Topic: Greedy + last index

Problem (summary)

Given the string s, split it into the maximum number of parts such that each letter appears in at most one part. Return the part sizes in order.

"ababcbacadefegdehijhklij" → [9,7,8]
"eccbbbbdec"               → [10]   (all 'e'..'c' interleave: a single part)

Pattern — what to memorize

Sweep with a “last occurrence” frontier: precompute the last index of each character. Walk the string keeping fim = the largest last-index among the characters already seen in the current part; when i == fim, the whole part closed (no character of it appears later) → slice fim - inicio + 1 and restart. Tell: each letter in at most one part + maximum number of parts → the current part only ends when all of its characters have “closed” (the last of all of them was seen). Greedy because extending to the frontier is forced, and cutting at the first safe point is optimal.

Python

class Solution:
    def partitionLabels(self, s: str) -> list[int]:
        ultimo = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(s)}   # last index per letter
        resp = []
        inicio = fim = 0
        for i, c in enumerate(s):
            fim = max(fim, ultimo[c])
            if i == fim:
                resp.append(fim - inicio + 1)
                inicio = i + 1
        return resp

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn partition_labels(s: String) -> Vec<i32> {
        let bytes = s.as_bytes();
        let mut ultimo = [0usize; 26];
        for (i, &b) in bytes.iter().enumerate() {
            ultimo[(b - b'a') as usize] = i;
        }
        let mut resp = Vec::new();
        let (mut inicio, mut fim) = (0usize, 0usize);
        for (i, &b) in bytes.iter().enumerate() {
            fim = fim.max(ultimo[(b - b'a') as usize]);
            if i == fim {
                resp.push((fim - inicio + 1) as i32);
                inicio = i + 1;
            }
        }
        resp
    }
}
}

C++

#include <algorithm>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> partitionLabels(string s) {
        int ultimo[26] = {0};
        for (int i = 0; i < (int)s.size(); ++i) ultimo[s[i] - 'a'] = i;
        vector<int> resp;
        int inicio = 0, fim = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < (int)s.size(); ++i) {
            fim = max(fim, ultimo[s[i] - 'a']);
            if (i == fim) {
                resp.push_back(fim - inicio + 1);
                inicio = i + 1;
            }
        }
        return resp;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
int* partitionLabels(char* s, int* returnSize) {
    int n = (int)strlen(s);
    int ultimo[26] = {0};
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) ultimo[s[i] - 'a'] = i;
    int* resp = malloc((size_t)n * sizeof(int));   /* at most n partitions */
    int inicio = 0, fim = 0, qtd = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        if (ultimo[s[i] - 'a'] > fim) fim = ultimo[s[i] - 'a'];
        if (i == fim) {
            resp[qtd++] = fim - inicio + 1;
            inicio = i + 1;
        }
    }
    *returnSize = qtd;
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — two passes (one for the last indices, one for the parts); signature with fixed [26], no hashmap.
  • Space: O(1) — the 26-slot array (the resp is the required output; in Python the dict is O(26) for a lowercase alphabet).

Pitfalls

  • Precompute the last indices BEFORE slicing: deciding “closed?” in a single pass only needs each letter’s final index — without it, at every cut you don’t know whether the letter reappears.
  • The first pass uses enumerate for the last indices — a repeated letter’s index is overwritten until only the last one remains ✓.
  • Single-character input → [1]; everything interleaving → [len(s)].
  • Characters outside ‘a’..‘z’ (if the problem varies): the [26] array of C/C++/Rust assumes lowercase; for general ASCII use [128]/[256].
  • In C, resp allocates n ints (max partition count = characters); returnSize is what tells the real size — LeetCode frees the return.
  • The slice fim - inicio + 1 must be computed BEFORE updating inicio = i + 1 (the classic off-by-one).

621. Task Scheduler (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/task-scheduler/ · Topic: Greedy + counting

Problem (summary)

A CPU runs tasks labeled in tasks; between two runs of the SAME task there must be at least n time units (you may fill them with other tasks or sit idle). Return the minimum total time to run all of them.

tasks = ["A","A","A","B","B","B"], n = 2 → 8   (A B _ A B _ A B)
tasks = ["A","A","A","B","B","B"], n = 0 → 6   (no cooldown: A A A B B B)

Pattern — what to memorize

The “compartment” formula: if max_freq is the count of the most frequent task and quantos_max is how many tasks tie on it, the worst case (filling with idles) has size (max_freq - 1) * (n + 1) + quantos_max.

Why? Split the most frequent task into max_freq runs; between two of them there are n free time units — that’s max_freq - 1 intervals, each with n + 1 slots (the task + the cooldown). In the last cycle, the quantos_max tied tasks close the queue with no idle. If there are enough tasks to fill the intervals, the real time is just len(tasks) (no idle) — answer = max(formula, len(tasks)). Tell: minimum interval between repeats + minimum total time → count per task + slot formula; greedy because filling the holes with other tasks is always optimal.

Python

from collections import Counter

class Solution:
    def leastInterval(self, tasks: list[str], n: int) -> int:
        contagem = Counter(tasks)
        max_freq = max(contagem.values())
        quantos_max = sum(1 for v in contagem.values() if v == max_freq)
        return max(len(tasks), (max_freq - 1) * (n + 1) + quantos_max)

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashMap;

impl Solution {
    pub fn least_interval(tasks: Vec<char>, n: i32) -> i32 {
        let mut contagem: HashMap<char, i32> = HashMap::new();
        for &t in &tasks {
            *contagem.entry(t).or_insert(0) += 1;
        }
        let max_freq = contagem.values().copied().max().unwrap_or(0);
        let quantos_max = contagem.values().filter(|&&v| v == max_freq).count() as i64;
        let formula = (max_freq as i64 - 1) * (n as i64 + 1) + quantos_max;
        (tasks.len() as i64).max(formula) as i32
    }
}
}

C++

#include <algorithm>
#include <vector>

using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int leastInterval(vector<char>& tasks, int n) {
        int cnt[26] = {0};
        int maxFreq = 0;
        for (char t : tasks) maxFreq = max(maxFreq, ++cnt[t - 'A']);
        int quantosMax = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 26; ++i) if (cnt[i] == maxFreq) ++quantosMax;
        long long formula = (long long)(maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + quantosMax;
        return (int)max((long long)tasks.size(), formula);
    }
};

C

int leastInterval(char* tasks, int tasksSize, int n) {
    int cnt[26] = {0};
    int maxFreq = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < tasksSize; ++i) {
        int c = ++cnt[tasks[i] - 'A'];
        if (c > maxFreq) maxFreq = c;
    }
    int quantosMax = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 26; ++i) if (cnt[i] == maxFreq) ++quantosMax;
    long long formula = (long long)(maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + quantosMax;
    return (int)((long long)tasksSize > formula ? (long long)tasksSize : formula);
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one pass to count (the fixed [26]); the final sweep is O(26).
  • Space: O(1) — array of 26 counters.

Pitfalls

  • n = 0: with no cooldown, the answer is len(tasks) — the formula gives (max-1)*1 + quantos_max ≤ len and the max resolves it.
  • Formula overflow: (max_freq - 1) * (n + 1) can overflow int with a large n — compute in long long/i64 and truncate in the max (without it, C/C++ is UB).
  • quantos_max counts the TIES on max_freq (not “who is greater than…”) — an off-by-one here adds extra idle to the formula.
  • Simulate the “varied enough” case: ["A","A","A","A","A","A", "B","C","D","E","F","G"], n = 2 → 6 As create 5 * 3 + 1 = 16, and since 12 tasks < 16, the answer is 16 (A B C A D E A …). If there were more varied tasks than holes, it would just be len(tasks).
  • max_freq comes from a Counter/cnt[]; in Rust unwrap_or(0) covers the empty input (the problem guarantees ≥ 1, but it’s defensive).
  • The labels are uppercase chars on LeetCode — the [26] of C/C++ assumes 'A'..'Z'; if the input varies, use [128].

57. Insert Interval (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/insert-interval/ · Topic: Intervals

Problem (summary)

Given a list of intervals already sorted by start with no overlaps between them, and a new interval, insert it in the correct position, merging with everything it touches. Return the resulting list.

intervals = [[1,3],[6,9]], newInterval = [2,5]            →  [[1,5],[6,9]]
intervals = [[1,2],[3,5],[6,7],[8,10],[12,16]], [4,8]     →  [[1,2],[3,10],[12,16]]

Pattern — what to memorize

Linear sweep in 3 phases — (1) copy the intervals that end before the new one starts; (2) merge the ones that touch the new interval (condition start <= end), stretching the new one on every touch; (3) copy what comes after. Because the input is already sorted, a single pass does it — the tell is “ordered” + “insert”: no re-sorting, no two pointers.

Python

class Solution:
    def insert(self, intervals: list[list[int]], newInterval: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        inicio, fim = newInterval
        antes, depois = [], []
        for intervalo in intervals:
            if intervalo[1] < inicio:        # ends before the new one starts
                antes.append(intervalo)
            elif intervalo[0] > fim:         # starts after the new one ends
                depois.append(intervalo)
            else:                            # touches/overlaps: stretch the new one
                inicio = min(inicio, intervalo[0])
                fim = max(fim, intervalo[1])
        return antes + [[inicio, fim]] + depois

No indices, no while — the elif already splits the 3 phases. This is the interview version: 8 lines, impossible to trip an off-by-one.

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn insert(intervals: Vec<Vec<i32>>, new_interval: Vec<i32>) -> Vec<Vec<i32>> {
        let (mut inicio, mut fim) = (new_interval[0], new_interval[1]);
        let mut resp: Vec<Vec<i32>> = Vec::new();
        let mut i = 0;
        // intervals that end before the new one starts: copy straight across
        while i < intervals.len() && intervals[i][1] < inicio {
            resp.push(intervals[i].clone());
            i += 1;
        }
        // merge everything that touches the new interval (boundaries included)
        while i < intervals.len() && intervals[i][0] <= fim {
            inicio = inicio.min(intervals[i][0]);
            fim = fim.max(intervals[i][1]);
            i += 1;
        }
        resp.push(vec![inicio, fim]);
        // and what comes after
        while i < intervals.len() {
            resp.push(intervals[i].clone());
            i += 1;
        }
        resp
    }
}
}

Cloning the intervals that pass through untouched is the honest way to not fight the borrow checker (the problem hands you the Vec by value anyway).

C++

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<vector<int>> insert(vector<vector<int>>& intervals, vector<int>& newInterval) {
        vector<vector<int>> resp;
        int inicio = newInterval[0], fim = newInterval[1];
        int i = 0, n = (int)intervals.size();
        // intervals that end before the new one starts: copy straight across
        while (i < n && intervals[i][1] < inicio)
            resp.push_back(intervals[i++]);
        // merge everything that touches the new interval (boundaries included)
        while (i < n && intervals[i][0] <= fim) {
            inicio = min(inicio, intervals[i][0]);
            fim = max(fim, intervals[i][1]);
            i++;
        }
        resp.push_back({inicio, fim});
        // and what comes after
        while (i < n)
            resp.push_back(intervals[i++]);
        return resp;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

int** insert(int** intervals, int intervalsSize, int* intervalsColSize,
             int* newInterval, int newIntervalSize, int* returnSize,
             int** returnColumnSizes) {
    (void)intervalsColSize;
    (void)newIntervalSize;
    int** resp = malloc((intervalsSize + 1) * sizeof(int*));
    *returnColumnSizes = malloc((intervalsSize + 1) * sizeof(int));
    int n = 0, i = 0;
    int inicio = newInterval[0], fim = newInterval[1];
    /* before: ends before the new one starts */
    while (i < intervalsSize && intervals[i][1] < inicio) {
        resp[n] = malloc(2 * sizeof(int));
        resp[n][0] = intervals[i][0];
        resp[n][1] = intervals[i][1];
        (*returnColumnSizes)[n] = 2;
        n++; i++;
    }
    /* merge everything that touches the new interval */
    while (i < intervalsSize && intervals[i][0] <= fim) {
        if (intervals[i][0] < inicio) inicio = intervals[i][0];
        if (intervals[i][1] > fim) fim = intervals[i][1];
        i++;
    }
    resp[n] = malloc(2 * sizeof(int));
    resp[n][0] = inicio;
    resp[n][1] = fim;
    (*returnColumnSizes)[n] = 2;
    n++;
    /* after */
    while (i < intervalsSize) {
        resp[n] = malloc(2 * sizeof(int));
        resp[n][0] = intervals[i][0];
        resp[n][1] = intervals[i][1];
        (*returnColumnSizes)[n] = 2;
        n++; i++;
    }
    *returnSize = n;
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one single pass; no sorting (the input is already sorted).
  • Space: O(n) — the answer holds at most n + 1 intervals.

Pitfalls

  • “Touching” counts as overlap: [1,2] plus a new [2,3] merges into [1,3]. The merge condition is intervals[i][0] <= fim, not < — the <= vs < mistake is the most common one in this problem.
  • New interval that touches nothing: it lands at the front (empty first phase) or at the back (empty third phase) — the 3-phase code covers both alone.
  • New interval that swallows several at once: phase 2 stretches inicio/fim cumulatively.
  • Empty input: return just the new interval.
  • C: the answer can hold n + 1 intervals — allocate (n + 1), not n. returnColumnSizes must be allocated with the same size.
  • C++: the signature takes vector<int>& — in the interview, always pass a named variable, never a loose {...} as an argument.

56. Merge Intervals (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/merge-intervals/ · Topic: Intervals

Problem (summary)

Given a list of intervals, merge all overlapping ones and return the resulting list with no overlaps (order doesn’t matter).

intervals = [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]  →  [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]
intervals = [[1,4],[4,5]]                 →  [[1,5]]

Pattern — what to memorize

Sort + sweep merging into the last one: sort by start, seed the answer with the first interval, and for each next one, if it touches the last interval in the answer (start <= last_end) extend the end with max; otherwise append it as new. Tell: merging overlapping intervals → the adjacent sorted pair is the only comparison needed; without sorting, two overlapping intervals far apart would force O(n²).

Python

class Solution:
    def merge(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> list[list[int]]:
        if not intervals:
            return []
        intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
        resp = [intervals[0]]
        for inicio, fim in intervals[1:]:
            if inicio <= resp[-1][1]:          # touches the last one built
                resp[-1][1] = max(resp[-1][1], fim)
            else:
                resp.append([inicio, fim])
        return resp

sort is stable and key=lambda x: x[0] is explicit — in Python, sort() without a key would already order by the whole pair, but the key makes the intent clear.

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn merge(intervals: Vec<Vec<i32>>) -> Vec<Vec<i32>> {
        let mut intervalos = intervals;
        intervalos.sort_by_key(|i| (i[0], i[1]));
        let mut resp: Vec<Vec<i32>> = Vec::with_capacity(intervalos.len());
        for intervalo in intervalos {
            if let Some(ultimo) = resp.last_mut() {
                if intervalo[0] <= ultimo[1] {
                    // touches the last one → extend the end (max)
                    ultimo[1] = ultimo[1].max(intervalo[1]);
                    continue;
                }
            }
            resp.push(intervalo);
        }
        resp
    }
}
}

last_mut() + continue is the idiomatic “mutate the last or push a new one” without indices — no borrow checker in the way.

C++

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<vector<int>> merge(vector<vector<int>>& intervals) {
        if (intervals.empty()) return {};
        sort(intervals.begin(), intervals.end());
        vector<vector<int>> resp;
        resp.push_back(intervals[0]);
        for (int i = 1; i < (int)intervals.size(); ++i) {
            if (intervals[i][0] <= resp.back()[1]) {
                // touches the last one → extend the end (max)
                resp.back()[1] = max(resp.back()[1], intervals[i][1]);
            } else {
                resp.push_back(intervals[i]);
            }
        }
        return resp;
    }
};

sort already orders by start (lexicographic on the pair) — no custom comparator.

C

#include <stdlib.h>

static int cmp_intervalo(const void* a, const void* b) {
    const int* x = *(const int* const*)a;
    const int* y = *(const int* const*)b;
    return (x[0] > y[0]) - (x[0] < y[0]); /* NEVER "x - y" (overflow) */
}

int** merge(int** intervals, int intervalsSize, int* intervalsColSize,
            int* returnSize, int** returnColumnSizes) {
    (void)intervalsColSize;
    qsort(intervals, intervalsSize, sizeof(int*), cmp_intervalo);
    int** resp = malloc(intervalsSize * sizeof(int*));
    *returnColumnSizes = malloc(intervalsSize * sizeof(int));
    if (intervalsSize == 0) {
        *returnSize = 0;
        *returnColumnSizes = NULL;
        return resp;
    }
    int n = 0;
    resp[n] = malloc(2 * sizeof(int));
    resp[n][0] = intervals[0][0];
    resp[n][1] = intervals[0][1];
    (*returnColumnSizes)[n] = 2;
    for (int i = 1; i < intervalsSize; i++) {
        if (intervals[i][0] <= resp[n][1]) {
            /* touches the last one → extend the end (max) */
            if (intervals[i][1] > resp[n][1]) resp[n][1] = intervals[i][1];
        } else {
            n++;
            resp[n] = malloc(2 * sizeof(int));
            resp[n][0] = intervals[i][0];
            resp[n][1] = intervals[i][1];
            (*returnColumnSizes)[n] = 2;
        }
    }
    *returnSize = n + 1;
    return resp;
}

The comparator receives a pointer to the array element — hence the double cast *(const int* const*)a. qsort reorders the array of pointers itself, so intervals comes back sorted in-place (acceptable on LeetCode).

Complexity

  • Time: O(n log n) — the sort dominates; the sweep is O(n).
  • Space: O(n) — the answer; in C, qsort adds O(log n) of stack.

Pitfalls

  • Sorting first is required: without it, “touches the last one” doesn’t hold.
  • Equality at the boundaries ([1,4] + [4,5]) merges — condition <=, not <. But [1,4] + [5,6] does not merge (5 > 4).
  • Contained intervals ([1,10] + [2,3]): the max on the end keeps the larger interval from shrinking.
  • Empty or single-element input: returns without exploding.
  • C: a qsort comparator that subtracts overflows (INT_MIN); use (a > b) - (a < b). The double const keeps -Wall quiet.
  • C++: resp.back() only exists because empty() was checked first — the first element enters by hand, no per-iteration conditional.

435. Non-overlapping Intervals (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/non-overlapping-intervals/ · Topic: Intervals

Problem (summary)

Given a list of intervals, return the minimum number of intervals to remove so that the rest don’t overlap. Two intervals that merely touch ([1,2] and [2,3]) are not an overlap.

intervals = [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[1,3]]     →  1              (remove [1,3])
intervals = [[1,2],[1,2],[1,2]]           →  2

Pattern — what to memorize

Greedy by “earliest end” (interval scheduling): sort by end and count how many intervals can stay — keep the current one if it starts after the previously kept one ended (start >= prev_end); the answer is simply “minimum to remove = total − kept”. Why sort by end and not by start? Whoever ends earlier frees up space faster, leaving maximum room for the rest — the same principle as “pick the meeting that ends first” from classic scheduling.

Python

class Solution:
    def eraseOverlapIntervals(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        # greedy by earliest end: keep whoever ends first
        intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])
        fim_anterior = float("-inf")
        mantidos = 0
        for inicio, fim in intervals:
            if inicio >= fim_anterior:   # doesn't touch the previously kept one
                mantidos += 1
                fim_anterior = fim
        return len(intervals) - mantidos

The answer is what’s left outside: solving “maximum number of intervals that fit” is easier than choosing what to remove.

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn erase_overlap_intervals(intervals: Vec<Vec<i32>>) -> i32 {
        let mut intervalos = intervals;
        // greedy by earliest end: keep whoever ends first
        intervalos.sort_by_key(|i| i[1]);
        let mut fim_anterior = i32::MIN;
        let mut mantidos = 0i32;
        for intervalo in &intervalos {
            if intervalo[0] >= fim_anterior {
                mantidos += 1;
                fim_anterior = intervalo[1];
            }
        }
        intervalos.len() as i32 - mantidos
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int eraseOverlapIntervals(vector<vector<int>>& intervals) {
        // greedy by earliest end: keep whoever ends first
        sort(intervals.begin(), intervals.end(),
             [](const vector<int>& a, const vector<int>& b) { return a[1] < b[1]; });
        int fimAnterior = INT_MIN, mantidos = 0;
        for (auto& iv : intervals) {
            if (iv[0] >= fimAnterior) { // doesn't touch the previously kept one
                mantidos++;
                fimAnterior = iv[1];
            }
        }
        return (int)intervals.size() - mantidos;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

static int cmp_por_fim(const void* a, const void* b) {
    const int* x = *(const int* const*)a;
    const int* y = *(const int* const*)b;
    return (x[1] > y[1]) - (x[1] < y[1]); /* NEVER "x - y" (overflow) */
}

int eraseOverlapIntervals(int** intervals, int intervalsSize, int* intervalsColSize) {
    (void)intervalsColSize;
    if (intervalsSize == 0) return 0;
    /* greedy by earliest end: keep whoever ends first */
    qsort(intervals, intervalsSize, sizeof(int*), cmp_por_fim);
    int fim_anterior = intervals[0][1];
    int mantidos = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i < intervalsSize; i++) {
        if (intervals[i][0] >= fim_anterior) { /* doesn't touch the kept one */
            mantidos++;
            fim_anterior = intervals[i][1];
        }
    }
    return intervalsSize - mantidos;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n log n) — the sort dominates; the sweep is O(n).
  • Space: O(1) beyond the sort (C: O(log n) of qsort stack).

Pitfalls

  • Sort by end, not by start — sorting by start breaks the greedy (the longest interval would win the spot it doesn’t deserve).
  • Touching is not overlapping: keeping requires start >= prev_end, not >.
  • Contained ([1,4] and [2,3]): the one with the larger end is dropped naturally — the smaller-end one ([2,3]) comes first under sort-by-end and [1,4] doesn’t touch the kept one, so it’s discarded.
  • All identical ([[1,2]]×3): keep 1, remove 2.
  • C/C++: i32::MIN/INT_MIN as sentinel works because the constraints are ≥ −10⁴ — point that out if the interviewer asks about the magic value.
  • Rust: sort_by_key on a Copy field; if the struct field weren’t Copy, sort_by would be needed to avoid moving.

252. Meeting Rooms (Easy · Premium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/meeting-rooms/ · Topic: Intervals (Premium)

Problem (summary)

Given a list of time intervals ([start, end) — the end is exclusive), say whether a single person can attend all the appointments: that is, whether no pair overlaps.

intervals = [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]]   →  false   (0–30 covers 5–10 and 15–20)
intervals = [[7,10],[2,4]]            →  true

Pattern — what to memorize

Sort by start + compare with the previous neighbor: after sorting, just check intervals[i][0] < intervals[i - 1][1] — if the current one starts before the previous one ends, there’s a conflict. This is Merge Intervals’ (56) close cousin: there we merge the ones that touch; here we only ask whether anything touches. If you memorized the merge, this one is 3 lines.

Python

class Solution:
    def canAttendMeetings(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> bool:
        intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
        for i in range(1, len(intervals)):
            if intervals[i][0] < intervals[i - 1][1]:  # starts before the previous ends
                return False
        return True

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn can_attend_meetings(intervals: Vec<Vec<i32>>) -> bool {
        let mut intervalos = intervals;
        intervalos.sort_by_key(|i| i[0]);
        // conflict if the next starts before the current ends
        for janela in intervalos.windows(2) {
            if janela[1][0] < janela[0][1] {
                return false;
            }
        }
        true
    }
}
}

windows(2) hands you the adjacent pairs with no index — and no risk of [-1]/off-by-one.

C++

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    bool canAttendMeetings(vector<vector<int>>& intervals) {
        sort(intervals.begin(), intervals.end());
        // conflict if the next starts before the current ends
        for (int i = 1; i < (int)intervals.size(); ++i) {
            if (intervals[i][0] < intervals[i - 1][1]) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

static int cmp_por_inicio(const void* a, const void* b) {
    const int* x = *(const int* const*)a;
    const int* y = *(const int* const*)b;
    return (x[0] > y[0]) - (x[0] < y[0]); /* NEVER "x - y" (overflow) */
}

bool canAttendMeetings(int** intervals, int intervalsSize, int* intervalsColSize) {
    (void)intervalsColSize;
    qsort(intervals, intervalsSize, sizeof(int*), cmp_por_inicio);
    for (int i = 1; i < intervalsSize; i++) {
        /* conflict if the next starts before the current ends */
        if (intervals[i][0] < intervals[i - 1][1]) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n log n) — the sort; the check is O(n).
  • Space: O(1) beyond the sort (C: O(log n) of qsort stack).

Pitfalls

  • [1,5] and [5,10] is true: the end is exclusive, so starting at the instant the other ends is not a conflict — condition <, not <=.
  • Premium: this is LeetCode 252, behind the paywall (password: saying "true if no pair overlaps" already is the summary; in a live interview, ask about closed/open boundaries before coding).
  • Empty or 1-element input → true (the loop doesn’t run).
  • No “booking rooms” or counting — it only asks conflict/no-conflict.

253. Meeting Rooms II (Medium · Premium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/meeting-rooms-ii/ · Topic: Intervals (Premium)

Problem (summary)

Given a list of meeting times ([start, end) — exclusive end), return the minimum number of rooms needed to fit all of them without overlap.

intervals = [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]]   →  2   (0–30 in one room; 5–10 and 15–20 can share the other)
intervals = [[7,10],[2,4]]            →  1   (they don't overlap)

Pattern — what to memorize

The minimum number of rooms is the peak of simultaneous overlap — at any instant, how many meetings are open at once. Two ways to count that peak:

1. Sweep line (chosen in the code below) — no heap: split all starts and all ends into two sorted arrays, and sweep with two pointers: each start before the next end is “+1 room”; each end before the next start is “−1 room”. A tie (start == end) goes to the end side (free the room before renting another — exclusive boundaries). The peak seen is the answer. O(n log n) sorting cost, no extra structure: it’s the version that pleases in C and skips heap debt.

2. Min-heap of ends: sort by start; the heap holds the ends of the meetings currently running. For each meeting, if the heap top <= start (the oldest meeting ended), pop it (room freed); then push the current end. The maximum heap size is the answer. Same idea, more machinery involved:

# alternative: min-heap
import heapq

class Solution:
    def minMeetingRooms(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
        fins = []                                   # heap of ends of open meetings
        for inicio, fim in intervals:
            if fins and fins[0] <= inicio:          # the oldest already ended
                heapq.heappop(fins)                 # free the room
            heapq.heappush(fins, fim)               # occupy
        return len(fins)                            # peak = max heap size

Memorize the relation between the two: the sweep line counts events over time (started/ended); the heap counts resources in use. In both, the peak is the answer — and start == end always frees first.

Tell for the pattern: “minimum number of rooms” + intervals → overlap peak → sweep line or heap.

Python

class Solution:
    def minMeetingRooms(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        # sweep line: start and end events, each in its own sorted array
        inicios = sorted(inicio for inicio, _ in intervals)
        fins = sorted(fim for _, fim in intervals)
        salas, max_salas = 0, 0
        i = j = 0
        while i < len(inicios):
            if inicios[i] < fins[j]:   # starts before somebody ends: +1 room
                salas += 1
                i += 1
            else:                      # a room freed first (tie = end first)
                salas -= 1
                j += 1
            max_salas = max(max_salas, salas)
        return max_salas

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn min_meeting_rooms(intervals: Vec<Vec<i32>>) -> i32 {
        // sweep line: start and end events, each in its own sorted array
        let mut inicios: Vec<i32> = intervals.iter().map(|i| i[0]).collect();
        let mut fins: Vec<i32> = intervals.iter().map(|i| i[1]).collect();
        inicios.sort_unstable();
        fins.sort_unstable();
        let (mut salas, mut max_salas) = (0i32, 0i32);
        let (mut i, mut j) = (0usize, 0usize);
        while i < inicios.len() {
            if inicios[i] < fins[j] {
                // starts before somebody ends: one more room needed
                salas += 1;
                i += 1;
            } else {
                // a room freed first (tie = end before start)
                salas -= 1;
                j += 1;
            }
            max_salas = max_salas.max(salas);
        }
        max_salas
    }
}
}

If you prefer the heap in this language: BinaryHeap<Reverse<i32>> (Rust’s heap is a max-heap; Reverse flips it) — but the version above is cheaper.

C++

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    int minMeetingRooms(vector<vector<int>>& intervals) {
        // sweep line: start and end events, each in its own sorted array
        vector<int> inicios, fins;
        inicios.reserve(intervals.size());
        fins.reserve(intervals.size());
        for (auto& iv : intervals) {
            inicios.push_back(iv[0]);
            fins.push_back(iv[1]);
        }
        sort(inicios.begin(), inicios.end());
        sort(fins.begin(), fins.end());
        int salas = 0, max_salas = 0, i = 0, j = 0;
        int n = (int)inicios.size();
        while (i < n) {
            if (inicios[i] < fins[j]) { // starts before somebody ends: +1
                salas++;
                i++;
            } else { // a room freed first (tie = end before start)
                salas--;
                j++;
            }
            max_salas = max(max_salas, salas);
        }
        return max_salas;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

static int cmp_int(const void* a, const void* b) {
    int x = *(const int*)a, y = *(const int*)b;
    return (x > y) - (x < y); /* NEVER "x - y" (overflow) */
}

int minMeetingRooms(int** intervals, int intervalsSize, int* intervalsColSize) {
    (void)intervalsColSize;
    if (intervalsSize == 0) return 0;
    /* sweep line: start and end events, each in its own sorted array */
    int* inicios = malloc(intervalsSize * sizeof(int));
    int* fins = malloc(intervalsSize * sizeof(int));
    for (int i = 0; i < intervalsSize; i++) {
        inicios[i] = intervals[i][0];
        fins[i] = intervals[i][1];
    }
    qsort(inicios, intervalsSize, sizeof(int), cmp_int);
    qsort(fins, intervalsSize, sizeof(int), cmp_int);
    int salas = 0, max_salas = 0, i = 0, j = 0;
    while (i < intervalsSize) {
        if (inicios[i] < fins[j]) { /* starts before somebody ends: +1 */
            salas++;
            i++;
        } else { /* a room freed first (tie = end before start) */
            salas--;
            j++;
        }
        if (salas > max_salas) max_salas = salas;
    }
    free(inicios);
    free(fins);
    return max_salas;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n log n) — sorting the two arrays (or O(log n) per heap operation in the equivalent). The sweep is O(n).
  • Space: O(n) — the two event arrays (or the max heap size).

Pitfalls

  • start == end frees the room first: with [1,5] and [5,10], a single room suffices. In the sweep line the else (end) wins the tie — condition inicios[i] < fins[j], never <=.
  • Peak, not sum: adding “pairwise overlapping” meetings gives the wrong answer; what matters is the simultaneous maximum.
  • Meeting order doesn’t matter — each array is sorted independently (that’s what makes the sweep line cheap: the two pointers never go back).
  • Empty → 0 rooms.
  • Heaps: Python/C++ heap pops min; Rust’s BinaryHeap is max — it needs Reverse (a house rule warning). The sweep line sidesteps this language pitfall for free.
  • C/C++: fins[j] never runs out of bounds because j only advances when a room frees — and there are only n frees total (invariant: j <= i).
  • Premium: problem 253 behind the paywall; in the interview, confirm the meaning of the boundaries (open/closed) before coding.

48. Rotate Image (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/rotate-image/ · Topic: Math & Geometry

Problem (summary)

Rotate a square n × n matrix 90° clockwise, in place — without allocating another matrix.

[[1,2,3],     [[7,4,1],
 [4,5,6],  →   [8,5,2],
 [7,8,9]]      [9,6,3]]

Pattern — what to memorize

Transpose + mirror the rows. A 90° rotation maps cell (i, j) → (j, n−1−i). The transposition swaps rows and columns: (i, j) → (j, i) (mirror along the main diagonal). Then mirroring each row horizontally reverses the column: (j, i) → (j, n−1−i). The composition is exactly the rotation — that’s why the trick works: two reflections whose composition is a rotation (the same mirror algebra physics uses). Two O(n²) in-place passes = zero extra memory.

Python

class Solution:
    def rotate(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> None:
        n = len(matrix)
        # 1) transpose: (i, j) <-> (j, i), only the triangle above the diagonal
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i + 1, n):
                matrix[i][j], matrix[j][i] = matrix[j][i], matrix[i][j]
        # 2) mirror each row: reverse the column order
        for linha in matrix:
            linha.reverse()

No %, no “chain of 4” arithmetic — each cell swap happens exactly once because the loop only walks the triangle above the diagonal.

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn rotate(matrix: &mut Vec<Vec<i32>>) {
        let n = matrix.len();
        // 1) transpose: (i, j) <-> (j, i), only the triangle above the diagonal
        for i in 0..n {
            for j in (i + 1)..n {
                let tmp = matrix[i][j];
                matrix[i][j] = matrix[j][i];
                matrix[j][i] = tmp;
            }
        }
        // 2) mirror each row: reverse the column order
        for linha in matrix.iter_mut() {
            linha.reverse();
        }
    }
}
}

iter_mut() + the Vec’s built-in reverse(): mirroring a row is native.

C++

#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    void rotate(vector<vector<int>>& matrix) {
        int n = (int)matrix.size();
        // 1) transpose: (i, j) <-> (j, i), only the triangle above the diagonal
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
            for (int j = i + 1; j < n; ++j)
                swap(matrix[i][j], matrix[j][i]);
        // 2) mirror each row: reverse the column order
        for (auto& linha : matrix)
            reverse(linha.begin(), linha.end());
    }
};

C

void rotate(int** matrix, int matrixSize, int* matrixColSize) {
    (void)matrixColSize;
    /* 1) transpose: (i, j) <-> (j, i), only the triangle above the diagonal */
    for (int i = 0; i < matrixSize; i++) {
        for (int j = i + 1; j < matrixSize; j++) {
            int tmp = matrix[i][j];
            matrix[i][j] = matrix[j][i];
            matrix[j][i] = tmp;
        }
        /* 2) mirror the row: reverse the column order */
        for (int l = 0, r = matrixSize - 1; l < r; l++, r--) {
            int tmp = matrix[i][l];
            matrix[i][l] = matrix[i][r];
            matrix[i][r] = tmp;
        }
    }
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n²) — each of the n² cells is visited a constant number of times (n/2 swaps in the transposition + n/2 in the per-row mirroring).
  • Space: O(1) — in place, only the swap temporary.

Pitfalls

  • In place is mandatory: allocating a fresh matrix “solves” it but fails the requirement — and the transpose+mirror trick exists precisely for this.
  • Transposition loop: j starts at i + 1, otherwise you undo the swap (transposing twice) — the diagonal (i == j) stays put.
  • The rotation is clockwise. If asked counter-clockwise: transpose + mirror the columns (or reverse rows before transposing).
  • n = 1: no loop runs, nothing breaks.
  • C: the matrix is int** (array of rows); matrixColSize is always n — ignore it with (void), don’t use it as the loop bound.
  • Rust/C++: reverse is in-place and O(n) — no building a new vector.

54. Spiral Matrix (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/spiral-matrix/ · Topic: Math & Geometry

Problem (summary)

Given an m × n matrix (possibly rectangular), return all elements in spiral order (clockwise): top → right → bottom → left, shrinking one layer per full loop.

[[1,2,3],         → [1,2,3,6,9,8,7,4,5]
 [4,5,6],
 [7,8,9]]
[[1,2,3,4],       → [1,2,3,4,8,12,11,10,9,5,6,7]
 [5,6,7,8],
 [9,10,11,12]]

Pattern — what to memorize

Shrink four boundaries (top/bottom/left/right) and walk the 4 sides of the current layer, updating the boundary right after each side. Each pass: → along the top, ↓ along the right, ← along the bottom, ↑ along the left; after the first row and the last column, before walking back, make sure there’s still an inner row/column (top <= bottom && left <= right). Tell from the statement: spiral + matrix → layer simulation with 4 boundary pointers. Watch out for non-square matrices: the last “loop” may have only 1 row or 1 column.

Python

class Solution:
    def spiralOrder(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
        resp: list[int] = []
        if not matrix:
            return resp
        cima, baixo = 0, len(matrix) - 1
        esq, dir = 0, len(matrix[0]) - 1
        while cima <= baixo and esq <= dir:
            for j in range(esq, dir + 1):            # top, left to right
                resp.append(matrix[cima][j])
            cima += 1
            for i in range(cima, baixo + 1):         # right, top to bottom
                resp.append(matrix[i][dir])
            dir -= 1
            if cima <= baixo:                        # bottom, right to left
                for j in range(dir, esq - 1, -1):
                    resp.append(matrix[baixo][j])
                baixo -= 1
            if esq <= dir:                           # left, bottom to top
                for i in range(baixo, cima - 1, -1):
                    resp.append(matrix[i][esq])
                esq += 1
        return resp

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn spiral_order(matrix: Vec<Vec<i32>>) -> Vec<i32> {
        let mut resp = Vec::new();
        if matrix.is_empty() {
            return resp;
        }
        let (mut cima, mut baixo) = (0usize, matrix.len() - 1);
        let (mut esq, mut dir) = (0usize, matrix[0].len() - 1);
        while cima <= baixo && esq <= dir {
            for j in esq..=dir {
                resp.push(matrix[cima][j]);
            }
            cima += 1;
            if cima > baixo {
                break;
            }
            for i in cima..=baixo {
                resp.push(matrix[i][dir]);
            }
            // dir can be 0 (1-column matrix): checked avoids usize underflow
            let Some(d) = dir.checked_sub(1) else { break };
            dir = d;
            if esq > dir {
                break;
            }
            for j in (esq..=dir).rev() {
                resp.push(matrix[baixo][j]);
            }
            baixo -= 1;
            for i in (cima..=baixo).rev() {
                resp.push(matrix[i][esq]);
            }
            esq += 1;
        }
        resp
    }
}
}

usize has no negatives: dir.checked_sub(1) is the handrail for the decrement — without it, a 1-column matrix panics at dir -= 1.

C++

#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> spiralOrder(vector<vector<int>>& matrix) {
        vector<int> resp;
        if (matrix.empty()) return resp;
        int cima = 0, baixo = (int)matrix.size() - 1;
        int esq = 0, dir = (int)matrix[0].size() - 1;
        while (cima <= baixo && esq <= dir) {
            for (int j = esq; j <= dir; ++j) resp.push_back(matrix[cima][j]);  // top →
            cima++;
            for (int i = cima; i <= baixo; ++i) resp.push_back(matrix[i][dir]); // right ↓
            dir--;
            if (cima <= baixo) {                                                // bottom ←
                for (int j = dir; j >= esq; --j) resp.push_back(matrix[baixo][j]);
                baixo--;
            }
            if (esq <= dir) {                                                   // left ↑
                for (int i = baixo; i >= cima; --i) resp.push_back(matrix[i][esq]);
                esq++;
            }
        }
        return resp;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

int* spiralOrder(int** matrix, int matrixSize, int* matrixColSize, int* returnSize) {
    *returnSize = 0;
    if (matrixSize == 0) return NULL;
    int cols = matrixColSize[0];
    int* resp = malloc(matrixSize * cols * sizeof(int));
    int cima = 0, baixo = matrixSize - 1;
    int esq = 0, dir = cols - 1;
    int n = 0;
    while (cima <= baixo && esq <= dir) {
        for (int j = esq; j <= dir; j++) resp[n++] = matrix[cima][j];  /* top → */
        cima++;
        for (int i = cima; i <= baixo; i++) resp[n++] = matrix[i][dir]; /* right ↓ */
        dir--;
        if (cima <= baixo) {                                            /* bottom ← */
            for (int j = dir; j >= esq; j--) resp[n++] = matrix[baixo][j];
            baixo--;
        }
        if (esq <= dir) {                                               /* left ↑ */
            for (int i = baixo; i >= cima; i--) resp[n++] = matrix[i][esq];
            esq++;
        }
    }
    *returnSize = n;
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(m·n) — every cell enters the answer exactly once.
  • Space: O(1) beyond the answer (which is the required output).

Pitfalls

  • Non-square matrix: the cima <= baixo / esq <= dir guards before the return sides are what avoid repeating the middle row/column in 1×n, n×1 and rectangular-core matrices.
  • 1 row ([[2,3]]) and 1 column ([[1],[2],[3]]) are the edge cases that break most naive implementations — test both.
  • The order of the 4 loops is fixed (→↓←↑); reversing one reverses the spiral.
  • Rust: decrementing usize with -= 1 panics at 0 — checked_sub (or work with i32 and cast at the index).
  • C/C++: indices are int (not size_t), so dir-- from 0 → −1 is safe — and the for (j = dir; j >= esq; --j) loop with negative dir simply doesn’t run.
  • C: returnSize = 0 and NULL for the empty matrix — LeetCode expects exactly that in the degenerate case.

73. Set Matrix Zeroes (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/set-matrix-zeroes/ · Topic: Arrays · Math

Problem (summary)

If an element of matrix is 0, zero out the entire row and column. Modify in place with O(1) extra memory.

[[1,1,1]        [[1,0,1]
 [1,0,1]   →     [0,0,0]
 [1,1,1]]        [1,0,1]]

Pattern — what to memorize

Use the first row and the first column as markers — two “free” zones of the matrix itself (O(1) memory) that record, respectively, “row i must zero” and “column j must zero”. Two extra flags preserve the fate of the borders themselves. Read/write order is what makes it work: first read the whole matrix writing markers (never zero before you finish reading — a zero you rewrote would become a false marker); then zero the interior consulting the markers ONLY; finally the borders, using the two flags from the original state. This trades the O(m·n) memory of a set of pairs for O(1).

Python

class Solution:
    def setZeroes(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> None:
        m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        # Border flags BEFORE using them as markers.
        primeira_linha = any(x == 0 for x in matrix[0])
        primeira_coluna = any(matrix[i][0] == 0 for i in range(m))

        # Markers: row i / column j will be zeroed.
        for i in range(1, m):
            for j in range(1, n):
                if matrix[i][j] == 0:
                    matrix[i][0] = 0
                    matrix[0][j] = 0

        # Zero the interior using ONLY the markers (never original zeros).
        for i in range(1, m):
            for j in range(1, n):
                if matrix[i][0] == 0 or matrix[0][j] == 0:
                    matrix[i][j] = 0

        # Borders last (the flags keep what was original).
        if primeira_linha:
            for j in range(n):
                matrix[0][j] = 0
        if primeira_coluna:
            for i in range(m):
                matrix[i][0] = 0

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn set_zeroes(matrix: &mut Vec<Vec<i32>>) {
        let (m, n) = (matrix.len(), matrix[0].len());

        // Border flags BEFORE using them as markers.
        let primeira_linha = matrix[0].iter().any(|&x| x == 0);
        let primeira_coluna = (0..m).any(|i| matrix[i][0] == 0);

        // Markers: row i / column j will be zeroed.
        for i in 1..m {
            for j in 1..n {
                if matrix[i][j] == 0 {
                    matrix[i][0] = 0;
                    matrix[0][j] = 0;
                }
            }
        }

        // Zero the interior using ONLY the markers.
        for i in 1..m {
            for j in 1..n {
                if matrix[i][0] == 0 || matrix[0][j] == 0 {
                    matrix[i][j] = 0;
                }
            }
        }

        // Borders last (the flags keep what was original).
        if primeira_linha {
            for j in 0..n {
                matrix[0][j] = 0;
            }
        }
        if primeira_coluna {
            for i in 0..m {
                matrix[i][0] = 0;
            }
        }
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    void setZeroes(vector<vector<int>>& matrix) {
        int m = matrix.size(), n = matrix[0].size();

        // Border flags BEFORE using them as markers.
        bool primeira_linha = false, primeira_coluna = false;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) if (matrix[0][j] == 0) primeira_linha = true;
        for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) if (matrix[i][0] == 0) primeira_coluna = true;

        // Markers: row i / column j will be zeroed.
        for (int i = 1; i < m; ++i)
            for (int j = 1; j < n; ++j)
                if (matrix[i][j] == 0) {
                    matrix[i][0] = 0;
                    matrix[0][j] = 0;
                }

        // Zero the interior using ONLY the markers.
        for (int i = 1; i < m; ++i)
            for (int j = 1; j < n; ++j)
                if (matrix[i][0] == 0 || matrix[0][j] == 0)
                    matrix[i][j] = 0;

        // Borders last (the flags keep what was original).
        if (primeira_linha)
            for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) matrix[0][j] = 0;
        if (primeira_coluna)
            for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) matrix[i][0] = 0;
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>

void setZeroes(int** matrix, int matrixSize, int* matrixColSize) {
    int m = matrixSize, n = matrixColSize[0];

    /* Border flags BEFORE using them as markers. */
    bool primeira_linha = false, primeira_coluna = false;
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) if (matrix[0][j] == 0) primeira_linha = true;
    for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) if (matrix[i][0] == 0) primeira_coluna = true;

    /* Markers: row i / column j will be zeroed. */
    for (int i = 1; i < m; i++)
        for (int j = 1; j < n; j++)
            if (matrix[i][j] == 0) {
                matrix[i][0] = 0;
                matrix[0][j] = 0;
            }

    /* Zero the interior using ONLY the markers. */
    for (int i = 1; i < m; i++)
        for (int j = 1; j < n; j++)
            if (matrix[i][0] == 0 || matrix[0][j] == 0)
                matrix[i][j] = 0;

    /* Borders last (the flags keep what was original). */
    if (primeira_linha)
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) matrix[0][j] = 0;
    if (primeira_coluna)
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) matrix[i][0] = 0;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(m·n) — three constant sweeps of the matrix.
  • Space: O(1) — just the two flags (the markers live in the matrix itself).

Pitfalls

  • The first-row/first-column flag is mandatory: matrix[0][0] is the crossing of the two markers — it doesn’t say which one zeroed whom. The flags decide.
  • Zero the interior before the borders: the markers sit on the border; if you zero the border first, you lose the information before using it.
  • Python: any(...) for the flags (one readable line) — or short-circuits.
  • Rust: matrix[0].iter().any(|&x| x == 0) — &x so you don’t move out of the iterator.
  • C/C++: matrix[i][0] with matrixColSize/n — the matrix arrives as int** (array of pointers), not a contiguous block; n is matrixColSize[0].
  • C: #include <stdbool.h> (no native bool before C23).
