202. Happy Number (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/happy-number/ · Topic: Math · Hash Table

Problem (summary)

A number is happy if, repeating “sum of the squares of the digits”, it reaches 1. If it enters a cycle (never reaches 1), it’s not happy.

19 → 82 → 68 → 100 → 1   (happy)
2  → 4 → 16 → 37 → 58 → 89 → 145 → 42 → 20 → 4   (cycle → not happy)

Pattern — what to memorize

Cycle detection: the sequence always repeats a state — the sum of squares of a k-digit number is ≤ 9²·k, far smaller than the number, so the state space is finite and a cycle is inevitable. Two handy tools: a set of visited states (simple, O(cycle) memory) or Floyd (tortoise-hare, O(1) memory — shown in all 4 languages; the set is the quick-interview default):

def is_happy_com_set(n: int) -> bool:
    def soma_quadrados(x: int) -> int:
        total = 0
        while x:
            x, d = divmod(x, 10)
            total += d * d
        return total
    visitados = set()
    while n != 1 and n not in visitados:
        visitados.add(n)
        n = soma_quadrados(n)
    return n == 1

Tell from the statement: “while not 1 and not in cycle” → cycle + finite state.

Python

class Solution:
    def isHappy(self, n: int) -> bool:
        # Floyd: the sequence ALWAYS cycles (back to a seen state) — if the
        # cycle doesn't contain 1, the number isn't happy.
        def soma_quadrados(x: int) -> int:
            total = 0
            while x:
                x, d = divmod(x, 10)
                total += d * d
            return total

        lento = n
        rapido = n
        while True:
            lento = soma_quadrados(lento)
            rapido = soma_quadrados(soma_quadrados(rapido))
            if rapido == 1:
                return True
            if lento == rapido:
                return False

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn is_happy(n: i32) -> bool {
        fn soma_quadrados(mut x: i32) -> i32 {
            let mut soma = 0;
            while x > 0 {
                let d = x % 10;
                soma += d * d;
                x /= 10;
            }
            soma
        }

        // Floyd: the sequence always cycles; if the cycle has no 1, not happy.
        let (mut lento, mut rapido) = (n, n);
        loop {
            lento = soma_quadrados(lento);
            rapido = soma_quadrados(soma_quadrados(rapido));
            if rapido == 1 {
                return true;
            }
            if lento == rapido {
                return false;
            }
        }
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    bool isHappy(int n) {
        auto soma_quadrados = [](int x) {
            int soma = 0;
            while (x > 0) {
                int d = x % 10;
                soma += d * d;
                x /= 10;
            }
            return soma;
        };
        // Floyd: the sequence always cycles; if the cycle has no 1, not happy.
        int lento = n, rapido = n;
        while (true) {
            lento = soma_quadrados(lento);
            rapido = soma_quadrados(soma_quadrados(rapido));
            if (rapido == 1) return true;
            if (lento == rapido) return false;
        }
    }
};

C

#include <stdbool.h>

static int soma_quadrados(int n) {
    int soma = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        int d = n % 10;
        soma += d * d;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return soma;
}

bool isHappy(int n) {
    /* Floyd: the sequence always cycles; if the cycle has no 1, not happy. */
    int lento = n, rapido = n;
    while (1) {
        lento = soma_quadrados(lento);
        rapido = soma_quadrados(soma_quadrados(rapido));
        if (rapido == 1) return true;
        if (lento == rapido) return false;
    }
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(log n · L) — each soma_quadrados costs O(log n) digits; L is the cycle length (small in practice, which is why the problem accepts both methods).
  • Space: O(1) for Floyd; O(L) for the set (L ≤ ~number of cycle states).

Pitfalls

  • Check rapido == 1 BEFORE lento == rapido in Floyd — for a happy n the two meet at 1; the order avoids a spurious false.
  • n < 10 is not a trivial case: 7 is happy (7 → 49 → 97 → 130 → 10 → 1), 8 is not.
  • Python: a single-loop divmod — no string indexing; no negative % to worry about.
  • Rust/C/C++: the sum never overflows i32 (≤ 10 digits, each square ≤ 81), but the digit loop is while x > 0 — 0 isn’t happy and returns false via the cycle.
  • C: bool needs #include <stdbool.h>; the soma_quadrados helper is static (file scope, no external symbol).

66. Plus One (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/plus-one/ · Topic: Arrays · Math

Problem (summary)

Array of digits representing an integer (most significant first, no leading zeros). Add 1 and return the array.

[1,2,3] → [1,2,4]        [9,9,9] → [1,0,0,0]   (grew a digit)

Pattern — what to memorize

Carry back to front, stopping at the first digit < 9. The +1 only “carries up” while it meets 9 (9+1=10, carry the 1). If the sweep reaches the end without stopping, ALL were 9 — the number becomes 100…0 and the array needs one more digit in front. The 99…9 case is the only one that allocates; otherwise the array is returned as it came (in C, with no allocation at all).

Python

class Solution:
    def plusOne(self, digits: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        # Carry back to front; no carry by the end = all were 9.
        for i in range(len(digits) - 1, -1, -1):
            if digits[i] < 9:
                digits[i] += 1
                return digits
            digits[i] = 0
        return [1] + digits  # 99…9 → 100…0 (allocates one more digit)

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn plus_one(mut digits: Vec<i32>) -> Vec<i32> {
        // Carry back to front; no carry by the end = all were 9.
        for i in (0..digits.len()).rev() {
            if digits[i] < 9 {
                digits[i] += 1;
                return digits;
            }
            digits[i] = 0;
        }
        // 99…9 -> 100…0: allocates one more digit in front.
        let mut nova = vec![0; digits.len() + 1];
        nova[0] = 1;
        nova
    }
}
}

C++

#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> plusOne(vector<int>& digits) {
        // Carry back to front; no carry by the end = all were 9.
        for (int i = (int)digits.size() - 1; i >= 0; --i) {
            if (digits[i] < 9) {
                digits[i]++;
                return digits;
            }
            digits[i] = 0;
        }
        // 99…9 -> 100…0: inserts the 1 in front (O(n), only happens on 99…9).
        digits.insert(digits.begin(), 1);
        return digits;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

int* plusOne(int* digits, int digitsSize, int* returnSize) {
    /* Carry back to front; no carry by the end = all were 9. */
    for (int i = digitsSize - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        if (digits[i] < 9) {
            digits[i]++;
            *returnSize = digitsSize;
            return digits; /* returns the very buffer (no allocation) */
        }
        digits[i] = 0;
    }
    /* 99…9 -> 100…0: allocates one more digit in front. */
    int* resp = (int*)malloc((digitsSize + 1) * sizeof(int));
    resp[0] = 1;
    memset(resp + 1, 0, (size_t)digitsSize * sizeof(int));
    *returnSize = digitsSize + 1;
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) worst case (99…9); O(1) average — most arrays end with a digit < 9 and exit on the first iteration.
  • Space: O(n) only in the 99…9 case (new array); otherwise O(1).

Pitfalls

  • [9] → [1,0] (size 2), but [0] → [1] (size 1) — don’t invent [1,0] for [0].
  • C++: digits.size() - 1 with size_t underflows on an empty array — the (int)digits.size() - 1 cast is deliberate (the statement guarantees ≥ 1 element).
  • C: the return is the same buffer when there’s no carry (avoids a copy); on 99…9 it allocates n+1 and uses memset for the zeros. Who frees? LeetCode frees the return.
  • Python: [1] + digits builds a new list — the C version above is the micro optimization; here clarity wins.
  • Rust: vec![0; len] + nova[0] = 1 — no needless insert(0, …).

50. Pow(x, n) (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/powx-n/ · Topic: Math · Recursion

Problem (summary)

Implement pow(x, n) — x real, n integer (-2³¹ ≤ n ≤ 2³¹−1). No native **/pow.

myPow(2.0, 10) = 1024.0        myPow(2.0, -2) = 0.25

Pattern — what to memorize

Iterative binary exponentiation: for each bit of the exponent, base keeps squaring (x, x², x⁴, x⁸…) and, where the bit is 1, accumulates into the answer. O(log n) multiplications instead of n. Negative exponent: invert the base (x → 1/x) and use |n| — and here’s the mandatory gotcha: n = INT_MIN and |n| overflows i32; the negation must happen in a wider type (long long/i64) BEFORE casting the exponent.

Python

class Solution:
    def myPow(self, x: float, n: int) -> float:
        exp = abs(n)          # Python: arbitrary int, no overflow
        base = x
        resp = 1.0
        while exp:
            if exp & 1:
                resp *= base
            base *= base
            exp >>= 1
        return resp if n >= 0 else 1.0 / resp

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn my_pow(x: f64, n: i32) -> f64 {
        let mut base = x;
        // i64 BEFORE negating: -INT_MIN doesn't fit in i32 (overflow).
        let mut exp = n as i64;
        if exp < 0 {
            base = 1.0 / base;
            exp = -exp;
        }
        let mut resp = 1.0;
        while exp > 0 {
            if exp & 1 == 1 {
                resp *= base;
            }
            base *= base;
            exp >>= 1;
        }
        resp
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    double myPow(double x, int n) {
        // long long BEFORE negating: -INT_MIN doesn't fit in int (overflow).
        long long exp = n;
        double base = x;
        if (exp < 0) {
            base = 1.0 / base;
            exp = -exp;
        }
        double resp = 1.0;
        while (exp > 0) {
            if (exp & 1) resp *= base;
            base *= base;
            exp >>= 1;
        }
        return resp;
    }
};

C

double myPow(double x, int n) {
    /* long long BEFORE negating: -INT_MIN doesn't fit in int (overflow). */
    long long exp = n;
    if (exp < 0) {
        x = 1.0 / x;
        exp = -exp;
    }
    double resp = 1.0;
    while (exp > 0) {
        if (exp & 1) resp *= x;
        x *= x;
        exp >>= 1;
    }
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(log |n|) — one square per bit, one multiplication per 1 bit.
  • Space: O(1) — just base, resp and the exponent (no recursion stack).

Pitfalls

  • -INT_MIN overflows int: long long exp = n (C/C++) / n as i64 (Rust) before exp = -exp — without it, myPow(2.0, INT_MIN) returns 1.0 instead of 0.0 (or loops forever).
  • Python: int is arbitrary precision, no overflow — but keep the same structure (abs(n)) so the code speaks one language across the 4.
  • n = 0 → answer 1.0 (the loop never runs).
  • x = 0 with negative n → 1.0/0.0 = inf (the statement doesn’t test that division).
  • Rust: exp & 1 == 1 needs the parentheses (precedence of ==); f64 has exact equality for powers of 2 in the tests.

43. Multiply Strings (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/multiply-strings/ · Topic: Math · Strings

Problem (summary)

Multiply two non-negative integers given as strings (up to 200 digits) and return the product as a string. The statement forbids BigInt/ eval and converting the whole number into a variable.

"123" × "456" = "56088"        "0" × "9133" = "0"

Pattern — what to memorize

Schoolbook multiplication into an m+n array. The contribution of digit i of num1 times digit j of num2 lands in two places: i+j (tens) and i+j+1 (units). Iterating back to front, the i+j+1 slot has already received the carry from more rightward multiplications — add into the product and spread product % 10 into i+j+1 and product / 10 into i+j. m+n slots suffice because the product of an m-digit by an n-digit number never exceeds m+n digits. Then strip the leading zeros (keeping the "0" case).

Python

class Solution:
    def multiply(self, num1: str, num2: str) -> str:
        if num1 == "0" or num2 == "0":
            return "0"
        m, n = len(num1), len(num2)
        resultado = [0] * (m + n)          # product fits in m+n digits
        for i in range(m - 1, -1, -1):
            for j in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
                # digit d1 of num1 × d2 of num2 lands in i+j and i+j+1;
                # the +resultado[i+j+1] propagates the carry already accrued.
                produto = (ord(num1[i]) - 48) * (ord(num2[j]) - 48) + resultado[i + j + 1]
                resultado[i + j + 1] = produto % 10
                resultado[i + j] += produto // 10
        inicio = 0
        while inicio < len(resultado) and resultado[inicio] == 0:
            inicio += 1                     # strip leading zeros
        return "".join(str(d) for d in resultado[inicio:]) or "0"

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn multiply(num1: String, num2: String) -> String {
        if num1 == "0" || num2 == "0" {
            return "0".to_string();
        }
        let (m, n) = (num1.len(), num2.len());
        let b1 = num1.as_bytes();
        let b2 = num2.as_bytes();
        let mut resultado = vec![0u8; m + n]; // product fits in m+n digits

        for i in (0..m).rev() {
            for j in (0..n).rev() {
                // digit i × digit j lands in i+j and i+j+1; the
                // +resultado[i+j+1] propagates the carry already accrued (we
                // iterate back to front, so the right-hand slot is ready).
                let produto = (b1[i] - b'0') * (b2[j] - b'0') + resultado[i + j + 1];
                resultado[i + j + 1] = produto % 10;
                resultado[i + j] += produto / 10;
            }
        }

        // Strip leading zeros (and never return an empty string).
        let inicio = resultado.iter().position(|&d| d != 0).unwrap_or(resultado.len());
        if inicio == resultado.len() {
            return "0".to_string();
        }
        resultado[inicio..]
            .iter()
            .map(|&d| (b'0' + d) as char)
            .collect()
    }
}
}

C++

#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class Solution {
public:
    string multiply(string num1, string num2) {
        if (num1 == "0" || num2 == "0") return "0";
        int m = num1.size(), n = num2.size();
        vector<int> resultado(m + n, 0); // product fits in m+n digits

        for (int i = m - 1; i >= 0; --i)
            for (int j = n - 1; j >= 0; --j) {
                // digit i × digit j lands in i+j and i+j+1; the
                // +resultado[i+j+1] propagates the carry already accrued.
                int produto = (num1[i] - '0') * (num2[j] - '0') + resultado[i + j + 1];
                resultado[i + j + 1] = produto % 10;
                resultado[i + j] += produto / 10;
            }

        // Strip leading zeros.
        int inicio = 0;
        while (inicio < (int)resultado.size() && resultado[inicio] == 0) ++inicio;

        string resp;
        resp.reserve(resultado.size() - inicio + 1);
        for (int k = inicio; k < (int)resultado.size(); ++k)
            resp.push_back('0' + resultado[k]);
        return resp.empty() ? "0" : resp;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

char* multiply(char* num1, char* num2) {
    if (!strcmp(num1, "0") || !strcmp(num2, "0")) {
        char* zero = (char*)malloc(2);
        zero[0] = '0'; zero[1] = '\0';
        return zero;
    }
    int m = (int)strlen(num1), n = (int)strlen(num2);
    int* resultado = (int*)calloc((size_t)(m + n), sizeof(int));

    for (int i = m - 1; i >= 0; i--)
        for (int j = n - 1; j >= 0; j--) {
            /* digit i × digit j lands in i+j and i+j+1; the
               +resultado[i+j+1] propagates the carry already accrued. */
            int produto = (num1[i] - '0') * (num2[j] - '0') + resultado[i + j + 1];
            resultado[i + j + 1] = produto % 10;
            resultado[i + j] += produto / 10;
        }

    /* Strip leading zeros. */
    int inicio = 0;
    while (inicio < m + n && resultado[inicio] == 0) inicio++;

    char* resp = (char*)malloc((size_t)(m + n - inicio) + 1);
    int k = 0;
    for (int p = inicio; p < m + n; p++)
        resp[k++] = (char)('0' + resultado[p]);
    resp[k] = '\0';

    free(resultado);
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(m·n) — the pair of nested loops over the digits.
  • Space: O(m+n) — the result array (besides the output string).

Pitfalls

  • “0” × anything → “0”: without the early case, the result becomes a string of zeros that the “strip leading zeros” erases completely — and the required return is "0" (never an empty string).
  • The digits come out from units to tens; the string is built from index inicio (first non-zero) onward.
  • Python: "".join(...) (loop concatenation would be O(n²)); ord(c)-48 instead of int(c) in the hot loop.
  • Rust: b1[i] byte indexing is safe — the digits are ASCII; the per-cell product never exceeds 81 + carry (fits u8; produto / 10 keeps each slot < 10).
  • C/C++: inputs are mutable char*/string — read-only; the result array is int/uint8_t; C allocates m+n+1 bytes for the answer and the \0.

2013. Detect Squares (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/detect-squares/ · Topic: Design · Hash Table

Problem (summary)

Structure with two methods: add(point) (inserts a point; duplicates count) and count(point) — how many squares with sides parallel to the axes have point as one vertex, counting each combination of points (duplicates multiply). Coordinates in 0..1000.

add (3,10), (11,2), (3,2)   →   count(11,10) = 1   (square of side 8)

Pattern — what to memorize

Hash map of counts point → number of copies. add is O(1): map[point]++. The count insight: instead of trying all 4 vertices, iterate the existing points as candidates for the OPPOSITE DIAGONAL of the square. If q=(x2,y2) is the opposite diagonal of p=(px,py), the other two corners are determined: (px,y2) and (x2,py) — and the square exists iff |dx| == |dy| (with dx ≠ 0, else zero area). Combinations = count(q) × count(px,y2) × count(x2,py). Since a square has exactly one opposite diagonal per vertex, every square is counted exactly once.

Python

class DetectSquares:
    def __init__(self):
        self.pontos: dict[tuple[int, int], int] = {}

    def add(self, point: list[int]) -> None:
        x, y = point
        self.pontos[(x, y)] = self.pontos.get((x, y), 0) + 1

    def count(self, point: list[int]) -> int:
        px, py = point
        total = 0
        # Every existing point is a candidate for the OPPOSITE DIAGONAL.
        for (x2, y2), contagem in self.pontos.items():
            dx, dy = x2 - px, y2 - py
            if dx == 0 or abs(dx) != abs(dy):
                continue                    # not a diagonal (or zero area)
            # The other two corners are (px, y2) and (x2, py).
            c1 = self.pontos.get((px, y2), 0)
            c2 = self.pontos.get((x2, py), 0)
            total += contagem * c1 * c2
        return total

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::collections::HashMap;

struct DetectSquares {
    pontos: HashMap<(i32, i32), i32>,
}

impl DetectSquares {
    fn new() -> Self {
        DetectSquares {
            pontos: HashMap::new(),
        }
    }

    fn add(&mut self, point: Vec<i32>) {
        *self.pontos.entry((point[0], point[1])).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }

    fn count(&self, point: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
        let (px, py) = (point[0], point[1]);
        let mut total = 0;
        // Every existing point is a candidate for the OPPOSITE DIAGONAL.
        for (&(x2, y2), &contagem) in self.pontos.iter() {
            let (dx, dy) = (x2 - px, y2 - py);
            if dx == 0 || dx.abs() != dy.abs() {
                continue; // not a diagonal (or zero area)
            }
            // The other two corners are (px, y2) and (x2, py).
            let c1 = self.pontos.get(&(px, y2)).copied().unwrap_or(0);
            let c2 = self.pontos.get(&(x2, py)).copied().unwrap_or(0);
            total += contagem * c1 * c2;
        }
        total
    }
}
}

C++

#include <map>
#include <utility>
using namespace std;

class DetectSquares {
    map<pair<int, int>, int> pontos; // point -> count
public:
    DetectSquares() {}

    void add(vector<int> point) {
        pontos[{point[0], point[1]}]++;
    }

    int count(vector<int> point) {
        int px = point[0], py = point[1];
        int total = 0;
        // Every existing point is a candidate for the OPPOSITE DIAGONAL.
        for (auto& [p, contagem] : pontos) {
            int x2 = p.first, y2 = p.second;
            int dx = x2 - px, dy = y2 - py;
            if (dx == 0 || abs(dx) != abs(dy)) continue; // not a diagonal
            // The other two corners are (px, y2) and (x2, py).
            auto it1 = pontos.find({px, y2});
            auto it2 = pontos.find({x2, py});
            if (it1 != pontos.end() && it2 != pontos.end())
                total += contagem * it1->second * it2->second;
        }
        return total;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

#define TAMANHO_GRADE 1001   /* coordinates 0..1000 */
#define CAPACIDADE 3000      /* max nº of distinct points (≤ 3000 calls) */

/* O(1) count grid per point + list of distinct points (so count iterates
   only the existing ones, not the ~1M cells of the grid). */
typedef struct {
    int* contagem;      /* [y * 1001 + x] */
    int* distintos_x;
    int* distintos_y;
    int n_distintos;
} DetectSquares;

DetectSquares* detectSquaresCreate(void) {
    DetectSquares* s = (DetectSquares*)malloc(sizeof(DetectSquares));
    s->contagem = (int*)calloc((size_t)TAMANHO_GRADE * TAMANHO_GRADE, sizeof(int));
    s->distintos_x = (int*)malloc(CAPACIDADE * sizeof(int));
    s->distintos_y = (int*)malloc(CAPACIDADE * sizeof(int));
    s->n_distintos = 0;
    return s;
}

void detectSquaresAdd(DetectSquares* s, int* ponto, int pontoSize) {
    (void)pontoSize;
    int x = ponto[0], y = ponto[1];
    int* contagem = &s->contagem[TAMANHO_GRADE * y + x];
    if (*contagem == 0) { /* first time this point: join the list */
        s->distintos_x[s->n_distintos] = x;
        s->distintos_y[s->n_distintos] = y;
        s->n_distintos++;
    }
    (*contagem)++;
}

int detectSquaresCount(DetectSquares* s, int* ponto, int pontoSize) {
    (void)pontoSize;
    int px = ponto[0], py = ponto[1];
    int total = 0;
    /* Every distinct point is a candidate for the OPPOSITE DIAGONAL. */
    for (int k = 0; k < s->n_distintos; k++) {
        int x2 = s->distintos_x[k], y2 = s->distintos_y[k];
        int dx = x2 - px, dy = y2 - py;
        if (dx == 0 || abs(dx) != abs(dy)) continue; /* not a diagonal */
        /* The other two corners are (px, y2) and (x2, py). */
        int c_diag = s->contagem[TAMANHO_GRADE * y2 + x2];
        int c1 = s->contagem[TAMANHO_GRADE * y2 + px];  /* (px, y2) */
        int c2 = s->contagem[TAMANHO_GRADE * py + x2];  /* (x2, py) */
        total += c_diag * c1 * c2;
    }
    return total;
}

void detectSquaresFree(DetectSquares* s) {
    free(s->contagem);
    free(s->distintos_x);
    free(s->distintos_y);
    free(s);
}

Complexity

  • Time: add O(1) (hash map); count O(n) — iterates the n distinct points.
  • Space: O(n) — the point→count map.

Pitfalls

  • dx != 0: without it, p itself (dx=dy=0) becomes “the diagonal” of itself and counts zero-area squares.
  • Multiplying the counts is what handles duplicates — count sums c_diag·c1·c2, not 1s; adding one more copy of (3,2) doubles the combinations.
  • Iterate distinct points (the map keys), not each copy — count is O(n) with n = distinct, not O(total points).
  • Rust: entry(point).or_insert(0) is the counter idiom; dx.abs().
  • C++: map<pair<int,int>, int> (ordered, no hash boilerplate for pair); use find instead of operator[] during the iteration (don’t insert into the map while iterating — it invalidates the loop).
  • C: no native hash map — the domain is small (1001×1001): a count grid at O(1) per point + a list of distinct points (so count iterates only the existing ones, not the ~1M cells of the grid); capacity = max number of calls.

136. Single Number (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/single-number/ · Topic: Array · Bit Manipulation

Problem (summary)

An array where every element appears twice except one that appears a single time. Find that element, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (the constraint that kills the hash-based solutions).

nums = [2,2,1]         → 1
nums = [4,1,2,1,2]     → 4

Pattern — what to memorize

XOR of all elements. The properties that solve it: x ^ x = 0 (a pair cancels out), x ^ 0 = x (the lone one survives) and XOR is commutative and associative (ORDER doesn’t matter — pairs cancel wherever they are). One pass, constant space, and you don’t even need a counter.

Clue in the statement: everything in pairs, one loner + O(1) space → XOR. The interview-worthy generalization: “one loner and the rest in groups of k” → count bits per position modulo k (see pitfalls).

Python

class Solution:
    def singleNumber(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        unico = 0
        for x in nums:
            unico ^= x  # x^x = 0, x^0 = x: pairs cancel out
        return unico

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn single_number(nums: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
        nums.iter().fold(0, |acc, &x| acc ^ x)
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    int singleNumber(vector<int>& nums) {
        int unico = 0;
        for (int x : nums) unico ^= x; /* x^x = 0, x^0 = x */
        return unico;
    }
};

C

int singleNumber(int* nums, int numsSize) {
    int unico = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < numsSize; i++) unico ^= nums[i];
    return unico;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one pass, each XOR is O(1).
  • Space: O(1) — a single accumulator integer.

Pitfalls

  • Negatives work: XOR is bitwise on two’s complement — -1 ^ -1 == 0 in all four languages; the [-1,-1,5] → 5 test covers it.
  • The initial 0 is the identity element — if the answer is 0, the algorithm correctly returns 0 ([0,0,3] → 3 involves 0 as a pair too).
  • It’s not addition: the naive alternative (sum and find what came out odd) doesn’t exist here — XOR is immune to overflow (Python doesn’t overflow, but C/C++ do; XOR has no such problem anywhere).
  • The k=3 generalization (LC 137): pairs become triples and XOR no longer works. The pattern that WINS is counting bits per position and taking % 3 — worth mentioning in the interview as a follow-up (“what if the rest appeared 3 times?”).

191. Number of 1 Bits (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-1-bits/ · Topic: Bit Manipulation · Divide and Conquer

Problem (summary)

Given a 32-bit unsigned integer (n), return the number of 1 bits in its binary representation (the “popcount”). n is a uint32_t/u32/int from the LeetCode signature.

n = 11  (0b1011)     → 3
n = 128 (0b10000000) → 1
n = 4294967293       → 31

Pattern — what to memorize

Kernighan’s trick: n = n & (n - 1) clears the least significant 1. Each iteration removes exactly one 1 bit — the loop counts until n hits zero and only runs popcount(n) times (better than the fixed 32-iteration loop). Understanding why it works: if bit 0 of n is 1, n-1 just flips it to 0; if it isn’t, the -1 “borrows” through the first 1 to the right, zeroing the borrow — either way n & (n-1) zeroes exactly the rightmost 1.

Clue in the statement: count bits of an integer → bit-by-bit. Valid alternatives to cite: a 32-loop with n & 1/n >>= 1, __builtin_popcount (C/C++), n.count_ones() (Rust) — in an interview, mention that the builtin compiles down to the CPU’s popcnt instruction.

Python

class Solution:
    def hammingWeight(self, n: int) -> int:
        # Kernighan: each iteration clears the least significant 1
        peso = 0
        while n:
            n &= n - 1
            peso += 1
        return peso

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn hamming_weight(n: u32) -> i32 {
        let (mut n, mut peso) = (n, 0);
        while n != 0 {
            n &= n - 1;
            peso += 1;
        }
        peso
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    int hammingWeight(uint32_t n) {
        int peso = 0;
        while (n) {          /* Kernighan: clears the rightmost 1 */
            n &= n - 1;
            peso++;
        }
        return peso;
    }
};

C

#include <stdint.h>

int hammingWeight(uint32_t n) {
    int peso = 0;
    while (n) {
        n &= n - 1;
        peso++;
    }
    return peso;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(k) with k = number of 1 bits (Kernighan) — ≤ 32 in practice; the fixed 32-loop would be O(32) = O(1) too.
  • Space: O(1).

Pitfalls

  • uint32_t/u32 signature: the problem explicitly states unsigned 32 bits. In C/C++, ~0 or n >> 1 on a negative int is UB if you use int — that’s why the signature and the implementation stay on uint32_t/u32.
  • Kernighan on n = 0: the loop never runs → returns 0 (mandatory test).
  • UINT32_MAX: all 32 iterations enter the n & (n-1) → 32. That’s the ceiling, and the 31 from UINT32_MAX - 1 (bit 0 zero) covers the “almost max” case.
  • Python has no bit limit, so n can arrive with unlimited leading zeros — the algorithm counts the real 1s; never apply ~n thinking in 32 bits (it becomes infinite leading 1s).
  • Rust has n.count_ones() and C/C++ have __builtin_popcount — cite them but know how to implement by hand (that’s what the interview asks when the topic is bit manipulation).

338. Counting Bits (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/counting-bits/ · Topic: Dynamic Programming · Bit Manipulation

Problem (summary)

Given an integer n, return an array resp where resp[i] is the number of 1 bits in the binary representation of i, for 0 <= i <= n. LeetCode asks for O(n) — recomputing the popcount of every number from zero is forbidden.

n = 2 → [0,1,1]          (0=00, 1=01, 2=10)
n = 5 → [0,1,1,2,1,2]    (0..5)

Pattern — what to memorize

DP with a bit shift: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1). The popcount of i is the popcount of i/2 (all bits except the least significant one) plus the least significant bit itself:

i    bin        dp[i>>1]   (i&1)   dp[i]
5    101        dp[2]=1     1       2
4    100        dp[2]=1     0       1

It’s a local recurrence (each i depends only on i >> 1, already computed) — that’s why it’s O(n). Two equivalent variants: counting the ranges [2^k, 2^(k+1)) that inherit the bits of [0, 2^k) plus 1 (dp[i] = dp[i - 2^k] + 1 for the largest 2^k <= i) — the same idea seen from another angle.

Clue in the statement: popcount of ALL numbers up to n + O(n) → one recurrence per number, not one popcount per number.

Python

class Solution:
    def countBits(self, n: int) -> list[int]:
        # dp: the least significant bit decides + the shifted remainder
        resp = [0] * (n + 1)
        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            resp[i] = resp[i >> 1] + (i & 1)
        return resp

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn count_bits(n: i32) -> Vec<i32> {
        let mut resp = vec![0; n as usize + 1];
        for i in 1..=n as usize {
            resp[i] = resp[i >> 1] + (i & 1) as i32;
        }
        resp
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> countBits(int n) {
        vector<int> resp(n + 1, 0);
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
            resp[i] = resp[i >> 1] + (i & 1); /* bits(i>>1) + lowest bit */
        return resp;
    }
};

C

#include <stdlib.h>

int* countBits(int n, int* returnSize) {
    *returnSize = n + 1;
    int* resp = malloc((size_t)(n + 1) * sizeof(int));
    resp[0] = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
        resp[i] = resp[i >> 1] + (i & 1);
    return resp;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one sum and one shift per number; no inner popcount.
  • Space: O(1) extra beyond the answer (the resp array of size n+1 is the required output itself).

Pitfalls

  • The recurrence depends on i >> 1 already being computed — the loop must start at i = 1 (and resp[0] = 0 is the base case). Starting at 0 reads resp[-1]/resp[unsigned usize].
  • Rust: vec![0; n as usize + 1] — when n == -1 (never in the problem, 0 <= n <= 10⁵), n as usize becomes a giant value; the cast to usize is safe here because of the range.
  • C: malloc without initialization + explicit resp[0] = 0 — everything else is overwritten by the loop; calloc would also work, just with the cost of zeroing everything.
  • i & 1 comes back as int/usize in C++/Rust: in Rust the sum needs the (i & 1) as i32 cast; in C/C++, the int promotion is automatic.
  • Case n = 0: returns [0] (a size-1 array). It’s the test that malloc(1 * sizeof(int)) usually gets wrong (writing resp[1]).

190. Reverse Bits (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/reverse-bits/ · Topic: Bit Manipulation · Divide and Conquer

Problem (summary)

Given a 32-bit unsigned integer (n), return the integer whose bits are the mirror of n’s bits — bit 0 becomes bit 31, bit 1 becomes bit 30, and so on. (If n were the string "ABCD", the answer would be "DCBA".)

n = 43261596  (0b00000010100101000001111010011100)
  → 964176192 (0b00111001011110000010100101000000)
n = 1         → 2147483648 (0x80000000)

Pattern — what to memorize

Shift and collect, one bit at a time, 32 iterations:

  1. invertido = (invertido << 1) | (n & 1) — “pushes” what was already collected to the left and slots in the current bit 0;
  2. n >>= 1 — discards the consumed bit.

It’s the same “iterate an integer’s bits” skeleton (appears in 191 counting, here reversing). A deeper alternative (divide and conquer, mention verbally): swapping halves in blocks with masks — (n >> 16) | (n << 16), then bytes, nibbles, pairs — solves it in fixed O(1) without a loop; worth mentioning in the interview, but the 32-loop is what you write without errors on the spot.

Clue in the statement: mirror the bits of a 32-bit integer → process bit-by-bit with shift/mask (and the iteration count is constant — the problem has no scalable “input”).

Python

class Solution:
    def reverseBits(self, n: int) -> int:
        invertido = 0
        for _ in range(32):
            invertido = (invertido << 1) | (n & 1)
            n >>= 1
        return invertido

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn reverse_bits(x: u32) -> u32 {
        let (mut n, mut invertido) = (x, 0u32);
        for _ in 0..32 {
            invertido = (invertido << 1) | (n & 1);
            n >>= 1;
        }
        invertido
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    uint32_t reverseBits(uint32_t n) {
        uint32_t invertido = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) {
            invertido = (invertido << 1) | (n & 1u);
            n >>= 1;
        }
        return invertido;
    }
};

C

#include <stdint.h>

uint32_t reverseBits(uint32_t n) {
    uint32_t invertido = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) {
        invertido = (invertido << 1) | (n & 1u);
        n >>= 1;
    }
    return invertido;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(1) — exactly 32 iterations regardless of the value (the 1 with 31 leading zeros costs the same as the maximum).
  • Space: O(1).

Pitfalls

  • Shifting an int with the high bit set is UB in C/C++ — n must be uint32_t (the standard LeetCode signature); in Rust, u32 with >>/<< is always defined.
  • Python doesn’t “have” 32 bits: n arrives as an integer with unlimited leading zeros. The 32-loop + >>= leaves exactly the relevant 32 bits — and (n & 1) never sees “the upper bits” because n >>= 1 discards them. Don’t apply ~n/one-shot masks here.
  • 0xFFFFFFFF is the ceiling case (mirror of itself); 1 → 0x80000000 is the test that catches someone flipping only the present bits (without shifting enough) — and 0xFFFFFFFE → 0x7FFFFFFF covers the opposite boundary.
  • Operator order: (invertido << 1) | (n & 1) — & binds tighter than | in C/C++; in Python, | and & also follow bitwise precedence with << above. Parenthesized, no doubt.

268. Missing Number (Easy)

https://leetcode.com/problems/missing-number/ · Topic: Array · Hash Table · Math · Bit Manipulation

Problem (summary)

An array of n distinct integers taken from {0, 1, 2, ..., n} — in other words, exactly one number of the range is missing. Find the missing one. The constraints demand O(1) extra space.

nums = [3,0,1]                        → 2
nums = [9,6,4,2,3,5,7,0,1]            → 8
nums = [0]                            → 1

Pattern — what to memorize

XOR of index with value: falta = n, then falta ^= i ^ nums[i] for every i. The XOR of the indices 0..n-1 plus the initial n forms exactly every number of the range {0..n}; XORing with the values cancels (pairwise) the ones that exist — what’s left is the missing one. A single accumulator, no hash, no overflow.

The two alternatives worth CITING in the interview:

  • Gauss sum: n(n+1)/2 - sum(nums) — O(n)/O(1), BUT in C/C++ it overflows int with n near 2·10⁹ (use long long — that’s why the 0LL in accumulate);
  • Sort — O(n log n), ruled out by the space (and time) constraint.

Clue in the statement: range 0..n, one missing → XOR index ↔ value (or interval sum). XOR wins because it doesn’t depend on integer size.

Python

class Solution:
    def missingNumber(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        # xor(indices) ^ xor(values): whatever remains is the missing one.
        falta = len(nums)
        for i, x in enumerate(nums):
            falta ^= i ^ x
        return falta

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn missing_number(nums: Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
        let mut falta = nums.len() as i32;
        for (i, &x) in nums.iter().enumerate() {
            falta ^= i as i32 ^ x;
        }
        falta
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    int missingNumber(vector<int>& nums) {
        int falta = (int)nums.size();
        for (int i = 0; i < (int)nums.size(); i++)
            falta ^= i ^ nums[i];
        return falta;
    }
};

C

int missingNumber(int* nums, int numsSize) {
    int falta = numsSize;
    for (int i = 0; i < numsSize; i++) falta ^= i ^ nums[i];
    return falta;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(n) — one pass.
  • Space: O(1) — a single accumulator.

Pitfalls

  • The XOR of the “index n” (the number that sits in no array position) is what closes the range: initialize with len(nums)/numsSize, not with 0 — otherwise [1] → 0 (wrong; the right answer is the missing 0… check: [1] → 0 ^ 1 ^ 1 = 0 ✓ with the initial n = 1 — with an initial 0 you get 0 ^ 0 ^ 1 = 1, wrong).
  • Gauss sum overflows: the statement allows n up to 2·10⁹ — a 32-bit int doesn’t hold n(n+1)/2. If you cite the sum, say long long/i64 (and accumulate’s 0LL); with XOR this is irrelevant by construction.
  • i vs nums[i] order: XOR’s associativity allows falta ^= i ^ nums[i] in one go; whoever splits the loops (^= all the is, then ^= all the values) also works — what does NOT work is forgetting the i (equivalent to pairing values with themselves → gives 0).
  • It’s not 191/338: here the XOR is over VALUES, not over the bits of a single number — don’t confuse the pattern with popcount.

371. Sum of Two Integers (Medium)

https://leetcode.com/problems/sum-of-two-integers/ · Topic: Math · Bit Manipulation

Problem (summary)

Given two integers a and b, return their sum without using the + and - operators. Only bitwise (&, |, ^, <<, >>) and loops.

a = 1,  b = 2   → 3
a = 2,  b = 3   → 5
a = -2, b = 3   → 1
a = -1, b = -1  → -2

Pattern — what to memorize

Bit-by-bit addition with carry in a loop:

  • a ^ b adds the bits WITHOUT considering the carry (“add without carry”);
  • (a & b) << 1 computes where there’s a carry into the next place (“carry”);
  • repeat with a = xor, b = carry until the carry reaches zero.
  a=5  b=3     xor      &     carry
  101  011     110      001   010
  110  010     100      010   100
  100  100     000      100  1000
  000 1000    1000      000   0000 → 8 ✓

The universal gotcha: 32-bit (or n-bit) arithmetic runs circularly — integers are two’s complement and the “ceiling” overflows back around. So:

  • Python has no natural overflow: a & 0xFFFFFFFF mask at each step simulates 32 bits, and the end converts back to signed;
  • C/C++ must work on unsigned int (shifting a negative signed is UB and the sign bit participates in the math);
  • Rust can use u32 with a final cast to i32 (WASM/CPU only see the bits).

Clue in the statement: add without + → think of the half-adder (xor + carry) from the digital electronics course.

Python

class Solution:
    def getSum(self, a: int, b: int) -> int:
        MASCARA = 0xFFFFFFFF          # Python has no overflow: simulate 32 bits
        while b:
            a, b = (a ^ b) & MASCARA, ((a & b) << 1) & MASCARA
        # convert the 32-bit unsigned result back to signed
        return a if a <= 0x7FFFFFFF else a - 0x100000000

Rust

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
impl Solution {
    pub fn get_sum(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
        // u32 keeps the math explicitly in 32 bits; i32<->u32 casts are
        // reinterpretations (two's complement), not value conversions.
        let (mut a, mut b) = (a as u32, b as u32);
        while b != 0 {
            let carry = (a & b) << 1; // bits that need to move left
            a ^= b;                  // add without carry
            b = carry;
        }
        a as i32
    }
}
}

C++

class Solution {
public:
    int getSum(int a, int b) {
        /* unsigned: shifting 'signed' data with the high bit set is UB in C++ */
        unsigned x = (unsigned)a, y = (unsigned)b;
        while (y) {
            unsigned carry = (x & y) << 1;
            x ^= y;
            y = carry;
        }
        return (int)x;
    }
};

C

int getSum(int a, int b) {
    unsigned x = (unsigned)a, y = (unsigned)b;
    while (y) {
        unsigned carry = (x & y) << 1; /* bits that need to move left */
        x ^= y;                        /* add without carry */
        y = carry;
    }
    return (int)x;
}

Complexity

  • Time: O(1) — worst case, a carry travels 32 places; the loop runs at most 32 iterations (constant).
  • Space: O(1).

Pitfalls

  • The 0xFFFFFFFF mask in Python is MANDATORY (the statement’s note): without it, a ^ b and the carry grow bits infinitely to the left (Python ints are arbitrary-precision) and the loop never zeroes the carry. The mask at each step simulates the 32-bit wrap; the final a - 0x100000000 returns the signed value (bit 31 set = negative).
  • C/C++: unsigned as the rule — (x & y) << 1 on an int with the high bit set is undefined behavior (shift of a negative); with unsigned it’s always defined. The -1 + -1 test is what exposes it.
  • Rust: shifting an i32 is defined (not UB like in C), but working with u32 keeps the “32 bits” invariant explicit — and (a & b) << 1 on i32 would also work; the u32/i32 cast is a reinterpretation, so 0xFFFFFFFF as i32 == -1. No wrapping_* needed with u32.
  • The carry’s << 1 can “spill” past the 32nd place — that’s exactly what should happen (the bit-31 carry disappears in the wrap); on unsigned values it’s discarded and the loop ends.
  • Case a == 0 or b == 0: the loop never runs (binary) — it returns the other number; a mandatory test (0 + 0 and 0 + x).

Review card

  • R1 (+1d) · [ ] R2 (+3d) · [ ] R3 (+7d, another language) · [ ] R4 (+21d) · [ ] R5 (+60d)

System Design — the 45-minute method

For a 5-year-experience profile, this is the round that decides. The template below is the skeleton of EVERY answer — drill it until it’s automatic.

The interview clock

PhaseTimeWhat to do
1. Requirements5–8 minAsk! Functional, non-functional, scale
2. Estimates3–5 minQPS, storage, bandwidth — back-of-the-napkin math
3. API + data5 minMinimal endpoints and tables
4. High level8–10 minBox-by-box diagram, justifying each box
5. Deep dive12–15 minWhere the offer is won: the bottleneck they pick
6. Trade-offs3–5 minWhat breaks, what you’d sacrifice, what you’d do with 10× more time

Phase 1 — questions that score points

  • How many active users? Read/write ratio?
  • Target latency? Availability (99.9%? 99.99%)?
  • Consistency or availability when you can’t have both? (CAP in practice)
  • Expected growth? Geo-distributed?

Never start by drawing. Whoever asks questions first draws better.

Phase 2 — napkin numbers (memorize)

Average QPS           = ops/day ÷ 86,400  (≈ 100k/day = ~1 QPS)
Peak                  ≈ 2–5× the average
1 year                ≈ 32 million seconds (π × 10⁷)
SSD random read       ~100 µs     RAM            ~100 ns
1 Gbps                ~125 MB/s   intra-DC round-trip ~0.5 ms
Transatlantic         ~150 ms     Redis cache hit ~1 ms
Sequential disk       ~30 MB/s (HDD) / ~500 MB/s (SSD)

Availability table: 99% = 3.65 days/yr of downtime · 99.9% = 8.8 h · 99.99% = 52 min · 99.999% = 5 min.

Phase 4 — the standard toolbox

Components that show up in 90% of designs (and the one-liner that justifies each):

  • Load balancer — “state lives outside the machine; any instance can serve”
  • Cache (Redis) — “hot reads never touch the DB; TTL + invalidation”
  • CDN — “static and media close to the user”
  • Queue (Kafka/SQS) — “decouple the write spike from consumption; retry”
  • Sharding — “horizontal partition by key; consistent hashing to rebalance without downtime”
  • Replication — “1 leader writes, N replicas read; failover and geo read”
  • Database — SQL (consistency, transactions) vs NoSQL (write scale, flexible schema) — justify the choice, never by taste

Mistakes that fail the interview

  1. Starting with the diagram, before requirements.
  2. Drawing boxes without saying WHY they exist.
  3. “I’ll add a Redis” with no invalidation/TTL policy.
  4. Ignoring the single point of failure you drew yourself.
  5. Monologue: system design is dialogue — check in at every phase (“am I making sense so far? which part do you want to go deeper on?”).
  6. Throwing out a number with no math to back it up.

How to drill with this book

1 problem/week (a dedicated page here in the book), timed, narrated out loud. Then compare with the model page. Review rotation: +7d and +30d (review card at the end of every page).

URL Shortener (TinyURL)

Category: key-value at scale · The classic of classics — almost every design interview starts with this or passes through it.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Shorten a long URL → short alias (e.g. ab3Xk9)
  • Redirect alias → original URL
  • Optional custom alias; optional expiration

Non-functional (with the interviewer):

  • Very heavy reads, moderate writes (ratio ~100:1)
  • Minimal redirect latency (every ms costs conversion)
  • High availability (dead link = broken product)
  • Aliases unique — collisions are unacceptable

Estimates (back-of-the-napkin):

  • 100 M new links/year → ~1,000 writes/s average, peak ~5,000/s
  • 100:1 → ~100,000 reads/s average, peak ~500,000/s
  • Record ~500 B → 100 M × 5 years ≈ 250 GB (fits in a SQL cluster; shard for convenience, not out of desperation)
  • Alias: base62 with 7 chars = 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion — plenty of headroom

2. API + data model

POST /api/shorten   { "url": "...", "custom": "abc"?, "expires_at": ts? }
                    → { "alias": "ab3Xk9", "short_url": "https://krl.ink/ab3Xk9" }
GET  /{alias}       → 302 Location: <original_url>

CREATE TABLE links (
  alias      TEXT PRIMARY KEY,   -- shard key
  url        TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
  expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL,
  clicks     BIGINT              -- async update (queue), never on the hot path
);

302 vs 301: 301 gets cached by the browser (less load, no analytics); 302 always passes through the server — that’s the choice when clicks matter (and interviewers love this trade-off).

3. High level

client → CDN (page/static)
   │
   ▼ GET /{alias}
Load Balancer → redirect servers (stateless, N instances)
   │                    │ miss
   ▼ hit                ▼
Cache Redis (LRU, hot aliases)      Sharded DB (alias → record)
                                        ▲
POST /shorten → LB → shorten service → ID generator (KGS) → DB
                          └→ clicks queue → analytics workers

Why each box: LB (state lives outside the machine), Redis (100:1 reads — hot keys never touch disk), shard (250 GB + 100k reads/s), KGS (alias generation with no collisions and no hot spot), queue (analytics off the redirect hot path).

4. Deep dive

a) Alias generation — the heart

Options and why KGS wins:

  1. Hash the URL (md5/murmur) + base62 + truncate: collisions need detection and retry; different URLs → different aliases for the same destination (duplicates).
  2. Global counter + base62: simple and collision-free, but a single counter = bottleneck/SPOF (you can shard the counter by range).
  3. Key Generation Service (KGS): servers pre-generate batches of unused random aliases and keep two pools: used and unused. Shorten takes a ready-made alias from the pool (O(1), no collision, no upfront query). Low pool → reload async. That’s the senior answer: it moves the problem off the hot path into a pre-computation.

base62: [0-9a-zA-Z]; convert id/random → 7-char string. Custom aliases check uniqueness at write time (SELECT ... ON CONFLICT).

b) Cache

  • LRU with TTL (e.g., 24 h) per alias; hot keys (viral campaign) = 1% of links driving 50% of clicks → high hit ratio with modest memory.
  • Invalidation: link expiration → event invalidates the key (pub/sub, or double-check the DB when expires_at exists).

c) Partitioning

  • Shard by alias (the lookup key — never by original URL, which isn’t in the redirect query).
  • Hash alias → shard; since aliases are random (KGS), distribution is uniform — no structural hot shard.
  • Replica per shard for reads + leader failover.

5. Trade-offs and bottlenecks

  • Breaks first: Redis (memory) and redirect bandwidth on a viral spike → mitigation: aggressive TTL, CDN edge-redirect for mega-hot aliases.
  • Conscious sacrifice: 302 (analytics) costs more load than 301; eventual consistency on click counters (queue) — nobody needs exact real-time clicks.
  • With 10× more time: URL dedupe (same destination → same alias, via indexed hash), abuse/malicious-shortener prevention (blocklist + rate limit per API key), geo-replication of redirects.
  • Common bonus question: “what if KGS hands out an alias that expired and was reused?” → expired aliases return to the pool only after a confirmed purge.

Review card

  • Narrated out loud, timed (45 min) · [ ] R1 (+7d) · [ ] R2 (+30d)

Rate Limiter

Category: resilience / edge · Difficulty: classic — the opening question of practically every platform interview. Master the algorithm table and the “where to put it” before drawing a single box.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Limit requests per client (IP, API key, authenticated user) within a time window
  • Exceeded → 429 Too Many Requests with headers that teach the client to behave (Retry-After)
  • Per-plan policy: free 10 req/s, pro 100 req/s (limit per key)
  • Optional: per-endpoint weights (login stricter than profile GET)

Non-functional:

  • Decision overhead < 1 ms; small memory per key
  • Distributed: N instances behind the LB enforce the SAME policy — the limit belongs to the client, not the instance (10 instances ≠ limit × 10)
  • Fail-soft of the limiter itself: if the decision source (Redis) dies, you explicitly choose pass (fail-open) or block (fail-closed)
  • Availability of the protected services: the limiter exists to protect, not to be a bigger SPOF than what it protects

Estimates (back-of-the-napkin):

  • 10 M active users, 30% active per day = 3 M DAU × 200 reqs/day = 600 M reqs/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ ~7,000 req/s average, peak 2–5× ≈ 35,000 req/s
  • Token bucket per key ≈ 40 B (2 numbers: tokens + last refill) → 10 M keys ≈ 400 MB — fits in a modest Redis, no drama
  • Latency: local in-memory decision ~µs; via Redis +1 intra-DC round-trip ~0.5–1 ms — within the gateway budget (which already has ~10 ms of slack)

2. API + data model

429 Too Many Requests
  body:   {"error":"rate limit exceeded"}
  headers: RateLimit-Limit: 100
           RateLimit-Remaining: 0
           RateLimit-Reset: 1737043200      (epoch seconds: when it resets)
           Retry-After: 8                   (RFC 6585 — HOW LONG to wait)

Storage in Redis (per client → key rl:{id}:...):

AlgorithmStructureCost per reqMemory per key
Token bucket2 numbers (tokens, last refill)O(1)fixed (~40 B)
Fixed windowINCR + TTLO(1)1 counter
Sliding window (log)ZSET of timestampsO(log n)∝ reqs in window
Sliding window (counter)2 counters + fractionO(1)2 counters

3. High level

clients → CDN/WAF → API Gateway (edge) ──► internal services
                     │
                     │  rate limiter middleware (on every gateway node)
                     ▼
              Redis (single, distributed decision)
  • Edge/gateway: the limiter lives AT THE EDGE — it blocks before traffic consumes auth, DB, or bandwidth of internal services (first trench against abuse/application DDoS).
  • Middleware on every node: every gateway applies the same policy by reading Redis — the decision belongs to the cluster, not the instance.
  • Redis: central key state; one request → one INCR/EVAL; the server serializes commands (single-threaded) — no race between nodes.
  • Library (alternative): an in-app limiter gives per-endpoint policy and avoids the round-trip, but every instance replicates state — it only works with per-client stickiness or if multiplying the limit by N is acceptable. The senior answer starts at the edge and cites the library as a variant when the requirement is “per-endpoint with minimum latency”.

4. Deep dive

a) The algorithm table — token bucket vs fixed vs sliding window

AlgorithmBurst at window edge?CostWhen to use
Token bucketallows burst up to capacity, average = rate rO(1), fixed memorygold standard (Stripe, Apigee)
Fixed windowyes, the classic: limit 10/min → 9 at 10:59 + 10 at 11:00 = 19 in 2 minO(1) INCRcoarse floodgate; 2× tolerance OK
Sliding window (log)no, exactO(log n) ZADD; memory ∝ reqs in windowwhen the edge can’t lie
Sliding window (counter)approximate (weights 2 fixed windows)O(1)“good enough” exactness at fixed-window price

Token bucket is the default because bursts are legitimate behavior (the user came back from coffee and hit refresh 5×) and the per-key cost is fixed — one counter and one clock, refill computed from time delta:

import time

class TokenBucket:
    """Burst up to `capacity`, average `rate_per_second`. Lazy refill:
    computes how much charged since the last call — no per-req timestamps."""

    def __init__(self, capacity: int, rate_per_second: float):
        self.capacity = float(capacity)
        self.rate = rate_per_second
        self._tokens = self.capacity
        self._last = time.monotonic()

    def allow(self, cost: float = 1.0) -> bool:
        now = time.monotonic()
        # lazy refill: min(capacity, balance + elapsed × rate)
        self._tokens = min(self.capacity, self._tokens + (now - self._last) * self.rate)
        self._last = now
        if self._tokens < cost:
            return False
        self._tokens -= cost
        return True

b) Redis + Lua — atomicity that’s non-negotiable

The decision is check-then-act: “already over? no → increment”. In two Redis calls (GET + INCR), N gateways pass together: two read “2 left”, both let through, and the counter hits 4. The fix is a Lua script executed inside Redis (EVAL) — the server’s single thread guarantees that check-and-add is one atomic operation:

-- Atomic fixed window (tested against Redis 8.8 on a throwaway instance:
-- limit 3 → responses 1,1,1,0,0; 60 s TTL set on the 1st INCR and NOT
-- reset by the following ones).
-- KEYS[1] = counter key (e.g., "rl:{client}:{window}")
-- ARGV[1] = limit  ·  ARGV[2] = window in seconds
local current = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if current == 1 then
    redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], tonumber(ARGV[2]))
end
if current > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then
    return 0        -- blocked
end
return 1            -- allowed

Exact sliding window with the same philosophy, using ZSET (prune → count → decide):

-- KEYS[1] ZSET key · ARGV[1] current timestamp · ARGV[2] window s
-- ARGV[3] limit · ARGV[4] unique request id (member; never repeats)
local now, window, limit = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]), tonumber(ARGV[3])
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], '-inf', now - window)
if redis.call('ZCARD', KEYS[1]) >= limit then
    return 0
end
redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], now, ARGV[4])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], window)
return 1

(Tested: limit 3 / window 10 → t0, t1, t2 allowed, t3 blocked; t11, t12, t13 free up as the old ones expire, t14 blocks again.)

c) Distributed vs per-instance — and Redis failing

  • Per-instance (local memory): ~µs decision, zero RTT — but N instances = N × the limit. Mitigation: hash client → fixed instance (loses balancing, creates a hot node, and when the node dies the limit “resets”).
  • Central (Redis): truly consistent (1 RTT ~1 ms per decision — fine up to ~100k decisions/s per Redis instance; beyond that, cluster by key hash). It’s the choice when requirement 2 (“same policy across the cluster”) is explicit — and at the edge it’s the norm.
  • Redis down? Explicit decision: fail-open (let through + alarm) is the platform default — a limiter that takes the product down is worse than occasional abuse; fail-closed only when the requirement is hard security (e.g., a password endpoint under attack). State the rule and the why before drawing.
  • 429 and the ecosystem: the junior dev who took down the upstream doesn’t blame the limiter — they blame the retry. An informed Retry-After header that the client honors (with jitter) turns 429 into a signal of cooperation, not an error.

5. Trade-offs and bottlenecks

  • Breaks first: Redis (latency + SPOF → replica + fail-open) and, in sliding log, memory ∝ reqs in window on a spike (35k req/s × a 60 s log = millions of members — watch the ZSET).
  • Conscious sacrifice: token bucket instead of exactness (accepts a short edge burst); a 429 without category distinction (a login 429 and a GET 429 weigh the same — counting 5xx and logins double comes later).
  • With 10× more time: cost-based limiting (per-endpoint weight), GCRA (token bucket without a per-key counter), per-account limits with per-IP fallback (a corporate NAT shouldn’t pay the price for one user), Redis clustering (failover + shard by key hash), and WAF integration for the coarse edge (DDoS) — the app limiter is the fine edge.
  • Common bonus question: “same client on 3 devices?” → limit per account (key rl:account:{id}), not per device; IP as an extra security layer against stolen accounts.

Review card

  • Narrated out loud, timed (45 min) · [ ] R1 (+7d) · [ ] R2 (+30d)

Chat / WhatsApp

Category: real-time messaging · Difficulty: advanced — the trial by fire of someone who has run a serious system. The words that need to come out of your mouth: per-conversation sequence, store-and-forward, group fan-out, receipts, presence — each with its why.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • 1:1 and group messages (up to ~1k members), delivered in ~100–300 ms when the recipient is online
  • Presence: “online now” and “last seen”
  • Order preserved PER CONVERSATION — everyone sees the same sequence
  • Offline → gets everything on reconnect (store-and-forward), nothing lost, nothing duplicated, in order
  • Receipts: ✓ delivered / ✓✓ read
  • E2E encryption: only the endpoints read; the server carries ciphertext
  • Optional: “typing…”, media (photo/audio), push to the phone

Non-functional:

  • Heavy write scale (~1:1 with reads — rare; social networks are 100:1, chat is the inverse)
  • Online latency < 300 ms; durability: an acknowledged message doesn’t disappear
  • Availability > 99.9% — a dead chat is a dead product
  • Consistency: exactly-once delivery + per-conversation order (neither global nor causal)

Estimates (back-of-the-napkin):

  • 500 M DAU × 40 msgs/day = 20 B msgs/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ ~230k msg/s average, peak 2–3× ≈ 500k/s
  • 1 KB per message with overhead → 20 B × 1 KB ≈ 20 TB/day ≈ 7 PB/year → sharding mandatory (with retention, 5 years ≈ 35 PB)
  • Concurrent connections: 10% of DAU active = 50 M WebSockets ≈ 20 KB per connection = ~1 TB of connection state on the gateways (50–200 nodes)
  • Group fan-out: mean 50 members; pure on-write → 230k × 50 ≈ 11.5 M deliveries/s — the single number that kills on-write for large groups

2. API + data model

WebSocket for the real-time flow + REST for catch-up:

WS  → {type:"msg", conversation_id, text, client_seq}
WS  ← {type:"ack",  conversation_id, server_seq}       # server assigned order
WS  → {type:"receipt", conversation_id, server_seq, type:"read"}
GET /conversations/{id}/messages?after_seq=N           # reconnect / history
POST /conversations/{id}/media                         # upload (metadata in DB)

conversations(id, type '1:1'|'group', created_at)
members(conversation_id, user_id, PK(conversation_id, user_id))
messages(conversation_id, server_seq, sender_id, text, created_at,
         PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, server_seq))    -- shard PER conversation
deliveries(conversation_id, server_seq, user_id, delivered_at, read_at,
         PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, server_seq, user_id))   -- receipts
presence(user_id PK, status, last_seen_at)             -- in Redis (TTL)
  • server_seq is the server’s, never the client’s: assigned by the conversation’s single writer (its shard) — that makes order comparable across clients. The client’s client_seq is only for dedupe (double send).
  • The PK (conversation_id, server_seq) makes redelivery idempotent: same seq → error/upsert, never a duplicated message.

3. High level

client → edge WS gateway (sticky) ──► messaging service (stateless)
   ▲                                      │  validates and assigns server_seq
   └───── delivery (WS/push) ←────────────┤
                                          ▼
                              delivery / notification queue
                                          │
                                          ▼
                     per-conversation sharded DB (messages, deliveries)
                                          ▲
                              fan-out workers (groups)
   Redis: presence (TTL), hot conversation cache, per-conversation seq
   counter (write-only counter — the real seq lives on the shard)
  • Sticky WS gateway: a connection has state (the thread writing to the socket); reconnect lands on the same node via L7 — socket state stays out of the services.
  • Messaging service: no connection state — scales horizontally; it’s the one that validates, orders, and writes.
  • Delivery queue: decouples the write spike (230k/s) from delivery to the recipient; it’s the store-and-forward and push channel.
  • Per-conversation sharded DB: all messages of one conversation on a single shard → order is a trivial ORDER BY server_seq, and the seq is born there.
  • Redis: presence and hot cache; never the owner of order truth.

4. Deep dive

a) Ordering: a sequence PER conversation, not global

The real requirement: “everyone sees the same order in that conversation”. So the clock is per conversation — a monotonic counter assigned by that conversation’s single writer (its shard). Why not:

  • Client timestamp: clocks lie, merges get random order.
  • Global seq: doesn’t scale (a single counter = bottleneck) and is pointless — a message in conversation A doesn’t compete with one in B.
  • Seq per (sender, conversation): only good for local dedupe; it doesn’t order both sides.

On reconnect, the client asks after_seq=N and receives in ascending order; the client renders in server_seq order, not in WebSocket arrival order (which network retries can shuffle).

# The rule in 20 lines (tested): server assigns per-conversation seq; offline
# lands in the mailbox (store-and-forward); reconnect delivers in order;
# receipts track delivery/read per (conversation, user).
class ChatSimulator:
    def __init__(self):
        self.next_seq = {}
        self.mailboxes = {}            # (conversation, user) -> [(seq, text)]
        self.last_delivered = {}
        self.last_read = {}

    def send(self, conversation: str, text: str, b_online: bool) -> int:
        seq = self.next_seq.get(conversation, 0) + 1     # single writer per conversation
        self.next_seq[conversation] = seq
        key = (conversation, "B")
        if b_online:
            self.last_delivered[key] = seq
        else:
            self.mailboxes.setdefault(key, []).append((seq, text))
        return seq

    def reconnect(self, conversation: str):
        key = (conversation, "B")
        pending = self.mailboxes.pop(key, [])
        for seq, _ in pending:                     # order = seq order
            self.last_delivered[key] = seq
        return pending

    def mark_read(self, conversation: str, seq: int):
        self.last_read[(conversation, "B")] = seq

b) Group fan-out: write vs read (the number decides)

  • On-write (copy per recipient): write the post into each member’s “mailbox” → reads are O(1). Write cost = O(members): 230k × 50 ≈ 11.5 M writes/s, even 100% async, heats the DB.
  • On-read (1 copy + pull): the message is single; each member fetches/is notified when they open. Writes O(1), reads O(members who pulled).
  • Hybrid by threshold — the senior answer:
    • groups ≤ ~100 members → on-write (materialized per-member mailbox, instant reads);
    • large groups (10k+; WhatsApp’s case) → on-read: single header + pointer to the message; the member pulls the body when opening.
    • The napkin becomes the criterion: state the threshold and show the math.
  • Receipts in a group: write into deliveries per member (asymmetric — an honest consequence; batch per read session).

c) Store-and-forward, receipts, presence, and E2E

  • Offline: the message (already stamped with server_seq) goes to the mailbox; when the recipient reconnects, GET ...?after_seq=N pulls everything in order — and N comes from the last persisted delivered seq, not from memory.
  • Receipts: client ack → delivered_at; opening the conversation → read_at. One row per (conversation, seq, user) — volume grows with member count and partitions with the conversation. A batched “read” marks the whole range (<= seq N), not a thousand rows.
  • Presence: WebSocket heartbeat (~30 s) refreshes Redis with TTL; “last seen” = last heartbeat. Simple, precise enough.
  • Push: a phone without a socket → APNs/FCM with “new message”; the real body only comes via encrypted pull.
  • E2E (high level, no cryptography in the interview): WhatsApp uses the Signal protocol — a per-pair session with a key ratchet; for groups, a shared sender-key among members. The point you make: the server carries ciphertext and can’t read the content — so it can’t index text, search, or anti-spam the body (search is encrypted on the device). The architectural price: fan-out, shard, and cache orchestration operate on metadata (sender, conversation, seq), never on content.

d) Sharding conversations

  • Shard by conversation_id — the key of ALL hot queries (messages WHERE conversation_id). A 1:1 can be a deterministic conversation id = min(a,b)_max(a,b) → find the shard with no extra index.
  • The seq counter lives only on the conversation shard’s leader (transactional): per-conversation sharding gives strong local order without paying for global ordering.
  • A giant group is the hot shard: the on-read from item (b) already relieves the writes — without it, a 100k group takes down its node.
  • Geo: shard by conversing region (a message doesn’t cross an ocean to be saved); rebalance with consistent hashing.

5. Trade-offs and bottlenecks

  • Breaks first: the WS gateways (state + 50 M connections; a node dies → mass reconnection on the neighbor) and the message DB on writes (230k/s
    • receipts).
  • Conscious sacrifice: strong per-conversation order = single writer per shard (conversation writes serialize — fine, an individual conversation writes little); durability by batch (fsync every 1–2 s → only what’s in the persisted log is “acknowledged”; ack-after-durable).
  • Sticky vs stateless gateway: a WS connection is long-lived and has state → sticky; the price is non-transparent failover: fast reconnect + history pull (the after_seq from item (c) solves it — losing the node loses the socket, not the message).
  • With 10× more time: message search (local encrypted index), media on CDN with direct signed-URL upload (keeps bytes out of the messaging server), “typing…” (ephemeral channel, nothing persisted), voice calls (WebRTC, signaling over the messaging path), reactions (a small third table beside deliveries), status (a 1:N message of the account itself).
  • Common bonus question: “same user on 2 devices?” → each device has its own delivery/receipt queue; the conversation seq is single and devices sync their after_seq pointer.

Review card

  • Narrated out loud, timed (45 min) · [ ] R1 (+7d) · [ ] R2 (+30d)

News Feed

Category: fan-out / social graph · Difficulty: classic — the feed question is to social what TinyURL is to key-value: the interviewer wants to hear your fan-out reasoning with the number on the tip of your tongue.

1. Requirements

Functional:

  • Feed with posts from people you follow, newest first (recency; simple ranking is a later evolution)
  • Publish a post; follow/unfollow; infinite pagination (scroll)
  • Out of scope for the 1st iteration: comments, reactions, ads, algorithm

Non-functional:

  • Very heavy reads (the feed is the product’s hottest path — every user opens it 10–20×/day); light writes (1–2 posts/day)
  • Feed-open latency < 500 ms
  • Eventual consistency acceptable: a published post may take seconds to reach feeds; the post itself needs immediate durability
  • Availability > 99.9% — a wall of shame on the home page is brand damage

Estimates (back-of-the-napkin):

  • 200 M DAU × 10 feed loads/day = 2 B loads/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ ~23k loads/s average, peak 2–3× ≈ 70k/s (each load returns ~100–200 posts → 2–4 M cache reads/s)
  • Posts: 200 M × 2/day = 400 M/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 4.6k posts/s of writes
  • Materialized feed: 200 M users × 100 ids × 8 B ≈ 160 GB in Redis (cluster, 24 h TTL)
  • On-write fan-out: 4.6k/s × mean 200 followers ≈ ~1 M feed-writes/s async — and a celebrity with 10 M followers is 10 M writes for a single post: the number that kills pure on-write

2. API + data model

POST /posts                    {text, media_uri?}         → {post_id}
GET  /feed?cursor=<opaque>&limit=20
                              → {posts: [{id, author, text, created_at}],
                                 next_cursor}
POST/DELETE /users/{id}/follow

users(id, name)
posts(id BIGINT UNIQUE, author_id, text, created_at)   -- shard by id
followers(follower_id, followed_id,
          PK (follower_id, followed_id))               -- shard by follower
-- materialized feed (Redis in practice; the SQL is the design):
feed_cache(user_id, post_id, score,
           PK (user_id, post_id))                      -- shard by user

A monotonic post_id (snowflake: time + node + seq) is what makes the feed sortable and the cursor trivial — uuid v4 doesn’t order, and order is the requirement.

3. High level

client → LB → feed service (stateless)
                 │
        feed cache (Redis: pages of post-ids per user)
                 │ miss
                 ▼
          posts/followers service → sharded DB
                 ▲
          fan-out queue → feed-materializing workers
  • Feed service: assembles the page from the cache; on a miss, queries the post/followers services and refills.
  • Redis: every user has their own list of post-ids (the page is pre-resolved — hot reads never touch the DB).
  • Fan-out queue + workers: the fan-out write spike must not stall publishing; process in batches and in order.
  • Sharded DB: posts and the follower graph are the durable truth; shard by post_id/follower_id for each load’s queries.

4. Deep dive

a) Fan-out: on-write vs on-read vs hybrid (the heart)

  • On-write: the published post goes to a queue; a worker copies the post_id into the feed_cache of every follower. Read = 1 Redis lookup (fast as hell). Write = O(followers) — and a 10 M celebrity blows up the queue and Redis on a single post.
  • On-read: nothing is materialized; on read, the feed fetches the latest posts of each followed user (N queries) and merges in sorted order. Write O(1), read O(followed) — 1,000 follows = 1,000 queries per load; great for people who follow little, terrible for power users (and power users live in the feed).
  • Hybrid (the senior answer):
    • users with few followers (the overwhelming majority) → on-write;
    • celebrities (a clear threshold, e.g., > 100k followers) → flagged at follow time; their posts stay a single copy;
    • on read, the feed = merge of the materialized feed + live pull of the celebrity posts that user follows (and each user follows few celebrities — few queries).
    • Result: the expensive write (10 M writes) becomes 1 write + a cheap pull per reader. The 1% of users generate the disproportionate share of writes; that’s the slice that leaves on-write.
  • The golden rule to memorize: writing once and pulling on read is always cheaper than writing N copies when N is large; the threshold decides where “large” starts.

b) Feed cache, invalidation, and hot keys

  • What’s cached: the user’s list of post-ids (not the posts — those come from a shared post cache, deduplicated across feeds). TTL 24 h + LRU eviction by usage.
  • Invalidation is rewrite, not delete: fan-out doesn’t delete — it appends the new post to the top of the list and evicts the oldest; event-based invalidation (post edit/removal) is rare and can be best-effort (a removed post disappears on the next page assembly).
  • Hot keys: a famous user reading constantly = the same hot Redis key → 2-layer cache (per-node local LRU + Redis) for the 1% mega-hot feeds; thundering herd on miss → a single placeholder that assembles the page and the rest wait on the same (distributed lock), instead of 1,000 identical queries.
  • The room number: 160 GB of feed cache + posts (plus duplication) — the Redis cluster is the physical bottleneck; the real bottlenecks are in item 5.

c) Cursor pagination vs offset + basic ranking

  • Cursor = post_id (opaque to the client): stable even when new posts arrive during the scroll — no duplicates, no skips. Offset breaks: a new post shifts the indices and the next page repeats an item (or skips one) — demonstrated below.
# (tested) cursor walks everything without duplicates; a post arriving in
# the middle of pagination does NOT enter the in-flight sequence (nor shifts
# it).
def page(feed, cursor, limit):
    remaining = feed if cursor is None else [p for p in feed if p[0] < cursor]
    chosen = remaining[:limit]
    next_ = chosen[-1][0] if chosen else None
    return chosen, next_

feed = [(10, "a"), (9, "b"), (8, "c"), (7, "d"), (6, "e")]
cur, collected = None, []
while True:
    slice_, cur = page(feed, cur, limit=2)
    if not slice_:
        break
    collected.extend(f[0] for f in slice_)
assert collected == [10, 9, 8, 7, 6]          # walked everything, no dups

# post 11 arrives BETWEEN pages: the old sequence stays intact
feed2 = [(10, "a"), (9, "b"), (8, "c"), (7, "d"), (6, "e")]
cur, collected = None, []
while True:
    slice_, cur = page(feed2, cur, limit=2)
    if not slice_:
        break
    collected.extend(f[0] for f in slice_)
    feed2.insert(0, (11, "new"))
assert collected == [10, 9, 8, 7, 6]          # stable: nothing dup/skips

# offset with a new post mid-stream → repeated page (here, 9 in both):
feed = [(10, "a"), (9, "b"), (8, "c"), (7, "d"), (6, "e")]
seen = [f[0] for f in feed[0:2]]              # page 1: 10, 9
feed.insert(0, (11, "new"))
seen += [f[0] for f in feed[2:4]]             # page 2: 9, 8  ← 9 repeated
seen += [f[0] for f in feed[4:6]]             # 7, 6
assert seen == [10, 9, 9, 8, 7, 6], seen       # duplicate: proven
  • Basic ranking: pure recency first (chronological — the id cursor already covers it). Evolution: score = f(age, estimated affinity, engagement) — and that changes the cache strategy: don’t cache the final order, cache the candidates and rank the page on read (100–200 items is cheap to sort in memory); a periodic job re-ranks the top of hot feeds.

5. Trade-offs and bottlenecks

  • Breaks first: the feed Redis (160 GB + hot keys + ~1 M/s fan-out writes) and the posts DB on writes (4.6k/s × post size + media via CDN with signed upload).
  • Conscious sacrifice: eventual consistency (a post takes seconds to arrive — fine); live pull for celebrity followers (slightly more expensive reads, much cheaper writes); feed cache with TTL (an inactive user’s “erased” feed is rebuilt on the next load).
  • With 10× more time: real ranking (ML: affinity, recency, content type), ads in the feed (real-time auction — then latency becomes a different-level requirement), memories/long-tail (old content needs a separate time-based index), per-user blocklists/filters, geo and moderation (a flagging queue removing posts from feeds via rewrite), media embedding.
  • Common bonus question: “what about a deleted post?” → a removal event walks the queue (fair), but the feed is eventual: visible removals are a fast-path (a removed-posts table checked at assembly, or a priority queue message) — mention that removing abusive content can’t wait for the fan-out tail.
